title: Why `this` Is Never What You Think

sections.title: The Button That Broke the Dashboard
sections.content:
📍 Maya has been staring at a broken console for 20 minutes

Maya: Alex, this makes absolutely no sense. I have a button that calls a method on my object. The method logs this.username, but it prints undefined. The object has a username property. It is right there.

const user = {
  username: 'maya_dev',
  greet() {
    console.log('Hello, ' + this.username);
  }
};

document.getElementById('greet-btn').addEventListener('click', user.greet);
// Clicked → logs: 'Hello, undefined'

Alex: Welcome to this. The most misunderstood word in JavaScript. The bug you just hit will follow you for your entire career unless you understand one rule: in JavaScript, this is determined by HOW a function is called, not where it is defined.

sections.title: What `this` Actually Means in JavaScript
sections.content:
📍 Alex explains the fundamental difference from other languages

Alex: In Python and Java, self / this always refers to the instance the method belongs to. Period. The language sets it when the class is instantiated. In JavaScript, this is set at the moment of the call. Not when you wrote the function. Not when you attached it. At the call.

// Python: self is always the instance
class User:
    def greet(self):        # self = guaranteed to be the User
        print(self.username)

// JavaScript: this depends on the call site
function greet() {
    console.log(this.username); // could be anything
}
// greet() → this = window or undefined (strict mode)
// user.greet() → this = user
// btn.addEventListener('click', greet) → this = btn

Maya: So when I passed user.greet to addEventListener, it detached the function from the object?

Alex: Exactly. You passed a reference to the function, not a bound method. When the browser calls it on a button click, this inside the function is the button element — because the button is the thing calling the function.

sections.title: The Four Rules of `this`
sections.content:
📍 Alex walks Maya through all four ways this gets its value

Alex: There are exactly four rules. They apply in priority order. The highest priority wins.

// Rule 1: new binding (highest priority)
// this = the newly created object
const u = new User('maya');  // inside constructor: this = u

// Rule 2: Explicit binding — .call / .apply / .bind
greet.call(user);        // this = user
greet.apply(user, []);   // this = user
const bound = greet.bind(user);  // returns fn where this = user permanently

// Rule 3: Implicit binding — dot notation at call site
user.greet();            // this = user (object left of the dot)

// Rule 4: Default binding (lowest priority)
greet();                 // this = window (sloppy) or undefined (strict mode)

Maya: My addEventListener case was Rule 3 but the browser was the one calling the function — not my object — so the dot notation pointed to the button?

Alex: Precisely. The DOM calls it as element.handler(), so this = the element. It has nothing to do with where you wrote the function.

sections.title: Arrow Functions — The `this` Shortcut
sections.content:
📍 Alex shows the ES6 solution that eliminates most this bugs

Alex: Arrow functions do not have their own this. They inherit it from the enclosing scope at the time they are defined. This makes them immune to the call-site problem.

// Problem: regular function in setTimeout
const timer = {
  seconds: 0,
  start() {
    setInterval(function() {
      this.seconds++;        // BUG: this = window, not timer
    }, 1000);
  }
};

// Fix 1: arrow function captures this from start()
const timer = {
  seconds: 0,
  start() {
    setInterval(() => {
      this.seconds++;        // OK: this = timer (from start())
    }, 1000);
  }
};

// Fix 2: store reference manually (old-school)
start() {
  const self = this;
  setInterval(function() {
    self.seconds++;          // OK: closure over self
  }, 1000);
}

Maya: So const self = this was the old hack before arrow functions existed?

Alex: Yes — or const that = this, or const vm = this. You will still see it in older codebases. Arrow functions obsoleted all of it.

sections.title: When Arrow Functions Break Things
sections.content:
📍 Arrow functions are not always the answer

Maya: Can I just use arrow functions for everything and stop worrying about this?

Alex: No — two places where arrow functions actively break this:

// 1. Object methods — this becomes the outer scope, not the object
const user = {
  username: 'maya',
  greet: () => {
    console.log(this.username); // undefined! arrow inherits window/module scope
  }
};
user.greet(); // BUG

// 2. Event handlers where you WANT this = the element
document.querySelector('.btn').addEventListener('click', () => {
  this.classList.toggle('active'); // BUG: this = outer scope, not the button
});

// For object methods and event handlers, use regular functions:
const user = {
  username: 'maya',
  greet() {                    // shorthand method = regular function
    console.log(this.username); // OK
  }
};

Maya: So the rule is: use arrow functions INSIDE methods for callbacks, use regular functions FOR the methods themselves?

Alex: That is the mental model. Object methods and event handlers: regular functions. Callbacks inside methods: arrow functions so you inherit the outer this.

sections.title: `.bind()` — Locking `this` Permanently
sections.content:
📍 Fixing Maya's original button bug properly

Alex: Going back to your original bug — when you need to pass a method as a callback but preserve its this, use .bind(). It returns a new function with this permanently locked.

// Option 1: .bind() at attachment
document.getElementById('greet-btn')
  .addEventListener('click', user.greet.bind(user));

// Option 2: arrow wrapper — most readable
document.getElementById('greet-btn')
  .addEventListener('click', () => user.greet());

// .call() and .apply() — one-time explicit call
greet.call(user);          // calls immediately, this = user
greet.apply(user, [arg1]); // same but args as array

// .bind() — deferred call, returns a new function
const boundGreet = greet.bind(user);
boundGreet(); // calls later, this = user (locked)

Maya: The arrow wrapper is cleaner than .bind(). Why would anyone use .bind()?

Alex: Partial application — you can pre-fill some arguments. Also, older React class components used it in the constructor before arrow class fields became standard. In modern code, arrow wrappers and arrow class fields cover 95% of cases.

sections.title: `this` in Class Methods — React and the Constructor Pattern
sections.content:
📍 Where the bind(this) pattern lives on in class-based code

Alex: If you ever read older React code, you will see this pattern in class component constructors — this was the canonical fix before class field arrow functions were introduced.

// Old React class component pattern (pre-2019)
class Counter extends React.Component {
  constructor(props) {
    super(props);
    this.state = { count: 0 };
    // Without this line, handleClick loses this when used in JSX
    this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this);
  }

  handleClick() {
    this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 });
  }
}

// Modern equivalent — class field arrow function
class Counter extends React.Component {
  state = { count: 0 };
  // Arrow field: this is captured at class construction, always bound
  handleClick = () => {
    this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 });
  };
}

Maya: So class field arrow functions are the modern way to make sure class methods always have the right this, without needing constructor binds?

Alex: Exactly. The constructor bind pattern is still valid — but class fields are shorter and the intent is clearer. Modern codebases prefer them.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• this is set at call time, not definition time — unlike Python/Java where it is always the instance
  • Four rules (priority order): new binding > explicit (.call/.bind/.apply) > implicit (dot notation) > default (window/undefined)
  • Arrow functions have no own this — they inherit from the surrounding scope at definition
  • Use regular functions for object methods and event handlers where you want this = the caller
  • Use arrow functions for callbacks inside methods to inherit the method's this
  • .bind(obj) returns a new function with this locked to obj permanently. Arrow wrapper () => obj.method() is usually cleaner
  • Class field arrow functions (handleClick = () => {}) are the modern replacement for constructor bind patterns
  • In strict mode, default this is undefined, not window — which makes bugs crash loudly instead of silently corrupting the global object

sections.title: Creating and Accessing Arrays
sections.content:
Arrays are ordered, zero-indexed lists. Use array literals — new Array() is rarely needed and behaves inconsistently with a single numeric argument.

const fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];
fruits[0];                  // 'apple'
fruits.length;              // 3
fruits[fruits.length - 1];  // 'cherry' — last element
fruits.at(-1);               // 'cherry' — cleaner, supports negative indices (ES2022)
Arrays are objects under the hood — typeof [] returns 'object'. Use Array.isArray(value) to check for an array specifically.

sections.title: Reading Methods — map, filter, find, some, every
sections.content:
These never mutate the original array — each returns a new value.

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

nums.map(n => n * 2);           // [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] — same length, transformed
nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);  // [2, 4] — subset that passes the test
nums.find(n => n > 3);          // 4 — first match, or undefined
nums.findIndex(n => n > 3);     // 3 — index of first match, or -1
nums.some(n => n > 4);          // true — at least one passes
nums.every(n => n > 0);         // true — all pass
nums.includes(3);               // true — value present (uses ===, handles NaN)

sections.title: Reducing and Iterating — reduce, forEach
sections.content:
reduce is the most powerful — and most misused — array method. Every method above can technically be written with it, but don't: use the specific method when one exists, reach for reduce when you're building up a single accumulated value.

const cart = [{ price: 10 }, { price: 25 }, { price: 5 }];

const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0); // 40

nums.forEach(n => console.log(n)); // no return value — side effects only, never chain off it
forEach cannot be stopped early (no break) and always returns undefined. Need to bail out mid-loop? Use a plain for...of loop instead.

sections.title: Mutating Methods — push, pop, splice, sort
sections.content:
Unlike the methods above, these change the array in place and most also return something other than the new array — easy to trip over.

const list = [3, 1, 2];

list.push(4);        // returns 4 (new length), list is now [3,1,2,4]
list.pop();           // returns 4 (removed item), list is now [3,1,2]
list.unshift(0);      // adds to front, returns new length
list.shift();         // removes from front, returns removed item

list.sort();          // MUTATES in place, returns the same array reference
                       // default sort is lexicographic — [10, 2, 1].sort() => [1, 10, 2]!
list.sort((a, b) => a - b); // correct numeric ascending sort

list.splice(1, 2);        // removes 2 items starting at index 1, returns removed items
list.splice(1, 0, 'x');   // inserts 'x' at index 1 without removing anything
Need the original array untouched? Copy first: [...list].sort(...) or the newer non-mutating list.toSorted(...) (ES2023).

sections.title: Objects — Creating, Reading, Shorthand
sections.content:
Object literals are the default way to group related data.

const name = 'Maya', role = 'Engineer';

const user = {
  name,               // shorthand for name: name
  role,
  greet() {           // shorthand method — same as greet: function() {...}
    return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`;
  },
  ['user_' + name]: true, // computed property key
};

user.role;            // dot notation — key must be a valid identifier
user['user_Maya'];    // bracket notation — required for dynamic/non-identifier keys
user.age ?? 'unknown'; // nullish coalescing — safe default for a missing key

sections.title: Object Utility Methods
sections.content:
Static Object.* methods for inspecting and transforming whole objects.

const point = { x: 1, y: 2 };

Object.keys(point);             // ['x', 'y']
Object.values(point);           // [1, 2]
Object.entries(point);          // [['x', 1], ['y', 2]] — pairs well with map/for-of

Object.assign({}, point, { z: 3 }); // shallow-merges into a NEW object: {x:1,y:2,z:3}
const merged = { ...point, z: 3 };   // spread syntax — same result, more common today

Object.freeze(point);           // prevents further changes (shallow — nested objects still mutable)

sections.title: Destructuring & Spread/Rest
sections.content:
Pulls values out of arrays/objects into named variables, or gathers/expands them.

// Array destructuring — position-based
const [first, second, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
// first = 10, second = 20, rest = [30, 40]

// Object destructuring — name-based, works with renaming and defaults
const { name: userName, age = 18 } = { name: 'Maya' };
// userName = 'Maya', age = 18 (default used — age wasn't present)

// Spread — expands an iterable/object
const combined = [...[1, 2], ...[3, 4]]; // [1, 2, 3, 4]
const cloned = { ...point };              // shallow clone

// Common in function signatures too
function greet({ name, role = 'Guest' }) {
  return `${name} (${role})`;
}

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Array read methods (map/filter/find/some/every/includes) never mutate — they return something new
  • Mutating methods (push/pop/splice/sort/reverse) change the array in place — copy first with [...arr] if you need the original untouched
  • Array.prototype.sort() defaults to lexicographic (string) order — always pass a comparator for numbers
  • reduce is for building a single accumulated value; don't reach for it when a more specific method already says what you mean
  • Object.keys/values/entries only return the object's own enumerable properties, not inherited ones
  • Spread (...) only does a shallow copy/merge — nested objects/arrays are still shared references
  • Destructuring defaults only kick in for undefined, not for null or other falsy values
  • typeof [] is 'object' — use Array.isArray() to actually detect an array

title: Fetching Real Data with the Fetch API

sections.title: Why Fetch Data At All?
sections.content:
Most real apps don't hardcode their data — they ask a server for it. The fetch() API is the browser's built-in way to make that request from JavaScript, replacing the older XMLHttpRequest.

Say you're building a weather widget. The temperature doesn't live in your HTML — it lives on a server, and changes by the minute. fetch is how your page asks for the current value and updates itself with the answer.

fetch() is available globally in every modern browser and in Node.js (18+) — no import needed.

sections.title: Your First fetch() Call
sections.content:
fetch(url) returns a Promise — it doesn't hand you data immediately, it hands you a placeholder for data that's still on its way over the network.

fetch('https://api.example.com/weather')
  .then(response => {
    console.log(response.status); // 200, 404, 500...
    console.log(response.ok);     // true only for 200-299
  });

Nothing about the actual weather data yet — response is metadata about the HTTP response, not the parsed content. That's the next step.

sections.title: Parsing the Body — response.json() Is Also Async
sections.content:
The response body arrives as a stream, so reading and parsing it is itself asynchronous — a second .then(), chained off the first.

fetch('https://api.example.com/weather')
  .then(response => response.json())  // returns ANOTHER promise
  .then(data => {
    console.log(data.temperature); // now we actually have the parsed object
  });
Getting plain text instead of JSON? Use response.text() instead of response.json() — both are async and both live on the response object.

sections.title: Handling Errors — fetch Doesn't Reject on 404s
sections.content:
This trips up almost everyone the first time: a 404 or 500 response is still a "successful" network request as far as fetch is concerned. The promise only rejects on a genuine network failure (offline, DNS failure, CORS block) — never because the server said "not found."

fetch('https://api.example.com/weather')
  .then(response => {
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  })
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error('Something went wrong:', error.message));
Skip the response.ok check and a 404 page's HTML gets silently passed to .json(), which then throws a confusing "Unexpected token <" parse error far from where the real problem is.

sections.title: Cleaner Syntax with async/await
sections.content:
async/await is the same Promise machinery underneath — just written to read top-to-bottom instead of chained. The error handling moves into an ordinary try/catch.

async function getWeather() {
  try {
    const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/weather');
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
    }
    const data = await response.json();
    return data;
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Something went wrong:', error.message);
    return null;
  }
}

await only works inside a function marked async — it pauses that function (not the whole program) until the promise settles.

sections.title: Sending Data — POST Requests
sections.content:
Fetching isn't just for reading — the second argument to fetch configures the request method, headers, and body for writing data too.

async function createUser(user) {
  const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/users', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(user),
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Create failed: ${response.status}`);
  }

  return response.json(); // most APIs echo back the created record
}

createUser({ name: 'Maya', role: 'Engineer' });
Forgetting Content-Type: application/json is the most common reason a server-side framework fails to parse the body — the raw JSON string gets sent, but the server doesn't know to parse it as JSON.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• fetch() returns a Promise that resolves with response metadata — call .json() (also async) to get the actual parsed data
  • fetch's promise only rejects on network failure — always check response.ok yourself for HTTP error statuses like 404/500
  • async/await is the same Promises underneath, just written linearly — wrap it in try/catch for error handling
  • await only pauses the async function it's inside, never the whole program
  • For POST/PUT requests, set method, headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, and body: JSON.stringify(data) explicitly — none of these default the way you'd expect
  • A missing/wrong Content-Type header is the most common reason a correctly-sent JSON body fails to parse server-side

sections.title: What JavaScript Actually Does
sections.content:
JavaScript is the programming language that makes web pages interactive. HTML builds the structure of a page and CSS styles it, but neither can react to a click, validate a form, or update content without reloading — that is JavaScript's job.

It runs directly inside the browser, which makes it the only language every browser understands natively. No plugin, no separate runtime to install — if you can open a browser, you can run JavaScript.

sections.title: Where JavaScript Runs
sections.content:
JavaScript started as a browser-only language, but it does not live there anymore.

  • Browser — the original home: buttons, forms, animations, single-page apps
  • Node.js — a runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser, on a server or your own machine
  • Mobile & desktop apps — frameworks like React Native and Electron use JavaScript to build native-feeling apps
Same language, different environment. Browser JavaScript can reach the page itself (document, window); Node.js instead gives you the file system and network, but no document.

sections.title: Dynamically Typed and Interpreted — What That Means for You
sections.content:
Two words describe JavaScript that you will hear constantly: dynamically typed and interpreted.

Dynamically typed means you never declare a variable's type — it is decided by whatever value you assign, and it can change later.

let value = 42;        // value is a number
value = 'hello';        // now it's a string — no error
value = true;           // now it's a boolean — still no error

Interpreted means there is no separate compile step before running — the browser (or Node) reads and runs your code directly.

Dynamic typing is convenient for quick scripts but is also the #1 source of confusing bugs in larger apps — a variable silently changing type is exactly what tools like TypeScript were built to catch.

sections.title: JavaScript vs. Java — Not Related, Despite the Name
sections.content: The similar name is a historical accident, not a relationship. JavaScript was created in 10 days in 1995 and named partly for marketing, riding on Java's popularity at the time. The two languages share a few syntax habits — curly braces, semicolons — but are otherwise unrelated: different type systems, different runtimes, different jobs.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• JavaScript adds interactivity to web pages — HTML is structure, CSS is style, JS is behavior
  • It runs natively in every browser, and also outside the browser via Node.js
  • It is dynamically typed — a variable's type is decided by its current value and can change
  • It is interpreted — code runs directly, without a separate compile step
  • "JavaScript" and "Java" are unrelated languages that happen to share part of a name

sections.title: What You Actually Need to Get Started
sections.content: You do not need to install anything to start writing JavaScript — every browser ships with a full JavaScript engine and a console built in. But for real development, three tools make the difference: a code editor, a way to run code outside the browser, and your browser's developer tools.

sections.title: A Code Editor
sections.content:
Any text editor can save a .js file, but a proper code editor adds syntax highlighting, autocomplete, and error checking as you type. VS Code is the most widely used free editor for JavaScript — first-class support out of the box, plus a huge extension ecosystem.

Install the "Prettier" and "ESLint" extensions early. They auto-format your code and flag common mistakes before you even run it — habits that compound over your whole career.

sections.title: Running JavaScript in the Browser Console
sections.content:
The fastest way to try a line of JavaScript: open any web page, open developer tools (F12, or right-click → Inspect), and click the Console tab. Type an expression and press Enter — it runs immediately.

2 + 2;                 // 4
'hello'.toUpperCase(); // 'HELLO'
document.title;        // the current page's title
The console has access to the actual page you are viewing — document refers to that real page, not a blank sandbox.

sections.title: Running JavaScript with Node.js
sections.content:
To run JavaScript as a standalone program — no browser, no HTML page — install Node.js from nodejs.org. It gives you a node command that runs any .js file directly from the terminal.

// save as hello.js, then run: node hello.js
console.log('Hello from Node!');

Node also gives you a REPL — type node alone in a terminal and you get an interactive prompt, just like the browser console, but outside the browser.

sections.title: The Script Tag — Connecting JavaScript to an HTML Page
sections.content:
To run JavaScript as part of a real web page, link a .js file with a <script> tag, placed just before the closing </body> tag so the page's HTML loads first.

<body>
  <h1>My Page</h1>
  <script src="app.js"></script>
</body>
Put the script tag where elements are not yet on the page (like <head> without defer) and your code will fail trying to find elements that don't exist yet. Either place it at the end of <body>, or add the defer attribute.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• No install needed to start — every browser has a built-in console and JavaScript engine
  • VS Code is the standard free editor, with Prettier and ESLint as day-one extensions
  • The browser console runs code against the actual page you are viewing
  • Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser — install it to run .js files from the terminal
  • Link a script to an HTML page with <script src="...">, placed at the end of <body> or marked defer

sections.title: Declaring Variables — let, const, and Why Not var
sections.content:
Three keywords declare a variable, but only two belong in modern code.

let age = 25;         // can be reassigned later
const name = 'Maya';   // cannot be reassigned
var score = 10;        // legacy — avoid in new code
var ignores block scope (it leaks out of if/for blocks) and allows redeclaring the same variable twice without error — both are common sources of bugs. Default to const, and use let only when you know the value will change.

sections.title: The Core Data Types
sections.content:
JavaScript has a small set of primitive types, plus objects for everything more complex.

let n = 42;             // number — no separate int/float type
let s = 'hello';        // string
let b = true;           // boolean
let u;                  // undefined — declared, no value assigned yet
let x = null;           // null — explicitly "no value"
let obj = { a: 1 };     // object — everything from here up is by reference

Use typeof to check a value's type at runtime — useful for debugging, but be aware typeof null famously returns 'object', a decades-old bug the language keeps for backward compatibility.

sections.title: Operators You Will Use Every Day
sections.content:
// Arithmetic
5 + 3;   // 8
10 % 3;  // 1 — remainder (modulo)
2 ** 8;  // 256 — exponent

// Comparison
5 === '5';  // false — strict equality, checks type too
5 == '5';   // true — loose equality, converts types first

// Logical
true && false; // false — AND
true || false; // true — OR
!true;         // false — NOT
Always prefer === over ==. Loose equality's type coercion produces surprising results (0 == false is true) — strict equality avoids that entire category of bug.

sections.title: Template Literals — Building Strings the Modern Way
sections.content:
Backticks let you embed expressions directly inside a string, and write multi-line strings without concatenation.

const name = 'Maya';
const age = 25;

// Old way
'Hi, ' + name + '. You are ' + age + '.';

// Template literal
`Hi, ${name}. You are ${age}.`;

sections.title: Comments
sections.content:
Comments are ignored when the code runs — use them to explain why, not to restate what the code already says.

// Single-line comment

/* Multi-line
   comment */

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Use const by default, let when a value needs to change, and avoid var
  • Primitive types: number, string, boolean, undefined, null — everything else is an object
  • typeof null returns 'object' — a known language quirk, not a bug in your code
  • Prefer ===/!== over ==/!= to avoid type-coercion surprises
  • Template literals (backticks) embed expressions with ${} and support multi-line strings

sections.title: console.log() Is Not the Whole Toolkit
sections.content:
console.log() is the first debugging tool everyone learns, and often the only one they ever use. The console object has several other methods that give more targeted information for the same effort.

console.log('basic output');
console.warn('shows as a yellow warning');
console.error('shows as a red error, with a stack trace');
console.table([{ name: 'Maya', age: 25 }, { name: 'Alex', age: 30 }]); // renders as an actual table

sections.title: Setting Breakpoints Instead of Logging
sections.content:
Adding console.log everywhere and rerunning the page works, but it is slow — you have to guess what to log before you see the problem. A breakpoint pauses execution at an exact line and lets you inspect every variable's live value at that moment.

In Chrome DevTools: open the Sources tab, find your file, and click the line number where you want to pause. Reload the page — execution stops there, and you can step through line by line.

You can also pause from inside your code with the debugger; statement — same effect as clicking a line number, but it travels with the code and works without hunting for the right file in DevTools.

sections.title: Reading a Stack Trace
sections.content:
When an error is thrown, the console prints a stack trace — the chain of function calls that led to the error, most recent call first.

function getUser(id) {
  return users.find(u => u.id === id).name; // throws if no match
}
getUser(999);
// Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')
//   at getUser (app.js:2)
//   at app.js:5

Read it top to bottom: the first line is the error itself, and the lines under it are the call chain — start debugging at the top-most line that is actually your code, not a library.

sections.title: The Network Tab — Debugging API Calls
sections.content:
When something is wrong with data from a server, the bug is often not in your JavaScript at all. The Network tab shows every request the page makes — status code, response body, headers, and timing — before you go looking for a bug in code that was never the problem.

A common wasted hour: chasing a bug in code that is working fine, when the real issue is a 500 response or a typo in the URL — visible immediately in the Network tab.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• console.warn, console.error, and console.table communicate more than plain console.log for the same effort
  • Breakpoints pause execution at a line and let you inspect live variable values — faster than guessing what to log
  • The debugger; statement sets a breakpoint from inside your code
  • Read a stack trace top to bottom — the error is first, the call chain follows
  • Check the Network tab before assuming a data problem is a JavaScript bug

sections.title: if / else — Branching on a Condition
sections.content:
const age = 20;

if (age >= 18) {
  console.log('Adult');
} else if (age >= 13) {
  console.log('Teenager');
} else {
  console.log('Child');
}

Conditions are checked top to bottom — the first one that is true runs, and the rest are skipped entirely, even if they would also be true.

sections.title: Truthy and Falsy — What Counts as True
sections.content:
An if condition does not need to be an actual boolean — JavaScript converts whatever you give it. Only eight values are falsy; everything else is truthy.

// Falsy — all 8, memorize this list:
false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN

// Truthy — everything else, including these surprising ones:
if ('0')  {} // truthy! non-empty string
if ([])   {} // truthy! empty array is still an object
if ({})   {} // truthy! empty object is still an object
An empty array or object is truthy, even though it "feels" empty. Check array.length === 0 or Object.keys(obj).length === 0 if you actually need to test for emptiness.

sections.title: The Ternary Operator — A One-Line if/else
sections.content:
const age = 20;
const status = age >= 18 ? 'Adult' : 'Minor';
// equivalent to:
// if (age >= 18) { status = 'Adult'; } else { status = 'Minor'; }
Ternaries are great for a simple value assignment. Nesting them trades a few saved lines for a much harder-to-read line — reach for a regular if/else once you have more than one condition.

sections.title: switch — Branching on One Value's Exact Match
sections.content:
const day = 'Mon';

switch (day) {
  case 'Sat':
  case 'Sun':
    console.log('Weekend');
    break;
  case 'Mon':
    console.log('Start of week');
    break;
  default:
    console.log('Midweek');
}
Forgetting break lets execution "fall through" into the next case — often unintentionally. case 'Mon': without a break would also run the default block below it.

sections.title: Loops — for, while, and for...of
sections.content:
// for — when you need an index
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2
}

// while — when you don't know the count in advance
let attempts = 0;
while (attempts < 3) {
  attempts++;
}

// for...of — the cleanest way to loop over an array's values
for (const fruit of ['apple', 'banana']) {
  console.log(fruit);
}

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• if/else if/else conditions are checked in order — the first true branch runs, the rest are skipped
  • Only 8 values are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN — everything else, including [] and {}, is truthy
  • Ternaries (cond ? a : b) are for simple one-line choices — do not nest them
  • switch needs a break in every case or execution falls through into the next one
  • for...of is the cleanest loop for array values; use a plain for when you need the index

sections.title: Declaring a Function — Three Ways
sections.content:
// Function declaration — hoisted, can be called before it's defined
function greet(name) {
  return `Hi, ${name}`;
}

// Function expression — not hoisted, stored in a variable
const greet2 = function(name) {
  return `Hi, ${name}`;
};

// Arrow function — shorter syntax, no own `this`
const greet3 = (name) => `Hi, ${name}`;
"Hoisted" means the function declaration is registered before any code runs, so it is safe to call above where it is written in the file. Function expressions and arrow functions are not — they only exist from the line they are defined onward.

sections.title: Parameters, Defaults, and Rest
sections.content:
// Default parameter — used only if the argument is omitted
function greet(name = 'Guest') {
  return `Hi, ${name}`;
}
greet(); // 'Hi, Guest'

// Rest parameter — gathers any number of extra arguments into an array
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
}
sum(1, 2, 3, 4); // 10

sections.title: Return Values — and What Happens Without One
sections.content:
A function without an explicit return statement returns undefined — this is one of the most common sources of a mystery undefined bug.

function add(a, b) {
  a + b; // computed, but never returned!
}
add(2, 3); // undefined — the calculation was thrown away
A function stops running the instant it hits return — any code written after it in the same block never runs.

sections.title: Scope — What a Function Can and Cannot See
sections.content:
A variable declared inside a function only exists inside that function. A function can read variables declared outside it, but the reverse is not true.

let outside = 'I am outside';

function show() {
  let inside = 'I am inside';
  console.log(outside); // OK — can read outer scope
}

show();
console.log(inside); // ReferenceError — inside doesn't exist out here

sections.title: Arrow Functions vs. Regular Functions — When It Actually Matters
sections.content:
Arrow functions are shorter, but they are not a drop-in replacement everywhere — the difference that matters most is that arrow functions do not have their own this.

Rule of thumb for now: use a regular function for an object's methods, and arrow functions for short callbacks (array.map(x => x * 2)). The full reasoning behind this — and where it goes wrong — is covered in its own lesson on the this keyword.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Function declarations are hoisted (usable before their line in the file); expressions and arrow functions are not
  • Default parameters (name = 'Guest') only apply when the argument is omitted entirely, not for null
  • Rest parameters (...args) gather any number of arguments into a real array
  • No explicit return means the function returns undefined — a very common source of unexpected bugs
  • return ends the function immediately — code after it in the same block never runs
  • A function can read variables from outside itself, but outside code cannot read a function's local variables

sections.title: What the DOM Actually Is
sections.content: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's live, in-memory representation of your HTML page — a tree of objects, one per element. JavaScript does not edit your HTML file directly; it edits this tree, and the browser redraws the screen to match.

sections.title: Selecting Elements
sections.content:
document.getElementById('title');              // single element by id
document.querySelector('.card');                // first match for any CSS selector
document.querySelectorAll('.card');              // ALL matches, as a NodeList
document.querySelector('#list li:first-child');  // any valid CSS selector works
querySelector/querySelectorAll accept any CSS selector, so you rarely need the older, more specific methods (getElementsByClassName, etc.) — one consistent way to select almost anything.

sections.title: Reading and Changing Content
sections.content:
const title = document.querySelector('h1');

title.textContent;                // reads the plain text
title.textContent = 'New Title';  // replaces it — safe, treats input as plain text

title.innerHTML = '<em>New</em> Title'; // parses and inserts as HTML
Never set innerHTML from user-provided input — anything typed by a user is inserted and executed as real HTML, a direct path to a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability. Use textContent for any text that came from a user.

sections.title: Changing Attributes and Classes
sections.content:
const btn = document.querySelector('button');

btn.setAttribute('disabled', 'true');
btn.getAttribute('disabled'); // 'true'
btn.removeAttribute('disabled');

btn.classList.add('active');
btn.classList.remove('active');
btn.classList.toggle('active'); // adds if missing, removes if present

sections.title: Creating and Inserting New Elements
sections.content:
const li = document.createElement('li');
li.textContent = 'New item';

document.querySelector('ul').appendChild(li); // adds at the end
document.querySelector('ul').prepend(li);      // adds at the start
An element must be created with createElement and then explicitly inserted with appendChild/prepend/etc. — creating it alone does not put it on the page.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• The DOM is a live tree of objects representing your page — JavaScript edits the tree, and the browser redraws to match
  • querySelector/querySelectorAll accept any CSS selector — the most flexible way to find elements
  • Use textContent for plain text, innerHTML only for trusted markup — never insert user input via innerHTML
  • classList.add/remove/toggle is the standard way to change an element's classes
  • A new element must be created and inserted (appendChild, etc.) — creating it alone does nothing visible

sections.title: The Checkout Button That Wouldn't Disable
sections.content:
📍 Maya's shopping cart page — the checkout button stays enabled even with an empty cart

Maya: Alex, I swear this if statement is lying to me. I wrote if (cart) { enableCheckout(); }, and cart is an empty array. It should be falsy. But the button stays enabled!

const cart = [];

if (cart) {
  enableCheckout(); // runs, even though cart is empty!
}

Alex: Your if is not lying — it is answering a different question than the one you think you are asking. It checks "is cart truthy," not "is cart empty." And an array — any array, even an empty one — is always truthy.

sections.title: Only Eight Values Are Falsy — Memorize Them
sections.content:
📍 Alex pulls up the full falsy list

Maya: Wait, so what actually counts as false in an if?

Alex: Exactly eight values, and that is the entire list. Everything else — including an empty array or empty object — is truthy.

// The complete falsy list:
false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN

// Everything else is truthy, including:
if ('0')  {} // truthy! non-empty string
if ([])   {} // truthy! empty array is still an object
if ({})   {} // truthy! empty object is still an object

Maya: So [] is truthy because... it is still an object, technically?

Alex: Right. typeof [] is 'object'. JavaScript is not checking whether the array has items — only whether the value exists at all.

sections.title: The Fix — Check What You Actually Mean
sections.content:
📍 Fixing the checkout bug properly

Alex: You did not want "does cart exist," you wanted "does cart have items." Say that directly.

const cart = [];

if (cart.length > 0) {
  enableCheckout(); // correctly skipped — cart is empty
}

Maya: That's it? I just needed to ask the right question.

The same trap applies to objects: if (errors) is true even when errors is {}. Check Object.keys(errors).length === 0 if you actually mean "no errors."

sections.title: The Second Lie — == vs ===
sections.content:
📍 Later that day — a different bug, same checkout flow

Maya: Okay, THIS one is really broken. if (discountCode == 0) is true even when discountCode is an empty string!

'' == 0;    // true  — both get coerced to compare
'' === 0;   // false — different types, no coercion, no match

if (discountCode == 0) {
  // true for '', for 0, for false, and for '0' — four different "empty" values, one branch
}

Alex: == converts both sides to the same type before comparing — an empty string becomes 0 for the purpose of that comparison. === refuses to convert anything. Different type on either side means an automatic false, no exceptions.

This is why loose equality (==) is banned in most style guides. It is not just "a bit looser" — it silently treats 0, '', and false as interchangeable in a comparison, which is almost never what you meant.

sections.title: One More Trap While We're Here — NaN
sections.content:
📍 Alex saves Maya one future bug report

Alex: Since we are collecting lies your if statements can tell you — one more. NaN is the only value in JavaScript that is never equal to itself.

NaN === NaN;        // false!
Number.isNaN(NaN);  // true — this is how you actually check for it

Maya: That feels like a bug in the language.

Alex: It is the IEEE 754 floating-point spec every language with decimal numbers follows, not a JavaScript-only quirk — but yes, it catches everyone exactly once.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Only 8 values are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN — arrays and objects are always truthy, even empty ones
  • Check array.length === 0 or Object.keys(obj).length === 0 to actually test for "empty," not just truthiness
  • Prefer === over == — loose equality's type coercion makes values like '', 0, and false compare as equal
  • NaN is never equal to itself, even to another NaN — use Number.isNaN() to check for it
  • A confusing if statement is usually asking the wrong question, not lying — restate what you actually mean to check

sections.title: Listening for Events
sections.content:
addEventListener is how you react to anything happening on a page — a click, a keystroke, a page load. It takes an event name and a function to run when that event fires.

const btn = document.querySelector('button');

btn.addEventListener('click', function () {
  console.log('Button was clicked');
});

// Arrow function works too, and is more common in modern code
btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('Clicked!'));
Prefer addEventListener over the older onclick = function() {} style — it lets you attach multiple listeners to the same element and event, and you can remove a specific one later with removeEventListener.

sections.title: The Event Object
sections.content:
Every event handler receives an event object as its first argument, carrying details about what happened.

document.querySelector('input').addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
  console.log(event.key);        // which key was pressed, e.g. 'Enter'
  console.log(event.target);     // the actual element the event happened on
  console.log(event.type);       // 'keydown'
});
event.target is the exact element that triggered the event. On a click inside a button that contains an icon and text, target could be the icon, not the button — this matters once you start checking what was clicked.

sections.title: Event Bubbling — Why Clicks Travel Upward
sections.content:
An event does not just fire on the element it happened on — it then "bubbles" upward through every ancestor element, firing their listeners too, all the way to document.

// Clicking the button fires BOTH listeners, inner first, then outer
document.querySelector('.card').addEventListener('click', () => console.log('card clicked'));
document.querySelector('.card button').addEventListener('click', () => console.log('button clicked'));

// Click order: 'button clicked', then 'card clicked'

This is by design, not a bug — it is what makes event delegation possible.

sections.title: Event Delegation — Listening Once Instead of Many Times
sections.content:
Instead of attaching a listener to every single item in a list — especially items that get added later — attach one listener to their shared parent, and use bubbling to figure out which child was actually clicked.

document.querySelector('ul').addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  if (event.target.matches('li')) {
    console.log('Clicked item:', event.target.textContent);
  }
});
// One listener now handles every <li>, including ones added to the list later
Delegation solves a real problem: a listener attached directly to an element only works for elements that existed when you attached it. A parent-level listener automatically covers new children too.

sections.title: preventDefault() and stopPropagation()
sections.content:
Two methods on the event object control what happens next, and they do different things.

form.addEventListener('submit', (event) => {
  event.preventDefault(); // stops the browser's default action (page reload)
  // ...validate and send the form data manually
});

child.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  event.stopPropagation(); // stops the event from bubbling up to ancestors
});
preventDefault() stops the browser's built-in behavior (like a form submitting or a link navigating) — it does not stop bubbling. stopPropagation() stops bubbling — it does not stop the default behavior. Confusing the two is a common source of "why did the page still reload" bugs.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• addEventListener(eventName, handler) is the standard way to react to events — prefer it over inline onclick attributes
  • The event object's target is the exact element the event happened on, which can be a child of the element you attached the listener to
  • Events bubble upward through ancestor elements by default — a click on a child also fires listeners on its parents
  • Event delegation uses bubbling to handle many (or dynamically added) children with a single listener on their parent
  • preventDefault() stops the browser's default action; stopPropagation() stops bubbling — they solve different problems

sections.title: Why 'ES6+' Matters
sections.content: ES6 (2015) was the biggest single update JavaScript has ever had, and "ES6+" now means everything from that release onward — let/const, arrow functions, classes, template literals, destructuring, and more. Almost all modern JavaScript code, and every framework you will touch, assumes you know this syntax.

sections.title: let/const and Block Scope
sections.content:
ES6 introduced let and const specifically to fix a long-standing problem with var: block scope.

if (true) {
  var x = 1;
  let y = 2;
}
console.log(x); // 1 — var leaked out of the if block
console.log(y); // ReferenceError — let stayed inside the block, as expected

sections.title: Arrow Functions
sections.content:
A shorter function syntax, with one meaningful behavior difference: no own this.

const double = (n) => n * 2;             // implicit return, no braces needed
const add = (a, b) => { return a + b; }; // explicit return, braces needed

[1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6] — arrow functions shine as short callbacks

sections.title: Destructuring
sections.content:
Pulls values out of arrays or objects directly into named variables, instead of accessing them one property at a time.

const user = { name: 'Maya', role: 'Engineer' };
const { name, role } = user; // name = 'Maya', role = 'Engineer'

const coords = [10, 20];
const [x, y] = coords; // x = 10, y = 20

function greet({ name, role = 'Guest' }) { // works directly in a parameter too
  return `${name} (${role})`;
}

sections.title: Default Parameters and Spread/Rest
sections.content:
// Default parameter
function greet(name = 'Guest') { return `Hi, ${name}`; }

// Spread — expands an array/object
const combined = [...[1, 2], ...[3, 4]]; // [1, 2, 3, 4]
const cloned = { ...user, role: 'Lead' }; // shallow clone with one field overridden

// Rest — gathers extra arguments into an array
function sum(...nums) { return nums.reduce((t, n) => t + n, 0); }
Spread and rest use the same ... syntax but do opposite jobs depending on where they appear — expanding on the right side of an assignment, gathering when it is a function parameter.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• "ES6+" refers to every JavaScript feature from the 2015 update onward — it is the baseline for all modern code
  • let/const are block-scoped, unlike var, which leaks out of if/for blocks
  • Arrow functions are shorter and have no own this — ideal for callbacks, not always for object methods
  • Destructuring pulls values out of arrays/objects into named variables in one line, including inside function parameters
  • ... expands a value (spread) on the right of an assignment, and gathers values (rest) as a function parameter

sections.title: try / catch / finally
sections.content:
try {
  const data = JSON.parse('not valid json'); // throws
} catch (error) {
  console.error('Parsing failed:', error.message);
} finally {
  console.log('This runs either way — success or failure');
}

Code in try runs normally until something throws. If it does, execution jumps straight to catch — everything else remaining in try is skipped. finally always runs, whether an error happened or not.

sections.title: Throwing Your Own Errors
sections.content:
function withdraw(balance, amount) {
  if (amount > balance) {
    throw new Error('Insufficient funds');
  }
  return balance - amount;
}

try {
  withdraw(100, 500);
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.message); // 'Insufficient funds'
}
Always throw new Error('message'), not a plain string. An Error object carries a .message, a .name, and a .stack trace — a thrown string has none of that, and makes debugging much harder.

sections.title: Built-in Error Types
sections.content:
JavaScript throws different error subtypes depending on what went wrong, and you can check error.name or use instanceof to react differently.

null.foo;              // TypeError — operating on the wrong type
undefinedVariable;      // ReferenceError — using something that doesn't exist
JSON.parse('{bad}');    // SyntaxError — malformed syntax
new RangeError('...');  // RangeError — a value outside its allowed range

try {
  riskyThing();
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof TypeError) {
    // handle specifically
  }
}

sections.title: Errors in Async Code
sections.content:
A regular try/catch does not catch errors thrown inside a .then() callback or a rejected promise on its own — you need .catch(), or try/catch around an await.

// Promise chain
fetchData()
  .then(data => process(data))
  .catch(error => console.error('Failed:', error.message));

// async/await — try/catch works here because await unwraps the promise
async function run() {
  try {
    const data = await fetchData();
    process(data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Failed:', error.message);
  }
}
A rejected promise with no .catch() and no surrounding try/catch does not just fail silently — in Node.js it can crash the process, and in the browser it logs an "Uncaught (in promise)" error. Always handle the rejection path.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• try runs until something throws, then execution jumps to catch; finally always runs regardless
  • Throw Error objects (throw new Error('...')), not plain strings — you lose .stack and .name otherwise
  • Common built-in types: TypeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError, RangeError — check with instanceof to handle them differently
  • A plain try/catch does not catch errors inside a .then() — use .catch() for promise chains, or await inside try/catch
  • An unhandled promise rejection is not a silent failure — it logs loudly, and can crash a Node process

sections.title: JSON.stringify and JSON.parse
sections.content:
JSON is text — JavaScript objects are not. These two methods convert between them.

const user = { name: 'Maya', age: 25 };

JSON.stringify(user);          // '{"name":"Maya","age":25}' — object to JSON text
JSON.parse('{"name":"Maya"}'); // { name: 'Maya' } — JSON text to object

JSON.stringify(user, null, 2); // pretty-printed, 2-space indent — useful for logging
JSON.stringify silently drops undefined values, functions, and Symbols from an object — they simply do not appear in the output, with no error.

sections.title: fetch() at a Glance
sections.content:
const response = await fetch(url);   // returns response metadata (status, ok, headers)
const data = await response.json();  // parses the body — itself async, second await

if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`); // fetch never rejects on 404/500 itself

sections.title: Query Parameters and Headers
sections.content:
const params = new URLSearchParams({ page: 1, limit: 20 });
fetch(`/api/items?${params}`); // '/api/items?page=1&limit=20'

fetch('/api/items', {
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
  },
});

sections.title: Common Response Patterns
sections.content:
// POST with a JSON body
fetch('/api/users', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Maya' }),
});

// Non-JSON responses
await response.text();   // plain text
await response.blob();   // binary data, e.g. an image

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• JSON.stringify (object → text) and JSON.parse (text → object) convert between JavaScript values and JSON
  • JSON.stringify silently drops undefined, functions, and Symbol values — no warning
  • fetch() resolves with response metadata, not data — call .json() (also async) to get the parsed body
  • response.ok must be checked manually — fetch's promise only rejects on a network failure, never on an HTTP error status
  • Use URLSearchParams to build a query string instead of concatenating strings by hand

sections.title: What a Closure Actually Is
sections.content:
A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that outer code has finished running.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0; // "private" to this function
  return function () {
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}

const counter = makeCounter();
counter(); // 1
counter(); // 2 — count was remembered between calls

makeCounter() already finished running, but the inner function still has access to its count variable. That is the closure.

sections.title: The Scope Chain — How JavaScript Looks Up a Variable
sections.content:
When code references a variable, JavaScript looks for it in the current function's scope first. If it is not there, it checks the next scope out, then the next, all the way to the global scope. This chain of nested lookups is the scope chain, and it is what makes closures possible — an inner function's scope chain includes every scope it was defined inside.

const outer = 'global';

function level1() {
  const outer2 = 'level1';
  function level2() {
    console.log(outer2); // found in level1's scope
    console.log(outer);  // not in level2 or level1 — found in global scope
  }
  level2();
}

sections.title: The Classic Loop Bug
sections.content:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100);
}
// Logs: 3, 3, 3 — not 0, 1, 2!

var is not block-scoped — there is only one shared i for the whole loop. By the time the timers fire, the loop has already finished and i is 3.

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100);
}
// Logs: 0, 1, 2 — correct
let creates a fresh binding of i for each loop iteration, so each closure captures its own separate copy — this is the real reason "just switch var to let" fixes this bug, not a special case for loops.

sections.title: A Practical Use — Private State
sections.content:
Closures are how you get real "private" variables in JavaScript, without a dedicated private keyword — a variable that outside code simply cannot reach directly.

function createAccount(startingBalance) {
  let balance = startingBalance; // inaccessible from outside

  return {
    deposit(amount) { balance += amount; },
    getBalance() { return balance; },
  };
}

const account = createAccount(100);
account.deposit(50);
account.getBalance(); // 150
account.balance;       // undefined — no direct access exists

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A closure is a function that keeps access to the variables from its creation scope, even after that outer function has returned
  • The scope chain is how JavaScript resolves a variable name — inward out, current scope first, then each enclosing scope
  • The classic loop-and-setTimeout bug happens because var shares one binding across the whole loop — let creates a new one per iteration
  • Closures are the standard way to create private state in JavaScript — variables accessible only through the functions that were defined alongside them

sections.title: Every Object Has a Prototype
sections.content:
When you access a property that does not exist directly on an object, JavaScript does not immediately give up — it checks the object's prototype, an object it is linked to, and keeps checking prototypes up the chain until it finds the property or runs out of chain.

const arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.push(4); // push isn't defined ON arr — it's found on Array.prototype

Object.getPrototypeOf(arr) === Array.prototype; // true

sections.title: class Is Sugar Over Prototypes
sections.content:
JavaScript's class syntax looks like classes in other languages, but underneath, it is still building the exact same prototype chain — class is a cleaner way to write what you could already do manually.

class User {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }
  greet() {
    return `Hi, ${this.name}`;
  }
}

const u = new User('Maya');
u.greet(); // methods defined in a class live on User.prototype, not on each instance
Object.getPrototypeOf(u) === User.prototype; // true
Because methods live on the prototype, not the instance, every object created from the class shares the exact same function in memory — creating 1,000 users does not create 1,000 copies of greet.

sections.title: Inheritance with extends
sections.content:
class Admin extends User {
  constructor(name, permissions) {
    super(name); // must call super() before using `this`
    this.permissions = permissions;
  }
  greet() {
    return `${super.greet()} (Admin)`; // calls User's greet, then extends it
  }
}

new Admin('Alex', ['delete']).greet(); // 'Hi, Alex (Admin)'
Forgetting to call super() in a subclass constructor before using this throws a ReferenceError — JavaScript will not let a subclass instance exist until its parent's constructor has run.

sections.title: Static Methods and Getters/Setters
sections.content:
class User {
  #email; // private field — truly inaccessible from outside the class

  constructor(name, email) {
    this.name = name;
    this.#email = email;
  }

  get email() { return this.#email; }       // accessed like a property: user.email
  set email(value) { this.#email = value; } // user.email = 'new@x.com'

  static fromJSON(json) {                    // called on the class itself: User.fromJSON(...)
    const data = JSON.parse(json);
    return new User(data.name, data.email);
  }
}

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Every object has a prototype — a linked object checked when a property is not found directly on the object itself
  • class is syntax over the same prototype system — methods defined in a class live on the shared prototype, not duplicated per instance
  • extends sets up the prototype chain between classes; super() must run before a subclass constructor uses this
  • get/set let a method be accessed like a plain property; static methods belong to the class itself, not to instances
  • #field syntax creates a genuinely private field — unlike a normal property, it cannot be accessed from outside the class at all

sections.title: The One Rule
sections.content: this is determined by how a function is called, not where it is written. The same function can have a different this every time it is called, depending on the call site.

sections.title: The Four Binding Rules, Ranked
sections.content:
// 1. new binding — highest priority
new User();              // this = the new object

// 2. Explicit binding
fn.call(obj); fn.apply(obj); fn.bind(obj);  // this = obj

// 3. Implicit binding
obj.method();             // this = obj (whatever is left of the dot)

// 4. Default binding — lowest priority
fn();                      // this = undefined (strict mode) or window (sloppy mode)

sections.title: Arrow Functions Don't Have Their Own this
sections.content:
const obj = {
  name: 'Maya',
  regular() { return this.name; },        // this = obj (rule 3)
  arrow: () => { return this.name; },      // this = enclosing scope, NOT obj
};
Arrow functions inherit this from where they are defined, permanently — they ignore all four binding rules above. That is exactly why they are the standard fix for callbacks that need to keep the outer this.

sections.title: Quick Diagnostic
sections.content:
When this is not what you expect, ask: "what's immediately to the left of the dot at the actual call site?" Not where the function is defined — where it is called.

btn.addEventListener('click', obj.method); // this = btn at call time, NOT obj — the method was detached
btn.addEventListener('click', () => obj.method()); // this = obj — arrow wrapper calls it through obj

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• this is set at call time based on how a function is invoked, not where it was defined
  • Priority order: new > explicit (call/apply/bind) > implicit (dot notation) > default
  • Arrow functions have no own this — they inherit it permanently from the surrounding scope where they were written
  • Passing a method as a bare callback (btn.addEventListener('click', obj.method)) detaches it — wrap it in an arrow function or use .bind() to keep this

sections.title: What a Regex Actually Is
sections.content:
A regular expression is a pattern that describes a shape of text — not a specific string, but rules like "one or more digits" or "an @ followed by a domain." JavaScript has regex support built directly into the language.

const pattern = /hello/;              // literal syntax — most common
const pattern2 = new RegExp('hello'); // constructor — useful when building a pattern dynamically

sections.title: Building a Pattern
sections.content:
/cat/        // matches the literal text 'cat'
/^cat/       // ^ anchors to the start of the string
/cat$/       // $ anchors to the end of the string
/c.t/        // . matches any single character — matches 'cat', 'cot', 'c9t'
/colou?r/    // ? makes the previous character optional — matches 'color' and 'colour'
/\d+/        // \d = any digit, + = one or more — matches '7' and '12345'
/\s/         // whitespace character
/[aeiou]/    // any one of the characters in the brackets
Flags go after the closing slash: /pattern/gi — g finds all matches instead of stopping at the first, i makes it case-insensitive.

sections.title: Testing and Matching
sections.content:
/\d+/.test('abc123');            // true — just checks yes/no
'abc123'.match(/\d+/);            // ['123', index: 3, ...] — returns match details
'a1 b2 c3'.match(/\d+/g);         // ['1', '2', '3'] — g flag returns ALL matches

sections.title: Replacing with a Pattern
sections.content:
'2024-01-15'.replace(/-/g, '/'); // '2024/01/15' — g flag replaces every match

// Capture groups — () saves part of the match for reuse
'2024-01-15'.replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)/, '$2/$3/$1'); // '01/15/2024'

sections.title: Common Patterns You'll Actually Use
sections.content:
/^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,}$/  // rough email shape check
/^\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}$/               // US phone format: 555-123-4567
A regex that "looks right" for email validation is never fully correct — real email addresses are far messier than most patterns account for. Use a simple shape check for UX feedback, but confirm on the server with an actual verification email, not a stricter regex.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A regex describes a pattern of text, not one exact string — written between slashes: /pattern/
  • ^ anchors to the start, $ to the end, . matches any character, \d/\s/\w match digit/whitespace/word characters
  • test() returns true/false; match() returns the actual matched text and position
  • The g flag matches all occurrences instead of stopping at the first; i makes matching case-insensitive
  • Capture groups (()) let you reference matched portions in a replacement string with $1, $2, etc.

sections.title: Why Modules Exist
sections.content:
Before modules, every script on a page shared one global scope — two files could easily define the same variable name and silently overwrite each other. Modules give each file its own private scope: nothing is visible outside a file unless you explicitly export it.

<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>

sections.title: Named Exports and Imports
sections.content:
// math.js
export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
export const PI = 3.14159;

// app.js
import { add, PI } from './math.js';
add(2, 3); // 5

import { add as sum } from './math.js'; // rename on import
import * as math from './math.js';      // import everything as one object
math.add(2, 3);

sections.title: Default Exports
sections.content:
// user.js — one default export per file
export default class User {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
}

// app.js — the import name is chosen by the importer, no braces needed
import User from './user.js';
import Person from './user.js'; // same class, any name works — there's no fixed name to match
Named exports are generally preferred for anything except a file's single "main" thing — they force a consistent name at every import site, which makes searching a codebase for usages far easier than a default export, where every file can rename it to anything.

sections.title: Dynamic Imports
sections.content:
// Static import — always loaded up front, at the top of the file
import { heavyChart } from './chart.js';

// Dynamic import — loaded only when actually needed, returns a Promise
button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
  const { heavyChart } = await import('./chart.js');
  heavyChart.render();
});
Dynamic import() is how code-splitting works in modern build tools — the chart code in this example is not downloaded at all until the button is actually clicked.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Modules give each file its own scope — nothing leaks into the global scope or other files unless explicitly exported
  • export/import { name } is a named export — the name must match at both ends (or be explicitly renamed with as)
  • export default allows exactly one per file, and the importer can name it anything
  • Dynamic import('./file.js') returns a Promise and loads code on demand — the basis of code-splitting
  • A <script type="module"> is required in the browser to use import/export syntax at all

sections.title: localStorage and sessionStorage
sections.content:
localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
localStorage.getItem('theme');   // 'dark'
localStorage.removeItem('theme');
localStorage.clear();             // wipes everything

sessionStorage.setItem('draftText', 'hello'); // same API, different lifetime
localStorage persists until explicitly cleared — closing the tab or browser does not remove it. sessionStorage is cleared automatically when the tab closes. Same methods, different lifetime.

sections.title: Storage Only Holds Strings
sections.content:
localStorage.setItem('user', { name: 'Maya' }); // stored as the string '[object Object]' — silently wrong!

// Correct way: serialize yourself
localStorage.setItem('user', JSON.stringify({ name: 'Maya' }));
const user = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('user'));
Storing an object directly without JSON.stringify does not throw an error — it silently converts to the useless string '[object Object]'. Always stringify before storing, and parse after reading.

sections.title: Cookies — When You Actually Need Them
sections.content:
Local/session storage never leaves the browser. Cookies do — they are automatically sent with every HTTP request to their matching domain, which is exactly why they are still used for session identification, even though they are clunkier to work with in JavaScript than storage.

document.cookie = 'theme=dark; max-age=3600'; // sets one cookie; reading requires manual parsing
Cookies are sent with every matching request automatically — including ones you did not intend, which is the root of CSRF attacks. Never store sensitive tokens in a cookie without the HttpOnly and Secure flags (set server-side, not from JavaScript).

sections.title: IndexedDB — For Real Data, Not Just Settings
sections.content:
localStorage is synchronous, string-only, and capped around 5–10MB — fine for settings and small flags, not for meaningful amounts of structured data. IndexedDB is a full asynchronous database built into the browser, for storing large amounts of structured data, including offline app data.

IndexedDB's raw API is verbose. In practice, most teams reach for a wrapper library (like idb) rather than writing against it directly — know that it exists and what it is for, and reach for a library when you actually need it.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• localStorage persists until cleared; sessionStorage clears when the tab closes — same API otherwise
  • Both only store strings — always JSON.stringify before storing an object, and JSON.parse after reading it back
  • Cookies, unlike storage, are automatically sent with matching HTTP requests — useful for sessions, but a CSRF risk if not flagged HttpOnly/Secure
  • IndexedDB is the browser's real database — for structured or large data, not just small settings

sections.title: What npm Actually Manages
sections.content: npm (Node Package Manager) installs and tracks the external code your project depends on — instead of copy-pasting a library's code into your project, you declare that you need it, and npm downloads the right version into a node_modules folder.

sections.title: package.json — The Project's Manifest
sections.content:
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.2"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "jest": "^29.0.0"
  },
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js"
  }
}
dependencies are needed for the app to run in production; devDependencies (testing tools, build tools) are only needed while developing — npm install --production skips them.

sections.title: Installing and Using a Package
sections.content:
// terminal: npm install express
const express = require('express'); // CommonJS
import express from 'express';       // ES module

// terminal: npm install --save-dev jest   (dev-only dependency)
// terminal: npm install                    (installs everything already in package.json)

sections.title: Understanding Semantic Versioning
sections.content:
// version format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, e.g. 4.18.2
// MAJOR — breaking changes
// MINOR — new features, backward compatible
// PATCH — bug fixes only

"express": "^4.18.2"  // ^ allows MINOR and PATCH updates (4.x.x), not 5.0.0
"express": "~4.18.2"  // ~ allows only PATCH updates (4.18.x)
"express": "4.18.2"   // exact version only, no updates
^ is npm's default and generally safe in theory, but a library that violates semver (ships a breaking change as a minor bump) can still break your build on a routine npm install. package-lock.json pins exact versions actually installed so this does not happen silently between installs.

sections.title: npm Scripts
sections.content:
// package.json
"scripts": {
  "start": "node index.js",
  "test": "jest",
  "build": "webpack --mode production"
}

// terminal:
// npm start     -> runs the "start" script (special case, no "run" needed)
// npm test      -> runs the "test" script (also special-cased)
// npm run build -> any other script needs "run"

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• npm installs and tracks external packages your project depends on, recorded in package.json
  • dependencies ship with the app; devDependencies are only needed during development
  • Semantic versioning is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — ^ allows minor+patch updates, ~ allows only patch updates
  • package-lock.json pins the exact versions actually installed, so a fresh npm install is reproducible
  • npm start and npm test are shortcuts; any other custom script needs npm run <script-name>

title: The Loop That Lost Its Numbers

sections.title: The Buttons That All Say the Same Thing
sections.content:
📍 Maya built three buttons, and clicking any of them logs the same wrong number

Maya: Alex, I built three buttons, numbered 0, 1, 2. I click button 0, it logs 3. I click button 1, it also logs 3. Every button logs 3, no matter which one I click!

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  const btn = document.createElement('button');
  btn.textContent = `Button ${i}`;
  btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(i));
  document.body.appendChild(btn);
}
// clicking any button logs: 3

Alex: That is not a DOM bug — it is a closures bug. All three click handlers are sharing the exact same variable i, not three separate copies of it.

sections.title: One Variable, Three Functions, Sharing It
sections.content:
📍 Alex draws the loop's actual memory model

Alex: var is function-scoped, not block-scoped. There is exactly one i for the entire loop — it does not get recreated each pass. All three arrow functions close over that same single i.

// There is ONE `i` in memory for this whole loop
// All three closures point to the SAME i
// By the time you click a button, the loop has already finished and i = 3

Maya: So the closures are not broken — they are doing exactly what closures do. They are just all pointing at the same box.

Alex: Exactly. The bug is not in how closures work. It is in assuming var gives you a new box every iteration. It does not.

sections.title: The One-Word Fix
sections.content:
📍 Fixing it
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  const btn = document.createElement('button');
  btn.textContent = `Button ${i}`;
  btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(i));
  document.body.appendChild(btn);
}
// clicking Button 0 logs 0, Button 1 logs 1, Button 2 logs 2 — correct

Maya: That's it? Just var to let?

Alex: Just that. let is block-scoped — the for loop creates a brand new i for every single iteration. Each closure now captures its own separate copy, not one shared one.

sections.title: Before let Existed — the IIFE Workaround
sections.content:
📍 Alex shows the old-school fix, for reading legacy code

Alex: Before let, people forced a new scope manually with an Immediately Invoked Function Expression — an IIFE. You will still find this pattern in old codebases.

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  (function (capturedI) {
    setTimeout(() => console.log(capturedI), 100);
  })(i); // i is passed in and captured fresh, right now, as an argument
}
// logs 0, 1, 2 — correct, but nobody writes this anymore

Maya: So the IIFE basically fakes what let now does for free?

Alex: Exactly — it manually creates a new scope, once per iteration, by wrapping the body in its own function call. let made the whole pattern obsolete.

sections.title: This Isn't Just a Loop Thing
sections.content:
📍 The same trap, outside a loop

Alex: The underlying lesson is not "loops are special" — it is that a closure captures a variable, not the value the variable happened to hold at that instant. If that variable changes later, every closure sees the new value.

let count = 0;
function logLater() { console.log(count); }

count = 5;
logLater(); // 5 — not 0. logLater closed over `count`, not its value at creation time.

Maya: So closures always see the current state of the variable, whenever they finally run?

Alex: Always. That is the whole rule this bug was hiding.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• var is function-scoped — a loop using var has exactly one shared variable across every iteration, not a fresh one each time
  • let is block-scoped — a loop using let creates a brand-new binding on every iteration, so each closure captures its own separate copy
  • The old fix, before let existed, was an IIFE — manually wrapping the loop body in a function call to force a new scope per iteration
  • A closure captures the variable itself, not a snapshot of its value — if the variable changes later, the closure sees the new value whenever it actually runs
  • This same trap applies anywhere a closure outlives the value it "should" have captured, not just inside loops

title: The Class That Wasn't Really a Class

sections.title: The Method That Appeared Out of Nowhere
sections.content:
📍 Maya adds a new method to a class... after objects already exist

Maya: Alex, this makes no sense. I already created a User object. Then I added a new method to the User class afterward. And the OLD object can suddenly use the new method too? In Java that's impossible — objects don't change after they're built!

class User {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
}
const maya = new User('Maya'); // created first

User.prototype.shout = function () { // method added AFTER maya exists
  return this.name.toUpperCase() + '!';
};

maya.shout(); // 'MAYA!' — works, even though shout didn't exist when maya was created

Alex: That is your first clue that JS classes are not real classes the way Java's are. They are a live link to a shared object, not a sealed blueprint.

sections.title: class Is a Disguise
sections.content:
📍 Alex reveals what's actually happening under class syntax

Alex: Every method you write inside a class body doesn't get copied onto each object. It gets attached to ONE shared object — the class's prototype. Every instance just links to that same prototype.

class User {
  constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
  greet() { return `Hi, ${this.name}`; }
}

const maya = new User('Maya');
const alex = new User('Alex');

maya.greet === alex.greet; // true — it's the literal same function in memory, not two copies
Object.getPrototypeOf(maya) === User.prototype; // true
