Maya: So class didn't create some separate blueprint. It just built an object — User.prototype — and links every instance to it?

Alex: Exactly. class is syntax. Underneath, it's the exact same prototype-linking system that's been in JavaScript since 1995. It just looks more familiar to people coming from other languages.

sections.title: Why This Actually Matters
sections.content:
📍 The consequence Maya didn't expect

Alex: Here's the part that trips people coming from class-based languages: because every instance shares ONE prototype object, changing the prototype changes what EVERY instance can do — even ones already created.

class Bug {}
const b1 = new Bug();

Bug.prototype.isSquashed = () => true; // added after b1 exists

b1.isSquashed(); // true — b1 gained a method it never had at creation time

Maya: In Java that would be terrifying. Objects aren't supposed to change shape after they exist.

Alex: In JavaScript it's just... how prototypes work. Not wrong, just different — and it's exactly why patching built-ins like Array.prototype is considered dangerous. You're not just changing your own code's behavior; you're changing it for every array in the entire program, including ones libraries create.

sections.title: Object.create — Doing It Without class at All
sections.content:
📍 Alex shows the mechanism with no class syntax involved

Alex: You can build the exact same prototype link with zero class syntax, to see there's no hidden magic.

const userProto = {
  greet() { return `Hi, ${this.name}`; },
};

const maya = Object.create(userProto); // maya's prototype IS userProto, directly
maya.name = 'Maya';
maya.greet(); // 'Hi, Maya' — no `class`, no `new`, same result

Maya: So class User {} really is just a nicer way to write what Object.create already does manually?

Alex: That's the whole trick. class, extends, super — all of it compiles down to prototype links and function calls. Nothing new exists under the hood, just a friendlier way to write it.

sections.title: Instance Fields vs. Prototype Methods
sections.content:
📍 One place where the sharing does NOT apply

Alex: One important exception: this.name = name inside the constructor is NOT shared. Every new User(...) call creates a fresh object, and each one gets its own copy of instance fields — only the methods live on the shared prototype.

class Counter {
  count = 0;               // instance field — a fresh copy on every instance
  increment() { this.count++; } // method — shared on the prototype
}

const a = new Counter();
const b = new Counter();
a.increment();
a.count; // 1
b.count; // 0 — b's own count, untouched — only methods are shared, not instance data

Maya: Okay, that part actually matches what I expected from Java. It's specifically the methods that are shared, not the data.

Alex: Right — and that's exactly why it works at all. If your own data were shared too, every object would corrupt every other object's state instantly.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• class is syntax over JavaScript's existing prototype system — it doesn't create a sealed blueprint the way classes in Java/C# do
  • Methods defined in a class live on ONE shared prototype object — every instance links to the same prototype, not a personal copy
  • Because the prototype is shared and live, adding a method to it later makes it available on objects that already exist, created before the method was added
  • Object.create(proto) builds the identical prototype link manually, with no class/new syntax at all — proof there's no hidden mechanism
  • Instance fields (set with this.x = ... in the constructor) are NOT shared — each instance gets its own copy; only methods on the prototype are shared

sections.title: The Call Stack — One Thing at a Time
sections.content:
JavaScript runs on a single thread — only one piece of code executes at any instant. The call stack tracks which function is currently running, and which functions called it.

function a() { b(); }
function b() { c(); }
function c() { console.log('here'); }
a();
// stack grows: a -> b -> c, then unwinds as each function returns

Nothing else can run while the stack is not empty — this is why a long-running synchronous function freezes the whole page.

sections.title: Where Async Callbacks Actually Go
sections.content:
setTimeout, a resolved Promise's .then(), a DOM event — none of these run their callback immediately, even with a delay of 0. The browser (or Node) hands the callback off to a queue, and it only runs once the call stack is completely empty.

console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
console.log('3');
// Logs: 1, 3, 2 — not 1, 2, 3
// setTimeout's callback waits for the stack to clear, even with a 0ms delay

sections.title: Microtasks vs Macrotasks — Two Separate Queues
sections.content:
There is not just one queue — there are two, and one always wins.

console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2 - macrotask'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3 - microtask'));
console.log('4');
// Logs: 1, 4, 3, 2
Promise callbacks (.then, async/await continuations, queueMicrotask) go on the microtask queue. setTimeout, DOM events, and I/O go on the macrotask queue. After every single macrotask, the entire microtask queue is drained completely before the next macrotask runs — that is why the Promise logs before the timer, even at 0ms.

sections.title: Putting It All Together
sections.content:
console.log('start');

setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log('promise 1'))
  .then(() => console.log('promise 2'));

console.log('end');

// Order: start, end, promise 1, promise 2, timeout
// 1. Synchronous code runs first, top to bottom
// 2. ALL queued microtasks run next, including ones added by other microtasks
// 3. Only then does the next macrotask (the timeout) run

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• JavaScript is single-threaded — the call stack runs one thing at a time, and nothing else runs while it is not empty
  • setTimeout, Promise callbacks, and DOM events do not run immediately — they are queued, and only run once the call stack is empty
  • Microtasks (Promise .then, async/await) always run before macrotasks (setTimeout, I/O), even when the timeout is 0ms
  • The entire microtask queue drains completely — including microtasks added by other microtasks — before the next macrotask is allowed to run
  • Synchronous code always runs first, top to bottom, before any queued callback of either kind

sections.title: What Makes Something Iterable
sections.content:
for...of, spread (...), and destructuring all work on arrays, strings, Maps, and Sets — because each of these implements the iterable protocol: an object with a Symbol.iterator method that returns an iterator.

const arr = [1, 2, 3];
typeof arr[Symbol.iterator]; // 'function' — this is what makes for...of work on it

const plainObject = { a: 1, b: 2 };
// for (const x of plainObject) {}  // TypeError — plain objects are NOT iterable by default

sections.title: Writing Your Own Iterator
sections.content:
An iterator is any object with a next() method that returns { value, done }.

function makeRangeIterator(start, end) {
  let current = start;
  return {
    next() {
      if (current < end) return { value: current++, done: false };
      return { value: undefined, done: true };
    },
  };
}

const it = makeRangeIterator(1, 4);
it.next(); // { value: 1, done: false }
it.next(); // { value: 2, done: false }
it.next(); // { value: 3, done: false }
it.next(); // { value: undefined, done: true }

sections.title: Generators — A Shortcut for Writing Iterators
sections.content:
Writing iterators by hand, tracking state manually, is tedious. A generator function (function*) writes the same logic as normal, readable code, and JavaScript builds the iterator for you.

function* range(start, end) {
  for (let i = start; i < end; i++) {
    yield i;
  }
}

for (const n of range(1, 4)) {
  console.log(n); // 1, 2, 3
}

[...range(1, 4)]; // [1, 2, 3] — spread works too, generators are iterable

sections.title: yield Pauses, It Doesn't Just Return
sections.content:
Unlike return, yield pauses the function's execution exactly where it is, and resumes from that exact point the next time next() is called.

function* logSteps() {
  console.log('step 1');
  yield;
  console.log('step 2'); // does NOT run until next() is called again
  yield;
  console.log('step 3');
}

const gen = logSteps();
gen.next(); // logs 'step 1', then pauses
gen.next(); // logs 'step 2', then pauses
gen.next(); // logs 'step 3', then finishes

sections.title: A Practical Use — Lazy Sequences
sections.content:
Because a generator only computes the next value when asked, it can represent a sequence that is infinite, or too large to build all at once.

function* naturalNumbers() {
  let n = 1;
  while (true) { // infinite — this would never finish as a regular array
    yield n++;
  }
}

function take(iterable, count) {
  const result = [];
  for (const value of iterable) {
    if (result.length >= count) break;
    result.push(value);
  }
  return result;
}

take(naturalNumbers(), 5); // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] — only 5 values were ever actually computed
This is the core idea behind lazy evaluation: nothing is computed until it is actually consumed. An infinite generator is completely safe as long as whatever reads from it eventually stops asking for more.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• An object is iterable if it has a Symbol.iterator method — that is what powers for...of, spread, and destructuring
  • An iterator is any object with a next() method returning { value, done }
  • A generator function (function*) builds an iterator for you from ordinary-looking, readable code
  • yield pauses execution at that exact line and resumes from there on the next next() call — it does not restart the function
  • Generators enable lazy sequences — including infinite ones — since a value is only computed when it is actually requested

sections.title: Property Descriptors — What a Property Actually Is
sections.content:
A property is not just a name and a value — JavaScript tracks metadata about it too: whether it can be changed, deleted, or shows up in a for...in loop.

const obj = { name: 'Maya' };
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(obj, 'name');
// { value: 'Maya', writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true }

Object.defineProperty(obj, 'id', {
  value: 42,
  writable: false,   // can't be reassigned
  enumerable: false, // won't appear in Object.keys() or for...in
});
obj.id = 999; // silently fails in sloppy mode, throws in strict mode
obj.id;        // still 42

sections.title: Getters and Setters, the Manual Way
sections.content:
const user = {
  firstName: 'Maya',
  lastName: 'Chen',
  get fullName() { return `${this.firstName} ${this.lastName}`; },
  set fullName(value) { [this.firstName, this.lastName] = value.split(' '); },
};

user.fullName;             // 'Maya Chen' — called like a property, not a method
user.fullName = 'Alex Kim'; // runs the setter — updates both firstName and lastName

sections.title: Proxy — Intercepting Operations on an Object
sections.content:
A Proxy wraps an object and lets you intercept fundamental operations — reading a property, writing one, checking if it exists — before they happen.

const target = { count: 0 };

const logged = new Proxy(target, {
  get(obj, prop) {
    console.log(`Reading ${String(prop)}`);
    return obj[prop];
  },
  set(obj, prop, value) {
    console.log(`Setting ${String(prop)} = ${value}`);
    obj[prop] = value;
    return true; // must return true to indicate success
  },
});

logged.count;      // logs 'Reading count', returns 0
logged.count = 5;  // logs 'Setting count = 5'
This is exactly how reactive frameworks like Vue 3 detect when your data changes — they wrap your data in a Proxy and react inside the set trap, without you writing any explicit "notify" calls.

sections.title: Reflect — Proxy's Natural Partner
sections.content:
Reflect provides the same fundamental operations as plain syntax (obj.prop, delete obj.prop), but as regular functions — which makes it the correct way to forward an operation from inside a Proxy trap.

const logged = new Proxy(target, {
  get(obj, prop, receiver) {
    console.log(`Reading ${String(prop)}`);
    return Reflect.get(obj, prop, receiver); // safer than obj[prop] inside a trap
  },
});
You will rarely reach for Proxy/Reflect directly in everyday app code — they are the tools underneath things like Vue's reactivity or ORM validation layers. Know what they do so a library's internals are not a mystery, more than as something to reach for daily.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Every property has descriptor metadata (writable, enumerable, configurable) beyond just its value — set with Object.defineProperty
  • get/set let a computed value be accessed with plain property syntax instead of a method call
  • Proxy wraps an object and intercepts operations on it (get, set, and more) before they happen — the mechanism behind reactive frameworks
  • Reflect mirrors the same fundamental operations as plain syntax, as callable functions — used inside Proxy traps to forward the original behavior correctly
  • These are foundational, low-level tools — most day-to-day code uses libraries built on them rather than calling them directly

sections.title: How Garbage Collection Actually Works
sections.content:
JavaScript manages memory automatically — you never call free(). The engine periodically looks for objects nothing can reach anymore (no variable, no closure, no reference chain leads to them) and reclaims their memory. This is called garbage collection, and the core idea is reachability, not how long ago something was created.

let user = { name: 'Maya' };
user = null; // nothing references the original object anymore — eligible for collection

sections.title: Memory Leaks — How 'Automatic' Cleanup Still Fails
sections.content:
A leak happens when something keeps a reference alive that you no longer actually need — the object is technically still reachable, so the garbage collector correctly leaves it alone, even though your program has moved on.

const cache = {};

function addToCache(key, largeData) {
  cache[key] = largeData; // never removed — cache grows forever
}

// Global event listener never removed — element is kept alive even after removal from the DOM
window.addEventListener('resize', () => updateLayout(hugeChartData));
The most common real-world leak is not a missing delete — it is an event listener or a timer (setInterval) that was never cleaned up, quietly keeping everything it references alive indefinitely.

sections.title: Debouncing and Throttling
sections.content:
Some events fire far more often than your code needs to react — scroll, resize, and keystroke events can fire dozens of times a second. Two patterns control that.

function debounce(fn, delay) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delay);
  };
}
// Waits until input STOPS for `delay` ms, then runs once — ideal for a search-as-you-type box

function throttle(fn, interval) {
  let last = 0;
  return (...args) => {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= interval) {
      last = now;
      fn(...args);
    }
  };
}
// Runs at most once per `interval` ms, no matter how often it's called — ideal for scroll handlers

sections.title: Measuring Before Optimizing
sections.content:
The DevTools Performance tab records exactly where time is spent — scripting, rendering, painting — and the Memory tab can take heap snapshots to compare over time and spot exactly what is growing.

Guessing at a performance problem and "optimizing" the wrong function is a classic waste of a day. Profile first, find the actual bottleneck, then fix that specific thing — most code is never the bottleneck people assume it is.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Garbage collection reclaims memory based on reachability — an object with zero remaining references becomes eligible for cleanup
  • A leak is not broken garbage collection — it is something (often an event listener or timer) unintentionally keeping a reference alive longer than needed
  • Debounce delays a function until activity stops (search-as-you-type); throttle caps how often it can run (scroll handlers)
  • Always remove event listeners and clear intervals/timeouts you no longer need — they are the most common real-world leak
  • Profile with DevTools before optimizing — fix the measured bottleneck, not a guessed one

sections.title: Why Automated Tests
sections.content: Manually clicking through an app after every change does not scale, and it is easy to miss a case you did not think to check. An automated test runs the same check every time, in seconds, and catches a regression the moment it is introduced — not weeks later in production.

sections.title: Writing Your First Test
sections.content:
// math.js
export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

// math.test.js
import { add } from './math.js';

test('adds two numbers', () => {
  expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5);
});

// terminal: npx jest

A test file pairs one behavior (test(...) or it(...), both work identically) with an assertion — a claim about what should be true if the code is correct.

sections.title: Matchers — Asserting What You Expect
sections.content:
expect(2 + 2).toBe(4);                       // exact equality (===)
expect({ a: 1 }).toEqual({ a: 1 });           // deep equality — for objects/arrays
expect([1, 2, 3]).toContain(2);
expect('hello world').toMatch(/world/);
expect(() => { throw new Error('bad'); }).toThrow();
expect(value).toBeNull();
expect(value).toBeUndefined();
toBe uses Object.is (effectively ===) — two different objects with identical contents will fail toBe even though they "look" equal. Use toEqual for objects and arrays.

sections.title: Mocking — Testing Code That Depends on Something Else
sections.content:
A function that calls a real API or reads a real database is not a good unit test — it is slow, unreliable, and not actually testing your logic. A mock replaces that dependency with a fake version you fully control.

const fetchUser = jest.fn(); // a fake function that records how it was called
fetchUser.mockResolvedValue({ name: 'Maya' }); // makes it return a resolved Promise

async function greetUser(fetchFn) {
  const user = await fetchFn();
  return `Hi, ${user.name}`;
}

const result = await greetUser(fetchUser);
expect(result).toBe('Hi, Maya');
expect(fetchUser).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); // assert HOW it was used, not just the result

sections.title: Setup, Teardown, and Async Tests
sections.content:
beforeEach(() => { /* runs before every test in this file */ });
afterEach(() => { /* runs after every test — good place to reset mocks */ });

test('fetches data', async () => {
  const data = await fetchData(); // async test functions just work with await
  expect(data).toBeDefined();
});

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Automated tests catch a regression immediately and repeatably — manual clicking through an app does not scale and misses cases
  • A test pairs a behavior with an assertion — expect(actual).matcher(expected)
  • toBe is exact equality (===); use toEqual for deep-comparing objects and arrays
  • Mocks (jest.fn()) replace a real dependency (API call, database) with a controllable fake, so a test stays fast and isolated
  • beforeEach/afterEach run setup/cleanup around every test; test functions can be async and use await directly

sections.title: Intersection Observer — Knowing When an Element Is Visible
sections.content:
Before this API existed, checking whether an element had scrolled into view meant listening to the scroll event and manually calculating positions on every single fire — expensive, and easy to get wrong. IntersectionObserver does the same job efficiently, built into the browser.

const observer = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  entries.forEach((entry) => {
    if (entry.isIntersecting) {
      console.log(`${entry.target.id} is now visible`);
    }
  });
});

document.querySelectorAll('.lazy-image').forEach((img) => observer.observe(img));
This is exactly what powers infinite scroll and lazy-loaded images — observe a "load more" element near the bottom of the list, and fetch the next page the moment it comes into view.

sections.title: Web Workers — Running Code Off the Main Thread
sections.content:
JavaScript is single-threaded — a heavy computation (parsing a huge file, complex math) blocks everything else, including the page's ability to respond to clicks. A Web Worker runs a script on a genuinely separate thread, communicating with the main page through messages.

// worker.js
self.onmessage = (event) => {
  const result = heavyComputation(event.data);
  self.postMessage(result);
};

// main.js
const worker = new Worker('worker.js');
worker.postMessage(input);
worker.onmessage = (event) => console.log('Result:', event.data);
A worker has no access to the DOM — it runs in complete isolation and can only communicate by passing messages back and forth. It is for computation, not for touching the page directly.

sections.title: The Clipboard API
sections.content:
await navigator.clipboard.writeText('Copied text!');
const text = await navigator.clipboard.readText(); // requires the page to have focus and permission

sections.title: Geolocation
sections.content:
navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(
  (position) => {
    console.log(position.coords.latitude, position.coords.longitude);
  },
  (error) => {
    console.error('Location denied or unavailable:', error.message);
  }
);
Always provide the error callback. A user denying the permission prompt is not an edge case — it is the expected path for a meaningful share of visitors, and an app that only handles the success callback breaks visibly for every one of them.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• IntersectionObserver efficiently detects when an element enters or leaves the viewport — the mechanism behind infinite scroll and lazy loading
  • A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a separate thread, for heavy computation that would otherwise freeze the page — it has no DOM access, only message passing
  • The Clipboard API's writeText/readText are async and require the page to have focus/permission
  • Geolocation is async and permission-gated — always handle the error/denial callback, not just the success case

sections.title: What a Design Pattern Actually Is
sections.content: A design pattern is not a library or a syntax feature — it is a named, reusable solution to a problem that comes up repeatedly. Learning the name matters because it lets a whole team talk about a shape of code in one word, instead of re-explaining the same structure every time it appears.

sections.title: Module Pattern
sections.content:
Groups related code together and controls exactly what is exposed to the outside — the same idea ES modules formalized, achievable with plain closures.

const CartModule = (function () {
  let items = []; // private — inaccessible from outside this closure

  return {
    add(item) { items.push(item); },
    getCount() { return items.length; },
  };
})();

CartModule.add('shirt');
CartModule.getCount(); // 1
CartModule.items;       // undefined — truly private

sections.title: Singleton Pattern
sections.content:
Guarantees exactly one instance of something exists, and gives every part of the app the same shared instance rather than a fresh one each time.

class Settings {
  static #instance;
  constructor() { this.theme = 'light'; }
  static getInstance() {
    if (!Settings.#instance) Settings.#instance = new Settings();
    return Settings.#instance;
  }
}

Settings.getInstance() === Settings.getInstance(); // true — always the same object
A module in JavaScript is already effectively a singleton — it only ever runs once no matter how many files import it. The explicit Singleton class pattern above shows up more often in other languages; in JS, reaching for a plain exported module usually solves the same problem more simply.

sections.title: Observer Pattern
sections.content:
Lets one or more "listeners" subscribe to be notified when something happens, without the source needing to know who is listening — this is the exact shape behind addEventListener.

class EventEmitter {
  #listeners = {};
  on(event, callback) {
    (this.#listeners[event] ??= []).push(callback);
  }
  emit(event, data) {
    (this.#listeners[event] ?? []).forEach((cb) => cb(data));
  }
}

const emitter = new EventEmitter();
emitter.on('login', (user) => console.log(`${user} logged in`));
emitter.emit('login', 'Maya'); // 'Maya logged in'

sections.title: Factory Pattern
sections.content:
Centralizes object creation behind a function, instead of scattering new SomeClass() calls throughout the codebase — useful when the exact type to create depends on some condition.

function createUser(type, name) {
  if (type === 'admin') return new AdminUser(name);
  if (type === 'guest') return new GuestUser(name);
  return new RegularUser(name);
}

createUser('admin', 'Alex'); // caller doesn't need to know which class this becomes

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring problem — the name is what makes it useful to talk about, not a special feature of the language
  • Module pattern uses a closure to keep state private and expose only a controlled public interface — the same idea ES modules formalized
  • Singleton guarantees exactly one shared instance — in JavaScript, a plain module import already behaves like one in most cases
  • Observer lets listeners subscribe to events without the source knowing who is listening — addEventListener is a built-in example
  • Factory centralizes object creation behind a function, hiding which exact class gets instantiated from the caller

sections.title: Pure Functions
sections.content:
A pure function always returns the same output for the same input, and does not change anything outside itself — no modifying an outer variable, no network call, no console.log as a side effect of the logic.

// Impure — depends on and modifies external state
let total = 0;
function addToTotal(n) { total += n; return total; } // same input can give different output

// Pure — same input always gives the same output, changes nothing outside itself
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
Pure functions are easy to test (no setup needed beyond the input) and easy to reason about (no need to check what else in the program might affect the result).

sections.title: Immutability — Not Changing, Replacing
sections.content:
Instead of mutating a value in place, functional style creates a new value with the change applied, leaving the original untouched.

// Mutating
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
nums.push(4); // original array changed

// Non-mutating — creates a new array instead
const nums2 = [1, 2, 3];
const nums3 = [...nums2, 4]; // nums2 is untouched, nums3 is the new version

const user = { name: 'Maya', age: 25 };
const older = { ...user, age: 26 }; // same idea for objects
Array methods split into two camps: map/filter/slice return a new array; push/splice/sort mutate in place. Mixing them up is a common source of a bug where "the original data" turns out to have silently changed somewhere else in the app.

sections.title: Higher-Order Functions
sections.content:
A function that takes another function as an argument, returns one, or both. map, filter, and reduce are the ones you already use daily.

function multiplyBy(factor) {
  return (n) => n * factor; // returns a new function
}

const double = multiplyBy(2);
double(5); // 10

[1, 2, 3].map(double); // [2, 4, 6] — map itself is also higher-order: it takes a function

sections.title: Function Composition
sections.content:
Building a complex transformation by chaining small, single-purpose functions together, instead of writing one large function that does everything at once.

const trim = (s) => s.trim();
const lower = (s) => s.toLowerCase();
const removeSpaces = (s) => s.replace(/\s+/g, '-');

function compose(...fns) {
  return (input) => fns.reduce((value, fn) => fn(value), input);
}

const slugify = compose(trim, lower, removeSpaces);
slugify('  Hello World  '); // 'hello-world'
Each function in the chain does exactly one thing and is trivial to test on its own — slugify itself is just wiring, not new logic.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and causes no side effects — easy to test and reason about
  • Functional style favors creating a new value over mutating an existing one — map/filter/spread instead of push/splice
  • A higher-order function takes a function as an argument, returns one, or both — map, filter, and reduce are everyday examples
  • Function composition builds complex behavior from small, single-purpose functions chained together, instead of one large function
  • Know which array methods mutate (push, splice, sort) and which do not (map, filter, slice) — mixing them up causes real bugs

title: The Callback That Cut in Line

sections.title: The Message That Always Arrives Too Late
sections.content:
📍 Maya's loading screen shows the wrong order every single time

Maya: Alex, I scheduled the 'still loading...' message with setTimeout(fn, 0) — zero delay, so it should run essentially immediately. But my Promise's success message always logs first, every single time. Zero delay should mean it runs FIRST, right?

console.log('Fetching...');
fetchUser().then(() => console.log('User loaded!'));
setTimeout(() => console.log('Still loading...'), 0);
// Logs: Fetching..., User loaded!, Still loading...
// The 0ms timeout ALWAYS loses to the promise, no matter what

Alex: 0ms does not mean "run immediately." It means "run as soon as possible" — and "as soon as possible" for a timer is never as soon as a Promise.

sections.title: Two Waiting Rooms, Not One
sections.content:
📍 Alex explains there are two separate queues

Alex: There is not one line of callbacks waiting their turn. There are two: the microtask queue and the macrotask queue. Promises go in the microtask queue. setTimeout goes in the macrotask queue.

// Microtask queue: Promise .then, async/await continuations, queueMicrotask
// Macrotask queue: setTimeout, setInterval, DOM events, I/O

Maya: Okay, but why does microtask always win, even at 0ms?

Alex: Because the rule is not "whichever queue you joined first." After the currently running code finishes, JavaScript drains the ENTIRE microtask queue — completely empty — before it is even allowed to look at the macrotask queue.

sections.title: Proving It — Stack Three Promises Against One Timer
sections.content:
📍 Alex stacks the deck to make the point unmistakable
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log('promise 1'))
  .then(() => console.log('promise 2'))
  .then(() => console.log('promise 3'));

// Logs: promise 1, promise 2, promise 3, THEN timeout
// All three promise callbacks run — even ones chained onto each other —
// before the single 0ms timeout ever gets a turn

Maya: So it's not even close. Three separate microtasks all cut in front of one macrotask?

Alex: All of them. Every time. The macrotask queue doesn't get a single turn until the microtask queue is completely, totally empty — even if new microtasks keep getting added while you're draining it.

sections.title: Fixing Maya's Loading Screen
sections.content:
📍 Applying the mental model to the actual bug

Alex: Your 'Still loading...' message isn't broken — it's doing exactly what a macrotask does. If you want it to always show first regardless of the Promise, don't compete with it — show it synchronously, before either queue even starts.

console.log('Fetching...');
console.log('Still loading...'); // shown synchronously, immediately, no race at all
fetchUser().then(() => console.log('User loaded!'));

Maya: So the fix wasn't about queue priority at all. It was realizing I didn't need a queue for this in the first place.

Alex: Right. The event loop isn't something to fight — once you know which queue something lands in, you stop guessing and start designing around it.

sections.title: Why This Design Exists At All
sections.content:
📍 The bigger picture

Alex: Microtasks jumping the line isn't an accident — it's deliberate. Promises are meant to resolve as soon as realistically possible once their value is ready, without waiting behind whatever else happened to be scheduled first. If a Promise had to wait its turn behind timers and DOM events, async/await would feel sluggish and unpredictable.

Maya: So the ordering isn't a quirk to memorize — it's the whole point of having two separate queues in the first place.

Alex: Exactly. Once you see it that way, the rule stops being a trivia question and starts being obvious.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• There are two separate queues, not one: the microtask queue (Promise .then, async/await) and the macrotask queue (setTimeout, DOM events, I/O)
  • After the currently running code finishes, JavaScript drains the ENTIRE microtask queue — completely — before running even one macrotask, no matter how many microtasks that takes
  • setTimeout(fn, 0) does not mean "run immediately" — it means "join the macrotask queue," which always loses to any pending microtask
  • Chained .then() calls each add a new microtask — a long promise chain can still fully finish before a single 0ms timeout ever runs
  • This ordering is deliberate, not incidental: Promises are designed to resolve as soon as possible, without waiting behind unrelated scheduled work

title: The Code Review That Changed Everything

sections.title: The Pull Request
sections.content:
📍 Maya submits her first solo feature — a notifications widget — for review

Maya: Okay, I finally finished the notifications widget. Approve it? I've been coding for six months, I think I've got this.

Alex: Give me ten minutes. I want to walk through this with you, not just approve it.

sections.title: Comment #1 — The this That Wasn't Bound
sections.content:
📍 Alex's first review comment
class NotificationBell {
  constructor() { this.count = 0; }
  increment() { this.count++; }
}

const bell = new NotificationBell();
socket.on('notify', bell.increment); // passed as a bare reference

Alex: This one will work in your local testing and break in production the first time a real notification arrives. You're passing bell.increment as a callback — it gets detached from bell. When the socket calls it, this won't be bell anymore.

Maya: Right — this depends on the call site, not where the function was written. I need to bind it, or wrap it in an arrow function.

Alex: Either works. This is the exact bug from your first week here — you've just met it in a new outfit.

sections.title: Comment #2 — The Closure Holding On Too Long
sections.content:
📍 Second comment, a subtler one
function setupBell(element) {
  const hugeHistory = fetchAllNotificationsEver(); // large array, needed briefly
  element.addEventListener('click', () => {
    console.log('Bell clicked'); // never actually uses hugeHistory
  });
}

Alex: Your click handler is a closure — and it keeps hugeHistory alive in memory for as long as this listener exists, even though the handler never touches it. It's not a bug today, but it's exactly the shape of a real memory leak once this list gets big.

Maya: Because a closure keeps its whole surrounding scope reachable, not just the variables it actually uses?

Alex: Right. If you don't need it in the closure, don't let it get captured — pull only what you need into scope first.

sections.title: Comment #3 — The Race Nobody Noticed
sections.content:
📍 Third comment
function loadNotifications() {
  showSpinner();
  fetchNotifications().then(renderList);
  hideSpinner(); // runs before renderList — every time, not just sometimes
}

Maya: Oh — hideSpinner() is synchronous, so it runs immediately, but renderList only runs later as a microtask once the fetch resolves. The spinner disappears before the data even arrives.

Alex: You caught that one yourself this time. That's the event loop again — synchronous code always finishes before any queued callback gets a turn, promise or not.

sections.title: Comment #4 — Reinventing a Pattern That Already Has a Name
sections.content:
📍 The last comment — not a bug, a naming
// Maya's code — works fine
const listeners = [];
function onNotify(cb) { listeners.push(cb); }
function fireNotify(data) { listeners.forEach(cb => cb(data)); }

Alex: This isn't wrong at all — it works. But you've just built the Observer pattern from scratch. There's no reason to hide that: name the file/class after it, and the next person who reads this immediately knows the shape without reverse-engineering it from the code.

Maya: So it's not about knowing more tricks. It's recognizing the shape of something I already know, and giving it its real name.

sections.title: What Actually Changed
sections.content:
📍 After the review

Maya: None of those were things I didn't know. this, closures, the event loop, Observer — I could have explained every single one of those in isolation on a quiz.

Alex: That's the actual shift happening right now. Knowing a rule and recognizing it live, inside code you just wrote yourself, under no pressure to perform — those are different skills. The first one you already had. You just built the second one, today.

Maya: So the review wasn't really about finding four bugs.

Alex: It never really is. Approved, by the way — once you push the fixes.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A method passed as a bare callback (obj.method, not () => obj.method()) detaches from its object — the same this-binding trap shows up in any callback-based API, not just event listeners
  • A closure keeps its entire surrounding scope reachable for as long as it exists — capturing more than a handler actually uses is a common, easy-to-miss memory leak
  • Synchronous code always finishes before any queued callback — a spinner hidden synchronously right after starting an async fetch will hide before the data even arrives
  • Recognizing a familiar pattern (Observer, Factory, Module) inside your own code — and naming it — makes that code instantly legible to the next person who reads it
  • Applying a rule you already "know" to code you're actually writing, under no quiz pressure, is a distinct skill from reciting the rule — and it's the one that actually matters day to day

sections.title: What Node.js Actually Is
sections.content:
Node.js is not a programming language. It's a runtime — a program that takes JavaScript, the same language browsers run, and executes it somewhere other than a browser. Specifically, on your own machine or a server.

It does this using V8, the same JavaScript engine that powers Google Chrome. V8's job is to take JavaScript code and turn it into fast, native machine code. Node.js wraps V8 and adds everything a browser normally gives JavaScript that a server doesn't need — and takes away things a server has that a browser doesn't, like direct file system access and network sockets.

Before Node.js existed (2009), JavaScript only ran inside a browser tab. If you wanted a backend, you reached for a completely different language — Python, Ruby, Java, PHP. Node.js meant a team could use one language across the whole stack.

Practically, this means Node.js is what lets you build a web server, a command-line tool, a script that processes files on disk, or the backend for a mobile app — all in JavaScript.

sections.title: Running Your First Script
sections.content:
Save a file called hello.js with one line:

console.log('Hello from Node.js');

Run it from your terminal:

node hello.js

Node.js reads the file top to bottom, executes it, and exits once there's no more work left to do — no browser tab, no HTML page, nothing to click.

The REPL

If you type node with no filename, you get the REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) — an interactive prompt where you can type JavaScript and see the result immediately. It's useful for quick experiments, but not for anything you want to keep or run more than once.

$ node
> 2 + 2
4
> .exit

sections.title: package.json and npm
sections.content:
Almost every real Node.js project has a package.json file at its root. It's the project's manifest: name, version, the scripts you can run, and — most importantly — the list of external packages (dependencies) your project needs.

Create one with:

npm init -y

npm (Node Package Manager) ships with Node.js and is how you install code other people have written. When you run:

npm install express

npm downloads the express package into a node_modules folder and adds it to package.json's dependencies list, so anyone who clones your project can run npm install and get the exact same packages.

Need to run a package's command-line tool just once, without installing it permanently? npx some-package downloads and runs it on the spot.

sections.title: require() and Your Own Modules
sections.content:
Node.js splits code across files using modules. To pull in code from another file — or a built-in module, or an installed package — you use require():

const fs = require('fs');          // built-in module
const express = require('express'); // installed package
const math = require('./math');     // your own file, note the ./

Whatever a file wants to expose to other files gets assigned to module.exports:

// math.js
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
module.exports = { add };

Anything not assigned to module.exports stays private to that file — a natural way to keep implementation details from leaking out.

sections.title: Global Objects You'll Use Often
sections.content:
A handful of objects are available in every Node.js file without requiring anything:

  • console — logging, same as in a browser (console.log, console.error, console.table for arrays of objects, console.time/timeEnd for quick timing).
  • process — information about and control over the currently running Node.js process. process.env holds environment variables, process.argv holds command-line arguments, process.exit() ends the process.
  • __dirname and __filename — the absolute path to the current file's folder and the file itself. Useful for building reliable paths: path.join(__dirname, 'data.json').
There is no window in Node.js. If a tutorial or Stack Overflow answer assumes one, it's written for the browser, not for Node.js.

sections.title: Managing Your Node.js Version
sections.content:
Node.js ships two kinds of releases: Current, which gets new features first but has a short support window, and LTS (Long Term Support), which trades the newest features for years of stability and security patches. Production apps almost always run on an LTS version.

Different projects on your machine may need different Node.js versions. Reinstalling Node.js by hand every time you switch projects gets old fast — a version manager like nvm lets you install several versions side by side and switch between them per-project.

nvm install 20
nvm use 20

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Node.js is a runtime, built on V8 — it lets JavaScript run outside a browser, with no window.
  • package.json is your project's manifest; npm install reads it and fills node_modules.
  • require() pulls a module in; module.exports decides what a file exposes.
  • process, console, __dirname are always available — no import needed.
  • Use an LTS release for production, and a version manager like nvm to juggle versions across projects.

sections.title: Why Node.js Cares So Much About Async
sections.content:
Node.js runs your JavaScript on a single thread. If that one thread ever sits and waits — for a file to finish reading, a database query to come back, a network request to complete — nothing else can happen while it waits. Every other request, every other piece of work, is stuck behind it.

Node.js avoids this with non-blocking I/O: instead of waiting, it starts the slow operation, registers what to do when it finishes, and immediately moves on to other work. When the operation completes, Node.js circles back and runs the code you registered for it.

The mechanism that manages all of this — deciding what runs next, and when a finished operation's callback gets its turn — is called the event loop. You don't control it directly, but almost every async pattern in Node.js exists to work well with it.

sections.title: Callbacks: The Original Pattern
sections.content:
The earliest and simplest way to say "run this when the async thing finishes" is a callback — a function you pass in, to be called later.

const fs = require('fs');

fs.readFile('data.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => {
  if (err) {
    console.error('Something went wrong:', err);
    return;
  }
  console.log(data);
});

Node.js callbacks follow the error-first convention: the first argument is always an error (or null if nothing went wrong), and the second is the actual result. You'll see this pattern across almost every built-in async function.

Nest enough callbacks inside callbacks and you get "callback hell" — code that drifts rightward with every new step, hard to read and easy to get wrong. This is the exact problem Promises were designed to solve.

sections.title: Promises: A Cleaner Abstraction
sections.content:
A Promise represents the eventual result of an async operation. It's always in one of three states: pending (still working), fulfilled (succeeded, with a value), or rejected (failed, with a reason).

const fs = require('fs/promises');

fs.readFile('data.txt', 'utf8')
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(err => console.error('Something went wrong:', err));

Promises also give you clean ways to coordinate several async operations at once:

  • Promise.all([p1, p2]) — waits for every Promise to succeed; rejects immediately if any one fails.
  • Promise.allSettled([p1, p2]) — waits for all of them regardless of outcome, and reports each result individually.
  • Promise.race([p1, p2]) — settles as soon as the first one settles, success or failure.
  • Promise.any([p1, p2]) — resolves with the first one that succeeds, ignoring failures unless every one fails.

sections.title: async/await: Async Code That Reads Like Sync Code
sections.content:
async/await is built directly on top of Promises — it's a different way to write the same thing, not a separate mechanism. An async function always returns a Promise, and inside it, await pauses execution until the awaited Promise settles.

const fs = require('fs/promises');

async function readConfig() {
  try {
    const data = await fs.readFile('config.json', 'utf8');
    return JSON.parse(data);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Could not read config:', err);
    throw err;
  }
}

Notice the error handling: a rejected await throws at that exact line, so a normal try/catch around it catches everything — no separate .catch() chain needed.

A very common bug: calling an async function inside array.forEach() and expecting it to wait. forEach() has no idea its callback is async — it fires every call and moves on immediately, without waiting for any of them. Use a for...of loop with await, or Promise.all(), instead.

sections.title: Why setTimeout(fn, 0) Doesn't Run Immediately
sections.content:
One thing that trips people up: synchronous code always finishes first, then all pending Promise callbacks (the microtask queue) run, and only after that does the event loop move on to things like timers (the macrotask queue) — even a timer set for 0 milliseconds.

console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
console.log('D');

// prints: A, D, C, B

This is why a Promise callback always "beats" a same-tick setTimeout(fn, 0), no matter how they're ordered in the code.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Node.js runs on a single thread — non-blocking I/O and the event loop exist so slow operations don't freeze everything else.
  • Callbacks are error-first: (err, result) => {}. Deep nesting of them is "callback hell."
  • A Promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected — .then()/.catch(), or Promise.all/allSettled/race/any to coordinate several.
  • async/await is Promises with synchronous-looking syntax — use try/catch around await for errors.
  • Synchronous code, then microtasks (Promises), then macrotasks (timers) — always, even at 0ms.

title: Working with Files and the Network

sections.title: Reading and Writing Files
sections.content:
The built-in fs module handles file access. It offers three flavors of almost every operation: synchronous, callback-based, and Promise-based.

const fs = require('fs');

// Synchronous — blocks until done. Only use in scripts or startup code.
const data = fs.readFileSync('notes.txt', 'utf8');

// Callback-based — non-blocking
fs.readFile('notes.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => { /* ... */ });

// Promise-based — pairs naturally with async/await
const data2 = await require('fs/promises').readFile('notes.txt', 'utf8');
Never use the synchronous *Sync functions inside a server's request handler — they freeze the entire process for every other request until they finish.

Writing works the same way. fs.writeFile() creates the file if it doesn't exist, and overwrites it if it does. If you're building up a log file line by line, you want fs.appendFile() instead, which adds to the end without erasing what's already there.

sections.title: Directories and File Metadata
sections.content:
const fs = require('fs/promises');

await fs.mkdir('uploads', { recursive: true }); // recursive creates missing parents too
const files = await fs.readdir('uploads');        // array of filenames
const info = await fs.stat('uploads/photo.jpg');   // metadata
console.log(info.isFile(), info.size, info.mtime);
await fs.unlink('uploads/old-file.txt');           // delete a file

fs.stat() is what you reach for before processing an uploaded file — checking whether it's actually a file (not a directory) and how large it is, before doing anything with its contents.

sections.title: Building a Server from Scratch
sections.content:
Before frameworks like Express add convenience on top, it's worth seeing what a Node.js server actually is underneath: the built-in http module.

const http = require('http');

const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/plain' });
  res.end('Hello World');
});

server.listen(3000);

The callback runs once per incoming request, with an IncomingMessage (req) and a ServerResponse (res). Notice that req.body isn't a thing here — the request body arrives as a stream of 'data' events you have to collect yourself. Frameworks like Express exist largely to do this collection-and-parsing step for you.

sections.title: Making Outbound Requests
sections.content:
To call another service, use http.get() (or https.get() for HTTPS URLs) without any extra dependency:

const https = require('https');

https.get('https://api.example.com/data', (res) => {
  let body = '';
  res.on('data', chunk => body += chunk);
  res.on('end', () => console.log(JSON.parse(body)));
});
Since Node.js 18, the global fetch() API is also built in — the same one browsers have. For most new code, await fetch(url) is simpler than the callback-and-chunks pattern above.

sections.title: Watching for Changes and Streaming Large Files
sections.content:
fs.watch(path, callback) watches a file or folder and fires whenever something changes — this is how tools like nodemon detect a saved file and restart your server automatically.

For large files, never load the whole thing into memory with readFile() just to send it somewhere else. Stream it instead:

const fs = require('fs');

fs.createReadStream('large-video.mp4').pipe(res);

pipe() connects a readable source directly to a writable destination, forwarding data in manageable chunks. Memory usage stays flat no matter how big the file is — a 500MB file and a 5MB file cost the same amount of memory to stream.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• fs has sync, callback, and Promise versions of everything — never use the sync versions in a server request handler.
  • writeFile() overwrites; appendFile() adds to the end.
  • http.createServer((req, res) => {}) is what frameworks like Express are built on top of.
  • The built-in fetch() (Node 18+) is the simplest way to make outbound requests today.
  • Stream large files with createReadStream().pipe() instead of loading them fully into memory.

title: Node.js Modules: CommonJS and ES Modules

sections.title: Two Module Systems, One Runtime
sections.content:
Node.js supports two different ways of splitting code across files: CommonJS (require()/module.exports), the original Node.js system, and ES Modules (import/export), the standardized system JavaScript itself eventually adopted, the same one browsers use.

This isn't just two ways of writing the same idea — they're genuinely different systems with different rules, and Node.js has to be told which one a given file is using before it can even parse it correctly.

sections.title: CommonJS: require() and module.exports
sections.content:
// math.js
function add(a, b) { return a + b; }
module.exports = { add };

// app.js
const { add } = require('./math');

This is Node.js's default for plain .js files, unless you tell it otherwise. It's synchronous — require() reads and runs the target file's code before your own code continues — and it caches by file path, so requiring the same file twice returns the exact same object both times, not two separate copies.

sections.title: ES Modules: import/export
sections.content:
// math.mjs
export function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

// app.mjs
import { add } from './math.mjs';

You opt into ES Modules two ways: name the file with a .mjs extension, or add "type": "module" to your package.json, which makes every plain .js file in that package an ES module.

ES Modules also unlock a couple of things CommonJS doesn't have: top-level await (you can await a Promise directly at the top of a file, no wrapper function needed) and always running in strict mode by default.

Switch on "type": "module" and every __dirname/__filename reference in your code will throw — those are CommonJS-only globals that don't exist in ES Modules. The replacement is import.meta.url, usually paired with fileURLToPath().

sections.title: Where the Two Worlds Meet
sections.content:
Node.js bridges the two systems, but only in one direction cleanly.

An ES module can import a CommonJS package without any special syntax — Node.js automatically treats that package's module.exports as the default export.

// works fine from an ESM file, even though old-package only has module.exports
import oldLib from 'old-cjs-package';

Going the other way is harder. A CommonJS file cannot require() an ESM-only package — require() is synchronous, and loading an ES module is inherently asynchronous. The fix is dynamic import, which returns a Promise:

// from a CommonJS file
const mod = await import('esm-only-package');

sections.title: Choosing for a New Project
sections.content:
For a brand new project, ES Modules is the more future-facing choice — it's the standard, and the ecosystem is steadily moving toward it. For an existing large CommonJS codebase, migrating everything at once is rarely worth the disruption; interop via dynamic import() lets you adopt ESM-only dependencies without a full rewrite.

If you're publishing a package for others to use, the "exports" field in package.json lets you ship both: consumers who import your package get the ESM build, and consumers who require() it get the CommonJS build, from the same published package.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• CommonJS (require/module.exports) is Node's original, synchronous module system.
  • ES Modules (import/export) is the JS-standard system — opt in via .mjs or "type": "module".
  • __dirname/__filename don't exist in ESM — use import.meta.url instead.
  • ESM can import CommonJS automatically; CommonJS needs dynamic import() to load ESM-only packages.
  • A package's "exports" field can ship both builds from one package.

sections.title: path: Building Cross-Platform File Paths
sections.content:
Windows uses backslashes in file paths; everything else uses forward slashes. String-concatenating paths by hand breaks the moment your code runs on a different OS. The path module handles this for you.

const path = require('path');

path.join('users', 'ana', 'notes.txt');   // 'users/ana/notes.txt'
path.basename('/a/b/notes.txt');           // 'notes.txt'
path.dirname('/a/b/notes.txt');            // '/a/b'
path.extname('notes.txt');                 // '.txt'

path.join() and path.resolve() look similar but do different things. join() just glues segments together with the right separator. resolve() builds an absolute path, working right to left, using the current working directory as the base if nothing absolute shows up along the way.

path.join('b', 'c');     // 'b/c'
path.resolve('b', 'c');  // '/current/working/dir/b/c'

sections.title: os: Information About the Machine
sections.content:
The os module reports on the machine Node.js is actually running on — useful for cross-platform tools and for sizing things like a cluster of worker processes.

const os = require('os');

os.platform();      // 'linux', 'darwin', 'win32'
os.cpus().length;   // number of logical CPU cores
os.totalmem();      // total system memory, in bytes
os.homedir();        // the current user's home directory
os.cpus().length is exactly what you'd loop over when forking one worker process per CPU core in cluster mode — the same code then scales correctly whether it's running on a 2-core laptop or a 32-core server.

sections.title: Buffer: Working with Raw Binary Data
sections.content:
Strings in JavaScript are text. Files, network packets, and images are often just raw bytes — not text at all. Buffer is Node's built-in way to represent a fixed chunk of binary data, sitting outside the normal JavaScript heap.

const buf = Buffer.from('hello', 'utf8');
console.log(buf);            // <Buffer 68 65 6c 6c 6f>
console.log(buf.toString()); // 'hello'

You'll meet Buffer constantly when working with files and network streams — a stream's 'data' event, for example, hands you chunks as Buffers by default.

sections.title: crypto: Hashing, Random Values, and Basic Security
sections.content:
The crypto module covers hashing, encryption, and generating secure random values.

const crypto = require('crypto');

crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('hex'); // a secure random token
crypto.createHash('sha256').update('data').digest('hex'); // a hash
Never use Math.random() for anything security-sensitive — session tokens, password reset codes — it's predictable, not cryptographically secure. Use crypto.randomBytes() instead.
Don't hash passwords with crypto.createHash('sha256') either. SHA-256 is fast — great for checking file integrity, terrible for passwords, since an attacker can brute-force billions of guesses per second on modern hardware. Password hashing needs a deliberately slow algorithm like bcrypt or argon2.

sections.title: readline: Reading Terminal Input
sections.content:
Building a command-line tool that needs to ask the user something? readline reads input from the terminal one line at a time.

const readline = require('readline');
const rl = readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin, output: process.stdout });

rl.question('What is your name? ', (name) => {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
  rl.close();
});

sections.title: zlib: Compression Without an External Dependency
sections.content:
Need to compress a large file before archiving or sending it, without pulling in a third-party library? zlib is built in, and works as a stream — you can pipe data straight through it.

const fs = require('fs');
const zlib = require('zlib');

fs.createReadStream('access.log')
  .pipe(zlib.createGzip())
  .pipe(fs.createWriteStream('access.log.gz'));

sections.title: A Few Small Utilities Worth Knowing
sections.content:
Three more built-ins that quietly solve specific problems well:

assert

Lightweight sanity checks without pulling in a full test framework — throws an AssertionError if a condition fails.

const assert = require('assert');
assert.strictEqual(2 + 2, 4);

perf_hooks

When Date.now() isn't precise enough — it's only millisecond-accurate — performance.now() gives high-resolution timing for measuring exactly how long a specific operation takes.

URLSearchParams

Building a query string by hand means remembering to URL-encode every value yourself — easy to get wrong. URLSearchParams handles the encoding automatically.

const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: 'node & express', page: '2' });
params.toString(); // 'q=node+%26+express&page=2'

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• path.join() concatenates; path.resolve() builds an absolute path from the current directory.
  • Buffer represents raw binary data — you'll meet it constantly around files and streams.
  • crypto.randomBytes() for secure tokens; bcrypt/argon2 (not crypto.createHash) for passwords.
  • zlib gives you gzip compression as a stream, no dependency needed.
  • assert, perf_hooks, and URLSearchParams each solve one small, specific problem well.

sections.title: EventEmitter: The Pattern Behind Half of Node.js
sections.content:
A huge amount of Node.js — HTTP servers, streams, child processes — is built on one pattern: something emits named events, and other code subscribes to react when they happen. That pattern has a name and a class: EventEmitter, from the built-in events module.

const { EventEmitter } = require('events');
const emitter = new EventEmitter();

emitter.on('greet', (name) => console.log(`Hello, ${name}`));
emitter.emit('greet', 'Ana'); // 'Hello, Ana'

Any class can extend EventEmitter to gain this behavior itself — which is exactly what streams, HTTP servers, and many npm packages do.

sections.title: on() vs once(), and Cleaning Up Listeners
sections.content:
.on(event, listener) fires every single time the event happens. .once(event, listener) fires only the first time, then automatically removes itself — useful for one-time setup events like a database connection's 'ready' event.

emitter.once('ready', () => console.log('Connected!'));

To remove listeners yourself, use emitter.off(event, listener) for one, or emitter.removeAllListeners() to clear everything at once — handy cleanup before discarding an emitter.

Node.js warns you if more than 10 listeners get added to a single event — it's a memory-leak detector, not a hard limit. If you legitimately need more (say, you're writing a library), emitter.setMaxListeners(n) raises the threshold — but check it isn't actually a leak first.

sections.title: The Four Kinds of Streams
sections.content:
A stream processes data piece by piece instead of loading it all into memory at once. Node.js has four flavors:

  • Readable — a source you read from: a file, an HTTP request body, process.stdin.
  • Writable — a destination you write to: a file, an HTTP response, process.stdout.
  • Duplex — both at once, independently. A TCP socket is the classic example: you read incoming data and write outgoing data through the same object.
  • Transform — a special Duplex that modifies data as it passes through, like gzip compression.

You can consume a Readable stream with modern async/await syntax, since streams are async-iterable:

for await (const chunk of readableStream) {
  console.log(chunk.length);
}

sections.title: Connecting Streams with pipe() and pipeline()
sections.content:
pipe() connects a Readable source to a Writable destination, forwarding data automatically:

fs.createReadStream('input.mp4').pipe(fs.createWriteStream('output.mp4'));

This copies a file in constant memory, no matter how large it is. The catch: if an error occurs mid-stream, pipe() doesn't clean up the destination stream automatically, which can leak file handles or leave a half-written file with no error surfaced.

stream.pipeline() fixes this — it properly closes every stream involved on error, and reports that error through a callback (or a Promise, via stream/promises):

const { pipeline } = require('stream/promises');

await pipeline(
  fs.createReadStream('input.mp4'),
  zlib.createGzip(),
  fs.createWriteStream('output.mp4.gz')
);
In modern code, prefer pipeline() over raw pipe() for exactly this reason.

sections.title: Backpressure: When the Writer Can't Keep Up
sections.content:
What happens if a Readable stream produces data faster than the Writable destination can consume it — reading a fast local file while writing over a slow network connection, say? Without any coordination, data would pile up in memory faster than it drains.

Node.js streams handle this automatically: when a Writable's internal buffer fills up, .write() returns false, signaling the source to pause. Once the buffer drains, a 'drain' event fires and reading resumes. This whole mechanism is called backpressure, and pipe()/pipeline() handle it for you — one more reason to use them instead of manually shuffling data between streams yourself.

sections.title: Streaming Objects, Not Just Bytes
sections.content:
Streams default to operating on Buffers or strings. If you want to stream arbitrary JavaScript objects instead — say, parsed database rows — pass { objectMode: true } when creating the stream:

const { Transform } = require('stream');

const toCsvLine = new Transform({
  objectMode: true,
  transform(row, encoding, callback) {
    callback(null, `${row.name},${row.email}\n`);
  },
});

This is the pattern behind streaming a large database export as CSV — rows come in as objects, get transformed to text, and stream straight out to the response without ever holding the whole result set in memory.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• EventEmitter underlies streams, HTTP servers, and a lot of the ecosystem — .on()/.emit()/.once() is the whole pattern.
  • Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform — four stream types, moving data in chunks instead of all at once.
  • Prefer stream.pipeline() over raw pipe() — it cleans up properly on error.
  • Backpressure is handled automatically by pipe()/pipeline() — the writer signals the reader to slow down.
  • { objectMode: true } lets a stream carry JS objects instead of raw bytes/text.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Errors
sections.content:
Not every error means your code is broken. It's worth splitting errors into two categories that need very different handling:

  • Operational errors — expected, recoverable failures: a user submits an invalid email, a network request times out, a file doesn't exist. Your code should anticipate these.
  • Programmer errors — actual bugs: a typo, calling a function with the wrong arguments, a null reference. These mean something needs to be fixed in the code itself.

Treating both the same way — a generic 500 error for everything — makes it impossible to tell, from the outside, which situation you're actually in.

sections.title: try/catch and Errors in async/await
sections.content:
try/catch catches a thrown error and lets execution continue instead of crashing. Inside an async function, it also catches a rejected awaited Promise — a rejection and a thrown error are handled identically here.

async function loadUser(id) {
  try {
    return await db.findUser(id);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Failed to load user:', err);
    throw err; // still let the caller know something went wrong
  }
}
Catching an error doesn't have to mean swallowing it. Log it, add context, and re-throw when the caller genuinely needs to know — silently catching and moving on hides real problems.

sections.title: Building Your Own Error Types
sections.content:
A custom error class lets your code, and whoever handles the error later, tell error types apart without parsing message text — which is fragile, since wording can change at any time.

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
    this.statusCode = 400;
  }
}

throw new ValidationError('Email is required');

A central error handler can then check error.statusCode or error.name to decide how to respond, instead of guessing from the message.

When you wrap a lower-level error to add context, keep the original around instead of losing it:

throw new Error('Could not save order', { cause: originalDbError });
Class-based checks like instanceof can break across boundaries — a worker thread, or an error serialized to JSON and parsed back. For anything that needs to survive that, use a plain string property like error.name instead.

sections.title: The Safety Nets: uncaughtException and unhandledRejection
sections.content:
Sometimes an error slips past every try/catch you wrote — a bug you didn't anticipate. Node.js gives you two process-level events as a last resort:

process.on('uncaughtException', (err) => {
  console.error('Uncaught:', err);
  process.exit(1);
});

process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => {
  console.error('Unhandled rejection:', reason);
  process.exit(1);
});
These are for logging and shutting down cleanly, not for keeping the process running. Once an error reaches this point, the process may be in a state you don't fully understand — a lock not released, a half-finished write. Log it, exit, and let a process manager restart you fresh, rather than trying to soldier on.

sections.title: Retrying Without Making Things Worse
sections.content:
A network call to a flaky service that fails occasionally shouldn't be given up on after one try — but retrying immediately, in a tight loop, can pile more load onto a service that's already struggling.

Exponential backoff is the standard fix: wait a bit before retrying, and double that wait after each subsequent failure, up to a capped maximum number of attempts.

async function withRetry(fn, maxAttempts = 4) {
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 2 ** attempt * 100));
    }
  }
}
Always cap the number of attempts. Unlimited retries assume every failure is temporary — but if the input itself is genuinely broken, it will fail forever and quietly block whatever's behind it in a queue.

sections.title: When to Give Up Gracefully
sections.content:
If a downstream service is completely down, retrying every request against it just wastes time waiting out the same timeout, over and over, while backing up your own capacity. The circuit breaker pattern addresses this directly: after enough consecutive failures, it "opens" and fails fast without even attempting the call, for a cooldown period — then lets one test request through to check whether the service has recovered.

For dependencies that aren't essential to the core experience, consider graceful degradation instead: if a recommendations service is down, show a plain product list rather than failing the whole page. The app keeps working with reduced functionality instead of failing outright.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Operational errors (expected) and programmer errors (bugs) need different handling — don't treat them the same.
  • Custom Error subclasses let you branch on a structured property, not fragile message text.
  • uncaughtException/unhandledRejection are last-resort safety nets — log and exit deliberately, don't try to keep running.
  • Retry with exponential backoff and a hard cap — never retry forever.
  • Circuit breakers stop hammering a known-down service; graceful degradation keeps the app usable when a non-critical dependency fails.

sections.title: The process Object, Beyond env and argv
sections.content:
You've likely already used process.env and process.argv. A few more properties are worth knowing:

process.memoryUsage(); // { rss, heapUsed, heapTotal, external, ... }
process.exitCode = 1;   // sets the exit code without forcing an immediate exit
process.pid;            // this process's ID

process.exitCode matters more than it looks. If a script hits an error partway through but never sets this (or calls process.exit(1)), Node.js quietly exits with code 0 once it runs out of work — meaning a CI pipeline calling this script has no way to know it actually failed.

Two more process events worth knowing: 'beforeExit' fires when the event loop has no more scheduled work, and code inside it can still schedule more, delaying exit further. 'exit' fires synchronously right at actual termination — no further async work can be started from it.

sections.title: Signals: How a Process Gets Told to Stop
sections.content:
A signal is how the outside world tells a running process something. Two you'll handle constantly:

  • SIGTERM — sent by process managers and orchestrators (Docker, Kubernetes, PM2) asking a service to shut down gracefully.
  • SIGINT — sent when a user presses Ctrl+C in a terminal.

Handling them properly means finishing in-flight work before actually exiting, instead of dropping active requests mid-response:

process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  server.close(() => {
    db.end();
    process.exit(0);
  });
});

server.close() stops accepting new connections but lets requests already in progress finish first — exactly what you want during a deployment.

sections.title: Running Other Programs
sections.content:
Sometimes you need to shell out to another program rather than doing something in pure JavaScript. Node.js gives you a few ways, with a real safety distinction between them.

const { exec, execFile } = require('child_process');

exec(`convert ${filename}`, callback);              // runs through a shell — risky with user input
execFile('convert', [filename], callback);           // runs directly, no shell involved
exec() passes your command through a shell, so string-concatenating any user-influenced value into it is a command injection risk — a filename like "a.jpg; rm -rf /" would actually execute that second command. execFile() (and spawn()) take arguments as a separate array and never involve a shell, so this class of attack doesn't apply.

exec() buffers the whole output in memory before handing it to your callback — fine for short commands, risky for anything producing a lot of output. spawn() streams stdout/stderr as they're produced, better suited to long-running processes or large output.

sections.title: fork() and Talking to a Child Process
sections.content:
child_process.fork() is specifically for spawning another Node.js process — running its own module, with its own V8 instance and event loop, plus a built-in communication channel between parent and child.

// parent.js
const { fork } = require('child_process');
const child = fork('./worker.js');
child.send({ task: 'process-report' });
child.on('message', (result) => console.log('Got:', result));

// worker.js
process.on('message', (msg) => {
  const result = doHeavyWork(msg.task);
  process.send(result);
});

This offloads CPU-intensive work to a separate process entirely, so it never blocks the main process's event loop while it runs.

sections.title: worker_threads for CPU-Heavy Work
sections.content:
worker_threads solves a similar problem to fork() — running CPU-bound work without blocking the main thread — but with threads instead of full separate processes. Threads are lighter weight than processes and, unlike fork(), can share memory directly through a SharedArrayBuffer.

const { Worker } = require('worker_threads');

const worker = new Worker('./resize-image.js', { workerData: { path: 'photo.jpg' } });
worker.on('message', (resizedPath) => console.log('Done:', resizedPath));
Reach for worker_threads for CPU-bound work like image processing or heavy parsing. For running a separate, independent Node.js program — or when you specifically want full process isolation — fork() is the better fit.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Always set process.exitCode on a failure path — an error being logged doesn't mean the exit code reflects it.
  • SIGTERM (from orchestrators) and SIGINT (from Ctrl+C) should trigger graceful shutdown: stop new connections, finish existing ones, then exit.
  • execFile()/spawn() with an arguments array avoid the command-injection risk of string-concatenating into exec().
  • fork() runs a whole separate Node.js process with built-in IPC; worker_threads runs lighter-weight threads that can share memory.

sections.title: npm install vs npm ci
sections.content:
npm install reads package.json, installs what's missing, and can update package-lock.json along the way. npm ci is stricter: it deletes node_modules first and installs exactly what the lock file says, failing outright if the lock file and package.json don't agree.

Use npm ci in CI/CD pipelines — it's faster and guarantees every environment installs the exact same dependency tree, rather than potentially drifting minor/patch versions apart over time.

sections.title: Understanding Semantic Versioning
sections.content:
Package versions follow MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: a PATCH bump is a bug fix, MINOR adds a backward-compatible feature, MAJOR means a breaking change. The prefix in front of a version in package.json controls how far npm install is allowed to drift:

"dependencies": {
  "express": "^4.18.0",  // allows any 4.x.x update
  "lodash": "~4.17.21"   // allows only 4.17.x patch updates
}

package-lock.json locks the exact resolved versions of every dependency and sub-dependency — commit it to git so every developer and CI run installs the identical tree, not just something that satisfies the same ranges.

sections.title: Scripts, Workspaces, and peerDependencies
sections.content:
The scripts section of package.json standardizes common commands across a team:

"scripts": {
  "start": "node dist/main.js",
  "dev": "nodemon src/main.ts",
  "test": "jest"
}

Run any of them with npm run <name> (start and test work without the run keyword).

For a repo with several related packages, npm workspaces let you manage them together — install dependencies once at the root, and let packages reference each other locally, instead of maintaining several separate repos.

A library sometimes lists a dependency like react as a peerDependency rather than a regular one. That signals the consuming app must provide its own copy — important so there's exactly one shared instance, not two conflicting ones bundled separately.

sections.title: Managing Secrets and Environment Config
sections.content:
Config that differs between dev, staging, and production — database URLs, API keys — belongs in environment variables, not in code. Locally, dotenv loads a .env file into process.env at startup:

require('dotenv').config();
console.log(process.env.DATABASE_URL);
The real .env file must be in .gitignore — once a secret is committed, it exists in Git history forever, even after you delete it from the latest commit.

To avoid new developers asking "what variables do I even need," commit a .env.example alongside the gitignored real one — same variable names, placeholder values, safe to share.

sections.title: Keeping a Node.js Process Alive in Production
sections.content:
