Hands-on testing every few months tells you more than reading about a new release ever will.

It also helps to pick a small number of sources you trust for AI news and ignore the rest, rather than trying to follow every announcement — the volume is not sustainable and most of it will not matter to your work. Stay skeptical of extreme claims in both directions: neither 'this changes everything overnight' nor 'this is all hype' has held up well as a general rule over the history of this field so far. The specific tools will keep changing; the habit of testing before trusting will not.

sections.title: What Won't Change Even as Models Do
sections.content:
New model families and new agent capabilities will keep appearing, but a few fundamentals are unlikely to change along with them. Confident-sounding output will still not be the same thing as verified output, so checking important facts against a real source will remain necessary no matter how advanced the underlying model becomes.

Accountability will also stay where it already is: with the person or organization using the tool, not with the tool itself, regardless of how autonomously a future system can act. And the underlying shape of what AI is good and bad at — strong at pattern recognition, drafting, and summarizing; weak at nuanced judgment and reliable facts — is likely to shift in degree over time rather than disappear entirely. Learning to evaluate a new AI tool using these same questions will serve you longer than learning the specifics of any one tool available today.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Specific model names, version numbers, and 'who's ahead' rankings change quickly — the underlying categories change much more slowly.
  • Model families are best understood by what they are built to do: general text conversation, image or video generation, code, or multimodal combinations.
  • An 'AI agent' takes a broader goal and carries out multiple steps toward it on its own, rather than producing one response to one prompt.
  • Agents matter because they shift AI from producing suggestions to directly producing outcomes, which raises new questions about permissions and accountability.
  • Stay current by periodically re-testing tools on your own real tasks, not by tracking every headline.
  • Confident output still is not verified output, and accountability still rests with the human or organization using the tool — that will not change as models improve.

sections.title: What Is HTML?
sections.content:
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard language used to describe the structure and content of every web page on the internet. Unlike a programming language such as JavaScript, HTML has no logic, loops, or calculations — it is a markup language, meaning it describes what a piece of content is rather than how to compute something.

When your browser opens an HTML file, it reads the markup and turns it into the visual page you see. A heading tag becomes large bold text, a paragraph tag becomes a readable block of text, and so on. Here is a tiny piece of HTML that describes one paragraph of text:

<p>Welcome to my first web page!</p>

Notice the word 'paragraph' never appears anywhere — the tag itself, p, tells the browser what this content is.

sections.title: HTML's Role in Web Development
sections.content:
Modern websites are built from three cooperating technologies, each with one job. HTML provides the structure and content — the text, images, and organization of a page. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how that structure looks: colors, fonts, spacing, and layout. JavaScript adds behavior — things that happen when you click a button or scroll the page.

A useful analogy is building a house. HTML is the wooden frame and rooms — it decides where the kitchen and bedrooms are. CSS is the paint, furniture, and decor. JavaScript is the electricity and plumbing that make things actually work. You can have a house made only of framing (plain HTML), but it will look plain and do nothing interactive until the other two are added.

This lesson series focuses only on HTML — learning to build a correct, well-structured 'frame' before decorating it.

sections.title: Tags: The Building Blocks
sections.content:
HTML content is written using tags. A tag is a keyword wrapped in angle brackets, such as p or h1. Most tags come in pairs: an opening tag marks where content begins, and a matching closing tag — the same name preceded by a forward slash — marks where it ends. Everything between the two tags, plus the tags themselves, is called an element.

<h1>Getting Started</h1>
<p>This paragraph is one element.</p>

In the example above, the h1 element is a heading and the p element is a paragraph. Tag names are conventionally written in lowercase, and every opening tag should have exactly one matching closing tag. Forgetting a closing tag is one of the most common beginner mistakes and can cause the rest of the page to render incorrectly.

sections.title: Attributes: Adding Detail to Tags
sections.content:
Tags can carry extra information called attributes. An attribute lives inside the opening tag, written as a name followed by an equals sign and a value in quotes: name='value'. Attributes never appear on the closing tag.

<img src='cat.jpg' alt='A sleeping orange cat'>

Here, the img tag has two attributes: src tells the browser which image file to load, and alt provides a text description used by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. Different tags support different attributes — you will meet many more as you learn specific elements like links and images. For now, remember the pattern: attributes sit inside the opening tag and always take the form name='value'.

sections.title: Nesting Elements
sections.content:
Elements can be placed inside other elements — this is called nesting. The element on the outside is the parent, and the element inside is the child. Nesting lets you combine simple elements into richer structures.

<p>Remember to save your work <strong>before</strong> closing the browser.</p>

Here, the strong element is nested inside the p element — the word 'before' is both a piece of emphasized text and part of the surrounding paragraph. A critical rule of nesting is that tags must close in the reverse order they were opened, like nested boxes: whatever opens last must close first. Overlapping tags — opening p, then strong, then closing p before strong — produce invalid, unpredictable HTML.

sections.title: Empty (Void) Elements
sections.content:
Not every tag wraps around content. Some elements are self-contained and never have a closing tag or inner content — these are called void elements (also known as self-closing or empty elements). Common examples include br (a line break), hr (a horizontal divider line), and img (an image), which you saw on the previous slide.

<p>First line of a poem.<br>Second line right below it.</p>
<hr>
<p>A new section starts after the divider above.</p>

Because void elements have nothing to contain, writing a separate closing tag for one is unnecessary and, in most cases, simply invalid. You can recognize a void element because it consists of a single tag with no matching pair.

sections.title: Comments in HTML
sections.content:
Sometimes you want to leave a note inside your HTML file that the browser will completely ignore — for reminders to yourself, explanations for other developers, or temporarily disabling a piece of markup without deleting it. This is done with an HTML comment, which wraps text between an opening marker and a matching closing marker, as shown below.

<!-- This is the site header, added on launch day -->
<p>Welcome to our shop!</p>

<!-- <p>This old greeting is hidden for now.</p> -->

Anything between the comment markers is invisible on the rendered page — only visible to someone reading the raw HTML source. Comments are extremely useful once pages grow larger and are shared between multiple people, but they add no value to the visitor, so use them sparingly and only when they genuinely help.

sections.title: Putting It Together: A First Web Page
sections.content:
Every real HTML file follows a standard skeleton around the elements you have just learned. You will study exactly what each structural line means in the next lesson, but here is a complete, valid web page so you can see how everything fits together:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang='en'>
  <head>
    <title>My First Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello, World!</h1>
    <p>This is my very <em>first</em> web page, and it has an image below.</p>
    <img src='hello.png' alt='A friendly waving hand'>
  </body>
</html>

Notice how the concepts from this lesson appear throughout: tags like h1 and p, the lang and src attributes, nesting (the em element inside the p element), and a void element (img) that needs no closing tag. This is the shape every HTML document shares.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure and content of a web page — it is not a programming language.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript split the work: structure, presentation, and behavior.
  • A tag is a keyword in angle brackets; an element usually pairs an opening and closing tag around content.
  • Attributes add extra information inside an opening tag, written as name='value'.
  • Elements can nest inside each other, and tags must close in reverse order of how they opened.
  • Void elements like br, hr, and img have no closing tag.
  • Comments let you leave notes in the source code that the browser never displays to visitors.

sections.title: Why Every Document Needs a Standard Skeleton
sections.content:
In the previous lesson you saw a complete web page for the first time, built from familiar tags like p and img. But that page was also wrapped in several unfamiliar lines: a doctype declaration, and the html, head, and body elements. These are not content elements — they form the required skeleton that every HTML document is built on.

Browsers expect this skeleton to be present and in a specific order. It tells the browser what kind of document it is looking at, separates information meant for the browser and search engines (the head) from information meant to be seen by visitors (the body), and establishes the single root element that contains everything else. This lesson walks through each part in the order it appears in a real file.

sections.title: The Doctype Declaration
sections.content:
Every HTML file begins with a doctype declaration. It is not a tag in the usual sense and has no closing tag — it is a special instruction to the browser that must be the very first line of the file.

<!DOCTYPE html>

This single line tells the browser: 'render this page using the modern HTML5 standard.' Without it, older browsers may fall back to a legacy rendering mode called 'quirks mode,' where spacing, sizing, and layout rules behave inconsistently and unpredictably. Modern doctype declarations are refreshingly simple — unlike older HTML versions, which required long, hard-to-remember doctype strings, HTML5 only needs this exact seven-word line, written once at the top of every page.

sections.title: The html Element: The Root
sections.content:
Directly after the doctype comes the html tag, which is the single root element of the page — every other element in the document lives inside it, and there is only ever one html element per page.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang='en'>
  ...
</html>

The lang attribute shown above declares the document's primary language using a standard code such as en for English, fr for French, or es for Spanish. This is not just a formality: screen readers use it to choose correct pronunciation rules, browsers use it to offer translation, and search engines use it to serve the page to the right audience. Always include a lang attribute on your html tag.

sections.title: The head Element: Information About the Page
sections.content:
Inside the html element, the first major section is head. Nothing placed in the head is displayed directly on the page — instead, it holds metadata: information about the document itself, used by the browser tab, search engines, and other tools rather than shown to a visitor reading the page.

<head>
  <title>My Bakery - Fresh Bread Daily</title>
</head>

Think of the head as a book's title page and copyright notice — a reader flipping through the story never lands on that page, but it carries essential information about the book as a whole. The next slide covers the specific elements that commonly live inside head.

sections.title: Essential Head Elements: title, charset, viewport
sections.content:
Three elements appear inside head on almost every modern page. title sets the text shown in the browser tab and in search results — every page should have exactly one, written as clear, descriptive text. A meta charset='UTF-8' tag tells the browser which character encoding to use so that letters, accented characters, and symbols from any language display correctly. A meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1' tag tells mobile browsers to size the page to the device's actual screen width instead of shrinking a desktop-sized layout to fit.

<head>
  <meta charset='UTF-8'>
  <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>
  <title>My Bakery - Fresh Bread Daily</title>
</head>

Skipping the viewport meta tag is one of the most common reasons a page looks fine on a computer but broken on a phone.

sections.title: The body Element: The Visible Content
sections.content:
After the head section closes, the body element holds absolutely everything a visitor actually sees and interacts with: headings, paragraphs, images, links, forms, and every other piece of visible content. A page has exactly one body element, and it comes after the head, never inside it.

<body>
  <h1>Welcome to My Bakery</h1>
  <p>We bake fresh sourdough every morning.</p>
</body>

A helpful way to separate the two sections: if a person browsing the live page would never notice it, it belongs in head; if it is something they read, look at, or click, it belongs in body. Nearly all of the tags you will learn in the rest of this course — headings, text formatting, links, lists, images — are written inside the body.

sections.title: Where Stylesheets and Scripts Are Loaded
sections.content:
Two more tags commonly appear in a full document, even though you will not study CSS or JavaScript in depth in this course. A link tag inside head connects an external CSS stylesheet to the page, and a script tag loads or contains JavaScript.

<head>
  <title>My Bakery</title>
  <link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <script src='app.js'></script>
</body>

Stylesheet links almost always go in the head so styling is ready before the page paints. Scripts are often placed near the end of the body so the visible content loads first and appears quickly, before any extra behavior is attached. You do not need to write CSS or JavaScript yet — just recognize these tags and know where they typically live when you encounter them.

sections.title: A Complete, Valid HTML Document
sections.content:
Putting every piece from this lesson together produces a fully valid, real-world HTML document — the same shape used by production websites, just smaller:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang='en'>
  <head>
    <meta charset='UTF-8'>
    <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>
    <title>My Bakery - Fresh Bread Daily</title>
    <link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Welcome to My Bakery</h1>
    <p>We bake fresh sourdough every morning, starting at 6 a.m.</p>
  </body>
</html>

Read it from top to bottom: doctype, then the single root html element, then a head full of metadata nobody sees directly, then a body full of the actual page content. Every HTML page you build from here on will start from this same shape.

sections.title: Common Structure Mistakes to Avoid
sections.content:
A handful of structural mistakes cause a surprising share of beginner bugs. Watch out for these:

  • Forgetting the doctype declaration entirely, which can trigger inconsistent rendering.
  • Placing visible content like a p or h1 element directly inside head, where it will not display correctly.
  • Writing more than one html, head, or body element in a single file.
  • Closing tags in the wrong order, such as closing html before body.
  • Omitting the lang attribute or the viewport meta tag.

Most of these are easy to catch simply by reading your file top to bottom and checking that it follows the same doctype-html-head-body shape shown on the previous slide.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A doctype declaration must be the very first line of every HTML file.
  • html is the single root element and should carry a lang attribute.
  • head holds metadata — title, charset, and viewport — that is never displayed directly on the page.
  • body holds everything a visitor actually sees and interacts with.
  • Stylesheets are usually linked in the head; scripts are often placed near the end of the body.
  • Every document has exactly one html, one head, and one body, always in that order.

sections.title: Headings: Organizing Content with h1 to h6
sections.content:
HTML provides six levels of headings, from h1 (the most important) down to h6 (the least important). Headings are not just for making text big and bold — they create an outline of the page's content, similar to chapter and section titles in a book, which is essential both for readers scanning a page and for screen readers navigating it.

<h1>Baking Sourdough Bread</h1>
<h2>Ingredients</h2>
<h3>For the Starter</h3>
<h2>Method</h2>

Use exactly one h1 per page for its main title, then nest lower levels underneath in order — do not skip from h1 straight to h4 just to make text smaller. If you want smaller text without changing the document's outline, that is a job for CSS, not for choosing the 'wrong' heading level.

sections.title: Paragraphs: p
sections.content:
The p element represents a paragraph of text — the most commonly used element on the web. Browsers automatically add space above and below each paragraph, visually separating one block of text from the next.

<p>Sourdough bread relies on a natural yeast culture called a starter, rather than commercial yeast, for its rise and flavor.</p>
<p>Feeding the starter daily keeps it active and ready to use.</p>

A common beginner mistake is using multiple br line breaks to fake the spacing between paragraphs instead of using separate p elements. This might look similar visually, but it loses the semantic meaning that this is two distinct paragraphs, which matters to screen readers, search engines, and anyone later styling the page with CSS. Always reach for a new p element when you are starting a new paragraph of thought.

sections.title: Strong Importance: strong
sections.content:
The strong element marks text as having strong importance — content the reader should pay special attention to, such as a warning or a key term. Browsers display it in bold by default, but the meaning is more important than the appearance: strong tells assistive technology, like screen readers, that this text truly matters, and some screen readers will change their tone of voice to reflect that.

<p><strong>Warning:</strong> the oven must be preheated to 475 degrees F before baking.</p>

Avoid reaching for strong purely because you want bold-looking text with no real emphasis behind it — that is a styling decision that belongs in CSS. Reserve strong for text that is genuinely more important than its surroundings.

sections.title: Emphasis: em
sections.content:
The em element marks text with stress emphasis — the way you might naturally raise your voice on a word when speaking it aloud. Browsers render it in italics by default, and, like strong, its meaning matters more than its look: screen readers can shift emphasis in speech when they encounter it.

<p>You <em>must</em> let the dough rest for at least an hour.</p>

It is easy to confuse strong and em since both change the visual style of text. A simple way to tell them apart: strong is about importance ('do not skip this'), while em is about emphasis in tone ('this is the word I'm stressing'). Both can be combined on the same piece of text when a phrase is both important and emphatic.

sections.title: Grouping Inline Text: span
sections.content:
Sometimes you need to select a small piece of text inside a sentence for styling or scripting purposes, without that piece having any special meaning like 'important' or 'emphasized.' The span element exists exactly for this — it is a generic inline container that changes nothing on its own.

<p>The price is <span>$12.50</span> per loaf.</p>

On its own, wrapping text in span has zero visible effect — no bold, no italics, nothing changes. Its entire purpose is to give you a 'hook': something CSS can later target to change color or size, or something JavaScript can later select to update. Because it carries no meaning, only use span when no more descriptive element, like strong or em, actually fits.

sections.title: More Inline Formatting: small, mark, sub, sup
sections.content:
A few more inline elements handle specific, common formatting needs. small represents 'fine print' — side comments, disclaimers, or legal text, typically rendered in a smaller font. mark highlights text as if with a highlighter pen, often used to show a search match. sub and sup render subscript and superscript text, positioned slightly below or above the normal line — essential for correct scientific and mathematical notation.

<p><small>Prices do not include delivery.</small></p>
<p>Search results for <mark>sourdough</mark> bread recipes.</p>
<p>Water is H<sub>2</sub>O. The footnote is marked<sup>1</sup>.</p>

Each of these carries real meaning beyond appearance, which is why they exist as dedicated elements rather than being left to CSS alone.

sections.title: Quotations: q and blockquote
sections.content:
HTML has two dedicated elements for quoting someone else's words. q is for a short, inline quotation within a sentence — browsers automatically wrap it in quotation marks, so you should not type quote marks yourself. blockquote is for a longer quotation set apart as its own block, typically indented by the browser.

<p>As the old saying goes, <q>good bread takes time.</q></p>

<blockquote>
  <p>Patience is the single most important ingredient in any sourdough recipe - rushing the rise is the most common cause of dense, flat loaves.</p>
</blockquote>

Both elements can take a cite attribute with a URL pointing to the quotation's source, which is useful for attribution even though it is not displayed visibly by most browsers.

sections.title: Line Breaks and Horizontal Rules: br and hr
sections.content:
Two void elements affect the flow of text without wrapping around any content. br forces a line break inside a block of text — useful for things like addresses or poem lines where the break matters but a whole new paragraph does not belong. hr draws a horizontal rule, a visual divider that represents a thematic break between sections of content.

<p>
  123 Baker Street<br>
  Springfield<br>
  Open daily, 6 a.m. to 2 p.m.
</p>
<hr>
<p>Catering orders are handled separately - see below.</p>

Because both are void elements, neither takes a closing tag. Use them sparingly: reaching for br repeatedly to create paragraph spacing, instead of using separate p elements, is a common misuse worth avoiding.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Headings h1 through h6 build a page's outline; use exactly one h1 and do not skip levels just to shrink text.
  • p defines a paragraph; use separate paragraphs instead of stacking br tags.
  • strong marks strong importance; em marks stressed emphasis — both carry meaning beyond their default bold or italic look.
  • span is a meaningless inline container used purely as a styling or scripting hook.
  • small, mark, sub, and sup handle fine print, highlighting, and scientific notation.
  • q is for short inline quotes; blockquote is for longer, block-level quotations.
  • br and hr are void elements with no closing tag.

sections.title: The Anchor Tag: a and href
sections.content:
Links are what make the web a web — connected pages instead of isolated documents. A link is created with the a element (short for 'anchor'), and its most important attribute is href ('hypertext reference'), which specifies the destination.

<a href='https://www.wikipedia.org'>Visit Wikipedia</a>

Everything between the opening and closing a tags becomes the clickable link text shown on the page — in this example, the words 'Visit Wikipedia'. Without an href attribute, an a tag creates no functional link at all, so always double-check that it is present and points to a real, correctly spelled destination.

sections.title: Absolute vs Relative URLs
sections.content:
The value of href can be written two ways. An absolute URL is the complete address of a page, including the protocol (https://) and domain name — it works from anywhere, including other websites. A relative URL describes a path to another file on the same website, relative to the current page's location, and is shorter and more portable.

<a href='https://www.example.com/about.html'>Absolute link</a>
<a href='about.html'>Relative link</a>

Use absolute URLs when linking to a different website entirely. Use relative URLs when linking between pages of your own site — if you ever move your whole site to a new domain, relative links keep working without any changes, while absolute links to your own pages would all need to be rewritten.

sections.title: Relative Paths in Practice: Folders and ../
sections.content:
Relative paths follow the same folder logic as a computer's file system. A bare filename like about.html looks for that file in the same folder as the current page. A path like products/shoes.html looks inside a subfolder called products. Two dots, ../, mean 'go up one folder,' letting you reach a file outside the current folder.

<a href='contact.html'>Same folder</a>
<a href='blog/latest-post.html'>Into a subfolder</a>
<a href='../index.html'>Up one folder, to the homepage</a>

A path that starts with a single slash, like /index.html, is relative to the site's root rather than the current page — it always points to the same file no matter how deep the current page is nested. Getting these paths wrong is one of the most common causes of broken links.

sections.title: Anchor Links: Jumping Within a Page
sections.content:
Links do not always have to go to a different page — they can also jump to a specific spot on the same page, which is extremely useful for long pages like documentation or a table of contents. This is done in two steps: give the target element an id attribute, then point a link's href at that id with a leading hash symbol.

<a href='#ingredients'>Jump to Ingredients</a>

<h2 id='ingredients'>Ingredients</h2>
<p>Flour, water, salt, and active starter.</p>

Clicking the link above scrolls the browser straight to the element whose id is ingredients, no matter how far down the page it sits. An id value must be unique within the page — never reuse the same id on two different elements.

sections.title: Linking to a Section of Another Page
sections.content:
Anchor links from the previous slide can be combined with a normal page link, letting you jump straight to a section of a different page instead of just the top of it. Simply add the hash and target id after the destination page's path.

<a href='recipe.html#ingredients'>See the ingredient list</a>

When a visitor clicks this link, the browser first loads recipe.html in full, then immediately scrolls down to the element with id='ingredients' on that page. This pattern is common in navigation menus, footers, and 'back to top' style links across multi-page sites, and it only works if the target page actually contains an element with that exact id.

sections.title: Controlling Where a Link Opens: target
sections.content:
By default, clicking a link replaces the current page in the same browser tab. The target attribute changes this behavior — the most common value, target='_blank', opens the link in a new tab or window instead, leaving the original page open.

<a href='https://www.example.com' target='_blank' rel='noopener noreferrer'>Open in a new tab</a>

Whenever you use target='_blank', it is a security and performance best practice to also add rel='noopener noreferrer': without it, the newly opened page can gain limited access to the original page's window, which has been used for phishing-style attacks. Use target='_blank' deliberately and sparingly — forcing every link into a new tab is a frequent source of visitor frustration.

sections.title: Special Link Types: Email and Telephone
sections.content:
The href attribute is not limited to web addresses. Using the mailto: scheme creates a link that opens the visitor's default email application with a new message already addressed; using the tel: scheme creates a link that starts a phone call, most useful on mobile devices.

<a href='mailto:hello@mybakery.com'>Email us</a>
<a href='tel:+15551234567'>Call (555) 123-4567</a>

You can extend a mailto: link with a pre-filled subject line by adding ?subject=Order%20Question after the address, where %20 represents a space. These special schemes are especially valuable on a business's contact page, where a visitor on their phone can tap once to call or email instead of copying an address by hand.

sections.title: Writing Accessible Link Text
sections.content:
The words placed inside an a tag matter for accessibility, not just appearance. Screen reader users often scan a page by jumping from link to link, hearing only the link text in isolation, out of its surrounding sentence. Text like 'click here' or 'read more' gives that listener zero useful information about where the link goes.

<p>Bad: <a href='menu.html'>Click here</a> to see today's menu.</p>
<p>Better: See <a href='menu.html'>today's full menu</a>.</p>

A well-written link describes its destination clearly enough to make sense entirely on its own — 'today's full menu' tells a listener exactly what to expect before they click, while 'click here' tells them nothing. This small habit meaningfully improves a site for visitors using assistive technology.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• The a element creates a link; its href attribute sets the destination, and text between the tags is the clickable label.
  • Absolute URLs include the full domain; relative URLs point to files on the same site and adapt automatically if the site moves.
  • A single slash at the start of a path (like /page.html) is relative to the site's root, not the current page.
  • An anchor link (href='#id') jumps to an element with a matching id, on the same page or by adding it after another page's path.
  • target='_blank' opens a link in a new tab and should be paired with rel='noopener noreferrer'.
  • mailto: and tel: links launch email and phone apps directly.
  • Write descriptive link text — never 'click here' — so it makes sense read on its own.

sections.title: Grouping Items with Unordered Lists
sections.content:
An unordered list groups related items when their order does not matter — a set of features, ingredients, or navigation links. Wrap the whole group in <ul> and put each individual item inside its own <li>. Browsers show a bullet in front of every item by default, but the real value is semantic, not visual: a screen reader announces 'list, 3 items' and lets a user jump between items, which plain paragraphs or line breaks can never do. Always reach for <ul> when you are presenting several related items, even if the list only has two entries.

<ul>
  <li>HTML</li>
  <li>CSS</li>
  <li>JavaScript</li>
</ul>

sections.title: Ordered Lists and Numbering Control
sections.content:
Use <ol> instead of <ul> whenever sequence matters — steps in a recipe, ranked results, or instructions that must be followed in order. Each item is still an <li>, but the browser numbers them automatically. Three attributes let you control that numbering: start sets the first number, reversed counts downward, and type switches the marker style between numbers, letters, or roman numerals (type='A', type='i', and so on). You never manually type the numbers yourself — that breaks the moment an item is added or removed.

<ol start='3' type='A'>
  <li>Preheat the oven</li>
  <li>Mix the batter</li>
  <li>Bake for 20 minutes</li>
</ol>

sections.title: Nesting Lists for Sub-Items
sections.content:
Lists can contain other lists to represent hierarchy, like a table of contents with sub-topics or a multi-level outline. To nest, place a whole new <ul> or <ol> directly inside an <li>, after any text that item already has. Browsers automatically indent nested lists and often switch bullet style at each level so the hierarchy is visually obvious. Keep nesting shallow — two or three levels is usually the limit before a list becomes hard to scan. Each nested list still needs its own <li> wrappers; you cannot put list items directly under another list item without an intermediate <ul>/<ol>.

<ul>
  <li>Frontend
    <ul>
      <li>HTML</li>
      <li>CSS</li>
    </ul>
  </li>
  <li>Backend</li>
</ul>

sections.title: Definition Lists for Term-Description Pairs
sections.content:
A definition list is a different shape entirely: instead of a flat set of items, it pairs a term with its explanation, making it ideal for glossaries, FAQs, or metadata like a key-value spec sheet. The whole group sits inside <dl>. Each term goes in a <dt> (definition term), immediately followed by one or more <dd> (definition description) elements holding the explanation. A single term can have several descriptions in a row, and browsers indent each <dd> under its <dt> by default, visually reinforcing the pairing.

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>The markup language used to structure web pages.</dd>
  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>The language used to style how HTML looks.</dd>
</dl>

sections.title: Starting a Table: Rows and Cells
sections.content:
A table lays data out in a grid of rows and columns — think a price list or a schedule. The outer wrapper is <table>, each horizontal row is a <tr> (table row), and each individual cell of data inside that row is a <td> (table data). Every row should contain the same number of cells so the columns line up correctly down the page. Tables are meant for genuinely tabular data, not for controlling page layout — using a table just to position unrelated content side by side confuses screen readers, which announce table structure aloud.

<table>
  <tr>
    <td>Laptop</td>
    <td>$999</td>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Mouse</td>
    <td>$25</td>
  </tr>
</table>

sections.title: Table Headers with th and scope
sections.content:
Column and row labels should use <th> (table header) instead of <td>. Browsers render <th> content bold and centered by default, but the more important effect is for accessibility: a screen reader can announce the matching header before reading each data cell, so a user hears 'Price: $999' instead of a bare '$999'. Add the scope attribute to make that association explicit — scope='col' for a header that labels a column, scope='row' for one that labels a row. Always use real <th> elements for labels; never fake them with bold <td> text.

<table>
  <tr>
    <th scope='col'>Product</th>
    <th scope='col'>Price</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Laptop</td>
    <td>$999</td>
  </tr>
</table>

sections.title: Organizing Tables with thead, tbody, and tfoot
sections.content:
Larger tables should group their rows into three sections: <thead> for the header row(s), <tbody> for the actual data rows, and an optional <tfoot> for summary rows like totals. This is purely structural — it does not change what a <tr> or <th>/<td> does inside each section — but it makes long tables easier to read in the source, lets browsers repeat the header when a table is printed across pages, and gives you clean CSS hooks to style headers and totals differently. Each of the three sections wraps one or more complete <tr> rows.

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Month</th><th>Sales</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>January</td><td>$4,200</td></tr>
    <tr><td>February</td><td>$3,900</td></tr>
  </tbody>
  <tfoot>
    <tr><td>Total</td><td>$8,100</td></tr>
  </tfoot>
</table>

sections.title: Merging Cells with colspan and rowspan
sections.content:
Sometimes one piece of data logically spans more than one column or row — a summary label that stretches across an entire table, or a value that applies to two rows at once. The colspan attribute on a <td> or <th> makes that cell stretch across the given number of columns; rowspan stretches it down that many rows. When a cell spans extra rows or columns, every other row it overlaps must have fewer cells to compensate, or the grid will misalign. Use spanning sparingly — it is powerful for summary rows and grouped labels, but overusing it makes a table's structure hard to follow.

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Region</th><th>Q1</th><th>Q2</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td rowspan='2'>North</td>
      <td>120</td>
      <td>140</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>130</td>
      <td>150</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td colspan='3'>Figures shown in thousands</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Use <ul> for unordered items and <ol> when the sequence matters; control numbering with start, reversed, and type.
  • Nest a whole new list inside an <li> to represent hierarchy — keep it shallow.
  • Use <dl>/<dt>/<dd> for term-description pairs like glossaries.
  • Build tables from <table>, <tr>, and <td>, keeping every row the same number of cells.
  • Label columns and rows with <th> and the scope attribute so assistive technology can announce them correctly.
  • Group large tables into <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> for readability.
  • Use colspan and rowspan to merge cells, making sure surrounding rows account for the overlap.

title: Images, Audio, and Video in HTML

sections.title: Adding Images with img
sections.content:
<img> is a void element — it has no closing tag and no content between tags, only attributes. Two attributes matter every time you use it: src points to the image file, and alt describes what the image shows. Unlike most elements you have seen so far, forgetting alt is not just sloppy — it is treated as a real accessibility failure by validators and screen readers alike. The browser fetches whatever file src points to and displays it inline as part of the page's content, sized at the image's natural dimensions unless you specify otherwise.

<img src='team-photo.jpg' alt='Five-person design team standing in the office'>

sections.title: Why the alt Attribute Matters
sections.content:
The alt attribute is read aloud by screen readers, displayed if the image fails to load, and used by search engines to understand image content — three jobs, one attribute. Write alt text that describes the image's purpose in context, not just its literal contents; 'chart showing 40% revenue growth' is more useful than 'a chart'. For purely decorative images that add no information — a divider graphic, a background flourish — set alt='' (present but empty) so screen readers skip over it silently. What you should never do is omit the alt attribute entirely; an image with no alt at all is announced as an unlabeled, confusing object.

<img src='quarterly-growth.png' alt='Bar chart showing 40% revenue growth in Q3'>
<img src='divider-swirl.png' alt=''>

sections.title: Controlling Image Dimensions
sections.content:
The width and height attributes tell the browser an image's intended size, in pixels, before the file has even finished downloading. This lets the browser reserve exactly that much space in the layout immediately, so the rest of the page does not visibly jump around as images load in — a jarring problem called layout shift. Set width and height to the image's real aspect ratio; stretching or squashing it with mismatched values distorts the picture. Fine-grained resizing across different screen sizes is better handled with CSS, but these two attributes remain valuable as an early layout hint on every image.

<img src='sales-chart.png' alt='Sales chart for 2024' width='600' height='400'>

sections.title: Embedding Audio with audio
sections.content:
The <audio> element embeds a playable sound file directly in the page — a podcast episode, a sound effect, a voice recording. On its own, <audio src='...'></audio> embeds the file but shows nothing and gives the visitor no way to play it. Add the controls attribute to make the browser draw its built-in play/pause button, seek bar, and volume slider. Without controls, the audio is technically present on the page but completely unusable by a visitor, so treat it as required in practice any time a real person needs to operate the player themselves.

<audio src='podcast-episode.mp3' controls></audio>

sections.title: Audio Attributes: controls, loop, and autoplay
sections.content:
Beyond controls, <audio> supports loop, which restarts the file automatically when it finishes — useful for background ambience — and autoplay, which starts playback the instant the page loads without any click. Most modern browsers block autoplay with sound entirely unless the visitor has already interacted with the site, precisely because unexpected audio is jarring and often mistaken for a bug or an ad. Prefer letting the visitor choose to press play; reserve autoplay for muted background video, never for audio a visitor did not ask to hear.

Avoid autoplay on audio. Even when a browser allows it, visitors experience unsolicited sound as intrusive, and many browsers will silently block it anyway.

<audio src='ambient-loop.mp3' controls loop></audio>

sections.title: Embedding Video with video
sections.content:
<video> works just like <audio> but displays a visual frame as well as playing sound. It needs the same controls attribute to give visitors a play button, seek bar, and volume control — without it, a video sits frozen on its first frame with no way to start it. You can set width and height exactly as you would on an <img>, both to size the player and to reserve layout space before the file loads. A video with no visible controls and no autoplay is effectively invisible content, so always include controls unless you are deliberately building a custom player with JavaScript.

<video src='product-demo.mp4' controls width='640' height='360'></video>

sections.title: Showing a Preview Frame with poster
sections.content:
By default, a video shows its very first frame before playback starts, which is often a blank or unflattering moment. The poster attribute lets you supply a separate image file to display instead, until the visitor presses play — like a thumbnail on a video-sharing site. This gives you full control over the first impression a video makes, independent of what its opening frame happens to look like. poster only affects the paused, pre-play state; once playback starts, the actual video frames take over.

<video src='product-demo.mp4' controls width='640' height='360' poster='demo-thumbnail.jpg'></video>

sections.title: Multiple Formats and Fallback with source
sections.content:
Not every browser supports every video or audio file format. Instead of a single src attribute, you can list several <source> child elements inside <video> or <audio>, each pointing to a different file with its type attribute set to that format's MIME type. The browser tries each <source> in order and plays the first one it can handle. Any plain text placed after the last <source>, inside the same tag, only displays in the rare case that the browser supports neither the element nor any listed source — a safety-net fallback message.

<video controls width='640' height='360'>
  <source src='demo.webm' type='video/webm'>
  <source src='demo.mp4' type='video/mp4'>
  Your browser does not support embedded video.
</video>

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• <img> is a void element that always needs both src and a meaningful alt attribute.
  • Use alt='' for purely decorative images; never omit alt entirely.
  • width and height on <img> reserve layout space and prevent content jumping as images load.
  • <audio> and <video> both need the controls attribute or visitors cannot operate them.
  • Avoid autoplay with sound — most browsers block it, and visitors dislike unsolicited audio.
  • Use poster to set a video's preview frame before playback begins.
  • List multiple <source> elements to offer format fallbacks, ordered by preference.

title: Building Forms with HTML Input Elements

sections.title: The form Element and Its Attributes
sections.content:
Every group of inputs that submits data together belongs inside a <form> element. Two attributes define where and how that submission happens: action is the URL the data is sent to, and method is either get (appends data to the URL, fine for searches) or post (sends data in the request body, required for anything sensitive or that changes data on the server, like a signup). Everything you place inside the <form> — text fields, checkboxes, buttons — is automatically included in that submission; nothing outside the <form> tags is sent.

<form action='/submit-feedback' method='post'>
  <label for='name'>Name</label>
  <input type='text' id='name' name='name'>
  <button type='submit'>Send</button>
</form>

sections.title: Labeling Inputs Correctly
sections.content:
Every input needs a visible, programmatically connected label — never rely on placeholder text or nearby paragraph text alone. The reliable pattern is a <label> whose for attribute matches the input's id. That connection does two things: clicking anywhere on the label text moves focus into the input (helpful for small checkboxes and radio buttons especially), and screen readers announce the label whenever the input receives focus. type='text' is the plain single-line text input — the most basic input type, and the default if type is omitted entirely.

<label for='full-name'>Full name</label>
<input type='text' id='full-name' name='fullName'>

sections.title: Choosing the Right Input Type
sections.content:
The type attribute changes far more than validation — it changes the actual keyboard and controls a device shows. type='email' brings up an @-key keyboard on mobile and flags obviously malformed addresses; type='password' masks characters as dots; type='number' shows numeric steppers and a numeric keypad; type='date' offers a native date picker; type='tel' shows a phone keypad. Choosing the specific type that matches your data is not cosmetic — it meaningfully improves the experience on touch devices and gives you free basic validation with zero JavaScript.

<input type='email' name='email'>
<input type='password' name='password'>
<input type='number' name='age' min='0' max='120'>
<input type='date' name='birthday'>

sections.title: Multi-line Text with textarea
sections.content:
A regular <input type='text'> only ever holds a single line. When a visitor needs to write something longer — a comment, a message, a bio — use <textarea> instead. It is a distinct element, not an input type, and it has its own opening and closing tags with the starting text placed between them rather than in a value attribute. The rows and cols attributes set its visible size in text lines and characters, though CSS is generally a better way to size it in a real page.

<label for='message'>Your message</label>
<textarea id='message' name='message' rows='4' cols='40'>Type here...</textarea>

sections.title: Radio Buttons for a Single Choice
sections.content:
Radio buttons let a visitor pick exactly one option out of a set — a subscription tier, a shipping method. The mechanism that makes them mutually exclusive is a shared name attribute: every <input type='radio'> with the same name belongs to one group, and selecting any one automatically deselects the others in that group. Each radio button still needs its own unique id, paired with its own <label>, and its own value, which is what actually gets submitted for that field.

<input type='radio' id='plan-basic' name='plan' value='basic'>
<label for='plan-basic'>Basic</label>

<input type='radio' id='plan-pro' name='plan' value='pro'>
<label for='plan-pro'>Pro</label>

sections.title: Checkboxes for Multiple Choices
sections.content:
Checkboxes look similar to radio buttons but behave independently of each other — a visitor can check none, one, or all of them, which makes checkboxes right for 'select all that apply' situations like interests or add-ons. Unlike radios, checkboxes sharing the same name do not exclude one another; each one submits its own value only if it is checked. Add the checked attribute directly in the HTML to make a box pre-selected when the page loads, such as a default subscribe-to-updates option.

<input type='checkbox' id='topic-html' name='topics' value='html' checked>
<label for='topic-html'>HTML</label>

<input type='checkbox' id='topic-css' name='topics' value='css'>
<label for='topic-css'>CSS</label>

sections.title: Dropdown Selection with select
sections.content:
When there are many options but only one (or a few) should be picked, a dropdown saves space compared to a wall of radio buttons. Wrap the whole dropdown in <select>, and list each choice as an <option> inside it. The text between the <option> tags is what the visitor sees; the value attribute is what actually gets submitted, and the two can differ. Add selected to one option to make it the default shown when the page loads, and give the <select> itself a matching <label> just like any other input.

<label for='country'>Country</label>
<select id='country' name='country'>
  <option value='us'>United States</option>
  <option value='in' selected>India</option>
  <option value='uk'>United Kingdom</option>
</select>

sections.title: Required Fields and Submitting the Form
sections.content:
Add the required attribute to any input, textarea, or select that must not be left empty. The browser then blocks submission and shows a built-in warning message if that field is empty, with no JavaScript needed at all. To actually submit the form, use <button type='submit'> (or <input type='submit'>) — pressing it triggers the browser to package up every named field's value and send it to the form's action URL using its method. A button with type='button', by contrast, does nothing on its own and is meant for custom JavaScript behavior.

<label for='email-req'>Email</label>
<input type='email' id='email-req' name='email' required>
<button type='submit'>Create account</button>

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Wrap inputs in <form> with action and method to control where and how data is sent.
  • Pair every input with a <label> whose for matches the input's id.
  • Pick a specific type (email, password, number, date, and more) to get the right keyboard and free validation.
  • Use <textarea>, not <input>, for multi-line text.
  • Group radio buttons with a shared name so only one can be selected; checkboxes stay independent.
  • Build dropdowns from <select> and <option>, marking a default with selected.
  • Add required for free browser-side validation, and submit with <button type='submit'>.

sections.title: What Semantic HTML Means
sections.content:
A semantic element names what its content actually is, not just how it should look. <div> and <span> carry no meaning at all — they are blank boxes that only exist to be styled or scripted — while elements like <nav>, <article>, and <footer> announce their role directly in the markup. That distinction sounds academic until you consider who else reads your HTML besides a browser rendering pixels: screen readers, search engine crawlers, browser reader-mode features, and the next developer who opens the file all benefit when structure and meaning line up. Semantic HTML costs nothing extra to write; it simply means picking the element that already matches your intent.

A useful test: if you replaced a semantic element with a generic <div>, would anything meaningful be lost? If yes, you chose the right tag.

sections.title: header and footer: Marking Introductions and Closings
sections.content:
<header> marks the introductory content of whatever it belongs to, and <footer> marks the closing content — but which container depends on where you put it. A <header> as a direct child of <body> is the page's overall banner, typically holding a logo and site title. A <header> nested inside an <article> instead introduces just that one article — its title and byline, for instance — and has nothing to do with the page as a whole. The same page-versus-section duality applies to <footer>.

<header>
  <p><strong>My Travel Blog</strong></p>
</header>

<article>
  <header>
    <p><strong>Hiking the Alps</strong> by Priya, June 2026</p>
  </header>
  <p>The trail began at sunrise...</p>
</article>

sections.title: nav: Marking Primary Navigation
sections.content:
<nav> should wrap a block of links that a visitor genuinely uses to navigate the site or page — a main menu, breadcrumbs, or pagination controls. It creates a navigation landmark that screen reader users can jump straight to, skipping past everything else, so reserve it for real navigation rather than wrapping every group of links you happen to have. A short list of related links buried in a footer or an article's body does not need <nav> — using it everywhere dilutes the landmark and defeats its purpose of highlighting the navigation that matters most.

<nav>
  <ul>
    <li>Home</li>
    <li>Articles</li>
    <li>About</li>
  </ul>
</nav>

sections.title: main: The One Primary Content Landmark
sections.content:
<main> wraps the content that is unique to the current page — the actual article, the actual product page, the actual search results — excluding anything that repeats across every page, like the site header, navigation, or footer. A document should contain exactly one visible <main>. Because of that uniqueness, assistive technology gives users a direct way to jump into <main> and skip straight past repeated boilerplate, which matters enormously to a screen reader user who would otherwise have to listen through the same navigation menu on every single page they visit.

<body>
  <header>Site banner</header>
  <nav>Site navigation</nav>
  <main>
    <p>Today's top story goes here.</p>
  </main>
  <footer>Site footer</footer>
</body>

sections.title: article vs section: Choosing the Right Wrapper
sections.content:
These two are the most commonly confused semantic elements. <article> marks content that is self-contained and would make sense on its own outside the page — a blog post, a news story, a single product card in a listing — the kind of thing that could be pulled into an RSS feed or shared independently and still be understandable. <section> marks a thematic grouping of content within a larger whole — a 'Reviews' chunk of a product page, or a distinct part of a long article — and generally makes sense only in the context of what surrounds it. A practical rule: if you would happily republish just that chunk elsewhere on its own, it is an <article>; if it only makes sense as one part of something bigger, it is a <section>. An <article> can contain several <section> elements.

<article>
  <p><strong>Review: The New Trail Shoes</strong></p>
  <section>
    <p><strong>Comfort</strong></p>
    <p>The cushioning held up well over 20 miles.</p>
  </section>
  <section>
    <p><strong>Durability</strong></p>
    <p>The outsole shows minimal wear after two months.</p>
  </section>
</article>

sections.title: aside: Complementary, Not Core, Content
sections.content:
<aside> marks content that relates to what is nearby but is not essential to understanding it — the main content should stand perfectly well without the aside present at all. Placed inside an <article>, it might be a pull-quote or a brief bio of the author. Placed at the page level, outside any <article>, it typically becomes a sidebar of related links, an advertisement slot, or a you-might-also-like widget. The test is the same either way: remove the <aside>, and the surrounding content should lose nothing essential — only a helpful extra.

<article>
  <p>The trail began at sunrise, climbing steadily for six miles...</p>
  <aside>
    <p><em>Tip: start before 6am to avoid the midday heat.</em></p>
  </aside>
</article>

sections.title: Semantic Structure Powers Accessibility
sections.content:
Every semantic element you have seen in this lesson creates a navigation landmark that assistive technology exposes directly to the user — a screen reader can present a full list of a page's landmarks (banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo) and let the visitor jump straight to any one of them, the same way a sighted visitor's eye jumps straight to the header or the sidebar. A page built entirely from unlabeled <div> elements offers none of that; a screen reader user must listen through the entire page linearly with no shortcuts. This is the single biggest practical payoff of choosing semantic tags over generic ones.

Try navigating any well-built site with a screen reader's landmark list — it is the clearest way to feel the real value of semantic HTML.

sections.title: Semantic Structure Also Helps SEO and Reader Views
sections.content: Search engines parse a page's semantic structure to judge what content actually matters. Text inside <main> and <article> is generally weighted as the substantive content of the page, while text inside <nav>, <header>, and <footer> is recognized as repeated boilerplate and weighted accordingly. Browser reader-mode features work the same way — they extract the <article> content and strip away the navigation and sidebars automatically, but only when the underlying markup actually distinguishes them. A page built purely from generic <div> soup gives neither search engines nor reader-mode features any of that structure to work with.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Choose semantic elements because they carry real meaning for browsers, screen readers, search engines, and other developers — not just for styling hooks.
  • <header> and <footer> can introduce or close either the whole page or just the section they sit inside.
  • Reserve <nav> for genuine navigation blocks, not every group of links.
  • Use exactly one <main> per page for the content unique to that page.
  • Use <article> for self-contained, independently distributable content; use <section> for a themed chunk that only makes sense within a larger whole.
  • <aside> marks helpful but non-essential complementary content.
  • Semantic structure creates accessibility landmarks and powers SEO and reader-mode features automatically.

sections.title: Why Client-Side Validation Matters
sections.content:
You already know how to build form inputs. Now the question is: how do you stop a visitor from submitting a form with a missing email, a two-character password, or a phone number typed as free text? HTML gives you built-in validation attributes that run entirely in the browser, before the form ever reaches a server.

Client-side validation is not a replacement for server-side validation — a user can always disable JavaScript or send a raw HTTP request straight past your form. But it is the fastest possible feedback loop: the browser stops a bad submission instantly and shows a message right next to the field, with zero network round-trip. That makes forms feel responsive and cuts down on wasted server requests for obviously invalid data.

Every validation attribute you will learn in this lesson works the same way: you add it to an <input>, <select>, or <textarea>, and the browser automatically blocks submission and displays a native error bubble if the constraint fails.

sections.title: The required Attribute
sections.content:
The simplest and most common validation attribute is required. Add it to any form control and the browser refuses to submit the form until that field has a value.

<label for='email'>Email address</label>
<input type='email' id='email' name='email' required>

<label for='plan'>Choose a plan</label>
<select id='plan' name='plan' required>
  <option value=''>-- Select --</option>
  <option value='basic'>Basic</option>
  <option value='pro'>Pro</option>
</select>

required is a boolean attribute — its presence alone turns it on, you never write required='true' or required='false'. It works on text inputs, checkboxes (the box must be checked), radio groups (one radio in the group must be selected), select menus, and textareas. For a <select>, pair it with an empty first <option value=''> so there is a genuinely 'unset' state for required to catch.

sections.title: Constraining Length: minlength and maxlength
sections.content:
Text-based inputs and textareas accept minlength and maxlength, which count characters typed into the field. maxlength is enforced live — the browser simply will not let the user type past the limit. minlength is checked at submission time, since a field can be too short at any point while the user is still typing.

<label for='username'>Username</label>
<input type='text' id='username' name='username'
       minlength='3' maxlength='20' required>

<label for='bio'>Short bio</label>
<textarea id='bio' name='bio' maxlength='280'></textarea>

A common mistake is assuming minlength blocks typing the way maxlength does — it does not. A user can type one character, pause, and the field simply will not be marked valid until they reach the minimum and try to submit. Both attributes only apply to inputs of type text, search, url, tel, email, and password, plus <textarea> — they have no effect on number inputs, which use a different pair of attributes covered next.

sections.title: Constraining Numbers: min, max, and step
sections.content:
For <input type='number'> and <input type='range'>, length limits do not make sense — instead you constrain the numeric value itself with min, max, and step.

<label for='qty'>Quantity (1-10)</label>
<input type='number' id='qty' name='qty'
       min='1' max='10' step='1' value='1' required>

<label for='rating'>Rating</label>
<input type='range' id='rating' name='rating'
       min='0' max='5' step='0.5'>

step defines the increment the value must land on relative to min. With min='1' and step='1', only whole numbers are valid; with step='0.5', half-steps like 2.5 are also accepted. If a typed number falls outside min/max or off the step grid, the field fails validation on submit. These same attributes also work on date, month, and time inputs, where min and max take date/time values instead of plain numbers.

sections.title: Pattern Matching with the pattern Attribute
sections.content:
When a field needs a specific shape that built-in input types cannot express — a product code, a postal code format, a username without spaces — use the pattern attribute with a regular expression. The browser wraps your pattern in an implicit ^(?:...)$, so it must match the entire value, not just part of it.

<label for='sku'>Product SKU (e.g. AB-1234)</label>
<input type='text' id='sku' name='sku'
       pattern='[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}'
       title='Two uppercase letters, a hyphen, then four digits'
       required>

<label for='zip'>US ZIP code</label>
<input type='text' id='zip' name='zip'
       pattern='[0-9]{5}(-[0-9]{4})?'>

pattern only applies to text-like inputs (text, search, url, tel, email, password) — not to number. Always pair it with a title attribute; many browsers display the title text inside the validation error bubble when the pattern fails, which turns a cryptic regex mismatch into a message the user can actually act on.

sections.title: Built-in Type Validation: email, url, tel
sections.content:
Before reaching for pattern, check whether an input type already does the validation for you. type='email' requires a syntactically valid email shape (something@something.something); type='url' requires a full URL with a scheme like https://; type='tel' accepts phone numbers but deliberately applies no format validation on its own, since phone formats vary wildly across countries.

<label for='site'>Website</label>
<input type='url' id='site' name='site'
       placeholder='https://example.com'>

<label for='phone'>Phone</label>
<input type='tel' id='phone' name='phone'
       pattern='[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}'
       placeholder='555-123-4567'>

Notice the tel example still adds pattern — that is the correct way to validate phone format, since type='tel' alone will not do it. For email and url, letting the built-in type validation handle the basic shape is simpler and less error-prone than writing your own regex, and you can still layer maxlength or required on top.

sections.title: Custom Error Messages with the title Attribute
sections.content:
By default, when a pattern or type constraint fails, browsers show a generic message like 'Please match the requested format.' That tells a user almost nothing about what the format actually is. The title attribute lets you supply a human-readable explanation that many browsers insert directly into that error bubble.

<label for='coupon'>Coupon code</label>
<input type='text' id='coupon' name='coupon'
       pattern='[A-Z0-9]{6,10}'
       title='6 to 10 characters, uppercase letters and numbers only'>

title is not exclusive to pattern — it is a general-purpose HTML attribute that also shows a plain tooltip on hover for any element. But paired with pattern specifically, it becomes your main tool for writing validation messages without touching JavaScript. Keep the wording short and concrete: describe the accepted format, not the rule you are enforcing internally, since the user only cares what they need to type differently.

sections.title: Turning Off Validation: novalidate and formnovalidate
sections.content:
Sometimes you want a form action to skip validation entirely — a 'Save as draft' button, for example, should let a user save incomplete work without being blocked by required fields. HTML gives you two escape hatches.

<form action='/submit' method='post'>
  <label for='title'>Title</label>
  <input type='text' id='title' name='title' required>

  <button type='submit'>Publish</button>
  <button type='submit' formnovalidate>Save as Draft</button>
</form>

Adding novalidate to the <form> tag itself disables validation for every submission of that form, no matter which button is pressed. Adding formnovalidate to a specific <button type='submit'> disables validation only when that particular button triggers the submit — other buttons in the same form still enforce validation normally. This is the cleanest way to support multiple submission behaviors from one form without writing any script.

sections.title: Styling Valid and Invalid Fields with CSS
sections.content:
HTML validation attributes automatically flip two CSS pseudo-classes on each field: :valid when the current value satisfies every constraint, and :invalid when it does not. You can use these to give visual feedback — a green or red border, for instance — without any JavaScript at all.

input:invalid {
  border: 2px solid #dc2626;
}

input:valid {
  border: 2px solid #16a34a;
}

/* avoid showing red before the user has interacted */
input:invalid:not(:focus):not(:placeholder-shown) {
  border-color: #dc2626;
}

A common usability problem is that an empty required field is :invalid from the moment the page loads, which paints every required field red before the user has even started. The :not(:placeholder-shown) trick above (combined with a real placeholder attribute on the input) is a pure-CSS way to only show the invalid style once a field has content and then loses focus, rather than on first paint.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• required is a boolean attribute that blocks submission until the field has a value.
  • minlength/maxlength constrain character count on text-like inputs and textareas; maxlength blocks typing live, minlength is checked on submit.
  • min, max, and step constrain numeric, range, and date/time inputs — not text length.
  • pattern applies a regular expression to text-like inputs and must match the entire value.
  • Prefer built-in types (email, url) over a custom pattern when one already exists.
  • Pair pattern with title so the browser's error bubble explains the expected format.
  • novalidate on a form (or formnovalidate on a button) skips validation for that submission.
  • The :valid and :invalid CSS pseudo-classes let you style fields based on validation state with no JavaScript.
  • Client-side validation improves user experience but never replaces server-side validation.

sections.title: Why Embed External Content
sections.content:
Not every piece of content on a page needs to be built from scratch. A huge amount of the web works by embedding content that lives on someone else's server: a YouTube video, a Google Map, a payment widget, a tweet, an ad. HTML supports this through the iframe element (short for 'inline frame'), which loads an entire separate HTML document inside a rectangular region of your page.

Whatever loads inside an <iframe> is its own independent browsing context — it has its own DOM, its own scripts, and its own security boundary, completely separate from the page that contains it. That isolation is exactly why embedding is safe by default: a map widget from a third party cannot casually reach into your page's data, and your page cannot casually reach into the map's internals either.

This lesson covers the practical side: how to size an iframe correctly, embed common services like YouTube and Google Maps, and keep embedded content secure and accessible.

sections.title: The iframe Element Basics
sections.content:
At minimum, an <iframe> needs a src attribute pointing at the page to load, plus explicit width and height attributes. Unlike an image, an iframe has no natural size of its own — without dimensions it collapses to a small default box.

<iframe
  src='https://example.com/widget'
  width='600'
  height='400'
  title='Example widget'>
</iframe>

The title attribute is not optional in practice, even though the browser will not stop you from omitting it — it is the only text a screen reader has to describe what the iframe contains, since the reader cannot see the visual content inside. Always write a specific title such as 'Store location map' rather than a generic one like 'embedded content'. Every iframe you embed from this point forward should include one.

sections.title: Embedding a YouTube Video
sections.content:
Video platforms like YouTube generate a ready-made iframe snippet for you (via their 'Share > Embed' option), but it helps to understand what that snippet is actually doing. YouTube's embed URLs follow the pattern https://www.youtube.com/embed/VIDEO_ID — not the normal watch URL.

<iframe
  width='560'
  height='315'
  src='https://www.youtube.com/embed/dQw4w9WgXcQ'
  title='YouTube video player'
  allow='accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture'
  allowfullscreen>
</iframe>

The allow attribute is a permissions policy specific to iframes — it grants the embedded page access to browser features it would otherwise be denied, such as autoplay or fullscreen. The allowfullscreen boolean attribute is what lets the video's own fullscreen button actually work; without it, clicking fullscreen inside the embed silently does nothing.

sections.title: Embedding a Google Map
sections.content:
Google Maps offers the same embed pattern: generate an embed URL from Maps' own 'Share > Embed a map' feature, then drop it into an <iframe>. The key difference from a video embed is that maps are typically wider and shorter, and rarely need allowfullscreen.

<iframe
  src='https://www.google.com/maps/embed?pb=!1m18!1m12...'
  width='600'
  height='450'
  style='border:0;'
  loading='lazy'
  title='Map showing our office location'>
</iframe>

Notice this example uses an inline style attribute inside the raw embed HTML — that is exactly how third-party services generate their snippets, and it is perfectly valid HTML on a real page. (Note that when authoring lesson content on this platform specifically, inline style attributes get stripped by the content sanitizer, so treat this as what you would paste into your actual project file, not into a lesson body.) The next slide covers the loading attribute shown here in more depth.

sections.title: Lazy Loading Embedded Content
sections.content:
An iframe loading a map, a video, or a heavy third-party widget can be one of the slowest parts of a page to load, because the browser has to fetch and render an entirely separate document. The loading attribute lets you defer that cost until it is actually needed.

<iframe
  src='https://example.com/heavy-widget'
  width='400'
  height='300'
  loading='lazy'
  title='Customer chat widget'>
</iframe>

With loading='lazy', the browser postpones fetching the iframe's content until the iframe scrolls near the visible viewport, similar to how lazy-loaded images work. This is especially valuable for embeds placed far down a long page — a map in the footer, for example — since visitors who never scroll that far never pay the loading cost at all. The default value, if you omit the attribute, is eager, meaning the browser loads it immediately along with the rest of the page.

sections.title: The sandbox Attribute for Security
sections.content:
Because an iframe can load a full, independent web page, embedding untrusted or third-party content carries risk — that page could run scripts, open popups, or submit forms. The sandbox attribute lets you lock down exactly what an embedded page is allowed to do, on top of the isolation an iframe already has by default.

<!-- No sandbox attribute at all = no restrictions beyond the default browsing-context isolation -->

<!-- sandbox with no value = maximum restriction: scripts, forms,
     popups, and same-origin access are ALL disabled -->
<iframe src='https://untrusted-widget.example.com' sandbox
        width='400' height='300' title='Untrusted widget'></iframe>

<!-- sandbox with specific tokens = allow only what you list -->
<iframe src='https://trusted-widget.example.com'
        sandbox='allow-scripts allow-popups'
        width='400' height='300' title='Trusted widget'></iframe>

An empty sandbox attribute is the strictest setting available. Adding specific tokens like allow-scripts or allow-forms re-enables just those individual capabilities. As a rule, only relax sandbox restrictions for embeds you actually trust, and grant the smallest set of tokens that makes the embed function correctly.

sections.title: Responsive Iframes
sections.content:
The width and height attributes on an iframe are fixed pixel values, which is a problem on a responsive page: a 560px-wide video embed will overflow a narrow mobile screen. The modern fix is CSS's aspect-ratio property combined with a fluid width.

.video-embed {
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  border: none;
}
<iframe
  class='video-embed'
  src='https://www.youtube.com/embed/dQw4w9WgXcQ'
  title='Product demo video'
  allowfullscreen>
</iframe>

Here the iframe still declares no fixed width/height HTML attributes; instead CSS stretches it to 100% of its container's width and uses aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 to derive a proportional height automatically, so the box keeps the video's correct shape at any screen size. This 16:9 ratio matches standard widescreen video; adjust it to match whatever content you are embedding.

sections.title: Other Ways to Embed Media
sections.content:
iframe is the general-purpose tool for embedding another web page, but HTML has a couple of narrower elements for embedding specific media types directly, without pulling in a whole separate document.

<!-- embed: a plug-in-rendered resource, e.g. a PDF viewer -->
<embed src='report.pdf' type='application/pdf' width='600' height='500'>

<!-- object: similar purpose, with fallback content support -->
<object data='report.pdf' type='application/pdf' width='600' height='500'>
  <p>Unable to display PDF. <a href='report.pdf'>Download it instead</a>.</p>
</object>

In modern practice, iframe has become the dominant choice for most embedding needs because browser support for it is universal and predictable, while embed and object depend more on what plugins or native viewers the browser has available. You will still encounter object used for PDF embedding with a graceful fallback, as shown above, since it is one of the few elements that lets you specify replacement content if the resource cannot be displayed.

sections.title: Accessibility for Embedded Content
sections.content:
Embedded content is easy to make inaccessible by accident, because it is content you did not author and often cannot modify. Two practices make a real difference: a meaningful title attribute on every iframe, and never relying on an embed as the only way to reach essential information.

<h2>Visit Our Store</h2>
<iframe
  src='https://www.google.com/maps/embed?pb=...'
  width='600' height='400' loading='lazy'
  title='Map showing our store at 123 Main Street'>
</iframe>
<p>123 Main Street, Springfield. Open 9am-6pm, Monday to Saturday.</p>

Notice the address and hours are repeated as plain text underneath the map, not left solely inside the embed. A screen reader user, or anyone whose network blocks the map's third-party domain, still gets the essential information. Treat every iframe as an enhancement layered on top of accessible page content, never as the sole carrier of information a visitor needs.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• An <iframe> loads an entire independent document inside your page and needs explicit dimensions since it has no natural size.
  • Always give an iframe a specific, descriptive title attribute — it is a screen reader's only description of the embed's content.
  • Use each service's own generated embed URL (e.g. YouTube's /embed/ path) rather than a normal page URL.
  • The allow and allowfullscreen attributes grant an embedded video specific browser permissions it needs to function.
  • Use loading='lazy' to defer fetching embeds that sit below the initial viewport.
  • The sandbox attribute restricts what an embedded page can do; start from the strictest setting and add only the tokens you need.
  • Make embeds responsive with CSS aspect-ratio and a fluid width, rather than fixed pixel dimensions.
  • embed and object exist for specific media/plugin resources; object uniquely supports fallback content.
  • Never make an embed the only source of essential information — repeat critical details as real page text.

sections.title: What Metadata Is and Where It Lives
sections.content:
Metadata is information about your page that is not part of the visible content itself — it describes the page rather than displaying inside it. Almost all of it lives inside the <head> element, using the <title> and <meta> tags.

<head>
  <meta charset='UTF-8'>
  <title>Best Hiking Trails in Colorado | TrailGuide</title>
  <meta name='description' content='Discover the top 20 hiking trails in Colorado, with difficulty ratings, maps, and trailhead directions.'>
</head>
