Search engines like Google read this metadata to decide how to summarize your page in search results, and social platforms like Facebook or LinkedIn read a related set of tags to build the preview card shown when someone shares your link. None of this metadata is rendered inside the page's visible body — it is read by machines (crawlers, browsers, sharing tools), not by a visitor scrolling the page.

sections.title: The title Tag: Your Most Important Signal
sections.content:
The <title> element is the single most important piece of SEO metadata on a page. It appears as the clickable blue link text in search results, as the browser tab label, and as the default text when someone bookmarks the page.

<title>Wireless Noise-Cancelling Headphones - AudioPro</title>

A good title is specific, under roughly 60 characters (longer titles get truncated with '...' in search results), and puts the most important, distinguishing words first — since users scanning results read left to right. Every page on your site should have a unique title; using the same generic title like 'Home' across every page gives search engines nothing to distinguish one page from another, which actively hurts how your pages rank against each other.

sections.title: The Meta Description
sections.content:
The description meta tag supplies the short paragraph of summary text that search engines often (though not always) display underneath your title in search results. It does not directly affect ranking, but a compelling description meaningfully affects whether someone actually clicks your result over a competitor's.

<meta name='description' content='Learn HTML from scratch with hands-on lessons covering tags, forms, accessibility, and SEO -- no prior experience required.'>

Keep descriptions around 150-160 characters; longer text gets cut off with an ellipsis in search results. Write it like ad copy: describe what the visitor gets and why it is worth clicking, using natural sentences rather than a stuffed list of keywords — search engines are good at detecting and penalizing keyword-stuffed descriptions, and human searchers ignore them anyway.

sections.title: Viewport and Charset Meta Tags
sections.content:
Two <meta> tags are not about SEO directly, but they are foundational enough that nearly every real page includes them, and their absence can silently break both rendering and search indexing.

<meta charset='UTF-8'>
<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>

charset='UTF-8' tells the browser (and search crawlers) which character encoding the page's text uses, so accented letters, currency symbols, and emoji render correctly instead of showing as garbled characters. The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers to render the page at the device's actual width rather than a shrunk-down desktop layout — Google explicitly uses mobile-friendliness, which depends on this tag, as a ranking factor, so omitting it has a real SEO cost, not just a visual one.

sections.title: Controlling Search Engines with the robots Meta Tag
sections.content:
Sometimes you want a page to exist on your site but not appear in search results — a thank-you page after checkout, an internal staging page, or duplicate content. The robots meta tag gives crawlers explicit instructions.

<!-- Do not index this page, but do follow links found on it -->
<meta name='robots' content='noindex, follow'>

<!-- Do not index, and do not follow any links on this page -->
<meta name='robots' content='noindex, nofollow'>

The two most common values are index/noindex (whether the page itself should appear in search results) and follow/nofollow (whether the crawler should treat links on this page as endorsements worth following to discover other pages). If you omit the tag entirely, the default behavior is index, follow — crawlers assume you want the page indexed unless you say otherwise.

sections.title: Canonical URLs
sections.content:
The same content is often reachable at more than one URL — with and without a trailing slash, with tracking parameters, or duplicated across http:// and https://. Search engines see each distinct URL as a separate page, which can split your ranking signal across duplicates. The canonical link tells search engines which URL is the 'real' one to credit.

<link rel='canonical' href='https://example.com/products/wireless-headphones'>

Place this tag in the <head> of every version of a page, including the canonical version itself, all pointing to the same single URL. This is especially important for e-commerce pages reachable through multiple category paths, or blog posts syndicated with tracking query parameters like ?utm_source=newsletter — without a canonical tag, search engines may treat the tracked and untracked URLs as competing duplicate pages.

sections.title: Open Graph Basics for Social Sharing
sections.content:
When someone pastes your page's link into Facebook, LinkedIn, or Slack, the resulting preview card — with an image, title, and description — is built from Open Graph tags, a metadata standard separate from (though similar to) plain SEO tags.

<meta property='og:title' content='Best Hiking Trails in Colorado'>
<meta property='og:description' content='20 hand-picked trails with maps, difficulty ratings, and directions.'>
<meta property='og:type' content='website'>
<meta property='og:url' content='https://example.com/colorado-trails'>

Notice these use property instead of name as the attribute — this is a real, intentional difference from standard meta tags, inherited from Open Graph's own specification. Without these tags, sharing platforms fall back to guessing from your <title> and <meta name='description'>, which often produces a worse or blank-looking preview card than an explicit Open Graph tag would.

sections.title: Open Graph Images and Article Types
sections.content:
The single Open Graph tag with the biggest visual impact is og:image — without it, most platforms show a plain text-only card with no thumbnail at all, which gets far less engagement than a card with an image.

<meta property='og:image' content='https://example.com/images/colorado-trails-hero.jpg'>
<meta property='og:image:width' content='1200'>
<meta property='og:image:height' content='630'>

1200×630 pixels is the widely recommended image size — large enough to look sharp on high-resolution displays, and at the aspect ratio most platforms crop preview images to. The og:image:width and og:image:height tags are optional but let the sharing platform render the correct-shaped placeholder immediately, before the image itself has finished downloading. For blog posts specifically, set og:type to article instead of website to unlock article-specific Open Graph fields like article:published_time.

sections.title: Twitter Card Tags
sections.content:
X (formerly Twitter) mostly respects Open Graph tags, but also supports its own Twitter Card tags, which give you finer control over how a link appears specifically on that platform.

<meta name='twitter:card' content='summary_large_image'>
<meta name='twitter:title' content='Best Hiking Trails in Colorado'>
<meta name='twitter:description' content='20 hand-picked trails with maps and directions.'>
<meta name='twitter:image' content='https://example.com/images/colorado-trails-hero.jpg'>

Unlike Open Graph, these use the ordinary name attribute rather than property. The twitter:card value summary_large_image is the most commonly used setting — it produces a card with a large, prominent image, versus the smaller thumbnail used by the plain summary value. If you already have complete Open Graph tags and no Twitter-specific tags, X will fall back to the Open Graph values, so adding Twitter Card tags is a refinement, not a requirement, once your Open Graph tags are in place.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Metadata lives in <head> and is read by machines — crawlers, browsers, sharing tools — not rendered as visible page content.
  • The <title> tag is the most important SEO signal; keep it unique per page and under roughly 60 characters.
  • The meta description drives click-through from search results but does not directly affect ranking; keep it around 150-160 characters.
  • charset and viewport meta tags affect rendering and mobile-friendliness, which is itself a ranking factor.
  • The robots meta tag controls indexing (index/noindex) and link-following (follow/nofollow) per page.
  • A canonical link tag prevents duplicate-URL versions of the same content from splitting your search ranking.
  • Open Graph tags (og:title, og:description, og:image) control how links look when shared on Facebook, LinkedIn, and Slack, and use property, not name.
  • An og:image around 1200×630px meaningfully increases engagement versus a text-only share card.
  • Twitter Card tags refine sharing on X specifically, and fall back to Open Graph values when absent.

sections.title: Why Accessibility Mechanics Matter
sections.content:
You have already learned why semantic tags matter as a general practice. This lesson goes one level deeper: the specific mechanical techniques that make a page actually usable for people relying on a screen reader, a keyboard instead of a mouse, or other assistive technology.

Screen readers do not see your page visually — they read through the DOM and announce elements, roles, and text to the user, often letting the user jump between headings, links, or form fields rather than reading top to bottom. A sighted mouse user can visually spot that a red border means an invalid field, or that an icon-only button means 'delete'; a screen reader user gets none of that unless the underlying HTML explicitly communicates it.

The techniques in this lesson — alt text, label association, ARIA roles and properties, keyboard focus — are the concrete tools that close that gap. None of them require JavaScript; they are attributes and patterns you apply directly to your markup.

sections.title: Writing Meaningful alt Text
sections.content:
The alt attribute on <img> is announced by screen readers in place of the image, and displayed as fallback text if the image fails to load. Good alt text describes the purpose of the image in context, not just what it visually contains.

<!-- Weak: describes pixels, not purpose -->
<img src='chart.png' alt='a bar chart'>

<!-- Strong: conveys the information the chart carries -->
<img src='chart.png' alt='Bar chart showing sales grew 40% from Q1 to Q4 2025'>

<!-- A logo used as a link home -->
<a href='/'><img src='logo.png' alt='Acme Corp home page'></a>

Notice the logo example: the alt text describes what happens when you click it ('home page'), not the visual appearance of the logo. As a rule, ask 'what does a sighted user learn from this image that a blind user would otherwise miss?' and write exactly that. Avoid redundant phrases like 'image of' or 'picture of' — screen readers already announce that it is an image before reading the alt text.

sections.title: Decorative Images and Empty alt
sections.content:
Not every image carries meaning. A purely decorative flourish, a spacer graphic, or a background pattern adds nothing for a screen reader user to know about — and forcing them to sit through a description of it is worse than saying nothing. HTML has an explicit mechanism for this: an empty alt attribute.

<img src='decorative-swirl.png' alt=''>

alt='' tells screen readers to skip the image entirely and announce nothing, which is exactly correct for decoration. This is different from omitting the alt attribute altogether — a missing alt attribute is a genuine authoring error, and screen readers commonly fall back to announcing the image's filename instead, which is a poor experience ('image, decorative dash swirl dot png'). Always include alt on every <img>; the only decision is whether it holds real descriptive text or is deliberately left empty.

sections.title: Associating Labels with Form Controls
sections.content:
A form field with no programmatically associated label is effectively unlabeled to a screen reader, even if there is text sitting visually right next to it — visual proximity alone does not create a relationship in the DOM. The fix is the for/id pairing you may already use, but it is worth understanding why it matters for accessibility specifically.

<!-- Broken: text and input are visually adjacent but not linked -->
<span>Email</span>
<input type='email' name='email'>

<!-- Correct: explicit for/id association -->
<label for='email-input'>Email</label>
<input type='email' id='email-input' name='email'>

When a <label>'s for attribute matches an input's id, a screen reader announces that label text every time the field receives focus, and clicking anywhere on the label text also focuses or activates the field — a real usability win for anyone with limited motor precision, not only screen reader users. Wrapping the input inside the label element (with no for/id needed) achieves the same association and is a valid alternative.

sections.title: ARIA Roles: Use Native HTML First
sections.content:
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes that describe roles, states, and properties to assistive technology, for cases where plain HTML cannot express what an element is doing. But there is a well-known guiding rule: if a native HTML element already provides the behavior and semantics you need, use it instead of recreating that behavior with ARIA. No ARIA is better than bad ARIA.

<!-- Avoid: reinventing a button with a div and ARIA -->
<div role='button' tabindex='0' onclick='submit()'>Submit</div>

<!-- Prefer: the native element already has this role, keyboard
     support, and focus behavior built in for free -->
<button type='submit'>Submit</button>

The <div role='button'> version requires you to manually wire up keyboard activation (Enter and Space), focus styling, and the correct announced role — and it is very easy to get one of those details wrong. The native <button> gets all of it correct automatically, with zero extra attributes. Reach for ARIA roles only when there is genuinely no native element that fits — a tab panel, a custom slider, a live chat notification — not as a substitute for elements HTML already gives you.

sections.title: Naming Elements with aria-label and aria-labelledby
sections.content:
Some elements have no visible text of their own but still need an accessible name — an icon-only button, for instance. aria-label supplies that name directly as a string. aria-labelledby instead points to the id of some other element on the page whose text should serve as the name.

<!-- aria-label: name supplied inline -->
<button aria-label='Close dialog'>×</button>

<!-- aria-labelledby: name borrowed from existing visible text -->
<h2 id='billing-heading'>Billing Address</h2>
<section aria-labelledby='billing-heading'>
  <!-- form fields here -->
</section>

Use aria-label when no suitable visible text exists anywhere on the page to reuse (like the icon-only close button, whose × symbol is not meaningful text). Use aria-labelledby when a heading or other text already visually serves as the label, so you are not duplicating the same words in two places. Both attributes override any visible text the element does have, so never add either one redundantly to an element like <button>Submit</button> that already has a perfectly clear accessible name from its own text content.

sections.title: Describing Errors with aria-describedby
sections.content:
A validation error message displayed near a field is only connected to that field visually, not programmatically, unless you link them. aria-describedby points to the id of supplementary descriptive text — a hint, a character counter, or a validation error — and screen readers announce that text right after the field's label when the field receives focus.

<label for='pwd'>Password</label>
<input type='password' id='pwd' name='pwd'
       aria-describedby='pwd-hint' minlength='8' required>
<p id='pwd-hint'>Must be at least 8 characters, including one number.</p>

Unlike aria-labelledby, which replaces an element's name, aria-describedby supplements it — the screen reader announces both the label and the described text, in that order. This is the single most effective way to make inline form hints and error messages accessible: without it, a screen reader user hears only 'Password, edit text' and has no idea the hint text even exists on the page.

sections.title: Keyboard Focus and tabindex
sections.content:
Many users navigate exclusively by keyboard — pressing Tab to move forward through focusable elements, Shift+Tab to move backward, and Enter or Space to activate them. This includes screen reader users, switch-device users, and anyone unable to use a precise pointing device. Every interactive element must be reachable and operable this way.

<!-- Natively focusable, no extra work needed -->
<a href='/pricing'>Pricing</a>
<button>Add to cart</button>

<!-- tabindex='0' inserts a non-interactive element into
     the natural tab order, at its normal DOM position -->
<div role='button' tabindex='0'>Custom control</div>

<!-- tabindex='-1' removes an element from tab order but still
     allows it to be focused programmatically (e.g. after opening a dialog) -->
<div tabindex='-1' id='dialog-heading'>Confirm Deletion</div>

Links, buttons, and form fields are focusable automatically — you never need tabindex on them. Avoid tabindex values greater than 0; they force an element earlier in the tab order than the page's natural DOM sequence, which creates a confusing, unpredictable navigation path that no longer matches the visual reading order.

sections.title: Announcing Dynamic Updates with aria-live
sections.content:
Content that changes after the page has already loaded — a 'saved successfully' toast, a live search result count, a shopping cart total — is invisible to a screen reader unless something actively tells it to announce the change. aria-live marks a region of the page as one to watch and announce automatically whenever its content updates.

<div aria-live='polite'>
  <!-- this text gets announced automatically whenever it changes,
       e.g. after an item is added via a script -->
  Cart: 3 items
</div>

<div aria-live='assertive' role='alert'>
  <!-- reserved for urgent, time-sensitive messages -->
</div>

aria-live='polite' is the right default for most status updates: the screen reader finishes whatever it is currently announcing before reading the change, so it never interrupts the user mid-sentence. aria-live='assertive' interrupts immediately and should be reserved for genuinely urgent messages, such as a session timeout warning, since overusing it is disorienting. Note that populating this content still requires a script; the HTML attribute only sets up which region gets watched and announced.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Write alt text that describes an image's purpose in context, not just its visual contents; avoid phrases like 'image of'.
  • Use alt='' for purely decorative images so screen readers skip them — never omit the alt attribute entirely.
  • Associate every form field with a <label> via matching for/id (or by wrapping); visual proximity alone is not a real association.
  • Prefer native HTML elements over ARIA-patched divs whenever a native element already provides the needed behavior — no ARIA is better than bad ARIA.
  • Use aria-label to name an element with no reusable visible text; use aria-labelledby to reuse text that is already visible.
  • Use aria-describedby to link hints and error messages to the field they describe, without replacing its name.
  • Every interactive element must be keyboard-reachable and operable; avoid positive tabindex values, which scramble the natural tab order.
  • Use aria-live='polite' to announce dynamic content changes without interrupting the user; reserve assertive for urgent messages.

sections.title: The "final_v2_ACTUALLY_final.docx" Problem
sections.content:
Every developer has lived through some version of the same folder: report.docx, report_final.docx, report_final_v2.docx, report_final_v2_ACTUALLY_final.docx. Each file is a guess at what changed and when, with no reliable way to see exactly what was different between two of them, who made a given change, or how to get back to a version from three days ago without digging through email attachments.

Source code has the same problem, except worse. A codebase is thousands of files edited by multiple people at once, and a single typo introduced last Tuesday can silently break something that is only noticed next month. Copying folders named project_backup and project_backup2 does not scale, and it tells you nothing about why something changed.

Version control systems exist to solve exactly this problem. A version control system (VCS) keeps a complete, searchable history of every change made to a set of files, tied to who made it, when, and ideally why. Git is the version control system used by the vast majority of professional software teams, and understanding the problem it solves makes every command that follows feel obvious rather than arbitrary.

Check whether Git is already available before going further:

git --version
# git version 2.43.0

sections.title: What a Version Control System Actually Tracks
sections.content:
A version control system does not just store files — it stores the history of changes to those files as a sequence of recorded states. Each recorded state is typically called a commit (or a "revision" in older systems). A commit captures the exact contents of the tracked files at one point in time, along with metadata: who made the change, when, and a message describing why.

This matters because it turns "what changed" from a guessing game into a question you can answer with a command. Instead of comparing two files by eye, you can ask Git directly what changed between any two points in history.

git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d Fix null check in login handler
# 9f8e7d6 Add password reset endpoint
# 4c5b6a7 Initial commit

Each line above is one recorded state of the project. That short hash (a1b2c3d) is a unique identifier for that exact snapshot — no two commits in a repository ever share one. Later lessons cover reading and filtering this history in depth; for now, the important idea is that this list exists at all, growing one entry at a time as work happens.

sections.title: Snapshots, Not Diffs: How Git Actually Stores History
sections.content:
Some older version control systems (and most naive "track changes" tools) store history as a series of diffs — a base file plus a chain of "here is what changed" patches. To reconstruct any given version, the system has to replay patches in order, which gets slower and more fragile the further back you go.

Git takes a different approach. Every commit stores a snapshot — essentially a complete picture of what every tracked file looked like at that moment. This sounds wasteful, but Git is efficient about it: if a file did not change between two commits, Git simply points the new commit at the exact same stored file rather than copying it again. Only files that actually changed get new content stored.

Think of each commit less like a "diff applied to the last one" and more like a full photograph of the project. Git computes diffs on demand for display purposes, but what it stores and what it hands back when you check out a commit is always a complete snapshot.

This design is why operations like switching between commits or branches in Git are fast — there is no chain of patches to replay, just a snapshot to restore. It is also why Git can confidently guarantee that the code you see at any commit is exactly the code that existed at that point, nothing more and nothing less.

sections.title: A Commit History Is a Timeline You Can Walk
sections.content:
Because every commit is a snapshot with a message and a parent pointer back to the commit before it, the full history of a project forms a timeline. Each commit knows what came immediately before it, so Git can walk backward from any point to see the entire sequence of decisions that produced the current state of the code.

This is more than a historical curiosity. A well-kept commit history lets a team answer real questions during real incidents:

  • What did this file look like before last week's refactor?
  • Which commit introduced this specific bug?
  • Who last touched this function, and what was their reasoning?
git log --oneline --graph
# * a1b2c3d Fix null check in login handler
# * 9f8e7d6 Add password reset endpoint
# * 4c5b6a7 Initial commit

The --graph flag draws the parent-to-child relationships as a visual line. Right now that line is straight because history is linear, but the branching lessons later in this course show how it fans out and reconverges when multiple lines of work happen at once. For now, the key idea is that history in Git is a connected chain, not a flat list of backups — and that chain is what every other Git feature is built on top of.

sections.title: Local First: Why Git Doesn't Need a Server to Work
sections.content:
Many people first meet Git through a hosted service like GitHub or GitLab, which can create the impression that Git requires an internet connection or a central server to function. It does not. Git is a distributed version control system: every clone of a repository is a complete, independent copy of the entire history, not just the latest files.

This is a meaningful difference from older centralized systems, where a single server held the only real history and every meaningful operation — committing, browsing history, comparing versions — required talking to that server. With Git, a developer on a plane with no internet access can still commit, branch, view the full log, and compare any two versions of the project, because all of that history is already sitting on their machine.

git log
# works fully offline -- the entire history is local

git commit -m "Refactor auth middleware"
# also works fully offline

A remote server like GitHub only becomes necessary when a developer wants to synchronize their local history with someone else's — pushing local commits up, or pulling other people's commits down. The remote is a convenient meeting point for collaboration, not a requirement for Git's core functionality. This distinction — local repository versus remote repository — becomes important the moment collaboration lessons introduce push and pull.

sections.title: The Three States: Working Directory, Staging Area, Repository
sections.content:
Git organizes a project's files into three conceptual states, and almost every Git command exists to move a change between them. Understanding these three states before typing a single command makes the rest of this course dramatically easier to follow.

  • Working directory — the actual files on disk, the ones opened in an editor. Edits here are just plain file changes; Git is aware of them but has not recorded anything yet.
  • Staging area (also called the index) — a holding area where changes are placed right before they become part of history. Staging lets a developer choose exactly which changes go into the next commit, even if the working directory has other, unrelated edits sitting alongside them.
  • Repository — the permanent, committed history, stored inside a hidden .git folder at the root of the project. Once a change reaches the repository as a commit, it is part of the recorded timeline.

A change always flows in one direction through these three states: edit a file in the working directory, stage it, then commit it. Nothing skips the staging area — that intermediate step is a deliberate feature, not an inconvenience, because it gives full control over what each commit contains.

sections.title: Watching a Change Move Through All Three States
sections.content:
The three states are easiest to understand by watching a single file move through all of them. Consider a plain text file called notes.txt that already exists in a Git-tracked project and gets one new line added.

git status
# On branch main
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified: notes.txt

At this point the edit exists only in the working directory. Git has noticed the file is different from the last commit, but nothing has been staged yet. Moving the change into the staging area is a deliberate action:

git add notes.txt
git status
# Changes to be committed:
#   modified: notes.txt

The change is now staged — recorded as "ready to go" but still not part of permanent history. The final step commits it, which moves it from the staging area into the repository as a new snapshot:

git commit -m "Add follow-up note"
git status
# On branch main
# nothing to commit, working tree clean

A clean git status output means the working directory, staging area, and the latest commit all agree — there is nothing pending in any of the three states. A later lesson covers this workflow command by command in far more depth; this walkthrough is only meant to make the three-state model concrete.

sections.title: git status: The Command You Will Run More Than Any Other
sections.content:
Of every Git command, git status is run the most often by far, because it answers the single most useful question at any point in a workflow: what state is everything in right now? It reports which files are modified but unstaged, which are staged and ready to commit, and which are entirely new and not yet tracked by Git at all.

git status
# On branch main
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified: app.js
#
# Untracked files:
#   new-feature.js

Notice the distinction: app.js is a file Git already knows about, and it has unstaged edits. new-feature.js is a brand-new file Git has never been told to track — it will remain invisible to commits until it is explicitly staged, even once, with git add.

Get in the habit of running git status before and after almost every other Git command. It costs nothing, it never changes anything, and it consistently catches mistakes — like forgetting to stage a file — before they become confusing later.

Because it is read-only and side-effect free, there is no such thing as running git status too often.

sections.title: Scenario: Reading a Project's History for the First Time
sections.content:
Imagine joining a team and being handed access to an existing Git-tracked project for the first time. Before writing a single line of code, the three-state model and the idea of a commit timeline already provide a way to get oriented.

First, confirm the current state of the working directory matches the last commit, so nothing unexpected is sitting around:

git status
# On branch main
# nothing to commit, working tree clean

Next, read the commit history to understand what has happened recently and who has been working on what:

git log --oneline
# 7d2f1a9 Add rate limiting to API gateway
# c3e9b40 Fix flaky integration test
# 88a1f02 Initial project scaffold

Three commits, three snapshots, each one a complete recorded state of the project with a clear description of intent. Nothing here required reading through folders named backup_final or guessing which file is the real one — the history is explicit, ordered, and queryable. That reliability, multiplied across a team of any size and a project of any age, is the entire reason version control exists. Every command covered in the rest of this course is really just a more precise way of moving changes through the working directory, staging area, and repository introduced here.

sections.title: Installing Git Without Overthinking It
sections.content:
Getting Git onto a machine is a one-time setup step and, on most systems, a short one. The installation method differs slightly by platform, but the goal is identical everywhere: get the git command working in a terminal.

  • Windows — install "Git for Windows," which bundles Git itself along with Git Bash, a Unix-like terminal.
  • macOS — Git often ships with Xcode Command Line Tools, or can be installed via a package manager like Homebrew.
  • Linux — install via the system package manager, for example apt on Debian/Ubuntu or dnf on Fedora.

Whichever route is used, confirm the install succeeded before doing anything else:

git --version
# git version 2.43.0

Any recent version is fine for everything covered in this course. Once git --version prints a version number instead of a "command not found" error, Git is installed and ready to be configured with an identity — the next required step before making a single commit.

sections.title: Why Every Commit Needs an Identity
sections.content:
Every commit in Git is permanently stamped with a name and an email address, recorded as the author of that exact snapshot. This is not optional metadata — it is baked into the commit itself, which is part of why Git history is trustworthy: anyone reading the log can see exactly who made a given change.

Until that identity is configured, Git will refuse to create a commit, or in some setups will fall back to a machine-generated guess that is rarely correct:

git commit -m "Add login form"
# *** Please tell me who you are.
# Run
#   git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
#   git config --global user.name "Your Name"

This is one of the first errors most people see the first time they use Git, and it is expected — it exists precisely so that no commit can ever be created anonymously. The fix is a two-line, one-time configuration covered next.

sections.title: Setting Your Name and Email Globally
sections.content:
The git config --global command sets a configuration value that applies to every repository on the current machine, for the current user. Name and email are the two values every setup needs first:

git config --global user.name "Alex Rivera"
git config --global user.email "alex.rivera@example.com"

Use the same name and email consistently across machines when possible — many hosting platforms (like GitHub) match commit authorship to a user account based on the email address, so inconsistent values can make history look like it came from multiple unrelated people.

Work commits and personal commits can use different identities. Set the personal identity with --global, then override it inside a specific work repository with git config user.email "you@work.com" (no --global flag) run from inside that repository's folder.

With name and email set, the earlier "Please tell me who you are" error goes away permanently, and every future commit on this machine carries a real, consistent identity.

sections.title: Choosing a Default Branch Name
sections.content:
Every new repository created with git init needs a name for its first branch. For a long time Git defaulted to master; most tooling and hosting platforms today default to main instead. Rather than accept whatever Git's built-in default happens to be, set it explicitly:

git config --global init.defaultBranch main

This setting only affects new repositories created after it is set — it has no effect on existing repositories, whose default branch name was fixed at the moment they were created. Setting it once now avoids a small but persistent annoyance: creating a new project locally, only to find its first branch has a different name than the main branch already sitting on the remote host, requiring an extra rename step.

git init
git branch
# * main

Branches themselves are covered in full in a later lesson; this configuration step simply ensures the naming is consistent from the very first repository created.

sections.title: Picking a Default Text Editor for Git
sections.content:
Some Git commands open a text editor automatically — most commonly git commit when run without a -m message, which opens an editor for writing a longer commit message. Without an explicit choice, Git falls back to whatever the system default is, which on many machines is a terminal editor like Vim — one that can be genuinely confusing to exit for anyone unfamiliar with it.

git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

The example above sets VS Code as the editor, using --wait so Git pauses until the file is closed. Other common choices:

  • nano — a simple terminal editor, easy to exit (Ctrl+X)
  • vim — powerful but has a real learning curve for beginners
  • "code --wait" — VS Code, if already installed and preferred
If git commit ever opens a screen that looks frozen with no obvious way to type or exit, it is very likely Vim. Press Esc, then type :wq and press Enter to save and quit, or :q! to quit without saving.

Setting a familiar editor once removes this entire class of confusion going forward.

sections.title: Saving Keystrokes with Aliases
sections.content:
Aliases let frequently typed Git commands be shortened to a few characters. They are configured the same way as any other setting, under the alias section:

git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.ci commit

After running these, git co main behaves exactly like git checkout main, and git st behaves exactly like git status. Aliases are purely a convenience layer — they do not change what a command does, only how much typing it takes to invoke it.

More elaborate aliases can bundle flags together, which is useful for a command that is always typed with the same options:

git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph"
git lg
# * a1b2c3d Fix null check in login handler
# * 9f8e7d6 Add password reset endpoint

Aliases are entirely optional and purely personal preference — nothing in this course assumes any alias exists, but they are worth knowing about early since most experienced Git users rely on a handful of them daily.

sections.title: Verifying Configuration with git config --list
sections.content:
After setting several values across a setup session, it helps to see everything Git currently has configured in one place, rather than checking each setting individually and hoping nothing was mistyped along the way:

git config --list
# user.name=Alex Rivera
# user.email=alex.rivera@example.com
# init.defaultbranch=main
# core.editor=code --wait
# alias.co=checkout
# alias.st=status

Any single value can also be checked in isolation, which is faster than scanning the full list when only one setting is in question:

git config user.email
# alex.rivera@example.com

git config user.name
# Alex Rivera

This is worth running right after initial setup, and again any time a commit shows up under an unexpected name or a familiar alias suddenly stops working — it is the fastest way to confirm exactly which identity and settings Git is currently using on this machine, without guessing.

Add --show-origin to see which file each value actually came from: git config --list --show-origin. This is the quickest way to settle any confusion about global versus local settings, covered next.

sections.title: Where Config Lives: --global vs --local vs --system
sections.content:
Git configuration exists at three levels, each stored in a different file, and each overriding the one below it in scope:

  • --system — applies to every user on the machine. Rarely used directly; stored in a system-wide file.
  • --global — applies to the current user, across all of that user's repositories. Stored in ~/.gitconfig. This is what every command in this lesson has used so far.
  • --local (the default when no flag is given) — applies only to the single repository the command is run from. Stored in .git/config inside that repository.

Local settings override global ones, which override system ones. This is what makes it possible to set a personal name and email globally, then override just the email inside one specific work repository:

cd work-project
git config user.email "alex@company.com"
# only applies inside work-project

Knowing these three scopes explains why a setting that works in one repository might not appear to apply in another — it may have been set with --local and never made global.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.content:
A handful of setup mistakes account for most early Git confusion, and all of them are easy to avoid once named explicitly.

  • Skipping identity setup and letting Git auto-guess it. Some environments fabricate a name and email from the operating system account instead of erroring out, silently attaching the wrong identity to every commit until someone notices.
  • Setting name and email locally per project and forgetting to also set them globally. The first commit in any brand-new repository will fail with "Please tell me who you are" if neither global nor local identity has been set.
  • Never touching core.editor and getting stuck in Vim. This is one of the most common first-week Git frustrations, and it is a one-line fix.
  • Assuming init.defaultBranch renames existing repositories. It only affects repositories created after the setting is changed — existing ones keep whatever branch name they already have.
  • Confusing which config file a setting landed in. Running git config --list --show-origin shows exactly which file each value came from, which resolves most "why isn't my setting applying" confusion instantly.

None of these mistakes are damaging or hard to fix, but avoiding them from the start means the very first real commit in the next lesson goes smoothly, with a correct identity, a sensible branch name, and an editor that will not get anyone stuck.

sections.title: git init vs git clone: Two Ways a Repository Begins
sections.content:
Every Git repository starts in one of exactly two ways: created fresh with git init, or copied from an existing repository with git clone. Understanding which situation applies avoids a surprising amount of early confusion, because the two commands solve opposite problems.

git init turns an ordinary folder — empty or already full of files — into a Git repository with no history yet. It is the right choice when starting something brand new that has never been tracked by Git before.

mkdir invoice-app
cd invoice-app
git init
# Initialized empty Git repository in invoice-app/.git/

git clone does the opposite: it copies an existing repository, history and all, from somewhere else (a teammate's machine, a hosting service like GitHub) down to the local machine.

git clone https://github.com/example-org/invoice-app.git
# Cloning into 'invoice-app'...

Both commands result in a fully functional local repository. The only difference is whether that repository starts with zero commits (init) or with the entire history of an already-existing project (clone).

sections.title: What git init Actually Does to a Folder
sections.content:
git init makes exactly one change to a folder: it creates a hidden subfolder named .git, which is where Git stores everything it needs to track history — configuration, the eventual commit history, and internal bookkeeping. Nothing else happens.

ls -a
# .  ..  .git

git status
# On branch main
# No commits yet
# nothing to commit
Running git init does not create any commits, does not touch any existing files in the folder, and does not automatically start tracking anything. It only makes Git aware that this folder is now a repository it should watch.

If git init is run inside a folder that already contains files, those files are left completely untouched on disk — they simply become visible to Git as untracked, ready to be staged and committed whenever that is wanted. This is a common way to bring an existing, previously unversioned project under Git's control for the first time.

sections.title: Cloning: Starting from Someone Else's History
sections.content:
git clone is how most developers actually begin working on an existing project. Given a repository URL, it downloads the complete history — every commit ever made — and checks out the latest snapshot into a new folder on disk.

git clone https://github.com/example-org/invoice-app.git
cd invoice-app
git log --oneline
# 7d2f1a9 Add rate limiting to API gateway
# c3e9b40 Fix flaky integration test
# 88a1f02 Initial project scaffold

Notice that git log works immediately after cloning, with no further commands needed — the entire history came down with the clone, not just the latest files. This is the distributed nature of Git in action, already introduced in the previous lesson: a clone is a full, independent copy, not a thin reference back to the original.

A clone also automatically remembers where it came from, recorded as a remote named origin, which later lessons on collaboration use for pushing and pulling changes. For now, the important point is simpler: after cloning, the working directory, staging area, and repository are all immediately populated and ready to use, with no separate setup step required.

sections.title: Inside the .git Folder, at a Glance
sections.content:
The .git folder is where all of a repository's actual data lives — it is the repository, in the sense that deleting it destroys all history while leaving the visible project files alone. A full tour of its internals is unnecessary for daily Git use, but a rough mental model helps demystify what commands are actually doing.

  • objects — where every snapshot Git has ever stored actually lives, compressed and identified by a unique hash.
  • refs — human-friendly pointers, like branch names, that point at a specific commit inside objects.
  • HEAD — a single file that records which branch (or commit) is currently checked out.
  • config — the local, repository-specific settings, exactly the file --local config values from the previous lesson are written into.
cat .git/HEAD
# ref: refs/heads/main
Almost nobody edits files inside .git by hand, and this course never asks for that. Every Git command is really just a structured way of reading or writing to this folder — knowing roughly what is in there just makes the commands feel less like magic.

sections.title: HEAD: Git's "You Are Here" Pointer
sections.content:
Among everything stored in .git, HEAD deserves special attention because it answers a question every other command depends on: which commit is currently checked out? HEAD almost always points at a branch name, and that branch name in turn points at a specific commit — the most recent one on that branch.

git log --oneline -1
# a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) Fix null check in login handler

The (HEAD -> main) annotation above is Git showing exactly this relationship: HEAD currently points to the main branch, and main currently points to commit a1b2c3d. Every new commit made moves the current branch's pointer forward to the new commit, and HEAD follows along automatically since it is pointing at the branch, not at a fixed commit.

This becomes especially relevant once branching is introduced: switching branches is really just moving HEAD to point somewhere else, which is why it happens instantly regardless of how large the project is — no files need to be copied, only a pointer needs to change.

sections.title: The Three-State Model in Practice
sections.content:
An earlier lesson introduced the working directory, staging area, and repository conceptually. With a real repository now in hand, the same flow can be walked through with actual commands, start to finish, inside a freshly initialized project.

git init
echo "# Invoice App" > README.md
git status
# Untracked files:
#   README.md

The new file exists only in the working directory so far — Git has noticed it but is not tracking it yet. Staging it moves it into the second state:

git add README.md
git status
# Changes to be committed:
#   new file: README.md

Committing moves it into the third and final state, permanently recorded in the repository's history:

git commit -m "Add project README"
git log --oneline
# 3f9a1c2 Add project README

This exact sequence — edit, git add, git commit — is the single most repeated pattern in all of Git, and it is the same pattern regardless of whether one file or a hundred files changed.

sections.title: git status as the Constant Companion Command
sections.content:
git status is the command that ties the three-state model together in daily use. Rather than memorizing which state a file is in, run git status and read the answer directly — it is completely safe to run at any time, since it never modifies anything.

git status
# On branch main
# Changes to be committed:
#   modified: invoice.js
#
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified: README.md
#
# Untracked files:
#   notes.txt

This single output describes three files in three different states simultaneously: invoice.js is staged and ready to commit, README.md has an edit that has not been staged yet, and notes.txt is a brand-new file Git has never tracked at all. All three can coexist at once, which is exactly why staging exists — it lets a commit be built up from precisely the changes that belong together, leaving unrelated edits for a later commit.

A common early habit worth building: run git status immediately before git add, and again immediately before git commit. It takes seconds and reliably prevents committing the wrong files.

sections.title: Reading Status Output Precisely
sections.content:
The exact wording in git status output is worth reading carefully, since it distinguishes between several genuinely different situations that are easy to conflate as a beginner.

  • Untracked files — files Git has never been told to track. They are invisible to commits until staged at least once.
  • Changes not staged for commit — files Git already tracks, with edits made since the last commit that have not yet been staged.
  • Changes to be committed — files currently staged; running git commit right now would include exactly these changes.
git status
# Changes to be committed:
#   modified: invoice.js
#
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified: invoice.js
The same filename can legitimately appear in both the staged and unstaged sections at once. That means the file was edited, staged, and then edited again — the staged version and the current working directory version are now different, and only the staged version would be included in the next commit.

When this happens, running git add again on the file brings the staging area up to date with the latest edit before committing.

sections.title: Scenario: A Complete Local Workflow from Nothing
sections.content:
Bringing everything in this lesson together, here is a full local workflow for a brand-new project, from an empty folder to a committed, verified change.

mkdir todo-cli
cd todo-cli
git init
# Initialized empty Git repository

echo "# Todo CLI" > README.md
git status
# Untracked files: README.md

git add README.md
git status
# Changes to be committed: new file: README.md

git commit -m "Add project README"
# [main (root-commit) 3f9a1c2] Add project README

git log --oneline
# 3f9a1c2 Add project README

git status
# nothing to commit, working tree clean

Every step above maps directly onto ideas from this lesson: git init created the .git folder and repository; the new file started in the working directory as untracked; git add moved it into the staging area; git commit moved it into the repository as a permanent snapshot; and a final clean git status confirmed all three states agree. Every future Git session, regardless of project size, is this same cycle repeated many times over.

sections.title: git add: Choosing What Goes Into the Next Commit
sections.content:
git add moves changes from the working directory into the staging area, marking them as "ready to be included in the next commit." It works on individual files, multiple files, or an entire project at once.

git add invoice.js
git add invoice.js receipt.js
git add .

git add . stages every changed and new file in the current directory and its subdirectories in one step. It is convenient, but it is also easy to accidentally stage a file that was not meant to be part of the next commit — a stray debug log, a locally modified config file, a half-finished edit in an unrelated part of the codebase.

Running git add . out of habit, without first checking git status, is one of the most common sources of messy commits — commits that mix an intended change with unrelated files that happened to be sitting in the working directory at the time.

Staging a specific file by name is always safer when only part of the working directory's changes belong in the next commit. The next section covers an even more precise tool for this: staging part of a single file.

sections.title: Selective Staging with git add -p
sections.content:
Sometimes a single file contains two unrelated edits — a bug fix and an unrelated cleanup, say — that really belong in two separate commits. git add -p (short for --patch) makes this possible by walking through a file's changes in small chunks called hunks, asking whether each one should be staged.

git add -p invoice.js
# Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,s,e,?]?

The most useful responses to that prompt:

  • y — stage this hunk
  • n — skip this hunk, leave it unstaged
  • s — split this hunk into smaller pieces, if possible
  • q — quit, staging nothing further

After answering prompts for every hunk in the file, git status shows the same file listed under both staged and unstaged changes — because part of it was staged and part was not. This is the tool that makes it possible to write commits that each represent exactly one logical change, even when the actual edits happened to land in the same file at the same time.

sections.title: git commit: Turning Staged Changes Into History
sections.content:
git commit takes everything currently in the staging area and permanently records it as a new snapshot in the repository, along with a message. The most common form passes the message inline with -m:

git commit -m "Add invoice PDF export"
# [main 7c4d2e1] Add invoice PDF export
#  1 file changed, 24 insertions(+)

Only staged changes are included — anything left unstaged in the working directory is left out of this commit entirely and will still show up in git status afterward, unchanged. This is the payoff of the staging step: a commit can be built deliberately from exactly the intended changes, regardless of what else happens to be edited at the time.

Running git commit without -m opens the configured text editor for writing a longer, multi-line message — useful when a change needs more explanation than a single line can hold. For most day-to-day changes, a well-written one-line message with -m is standard practice.

sections.title: What Makes a Good Commit Message
sections.content:
A commit message is read far more often than it is written — by teammates reviewing a pull request, by anyone running git log months later trying to understand why a line of code exists, by the same developer six months from now with no memory of the change. A vague message throws that context away.

# Weak: says nothing about what actually changed
git commit -m "fixed bug"

# Better: specific, describes the actual change
git commit -m "Fix null check in login handler"

A few conventions consistently produce clearer history:

  • Imperative mood — "Add," "Fix," "Remove," not "Added," "Fixed," "Removing." Read it as completing the sentence "If applied, this commit will <message>."
  • Specific, not vague — name the actual thing that changed, not just that "something" was fixed.
  • One logical change per commit — a commit that mixes a bug fix with an unrelated formatting pass is harder to review and harder to revert cleanly later.

None of this needs to be elaborate. "Fix null check in login handler" takes no longer to type than "fixed bug," and it is dramatically more useful to every future reader of the history, including the person who typed it.

sections.title: git log: Reading the Project's History
sections.content:
Plain git log lists every commit reachable from the current branch, most recent first, with the full commit hash, author, date, and message:

git log
# commit a1b2c3d4e5f6...
# Author: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@example.com>
# Date:   Wed Sep 10 14:22:03 2026 -0700
#
#     Fix null check in login handler

This full form is useful when the author or exact date of a change matters, but it is verbose for quickly scanning recent history — each commit takes several lines. For everyday browsing, a more compact view is usually more useful, covered next.

By default, output longer than one screen is shown through a pager, which can be exited by pressing q. This surprises a lot of new users who expect the terminal to return immediately after running the command.

sections.title: Shaping Log Output: --oneline and --graph
sections.content:
git log --oneline condenses each commit to a single line — a short hash and the first line of the commit message — which makes it far easier to scan a project's recent history at a glance:

git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d Fix null check in login handler
# 9f8e7d6 Add password reset endpoint
# 4c5b6a7 Initial commit

Adding --graph draws the branch and merge structure alongside the commits using simple line-drawing characters:

git log --oneline --graph
# * a1b2c3d Fix null check in login handler
# * 9f8e7d6 Add password reset endpoint
# * 4c5b6a7 Initial commit

On a single-branch project the graph is just a straight line, as shown above, but on a project with multiple branches and merges it becomes genuinely useful for visualizing how lines of work diverged and came back together — a topic covered in the branching lesson. Because this combination is typed constantly, it is a very common candidate for the kind of alias set up in an earlier lesson, for example git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph".

sections.title: git diff: Seeing Exactly What Changed
sections.content:
Where git status reports which files changed, git diff reports exactly what changed inside them, line by line. Run with no arguments, it shows changes in the working directory that have not yet been staged:

git diff
# diff --git a/invoice.js b/invoice.js
# --- a/invoice.js
# +++ b/invoice.js
# @@ -12,6 +12,7 @@
#  function generateInvoice(order) {
#-   return renderTemplate(order);
#+   const total = calculateTotal(order);
#+   return renderTemplate(order, total);
#  }

Lines prefixed with - were removed, lines prefixed with + were added, and unprefixed lines are shown only as context. Reading a diff before staging it is one of the simplest habits that consistently catches mistakes — a leftover console.log, an accidental change to an unrelated line, a file that should not have been touched at all.

On a file with a lot of unrelated changes, git diff output can get long. Scrolling through it is normal; the pager can be exited with q, same as with git log.

sections.title: git diff --staged: Reviewing Before You Commit
sections.content:
Plain git diff only shows unstaged changes — once a file is staged with git add, it disappears from that output, which surprises people expecting it to keep showing everything. To see exactly what is staged and about to be committed, use git diff --staged (equivalently, --cached):

git add invoice.js
git diff
# (no output -- invoice.js is staged, nothing else changed)

git diff --staged
# diff --git a/invoice.js b/invoice.js
# +   const total = calculateTotal(order);
# +   return renderTemplate(order, total);

This distinction matters most when a file has been edited more than once between staging steps. git diff shows what would be added if staged right now; git diff --staged shows what will actually be included the moment git commit runs. Checking git diff --staged immediately before committing is a reliable last line of defense against committing something unintended.

sections.title: Scenario: Shipping a Small Feature End to End
sections.content:
Consider adding a small feature — a total calculation to an invoice generator — using every command from this lesson in sequence.

git status
# modified: invoice.js

git diff
# @@ -12,3 +12,4 @@
#  function generateInvoice(order) {
#+   const total = calculateTotal(order);
#    return renderTemplate(order);
#  }

git add invoice.js
git diff --staged
# (confirms the exact change about to be committed)

git commit -m "Add order total to invoice generation"
# [main 7c4d2e1] Add order total to invoice generation

git log --oneline
# 7c4d2e1 Add order total to invoice generation
# a1b2c3d Fix null check in login handler

Four commands, each with a distinct job: git diff confirmed what actually changed before staging anything, git add moved the intended change into the staging area, git diff --staged confirmed exactly what was about to be committed, and git commit recorded it with a clear, specific message. This exact rhythm — check, stage, verify, commit — scales from a one-line fix to a large feature without needing any new commands.

sections.title: A Branch Is Just a Movable Pointer
sections.content:
Branches are often introduced as if they were separate copies of a project, which makes them sound heavyweight and mysterious. They are not. A branch in Git is nothing more than a lightweight, movable pointer to a single commit. Creating one does not copy any files, and switching between branches does not duplicate anything on disk.

git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) Add order total to invoice generation

The label main in that output is exactly this kind of pointer — it currently points at commit a1b2c3d. When a new commit is made on main, Git does not create a new branch; it simply moves the main pointer forward to the new commit. Every branch works this way, without exception.

This is why creating a branch in Git is instantaneous even on a huge project with years of history: nothing is being copied, only a small pointer file is being created, pointing at whatever commit is currently checked out.

Everything that follows in this lesson — creating branches, switching between them, merging them back together — is really just different ways of creating, moving, and combining these pointers.

sections.title: git branch: Listing and Creating Branches
sections.content:
Run with no arguments, git branch lists every branch in the repository, marking the currently checked-out one with an asterisk:

git branch
# * main

Passing a name creates a new branch — but only creates it, it does not switch to it. The new branch starts out pointing at exactly the same commit as whatever branch was checked out at the time:

git branch add-export-feature
git branch
# * main
#   add-export-feature

Notice the asterisk is still on main — creating add-export-feature did not move to it. This two-step nature (create, then separately switch) is exactly why the combined command introduced in the next section exists: creating and moving to a new branch is such a common pairing that Git provides a shortcut for doing both at once.

sections.title: Creating and Switching in One Step
sections.content:
git switch -c (or the older, still very common git checkout -b) creates a new branch and immediately moves HEAD to point at it, combining the two steps from the previous section into one command:

git switch -c add-export-feature
# Switched to a new branch 'add-export-feature'

git branch
#   main
# * add-export-feature

The older equivalent, still seen constantly in existing scripts and documentation:

git checkout -b add-export-feature

Both produce an identical result. git switch is the newer, purpose-built command for moving between branches — git checkout is older and does several unrelated things depending on its arguments (including restoring individual files), which is part of why git switch was introduced as a clearer, more focused alternative specifically for branch switching.

Moving back to an existing branch, with either command, requires no -c flag since nothing new is being created:

git switch main

sections.title: Committing on a Branch: Where the Pointer Actually Moves
sections.content:
Once a branch is checked out, every commit made behaves exactly as it always has — git add, then git commit — with one important difference: the pointer that moves forward is whichever branch is currently checked out, leaving every other branch's pointer exactly where it was.

git switch add-export-feature
echo "exportToCSV()" >> invoice.js
git add invoice.js
git commit -m "Add CSV export for invoices"
# [add-export-feature 9d3e1f2] Add CSV export for invoices

git log --oneline --graph --all
# * 9d3e1f2 (HEAD -> add-export-feature) Add CSV export for invoices
# * a1b2c3d (main) Add order total to invoice generation

The (main) label above is still sitting on the older commit — main was not touched by this commit at all, because add-export-feature was checked out when it happened. This is the entire mechanism that makes branches useful: work can happen on add-export-feature for as long as needed, with as many commits as needed, while main stays completely untouched and stable in the meantime.

sections.title: git merge: Bringing a Branch's Work Back In
sections.content:
Once work on a branch is ready to be combined back into another branch — typically main — git merge does that combining. The command is run from the branch that should receive the changes, naming the branch whose changes should be pulled in:

git switch main
git merge add-export-feature
# Updating a1b2c3d..9d3e1f2
# Fast-forward
#  invoice.js | 1 +
#  1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

After this completes, main includes every commit that was made on add-export-feature, and both branch pointers now point at the same commit:

git log --oneline --graph --all
# * 9d3e1f2 (HEAD -> main, add-export-feature) Add CSV export for invoices
# * a1b2c3d Add order total to invoice generation

Notice the word Fast-forward in the merge output above. That is not incidental phrasing — it names one of two genuinely different things git merge can do, depending on whether history diverged in the meantime. The next two sections cover exactly that distinction.

sections.title: Fast-Forward Merges: When Git Just Moves the Pointer
sections.content:
A fast-forward merge happens when the branch being merged into (main, in the previous example) has not received any new commits of its own since the other branch was created. In that situation, merging requires no actual combining of changes at all — the commits on add-export-feature already build directly on top of main's current position, so Git can simply slide main's pointer forward to match.

git merge add-export-feature
# Fast-forward

In prose form, before the merge the history looked like a single line with a branch label further along it:

# main:                a1b2c3d
# add-export-feature:  a1b2c3d -- 9d3e1f2

After a fast-forward merge, main simply points at 9d3e1f2 too — nothing new was created, no merge commit was added, the history stays a single straight line. This is the simplest and cleanest kind of merge, and it is only possible because main stood still the entire time add-export-feature was being worked on.

sections.title: Three-Way Merges: When History Has Actually Diverged
sections.content:
A fast-forward is only possible when one branch is a straight-line continuation of the other. If main also received new commits of its own while the feature branch was being worked on, the two branches have diverged, and Git has to actually combine two different sets of changes. This is a three-way merge.

# main:                a1b2c3d -- 5e6f7a8
# add-export-feature:  a1b2c3d -- 9d3e1f2

git switch main
git merge add-export-feature
# Merge made by the 'recursive' strategy.
#  invoice.js | 1 +
#  1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

The name "three-way" refers to what Git compares: the tip of main, the tip of add-export-feature, and their common ancestor commit (a1b2c3d above). Git works out what changed on each side since that shared ancestor and combines both sets of changes automatically wherever possible, producing a new merge commit with two parents instead of one:

git log --oneline --graph --all
# *   f4a9c21 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'add-export-feature'
# |\
# | * 9d3e1f2 Add CSV export for invoices
# * | 5e6f7a8 Fix rounding in total calculation
# |/
# * a1b2c3d Add order total to invoice generation
When both branches changed the same lines of the same file, Git cannot automatically decide which version to keep — this produces a merge conflict, resolved in a dedicated lesson later in this course.

sections.title: Cleaning Up with git branch -d
sections.content:
Once a branch has been merged, the branch pointer itself has served its purpose — every commit it pointed to is now also reachable from main, so the separate branch label is no longer needed. Deleting it keeps the branch list from accumulating clutter over time:

git branch -d add-export-feature
# Deleted branch add-export-feature (was 9d3e1f2)

Lowercase -d is a safety-checked delete: Git refuses to run it if the branch contains commits that have not been merged anywhere yet, preventing accidental loss of unmerged work:

git branch -d unfinished-branch
# error: the branch 'unfinished-branch' is not fully merged
Uppercase -D force-deletes a branch regardless of merge status, discarding any commits on it that exist nowhere else. It is a legitimate command, but it should be used deliberately, never as a reflex substitute for a failed -d.

Deleting a branch only removes the pointer, never the commits themselves, as long as at least one other reachable branch or pointer still points to them — which is exactly what the safety check in -d confirms before allowing the delete.

sections.title: Scenario: A Complete Feature Branch from Start to Finish
sections.content:
Bringing every command in this lesson together: a small feature is built on its own branch while main continues to receive an unrelated fix at the same time, and both are reconciled with a merge.

git switch -c add-export-feature
echo "exportToCSV()" >> invoice.js
git add invoice.js
git commit -m "Add CSV export for invoices"

git switch main
echo "// rounding fix" >> invoice.js
git add invoice.js
git commit -m "Fix rounding in total calculation"

git merge add-export-feature
# Merge made by the 'recursive' strategy.

git log --oneline --graph --all
# *   f4a9c21 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'add-export-feature'
# |\
# | * 9d3e1f2 Add CSV export for invoices
# * | 5e6f7a8 Fix rounding in total calculation
# |/
# * a1b2c3d Add order total to invoice generation

git branch -d add-export-feature
# Deleted branch add-export-feature (was 9d3e1f2)

Because main had moved forward with its own commit while the feature branch was being worked on, this merge could not fast-forward — Git produced a real three-way merge commit combining both lines of work, exactly as described earlier in this lesson. Once the merge succeeded, the feature branch had done its job and was safely deleted with -d, leaving main with a complete, honest record of both changes and how they came together.

sections.title: Why Two Branches Can Disagree About the Same Line
sections.content:
A merge conflict happens when Git tries to combine two branches and finds that both branches changed the same lines of the same file in different ways. Git is very good at automatically merging changes that touch different parts of a file, or even different files entirely — it only asks for help when it genuinely cannot decide which version you want.

Picture two developers working from the same starting point. One edits line 12 of config.js to fix a typo. The other edits line 12 of the same file to add a new setting. Both commits are valid on their own branch, but when you try to merge them, Git has two different versions of line 12 and no way to know which one is correct — or whether you want both.

This is not a bug or a sign that something went wrong. Conflicts are a normal, expected part of working with branches, especially on a team. The only thing that matters is knowing how to read what Git is telling you and resolve it deliberately.

sections.title: What Merge Does Before It Gives Up
sections.content:
When you run git merge, Git compares the two branches against their common ancestor commit and tries to apply every change automatically. For the vast majority of a merge, this works silently — most changes touch different lines or different files, so Git combines them without asking you anything.

git checkout main
git merge feature/pricing-update
# Auto-merging src/config.js
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/config.js
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

Notice what happens here: Git does not abandon the merge entirely. It pauses mid-merge, leaves the repository in a special "merging" state, and marks exactly which file(s) contain unresolved conflicts. Every file that merged cleanly is already updated and staged. Only the conflicting file needs your attention.

Run git status at this point and Git will list the conflicted file under "Unmerged paths", along with a reminder of the commands you need next.

sections.title: Reading the Conflict Markers Line by Line
sections.content:
Open the conflicted file and you will find that Git has inserted special markers directly into the text to show you both versions side by side. Understanding these markers is the whole skill of resolving conflicts.

<<<<<<< HEAD
const maxRetries = 3;
=======
const maxRetries = 5;
>>>>>>> feature/pricing-update
  • <<<<<<< HEAD marks the start of "your" version — the content currently on the branch you are merging into.
  • ======= is the dividing line between the two versions.
  • Everything between ======= and >>>>>>> feature/pricing-update is the incoming version from the branch you are merging in.
  • >>>>>>> feature/pricing-update marks the end of the incoming block, labeled with the branch or commit it came from.

Git never guesses which side is "right" — it shows you both and steps back. A file can contain multiple conflicted blocks like this one, each needing its own decision.

sections.title: A Concrete Conflict, Walked Through
sections.content:
Consider a real scenario. Your team's README.md has a single-line project description. On main, a teammate updated it to mention a new feature. On your branch feature/docs-fix, you fixed a typo in that same line. When you merge, Git shows:

<<<<<<< HEAD
Codemerit helps developers practice real interview questions.
=======
Codemerit helps developers practise for technical interviews.
>>>>>>> feature/docs-fix

Both versions are reasonable. The HEAD side (main) mentions "real interview questions"; the incoming side fixes "practise" to the correct spelling for your audience but drops that phrase. The right resolution here is neither line alone — it is a combination: keep the feature mention and the spelling fix.

This is the key insight beginners miss: resolving a conflict does not mean picking one block and deleting the other. It means deciding what the final, correct content should be, which is sometimes one side, sometimes the other, and sometimes a blend of both.

sections.title: Editing the File to Decide the Outcome
sections.content:
Resolving a conflict is plain text editing. Open the file in any editor, delete the marker lines themselves (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>), and leave behind exactly the content you want to keep.

For the README example above, the resolved line might read:

# Before (with markers) — 5 lines
# After resolving — 1 line:
Codemerit helps developers practise real interview questions.

Every marker must be removed. If you leave a stray <<<<<<< in the file, Git will not stop you from committing it, and it will sit in your codebase as broken syntax or nonsense text — a common and easily avoided mistake.

Most code editors (VS Code, IntelliJ, and others) highlight conflict markers and offer one-click "Accept Current", "Accept Incoming", or "Accept Both" buttons. These are convenient, but always read the result afterward — they resolve the marker, not necessarily the intent.

If the file is code, don't just resolve the text conflict — check that the merged result still makes sense logically and, where possible, still runs.

sections.title: Telling Git You're Done: git add
sections.content:
Once a conflicted file looks correct, stage it the same way you stage any other change:

git add src/config.js
git status
# All conflicts fixed but you are still merging.
#   (use "git commit" to conclude merge)

git add during a conflict has a special meaning beyond just staging content — it is how you tell Git "I have resolved this file's conflict." Git tracks, per file, whether it is still unmerged. Staging a formerly-conflicted file marks it resolved.

If a merge touched several files and only some conflicted, the non-conflicting files were already staged automatically when the merge ran. You only need to explicitly git add the files that showed up under "Unmerged paths".

Run git diff before staging if you want to double check exactly what changed and confirm no marker lines remain.

sections.title: Finishing the Merge with git commit
sections.content:
After every conflicted file has been resolved and staged, run git commit with no arguments needed:

git commit
# Merge branch 'feature/pricing-update'
#
# Conflicts:
#       src/config.js
#

Git already prepares a merge commit message for you, listing which files had conflicts, so you usually just save and exit the editor that opens. This commit is special: it has two parent commits — the tip of the branch you were on, and the tip of the branch you merged in. That two-parent shape is what makes it a merge commit rather than a regular one.

If you try to commit before every conflict is resolved, Git will refuse:

git commit
# error: Committing is not possible because you have unmerged files.

Run git status again to see which file still needs attention.

sections.title: Conflicts in Multiple Files
sections.content:
Larger merges often conflict in more than one file at once. Git lists every conflicted file up front, and the process is identical for each — you just repeat it:

git status
# Unmerged paths:
#   both modified:   src/config.js
#   both modified:   src/routes.js
#   both modified:   package.json

Work through them one at a time: open the file, resolve the markers, git add it, and move to the next. There is no requirement to resolve them in any particular order.

Some files are easier to get wrong here than others. package.json and similar structured files (lock files, config files) are especially error-prone because a misplaced comma or brace after removing markers can silently break the file. Always validate structured files after resolving — run a linter, or at minimum open the file and read it fully.

Do not run git add . out of habit mid-conflict without reviewing each file first. It is easy to accidentally stage a file that still has marker lines in it.

sections.title: git merge --abort: The Escape Hatch
sections.content:
Sometimes, partway through resolving a conflict, you realize the merge itself was a mistake — wrong branch, not ready yet, or the conflicts are more tangled than expected and you want to think it through first. Git gives you a clean way out:

git merge --abort

This command cancels the merge entirely and restores your working directory to exactly how it looked before you ran git merge — no conflict markers, no partial resolutions, no merge commit. It only works while the merge is still in progress (before you run git commit); once the merge commit is made, aborting is no longer available and you would need other tools to undo it.
