If you are ever unsure whether an in-progress conflict resolution is correct, aborting and starting over costs you nothing but a few minutes. There is no shame in backing out of a messy merge and re-approaching it calmly.

You can confirm you are mid-merge at any time with git status — it will explicitly say "You have unmerged paths" or similar at the top of the output.

sections.title: Scenario: A Calm Conflict Resolution
sections.content:
You pull the latest main into your local feature/checkout-fix branch before opening a pull request, and Git reports a conflict in src/checkout.js:

git checkout feature/checkout-fix
git merge main
# Auto-merging src/checkout.js
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/checkout.js
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

You open checkout.js and find one conflicted block: main added input validation for the discount code field, while your branch changed the same function to fix a currency rounding bug. Both changes are valid and don't actually contradict each other — they just happen to touch nearby lines.

You remove the conflict markers and manually combine both changes: the validation logic from main, followed by your rounding fix. You save the file, then run:

git add src/checkout.js
git status
# All conflicts fixed but you are still merging.
git commit

Git opens the prepared merge commit message; you accept it as is. The merge completes, your branch now has both the validation logic and the rounding fix, and you push your branch knowing exactly what changed and why — no guessing, no panic.

sections.title: What a "Remote" Actually Is
sections.content:
Every Git repository you have worked with so far has been local — living entirely on your own machine. A remote is simply another copy of that same repository, usually hosted on a server like GitHub, GitLab, or a company's internal Git server, that you and your teammates can all connect to.

There is nothing structurally special about a remote repository. It has the same commits, branches, and history format as your local one. The only difference is where it lives and that multiple people can push to and pull from it, which is what makes it useful as a shared point of coordination for a team.

A single local repository can be connected to more than one remote at once — for example, your own fork on GitHub and the original project you forked from. Each remote is given a short name so you can refer to it in commands instead of typing a full URL every time.

"The cloud" is not doing anything magical here — a remote is just a Git repository, reachable over a network, that happens to be treated as the shared source of truth.

sections.title: Connecting a Local Repo to a Remote: git remote add
sections.content:
If you start a project locally with git init and later want to push it to GitHub, you need to tell your local repository where that remote lives:

git remote add origin https://github.com/your-team/project.git
git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/your-team/project.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/your-team/project.git (push)

git remote add takes two arguments: a short name for the remote (origin is the near-universal convention for your main remote) and its URL, which can be an HTTPS address or an SSH address depending on how you authenticate.

After adding a remote, your local branches still know nothing about it until you push or pull. Adding the remote only registers where it lives — it does not transfer any data by itself.

git push -u origin main

That command performs the first actual data transfer, sending your local main branch history to the newly registered origin.

sections.title: git clone Revisited: Cloning Sets Up the Remote For You
sections.content:
In practice, most developers never type git remote add for their primary remote, because git clone does it automatically. When you clone a repository:

git clone https://github.com/your-team/project.git
cd project
git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/your-team/project.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/your-team/project.git (push)

Git creates the local repository, copies over the full commit history, checks out the default branch, and — critically for this lesson — automatically names the source you cloned from origin and remembers its URL. That is why you have been able to git push and git pull without ever manually configuring a remote in earlier lessons.

git remote add becomes necessary in two situations: starting a brand-new repository locally with git init before it exists remotely, or connecting an existing local repository to an additional remote later on.

sections.title: Sending Your Work: git push
sections.content:
git push uploads your local commits to a remote repository, updating the remote branch to match your local one:

git push origin feature/login-page
# Enumerating objects: 12, done.
# Writing objects: 100% (8/8), 942 bytes | 942.00 KiB/s, done.
# To https://github.com/your-team/project.git
#  * [new branch]      feature/login-page -> feature/login-page

The syntax is git push <remote> <branch>. This pushes only the commits that exist locally and are missing from the remote — Git compares histories and transfers the difference, not the entire repository every time.

If the remote branch has commits your local branch does not have — because a teammate pushed in the meantime — Git will refuse the push to protect you from silently overwriting their work:

git push origin main
# ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
# error: failed to push some refs

The fix is to pull first, resolve anything that needs resolving, and push again — never force the issue without understanding why it was rejected.

sections.title: git fetch vs git pull — The Difference That Trips Everyone Up
sections.content:
These two commands are often confused, but they do meaningfully different things.

git fetch downloads new commits, branches, and tags from the remote into your local repository, but does not change any of your working files or local branches. It updates your knowledge of the remote (visible as origin/main, for example) without touching your current branch at all.

git fetch origin
git log origin/main --oneline -3
# see what's new on the remote without merging it yet

git pull does two things in sequence: it runs git fetch, then immediately merges the fetched changes into your current local branch.

git pull origin main
# equivalent to:
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main

In short: fetch is "show me what changed, I'll decide what to do"; pull is "get the changes and merge them into what I'm working on right now." When you are unsure whether merging is safe — for example, you have uncommitted work — fetching first and inspecting before merging is the more cautious habit.

sections.title: Tracking Branches: Why git push -u Matters
sections.content:
The first time you push a new local branch, Git does not yet know it should be linked to a corresponding branch on the remote. Pushing with -u (short for --set-upstream) establishes that link:

git push -u origin feature/checkout-redesign

This does two things: it pushes the branch, and it configures your local feature/checkout-redesign to track origin/feature/checkout-redesign. Once tracking is set up, every future push and pull on that branch can be run with no arguments at all:

git push
git pull

Without a tracking relationship, Git does not know which remote branch a bare git push should target and will tell you so:

git push
# fatal: The current branch feature/checkout-redesign has no upstream branch.
# To push the current branch and set the remote as upstream, use
#     git push --set-upstream origin feature/checkout-redesign

You only need -u once per branch, on its first push. After that, the tracking relationship persists in your local Git configuration.

sections.title: Checking What Remotes You Have
sections.content:
As a repository accumulates history, it is worth knowing how to inspect its remote configuration directly instead of guessing:

git remote
# origin

git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/your-team/project.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/your-team/project.git (push)

git remote show origin
# * remote origin
#   Fetch URL: https://github.com/your-team/project.git
#   Push  URL: https://github.com/your-team/project.git
#   HEAD branch: main
#   Remote branches:
#     main tracked

git remote show <name> is especially useful when a push or pull is not behaving as expected — it reports exactly which branches are tracked and whether your local branches are ahead, behind, or diverged from the remote.

If a remote's URL changes — for example, your team moves from one hosting provider to another — update it without removing and re-adding:

git remote set-url origin https://newhost.example.com/project.git

sections.title: origin vs upstream: Naming Convention for Forks
sections.content:
origin is just a convention, not a Git requirement — but it is such a strong convention that deviating from it without reason will confuse anyone else reading your commands. It gets more interesting once forking enters the picture.

When you contribute to an open-source project you don't have write access to, the typical workflow is: fork the project on GitHub into your own account, then clone your fork. That clone automatically names your fork origin. To stay in sync with the original project, you add a second remote, conventionally named upstream:

git clone https://github.com/your-username/project.git
cd project
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/project.git
git remote -v
# origin    https://github.com/your-username/project.git (fetch/push)
# upstream  https://github.com/original-owner/project.git (fetch only, typically)

With this set up, you push your own work to origin (your fork), and pull changes from the original project's ongoing development with git fetch upstream or git pull upstream main to keep your fork current.

This origin/upstream split matters only in the fork-and-pull-request model. On a team where everyone shares direct write access to one repository, there is usually just a single remote, origin.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.content:
A few mistakes come up repeatedly for people new to working with remotes:

  • Confusing fetch and pull, then being surprised by a merge. Running git pull when you only meant to check for updates can create an unexpected local merge commit. If you just want to look, use git fetch.
  • Force-pushing to fix a rejected push without understanding why it was rejected. A rejected git push almost always means the remote has commits you don't have locally. Pull and merge first; reach for --force only when you deliberately intend to overwrite remote history and understand the consequences for anyone else using that branch.
  • Forgetting -u on the first push of a new branch, then being confused why subsequent bare git push commands fail with "no upstream branch".
  • Assuming origin always means "the official project". In a fork, origin is your own copy — the official project is upstream. Pushing to the wrong one is a common early mix-up.
  • Not checking git remote -v before troubleshooting a push/pull problem. Half of remote-related confusion resolves itself once you confirm which URL you are actually talking to.

None of these mistakes cause permanent damage on their own — remotes are just URLs, and reconfiguring one is always safe. The goal is simply to build an accurate mental model of what each command actually does before running it under time pressure.

sections.title: Keeping Noise Out With .gitignore
sections.content:
Not everything in a project folder belongs in version control. Dependency folders like node_modules, build output like dist, secrets like .env, and editor files like .DS_Store are either regenerable, huge, or sensitive — committing them clutters history, bloats the repository, and in the case of secrets, can leak credentials publicly.

A .gitignore file, placed at the root of your repository, tells Git which paths to never track:

# .gitignore
node_modules/
dist/
.env
*.log
.DS_Store

Each line is a pattern. A trailing slash matches a directory and everything inside it; * matches any sequence of characters, so *.log ignores every file ending in .log anywhere Git looks. Once a pattern is listed, git status stops mentioning matching files as untracked, and git add . will silently skip them.

GitHub maintains a large collection of ready-made .gitignore templates per language and framework — starting from one of those and adjusting it is usually faster and safer than writing your own from scratch.

sections.title: Untracking a File Git Is Already Watching
sections.content:
.gitignore only prevents Git from tracking a file it does not already know about. If a file was committed before it was added to .gitignore — a common mistake — the ignore rule alone will not remove it from tracking:

echo "config/secrets.json" >> .gitignore
git status
# still shows config/secrets.json as tracked and modified

To stop tracking a file while keeping it on disk, use git rm --cached:

git rm --cached config/secrets.json
git commit -m "Stop tracking secrets.json"

The --cached flag is the important part — without it, git rm deletes the file from your working directory too, which is usually not what you want. With --cached, the file stays exactly where it is on your machine; it just leaves Git's index and, once committed, future changes to it are ignored.

This does not remove the file from your history — anyone who checks out an older commit will still see it. If a real secret (a password, API key) was committed, rotate that credential; removing the file going forward is not enough to undo an already-public leak.

sections.title: Undoing Unstaged Changes: git restore
sections.content:
You are editing a file, decide the direction was wrong, and want your local edits gone — back to how the file looked in the last commit. This is one of the safest undo operations in Git, and there is no need to be nervous about it:

git status
# modified:   src/utils/formatDate.js  (not staged)

git restore src/utils/formatDate.js
git status
# nothing to commit, working tree clean

git restore <file> discards uncommitted, unstaged changes to that file and replaces it with the version from the last commit. It only affects your working directory — nothing about your commit history changes, because there was nothing committed to undo in the first place.

This does permanently discard the uncommitted edits themselves — there is no "undo the undo" for changes that were never committed or stashed. If you are even slightly unsure whether you want to keep an edit, consider git stash instead, which sets changes aside without deleting them.

To restore every modified file at once instead of one at a time, use git restore . from the repository root.

sections.title: Unstaging Without Losing Your Edits: git restore --staged
sections.content:
A different, equally common situation: you ran git add on a file, then changed your mind about including it in this commit — but you still want to keep the edits, just not stage them yet.

git add src/config.js
git status
# Changes to be committed:
#   modified:   src/config.js

git restore --staged src/config.js
git status
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified:   src/config.js

This is the calm, reassuring detail worth remembering: git restore --staged only moves the file back from "staged" to "modified." It does not touch the file's actual content at all. Your edits are still sitting right there in the working directory, completely intact — you have simply told Git not to include them in the next commit yet.

This is the direct opposite operation of git add, and the two are safe to run back and forth as many times as you like while you decide exactly what belongs in a commit.

sections.title: Fixing the Last Commit: git commit --amend
sections.content:
You just committed, and immediately notice a typo in the message, or realize you forgot to include a file. Rather than making an awkward follow-up "fix typo" commit, amend the previous one:

git commit --amend -m "Fix null check in login form"

# or, to add a forgotten file to the same commit:
git add src/login.js
git commit --amend --no-edit

--amend replaces the most recent commit with a new one that combines your staged changes (if any) with the previous commit's content, letting you also edit the message. --no-edit keeps the existing message unchanged if only the content needs fixing.

Technically, this creates a brand-new commit with a new identifier and discards the old one — it is not literally editing history in place, it is replacing it. For a commit that only exists locally and has not been pushed, this is completely safe.

Avoid amending a commit that has already been pushed and that others may have pulled. Because amending changes the commit's identity, it will diverge from what they have, requiring a force-push and causing sync problems for anyone who already pulled the original.

sections.title: git reset: Moving the Branch Pointer
sections.content:
git reset moves your current branch pointer to a different commit, effectively rewriting what your branch's history looks like from that point forward.

git log --oneline -3
# a1b2c3d Fix typo in README
# 9f8e7d6 Add login validation
# 5c4b3a2 Initial commit

git reset --soft HEAD~1
# undoes the last commit, but keeps its changes staged

git reset --mixed HEAD~1
# undoes the last commit, keeps changes but unstaged (this is the default mode)

git reset --hard HEAD~1
# undoes the last commit and discards its changes entirely

The three modes differ only in what happens to the changes from the undone commit(s): --soft keeps them staged, --mixed (the default) keeps them as unstaged edits, and --hard deletes them from the working directory too — the most destructive option, since uncommitted work discarded this way cannot easily be recovered.

Reset literally moves the branch pointer, erasing commits from that branch's history as Git sees it. If you have already pushed those commits and a teammate has pulled them, resetting locally and force-pushing rewrites history out from under them — their clone now disagrees with yours, causing confusing conflicts. Never reset commits that others may have already based work on.

sections.title: git revert: Undoing Safely on Shared History
sections.content:
git revert solves the same underlying problem as reset — "I want to undo a commit" — but in a fundamentally safer way for anything that is already shared with other people.

git log --oneline -3
# a1b2c3d Add experimental caching layer
# 9f8e7d6 Fix login validation
# 5c4b3a2 Initial commit

git revert a1b2c3d
# creates a NEW commit that applies the exact opposite of a1b2c3d's changes

Instead of erasing the commit from history, revert adds a brand-new commit on top that undoes its effect. The original commit stays in the log, visible and intact, alongside the new commit that cancels it out. Anyone who already has the original commit in their local history is completely unaffected — they just pull the new revert commit like any other, and their history stays consistent with yours.

This is why git revert is the standard tool for undoing something on main or any branch other people are actively working from, while git reset is reserved for local, not-yet-shared history.

sections.title: Choosing Between reset and revert
sections.content:
A simple rule settles almost every case:

  • Undoing a commit that only exists on your machine and has never been pushed — reset is fine. Nobody else's history depends on it.
  • Undoing a commit that has been pushed and others may have pulled or built on — use revert. It adds new history instead of erasing shared history.
  • Not sure which category you're in — check with git log and git status, and lean toward revert. Reverting an already-safe local commit costs you nothing but an extra commit; resetting a shared one can cost a teammate real time untangling a broken clone.

Both commands answer "how do I undo a commit," but they answer different questions underneath: reset asks "what should my branch's history look like," while revert asks "what new change cancels this one out." Keeping that distinction in mind makes the choice far less intimidating.

If you are ever unsure whether a reset is safe, run git log origin/main..HEAD — commits it lists are local-only and unpushed, safe to reset freely. Commits missing from that list are already shared.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.content:
Mistakes with undo commands feel scarier than they are. Keep these in mind and you will rarely lose real work:

  • Reaching for git reset --hard out of habit. It is the only command in this lesson that can permanently discard uncommitted work. When in doubt, try --mixed or --soft first, or commit/stash your work before resetting anything.
  • Force-pushing after a reset without checking who else uses the branch. On a shared branch, that is almost always a job for git revert instead.
  • Forgetting that .gitignore does not retroactively untrack a file. Pair it with git rm --cached when a file was already committed.
  • Panicking and doing nothing. Git rarely deletes anything immediately — commits stick around even after a reset for a while and are recoverable through git reflog (covered in a later lesson) in many cases. Take a breath, run git status and git log, and figure out exactly what state you're in before running another command.

Every command in this lesson exists precisely because mistakes are normal and expected in daily Git use. The workflow is designed around the assumption that you will stage the wrong thing, commit too early, or change your mind — and it gives you a calm, deliberate way back every time.

sections.title: From Solo Branch to Team Workflow
sections.content:
Branching and merging locally is only half the picture. On a real team, changes rarely go straight from a feature branch into main with a simple git merge run by the same person who wrote the code. Instead, teams route changes through a pull request (GitHub's term) or merge request (GitLab's term) — the same concept under two different names.

A pull request is a proposal: "here is a branch with some commits, please review it and merge it into main when it's ready." It wraps the plain git merge you already know with a review step, a discussion thread, and often automated checks, before the merge actually happens.

This lesson walks through that full workflow end to end — from branching, to opening the request, through review and revision, to the merge itself — the way it plays out on a real team day to day.

sections.title: Step One: Branch, Then Push
sections.content:
The workflow starts exactly where earlier lessons left off: create a branch for the change, commit your work on it, and push it to the remote.

git checkout -b feature/add-export-button
# ... make changes, commit ...
git add src/components/ExportButton.tsx
git commit -m "Add CSV export button to reports page"
git push -u origin feature/add-export-button

Nothing here is different from working solo — the branch lives on the remote now, but main is untouched. Pushing a feature branch does not merge anything by itself; it simply makes the branch and its commits visible to anyone else with access to the remote, which is a prerequisite for opening a pull request against it.

Most hosting platforms (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) will show a banner immediately after you push a new branch, offering a one-click link to open a pull request from it — you rarely need to hunt for the button.

sections.title: Opening a Pull Request
sections.content:
On the hosting platform, opening a pull request means picking a source branch (yours, feature/add-export-button) and a target branch (usually main), then writing a description of the change.

A good pull request description typically includes:

  • What changed and why, in plain language.
  • How to test or verify it, if that's not obvious.
  • Links to a related ticket, issue, or design discussion.
  • Screenshots or a short clip, for anything visual.

Behind the scenes, the pull request is really just a pointer to a comparison between two branches — it does not duplicate your commits or create new history on its own. You can keep committing and pushing to the same branch after opening the PR, and it will simply reflect the growing diff between your branch and the target.

Once opened, the pull request becomes the central place for discussion, automated check results, and eventually the merge button — a single page that tracks the entire lifecycle of that change from proposal to merge.

sections.title: Requesting Review — What Reviewers Actually Look At
sections.content:
Most teams require at least one other person to review a pull request before it merges. You typically add a reviewer explicitly, or the platform assigns one automatically based on a configured rule (for example, whoever owns the touched files).

A reviewer is not just re-reading your diff for typos. They are usually checking for:

  • Correctness — does the logic actually do what the description claims?
  • Consistency with existing patterns in the codebase.
  • Edge cases and error handling that might be missing.
  • Whether tests were added or updated for the change.
  • Readability — will the next person to touch this code understand it?

Reviews come back as inline comments attached to specific lines, general comments on the PR as a whole, and an overall verdict — commonly "approve," "comment," or "request changes." A "request changes" verdict on most platforms blocks the merge button until it's resolved, which is precisely the mechanism that makes review meaningful rather than optional.

sections.title: Fork-and-PR vs Shared-Repository Model
sections.content:
There are two common shapes this workflow takes, and which one applies depends on whether you have write access to the repository.

Shared-repository model — typical inside a company. Everyone with write access branches directly off the same repository:

git clone https://github.com/your-company/product.git
git checkout -b feature/add-export-button
git push -u origin feature/add-export-button
# open a PR: feature/add-export-button -> main, same repository

Fork-and-PR model — typical for open source, where most contributors don't have write access to the original repository. You fork it into your own account first, push branches there, and open a PR from your fork back to the original project:

git clone https://github.com/your-username/project.git
cd project
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/project.git
git checkout -b fix-typo-in-docs
git push -u origin fix-typo-in-docs
# open a PR: your-username/project:fix-typo-in-docs -> original-owner/project:main

Both models converge on the same review-and-merge process once the PR is open — the difference is only in where your branch physically lives before that point.

sections.title: What "Protecting main" Means in Practice
sections.content:
Most teams configure main (and often other long-lived branches) as protected, meaning the hosting platform enforces rules that no individual, including admins in some configurations, can casually bypass:

  • No direct pushes. Nobody, including the original author, can run git push origin main straight to the protected branch — all changes must go through a pull request.
  • Required reviews. A configurable number of approvals (often one or two) must be given before the merge button becomes active.
  • Required status checks. Automated checks (tests, linting, builds) must pass before merging is allowed, regardless of human approval.
  • Up-to-date branch requirement, in stricter setups — your branch must be rebased or merged with the latest main before merging, so it's tested against current code, not a stale snapshot.

The point of these rules is not distrust of any individual developer — it is removing the possibility of an honest mistake (a typo'd command, a rushed late-night push) reaching production code with no second set of eyes and no automated safety net. It turns "please review this" from a polite request into a structural guarantee.

sections.title: Required CI Checks: Automating the Gate
sections.content:
Alongside human review, most protected branches also require continuous integration (CI) checks to pass — automated jobs that run every time a pull request is opened or updated:

# triggered automatically on push to the PR branch, not run manually:
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build

These checks appear directly on the pull request page as a list with pass/fail status next to each one. A required check that fails blocks the merge button exactly like a missing review does — the platform will not let the merge happen until it's green, no matter how confident the author or reviewer feels.

This matters because human review is good at catching logic and design problems but is slow and inconsistent at catching things a machine checks instantly and every single time: a failing test, a lint violation, a build that no longer compiles. Splitting the gate between "a human confirms this is a good idea" and "a machine confirms this doesn't break anything mechanical" catches more problems than either check alone.

sections.title: Addressing Review Feedback Without Starting Over
sections.content:
When a reviewer requests changes, you do not close the pull request and start fresh. You keep working on the exact same branch, and the same pull request tracks the update automatically:

# reviewer commented: "this should handle the empty-list case"
git checkout feature/add-export-button
# ... make the fix ...
git add src/components/ExportButton.tsx
git commit -m "Handle empty list in CSV export"
git push

Because the pull request is just a live comparison between your branch and the target branch, pushing new commits to feature/add-export-button immediately updates the PR — no new PR, no re-linking, nothing to reconfigure. The reviewer sees the new commits appear and can re-review just the delta, or the whole diff again, depending on the platform.

Address each review comment with its own small, focused commit rather than one giant "address feedback" commit. It gives the reviewer an easy way to confirm each specific point was handled, and keeps the history readable afterward.

Once the reviewer is satisfied, they change their verdict to "approve," and once required checks are also green, the merge button unlocks.

sections.title: Scenario: A PR Gets Change Requests
sections.content:
A developer, Priya, opens a pull request for feature/export-filters that lets users filter a CSV export by date range. CI runs automatically and passes. A teammate reviews the code and leaves two comments: one asking why an unused import was left in, and another pointing out that an empty date range silently exports nothing instead of showing an error message. The reviewer sets the verdict to "request changes."

git status
# On branch feature/export-filters

git add src/utils/exportFilters.js
git commit -m "Remove unused import and validate empty date range"
git push

Priya does not open a new pull request or ask the reviewer to re-review from scratch. She stays on the same branch, makes both fixes in one focused commit, and pushes. The existing pull request updates automatically — the new commit appears in its history, and CI reruns against the updated branch without anyone touching a setting.

The reviewer gets notified, checks the new commit addresses both comments, and switches their verdict to "approve." With one approval and a passing CI run — the two conditions the protected main branch requires — the merge button becomes active, and Priya merges the pull request into main herself, right from the same page where the whole conversation happened.

sections.title: Two Ways to Combine Histories: Merge vs Rebase
sections.content:
Both git merge and git rebase solve the same underlying problem — bringing changes from one branch into another — but they produce very different-looking history, and picking the right one for a situation matters.

git merge combines two branches by creating a new merge commit with two parents, leaving both branches' original commits exactly as they were:

*   7f3a2c1 Merge branch 'main' into feature/search
|\
| * 9d8e7f6 Fix pagination bug (main)
* | 4b3c2d1 Add search input debounce (feature/search)
|/
* 1a2b3c4 Initial commit

git rebase instead takes your branch's commits and replays them one by one on top of a new base, producing a straight line with no merge commit at all:

* 5e6f7a8 Add search input debounce (feature/search, rebased)
* 9d8e7f6 Fix pagination bug (main)
* 1a2b3c4 Initial commit

Same end content, meaningfully different shape: merge preserves exactly what happened and when branches diverged and rejoined; rebase rewrites your commits as if they had been written starting from the new base all along, producing a cleaner, linear-looking log at the cost of the commits' original identity.

sections.title: What Rebase Actually Does, Commit by Commit
sections.content:
"Replay" is not just a metaphor — it describes the literal mechanism. Given a feature branch with three commits diverged from main, git rebase main does the following internally:

  • Finds the common ancestor of your branch and main.
  • Temporarily sets your branch aside and moves to the tip of main.
  • Takes your first diverged commit's changes and reapplies them on top of main's tip, creating a brand-new commit with the same change content but a new identifier (a new hash).
  • Repeats this for each subsequent commit on your branch, in original order, each one now built on top of the previous replayed commit.
  • Moves your branch pointer to the last newly-created commit.

This is why rebased commits get new hashes even though their content is identical — from Git's perspective, a commit's identity is a hash of its content plus its parent, and rebase changes every commit's parent by definition. Anyone still holding the old commits (because they pulled your branch before the rebase) now has commits that no longer exist on your rebased branch — this single fact is the reason the golden rule later in this lesson exists.

sections.title: Updating a Feature Branch: git rebase main
sections.content:
A common, safe use of rebase: your feature branch has fallen behind main, and you want your work built on the latest code before opening a pull request.

git checkout feature/search-improvements
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# First, rewinding head to replay your work on top of it...
# Applying: Add search input debounce
# Applying: Fix search results ordering

Your two commits are removed from their old position, main's new commits become the base, and your commits are reapplied on top — one at a time, in order. The result reads as if you had branched off today's main from the start, rather than showing the messy back-and-forth of when each side actually happened.

This is the most common everyday use of rebase: keeping a not-yet-shared feature branch current with main before opening or updating a pull request, producing a clean, easy-to-review diff.

If your branch has already been pushed and reviewed by others, check the golden rule later in this lesson before rebasing it.

sections.title: Resolving Conflicts During a Rebase
sections.content:
Because rebase replays commits one at a time, a conflict can occur on any individual commit, not just once for the whole branch. When it happens, Git pauses mid-replay:

git rebase origin/main
# Applying: Fix search results ordering
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/search.js
# error: could not apply 4b3c2d1... Fix search results ordering

Resolve it the same way you would resolve any conflict — open the file, edit out the markers, decide the correct content — then continue the rebase instead of committing:

git add src/search.js
git rebase --continue

If a later commit in the sequence also conflicts, the same cycle repeats: resolve, git add, git rebase --continue. If at any point you want out entirely, exactly like a merge:

git rebase --abort

This restores your branch to exactly how it looked before the rebase started, as if it never happened.

sections.title: Interactive Rebase: git rebase -i HEAD~3
sections.content:
Interactive rebase uses the same replay mechanism, but instead of running automatically, it opens an editor listing your recent commits and lets you decide what happens to each one before they're replayed:

git rebase -i HEAD~3
pick 9d8e7f6 Add search input field
pick 4b3c2d1 fix typo
pick 5e6f7a8 Actually fix the debounce bug

HEAD~3 means "the three most recent commits on this branch." The editor lists them oldest-first, each prefixed with the action pick, which just means "keep this commit as is." Changing the word in front of a commit changes what rebase does with it when it replays.

The common actions:

  • pick — keep the commit unchanged.
  • reword — keep the changes, but stop to let you edit the commit message.
  • squash — combine this commit into the one above it, merging their messages.
  • fixup — combine this commit into the one above it, discarding this commit's message entirely.
  • drop — remove the commit entirely.

Save and close the editor, and Git replays the commits according to your instructions.

sections.title: Squashing Commits Into One
sections.content:
A frequent use of interactive rebase is cleaning up a messy commit trail before a pull request — several "work in progress" and "fix typo" commits that add no value to the permanent history.

Before:

9d8e7f6 Add search input field
4b3c2d1 fix typo
5e6f7a8 Actually fix the debounce bug
2c1b3a4 wip

Running git rebase -i HEAD~4 and editing the plan:

pick   9d8e7f6 Add search input field
squash 4b3c2d1 fix typo
squash 5e6f7a8 Actually fix the debounce bug
squash 2c1b3a4 wip

After saving, Git combines all four commits into one, opening an editor pre-filled with all four commit messages so you can write a single clean summary:

Add search input field with debounce

After:

a1b2c3d Add search input field with debounce

One commit, one clear message — much easier for a reviewer or a future git log reader to understand than four commits describing the messy path it took to get there.

sections.title: Rewording, Reordering, and Dropping Commits
sections.content:
Interactive rebase supports more than squashing. Three other adjustments come up regularly:

Rewording a commit message without touching its content:

pick   9d8e7f6 Add search input field
reword 4b3c2d1 fx bug
# change "reword" and Git will stop to let you retype the message for that commit only

Reordering commits is done simply by rearranging the lines in the editor before saving — Git replays them in whatever order the lines appear, top to bottom:

# before: input field, then debounce fix
pick 9d8e7f6 Add search input field
pick 5e6f7a8 Actually fix the debounce bug

# after reordering the lines:
pick 5e6f7a8 Actually fix the debounce bug
pick 9d8e7f6 Add search input field

Dropping a commit removes it from history entirely — either by changing its action to drop, or simply deleting its line from the plan altogether, which has the same effect:

pick 9d8e7f6 Add search input field
drop 4b3c2d1 Accidentally committed debug console.log
Reordering commits that depend on each other (one edits a file the earlier one created) can produce conflicts during the replay — Git will pause exactly as it does for any other rebase conflict, and the same resolve/add/continue cycle applies.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Never Rebase Shared History
sections.content:
Everything in this lesson so far has been safe because it assumed one condition: the commits being rebased exist only on your machine, or on a branch nobody else has based work on yet. That condition is not optional — it is the single most important rule about rebasing.

The golden rule of rebasing: never rebase commits that have already been pushed and that someone else may have pulled or built work on top of. Rebasing rewrites those commits into new ones with new hashes. Anyone who already has the old commits now has a history that has diverged from yours in a way git pull cannot cleanly reconcile.

This rule applies specifically to shared branches — typically main, and any long-lived branch other people actively pull from. A private feature branch that only you push to is generally safe to rebase, even after pushing, as long as you are certain nobody else has pulled it.

Repeat it plainly, because it is worth repeating: rebase freely on branches only you touch, never on branches other people are already working from. When a feature branch becomes a shared pull-request branch with someone else's commits added to it, or once other people have explicitly pulled it, treat it as shared from that point on.

sections.title: What Breaks When You Rebase Shared Commits Anyway
sections.content:
Understanding what actually goes wrong makes the golden rule stick better than just being told to follow it. Say you rebase a branch that a teammate already pulled:

git rebase -i HEAD~3
git push
# ! [rejected]        feature/search -> feature/search (non-fast-forward)
# error: failed to push some refs

Git rejects the plain push immediately, because your local branch and the remote branch no longer share the same commit history — from the remote's point of view, your rebased commits are entirely new and unrelated to what it already has. The only way to push a rebased branch over its old remote version is a force push:

git push --force-with-lease

That command succeeds, but now your teammate's local branch still points at the old, now-discarded commits. Their next git pull either produces confusing duplicate-looking commits, or a merge conflict between commits that are actually the same change under two different hashes. They typically have to manually reset their local branch to match yours to recover cleanly — real, avoidable disruption to their work caused entirely by a rebase that should have been a merge, or should have been coordinated with them first.

Prefer --force-with-lease over plain --force when you do intentionally need to force-push your own branch — it refuses the push if the remote has commits you haven't seen yet, protecting against overwriting someone else's work you didn't know about.

sections.title: Scenario: Cleaning Up Before, Not After, a Push
sections.content:
A developer is working on feature/report-export alone, with three messy commits: "add button," "wip," and "fix export bug." Before opening a pull request, they clean it up:

git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# replays the three commits on top of the latest main, resolving one small conflict

git rebase -i HEAD~3
# squash the three commits into one, rewrite the message:
# "Add CSV export button to reports page"

git push -u origin feature/report-export

Because this branch was never pushed before this point, nobody else has a copy of the old, messy commits — there is nothing to break. The pull request opens showing one clean commit built on current main, easy for a reviewer to read top to bottom.

A week later, a reviewer asks for a small change. The developer's instinct is to rebase again to keep history tidy — but the branch has since been pushed, reviewed, and another teammate pulled it locally to test the export feature. This time, rebasing would rewrite commits that teammate already has. Following the golden rule, the developer instead commits the fix normally and pushes it as a new commit on top, leaving the existing history untouched — the pull request updates cleanly, and nobody's local branch is disrupted.

sections.title: The Mid-Feature Interruption
sections.content:
Picture this: three hours into refactoring the checkout module, files across four directories are half-edited, and nothing compiles cleanly yet. Nothing is ready to commit. Then a message arrives — production is throwing errors and a customer cannot complete payment. The task is to switch to main, cut a hotfix branch, and ship a fix in the next ten minutes.

Committing broken work just to switch branches pollutes history with a commit that will need to be undone or amended later. Discarding the changes loses three hours of work. Neither option is acceptable.

This is exactly the situation git stash exists for. It takes uncommitted changes — staged and unstaged — and saves them on a hidden stack separate from any branch, restoring the working directory to a clean state matching the last commit. Branches can then be switched freely, the urgent work done, and the original changes brought back exactly as they were.

Stash is local-only and temporary by design. It is not meant to replace commits for anything meant to be kept long-term or shared with teammates — it is a scratch space for exactly this kind of interruption.

sections.title: Saving Work With git stash push
sections.content:
The simplest form stashes everything tracked and modified in one step:

git stash
# Saved working directory and index state WIP on feature/checkout-refactor: a1b2c3d Add discount logic

This is shorthand for git stash push, the full command. Always prefer adding a message so the stash is identifiable later — with several stashes queued up, "WIP on feature/checkout-refactor" tells nothing useful:

git stash push -m "mid-refactor, discount calc not yet wired up"
# Saved working directory and index state On feature/checkout-refactor: mid-refactor, discount calc not yet wired up

After either command, git status shows a clean working tree, as if the changes never happened. They have not been lost; they have been moved onto the stash stack. Another branch can now be checked out safely:

git checkout main
git checkout -b hotfix/payment-500-error

Stashing only ever touches the local working directory and index. It never affects the remote or any other branch, which is what makes it safe to reach for mid-crisis.

sections.title: Tracking Multiple Stashes
sections.content:
Stash is a stack, not a single slot. Stashing can happen more than once, and each entry is kept until it is explicitly removed:

git stash list
# stash@{0}: On feature/checkout-refactor: mid-refactor, discount calc not yet wired up
# stash@{1}: On feature/user-profile: WIP avatar upload validation

Each entry is addressed by its stash@{n} reference, with stash@{0} always the most recently created. This matters once more than one stash exists — commands that act on "the stash" without an explicit reference always target stash@{0}, so an old forgotten stash from last week can silently sit at stash@{2} while work continues on top of it.

It is worth developing the habit of running git stash list before stashing new work, simply to notice anything left over from a previous interruption. A stash that has sat for weeks is a signal it should either be applied and finished, or dropped because it is no longer needed.

Name every stash with -m. "WIP" six times over in git stash list is indistinguishable and forces inspecting each one just to find the right work.

sections.title: Pop vs Apply: Why the Difference Matters
sections.content:
Bringing stashed changes back has two commands that look similar but behave differently:

git stash pop
# reapplies stash@{0} to the working directory AND removes it from the stash list

git stash apply
# reapplies stash@{0} to the working directory but LEAVES it on the stash list

pop is the more common choice: it restores the changes and cleans up the stash entry in one step, since most of the time work is stashed with the intent of resuming it immediately and only once.

apply is useful when the same stashed changes need to be reused in more than one place — for example applying an experimental change to two different branches to compare results, or when there is uncertainty about whether the apply will go cleanly and the stash should remain as a safety net.

A critical detail: if applying a stash produces a conflict, neither pop nor apply removes the stash entry, even though pop normally would. Git leaves the stash in place until the conflict is resolved and it is explicitly dropped, so a failed pop never silently loses work.

git stash apply stash@{1}

Either command accepts a specific stash reference; without one, both default to stash@{0}.

sections.title: Inspecting a Stash Before Touching It
sections.content:
Applying a stash blind, especially an old one, is a common source of surprise conflicts. git stash show allows a look before committing to reapply anything:

git stash show
#  src/checkout/discount.ts | 14 +++++++-------
#  src/checkout/cart.ts     |  6 ++++--
#  2 files changed, 11 insertions(+), 9 deletions(-)

That gives a summary of files touched, but not the actual changes. Add -p (patch mode) to see the full diff, exactly as git diff would show it:

git stash show -p stash@{1}

This is especially valuable when git stash list turns up an entry from weeks ago with a vague or missing message. Reviewing the patch reveals whether it is still relevant, whether the surrounding code has since changed enough that applying it would conflict, or whether it is safe to simply drop.

Treat git stash show -p as a read-only preview. It does not touch the working directory at all, so there is no risk in checking an uncertain stash before deciding what to do with it.

sections.title: Stashing Untracked and Ignored Files
sections.content:
By default, git stash only stashes changes to files Git already tracks. Brand-new files created but not yet git added are left sitting in the working directory untouched:

git status
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified: src/checkout/cart.ts
# Untracked files:
#   src/checkout/discount-preview.ts

If a clean switch to another branch is required, that leftover untracked file can cause a checkout to fail, or worse, silently carry over onto the branch being switched to since it was never part of any commit. Include untracked files in the stash with -u:

git stash push -u -m "mid-refactor including new discount preview file"

There is also -a (--all), which goes further and stashes ignored files too — files matched by .gitignore, such as local build output. This is rarely what is needed and can stash things like node_modules if ignore rules are broad, so reach for -u as the default and reserve -a for the specific case where an ignored file genuinely needs to travel with the stash.

sections.title: When a Stash Pop Conflicts
sections.content:
If the branch has moved on since stashing — someone else's commits landed, or new local changes were made — reapplying a stash can conflict just like a merge:

git stash pop
# Auto-merging src/checkout/cart.ts
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/checkout/cart.ts
# The stash entry is kept in case you need it again.

Git leaves conflict markers in the affected files, exactly as it does for a merge conflict. Resolve them the same way: open each conflicted file, choose or combine the correct content, remove the markers, then stage the result:

git add src/checkout/cart.ts

Note the important difference from a normal pop: because the pop encountered a conflict, Git does not automatically drop the stash entry, even after resolution and staging finish. Check git stash list once resolution is done, and drop it manually if it is no longer needed:

git stash drop stash@{0}
If a stash pop conflict looks too tangled to sort out by hand, git stash drop is not the escape hatch — that deletes the stash entirely. Resolve the conflict, or discard the working-file changes with git checkout -- . and leave the stash for later.

sections.title: Cleaning Up the Stash Stack
sections.content:
Stash entries do not expire and are not cleaned up automatically. Left unmanaged, git stash list can accumulate entries from months of interruptions, most of them stale or already superseded by other changes.

git stash drop stash@{2}
# drops a single named entry

git stash clear
# removes every stash entry -- use with real caution

git stash drop removes one specific entry and is the safer, deliberate choice. git stash clear wipes the entire stack in one shot with no confirmation and no way to recover the entries afterward — reserve it for situations where every single stash is confirmed to be junk, such as after a cleanup pass where each one was individually reviewed with show -p first.

Stashes are not backed up anywhere and are not part of any branch history. If a stashed change genuinely matters, get it applied and committed rather than leaving it parked indefinitely on the stack.

A useful habit on a team: treat an old, unexplained stash entry the same way as an old, unexplained branch — either finish what it represents or delete it, rather than letting it linger as unreadable clutter.

sections.title: End to End: From Refactor to Hotfix and Back
sections.content:
Return to the opening scenario and walk it through with the actual commands. Three hours into the checkout refactor, the production alert comes in:

git stash push -u -m "mid-refactor: discount calc + new preview file"
git status
# working tree clean

Switch to main, branch for the fix, and ship it:

git checkout main
git pull
git checkout -b hotfix/payment-500-error
# ...fix the bug...
git add src/payments/gateway.ts
git commit -m "Fix null reference on payment gateway timeout"
git push -u origin hotfix/payment-500-error

Once the hotfix is merged and production is stable, return to the interrupted feature branch:

git checkout feature/checkout-refactor
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On feature/checkout-refactor: mid-refactor: discount calc + new preview file
git stash pop

The working directory comes back exactly as it was left, the stash entry is removed automatically since the pop applied cleanly, and the refactor continues without the interruption ever touching the branch's commit history.

sections.title: Why Branches Aren't Enough for Releases
sections.content:
A branch is a moving pointer — every new commit on main shifts what main points to. That behavior is exactly right for ongoing development, but wrong for marking a release. Six months from now, "the commit that was main when version 2.1.0 shipped" is not something a branch can answer, because main has moved hundreds of commits since.

A tag solves this by pointing at one specific commit permanently. Unlike a branch, a tag never moves on its own — once created, v2.1.0 refers to that exact commit forever, regardless of how much further development happens afterward.

git tag v2.1.0

This is the core reason tags exist: to give a permanent, human-readable name to a specific point in history — almost always the exact commit that was built and shipped as a release — so that commit can be found again unambiguously at any point in the future, for debugging a production issue, auditing what changed between releases, or rolling back.

sections.title: Lightweight Tags
sections.content:
The simplest tag is a lightweight tag — just a named pointer to a commit, with no additional metadata:

git tag v0.1.0-internal

This creates a reference at the current HEAD. It behaves almost like a branch name that never moves: no author, no date, no message is stored, only the pointer itself. Lightweight tags are fine for quick, private, throwaway markers — flagging a commit before trying something risky, or marking a build for local testing that will never be referenced again.

They are generally not what is wanted for anything representing an actual software release. Because they carry no metadata, there is no record of who created the tag, when, or why — information that matters the moment someone needs to understand a release months later.

git tag
# v0.1.0-internal
# v1.0.0

Running git tag with no arguments lists every tag in the repository, lightweight and annotated together — nothing in the output distinguishes which is which without inspecting each one individually.

sections.title: Annotated Tags: The Standard for Real Releases
sections.content:
An annotated tag is a full object in Git's database, not just a pointer. Creating one requires -a and a message with -m:

git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0: add SSO login, fix export timeout"

Unlike a lightweight tag, this stores the tagger's name and email, the date it was created, and the message — the same kind of metadata a commit carries. Because it is a real object, git show displays that metadata alongside the commit it points to:

git show v1.2.0
# tag v1.2.0
# Tagger: Priya Shah <priya@example.com>
# Date:   Wed Sep 17 10:04:22 2026 +0000
#
# Release 1.2.0: add SSO login, fix export timeout
#
# commit a1b2c3d...

This is why annotated tags are the standard for anything representing an actual release, version, or build that gets deployed. The metadata answers exactly the questions that matter later: who cut this release, when, and what changed. Treat lightweight tags as scratch markers and annotated tags as the real thing.

Default to -a for every tag unless it is a genuinely throwaway local marker known to never be pushed or referenced again.

sections.title: Semantic Versioning Basics
sections.content:
Most projects that tag releases follow semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, for example v2.4.1. Each position means something specific, and bumping the wrong one sends the wrong signal to anyone depending on the software:

  • MAJOR — incremented for breaking changes: anything that could require consumers to update their own code to keep working (e.g. 1.9.3 to 2.0.0).
  • MINOR — incremented for new functionality that remains backward compatible: new features, new optional parameters, nothing that breaks existing usage (e.g. 2.0.0 to 2.1.0).
  • PATCH — incremented for backward-compatible bug fixes only, no new functionality (e.g. 2.1.0 to 2.1.1).
git tag -a v2.1.1 -m "Patch: fix off-by-one error in pagination"

The discipline matters because tools and teammates often make real decisions based on the version number alone — an automated dependency updater might auto-apply patch and minor bumps but require manual review for a major bump. Mislabeling a breaking change as a minor version defeats that safeguard entirely.

sections.title: The Push Surprise: Tags Don't Go With git push
sections.content:
This catches nearly everyone the first time: creating a tag locally does not send it to the remote, even after a normal git push:

git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0"
git push
# pushes commits, but v1.2.0 is nowhere on the remote

Tags are pushed explicitly, either one at a time or all at once. To push a single tag:

git push origin v1.2.0

To push every local tag not yet on the remote:

git push --tags

The one-at-a-time form is usually the better habit on a shared repository, since --tags pushes every local tag indiscriminately, including any private or experimental ones never meant to be shared. Push the specific tag a release actually needs.

A tag that exists only locally provides none of the benefit tags are for — nobody else, no CI pipeline, and no deployment tool can see it. If a release process depends on a tag existing, confirm it was actually pushed, not just created.

sections.title: Listing, Finding, and Deleting Tags
sections.content:
Beyond a plain git tag, patterns and searches narrow down a long tag list:

git tag -l "v1.*"
# v1.0.0
# v1.1.0
# v1.2.0

To see a tag's message alongside its name in one pass:

git tag -n

Deleting a tag has to happen in two places, since it exists locally and, if pushed, on the remote as well. Deleting locally does not touch the remote copy:

git tag -d v1.2.0-beta
# Deleted tag 'v1.2.0-beta' (was a1b2c3d)

git push origin --delete v1.2.0-beta

Deleting a tag that other people or systems already depend on — a CI pipeline that deploys from it, or a colleague who already checked it out — is disruptive, since the reference simply disappears out from under them. Reserve tag deletion for tags created by mistake rather than as routine cleanup.

sections.title: Checking Out a Tag to Inspect Old Code
sections.content:
Because a tag points at an exact commit, checking one out is the reliable way to see precisely what shipped in a given release:

git checkout v1.2.0
# Note: switching to 'v1.2.0'.
# You are in 'detached HEAD' state...

Git warns about detached HEAD because a tag is not a branch — there is no branch pointer moving forward while looking around, only a direct reference to one commit. New commits made in this state are not attached to any branch and can be lost once switching away, unless explicitly saved onto a new branch first.

git checkout -b hotfix/from-v1.2.0

For pure inspection — reading old code, running an old build locally, comparing behavior against the current version — detached HEAD is completely fine and expected; just check out a different branch when finished. A full explanation of detached HEAD and how to recover from it belongs in its own lesson; the short version here is: checking out a tag is safe to look, risky to edit without branching first.

sections.title: Tagging a Commit That Already Happened
sections.content:
Tags do not have to be created at HEAD. A release is sometimes tagged after the fact — for example, discovering that the commit that should have been tagged v1.3.0 was three commits back, since work continued on main before anyone remembered to tag it:

git log --oneline -5
# f4e5d6c Update changelog for next cycle
# c9d8e7f Start work on next feature
# a1b2c3d Fix export timeout (this is the real release commit)
# ...

git tag -a v1.3.0 a1b2c3d -m "Release 1.3.0: fix export timeout"
git push origin v1.3.0

Appending the commit hash after the tag name and message points the new tag at that specific commit rather than the current HEAD. This is a normal, supported operation — nothing about tagging requires the target commit to be the newest one in the repository.

The same technique works for backfilling tags on a project that never tagged releases from the start: walk the log for the commits corresponding to each past release and tag them retroactively, giving the project's history the same permanent markers going forward.

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
sections.content:
• Forgetting to push the tag. A tag created and never pushed is invisible to CI, deployment tooling, and teammates — confirm with git ls-remote --tags origin that it actually landed.
  • Using lightweight tags for real releases. Without -a and a message, there is no record of who tagged the release or why — reach for annotated tags by default.
  • Mislabeling the version bump. Shipping a breaking change under a minor or patch version number breaks the trust automated tooling and teammates place in semantic versioning.
  • Committing while in detached HEAD after checking out a tag. Work done there is not attached to any branch and can be lost — branch off first with git checkout -b before making any real changes.
  • Deleting a tag other systems already depend on. If a pipeline deploys from a tag, deleting it can break that pipeline with no warning; confirm nothing depends on a tag before removing it.
  • Reusing a tag name for a different commit. Retagging v1.2.0 onto a new commit means anyone who already has the old tag now disagrees with the remote about what it points to — treat pushed tag names as permanent.

sections.title: When Conflicts Show Up Mid-Operation
sections.content:
A basic merge conflict is disruptive but familiar: run git merge, get conflict markers, resolve them, make one commit, done. Conflicts get more confusing the moment they show up in the middle of a multi-step operation — a rebase replaying ten commits one at a time, or a cherry-pick applying a single commit onto an unrelated branch.

The confusion is not really about the conflict itself — the markers look identical either way. It is about what happens next. A merge conflict resolves into a single new commit. A rebase or cherry-pick conflict resolves into continuing an operation that is already partway through, and using the wrong next command leaves the repository in a half-finished, confusing state.

git rebase main
# Auto-merging src/api/client.ts
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/api/client.ts
# error: could not apply c9d8e7f... Add retry logic

This lesson covers exactly that distinction, plus the tools for handling a conflict too messy to sort out by reading raw markers.

sections.title: Rebase Conflicts: Resolve, Add, Continue
sections.content:
A rebase replays each commit, one at a time, onto a new base. When a commit's changes cannot apply cleanly, the rebase pauses on that exact commit and leaves conflict markers in the affected files, the same format as any other conflict:

git status
# rebase in progress; onto 7f8e9d0
# You have unmerged paths.
#   both modified:   src/api/client.ts

Edit the file, choose the correct content, and remove the markers. Then stage the resolved file — but do not commit it:

git add src/api/client.ts
git rebase --continue

git rebase --continue finishes applying the current commit using the staged resolution as its new content, then moves on to replay the next commit in the sequence. If that next commit also conflicts, the same cycle repeats: resolve, add, rebase --continue, until every commit has been replayed.

Never run git commit directly during a rebase conflict. The rebase machinery expects --continue to create the commit itself from the staged resolution — committing manually can leave the rebase state confused about what step it is on.

sections.title: Cherry-Pick Conflicts Work the Same Way
sections.content:
git cherry-pick applies a single commit from elsewhere onto the current branch — useful for pulling one specific fix onto a release branch without bringing along everything else from the source branch. It can conflict for the same reason a rebase step can: the surrounding code on the target branch has diverged from what the commit expects.

git cherry-pick a1b2c3d
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/payments/gateway.ts
# error: could not apply a1b2c3d... Fix null reference on timeout

The resolution pattern mirrors rebase exactly: resolve the markers, stage the result, then continue the operation rather than committing directly:

git add src/payments/gateway.ts
git cherry-pick --continue

Because a cherry-pick applies only one commit, --continue finishes that single commit and the operation ends there — unless multiple commits were cherry-picked in one invocation (git cherry-pick A B C), in which case it moves on to the next one just as a rebase would.

sections.title: Backing Out Cleanly: --abort
sections.content:
Sometimes a conflict, once actually opened up, turns out to be more than can be safely resolved in the moment — the change is more invasive than expected, or it becomes clear the wrong commit was picked entirely. Both rebase and cherry-pick support a full, clean bailout:

git rebase --abort
git cherry-pick --abort

Either command returns the branch to exactly the state it was in before the operation started — as if the rebase or cherry-pick had never been run. Any conflict markers, partial resolutions, or staged changes from the interrupted attempt are discarded entirely.

This is the safe default when a conflict resolution goes sideways under time pressure. Trying to force through a resolution that is not actually understood risks silently introducing a bug that looks like a clean merge but is functionally wrong. Abort, take a breath, and either resolve it more carefully or ask for a second pair of eyes before retrying.

There is also git rebase --skip, which drops the current conflicting commit entirely and moves to the next one — different from --abort, and rarely the right choice unless that specific commit's changes are confirmed to no longer be needed.

sections.title: Reading git diff During a Conflict
sections.content:
Conflict markers show both sides stacked together, which gets hard to read once a file has more than one conflicting hunk. git diff, run while a conflict is unresolved, gives a clearer view of exactly what changed on each side:

git diff
# diff --cc src/api/client.ts
# index a1b2c3d,c9d8e7f..0000000
# --- a/src/api/client.ts
# +++ b/src/api/client.ts

This combined diff format marks lines that differ between the two sides with a leading plus or minus per side, rather than the raw marker block. For a conflict during a rebase specifically, it helps to think of the two sides precisely:

  • During a rebase, "ours" is the branch being rebased onto (the new base), and "theirs" is the commit currently being replayed — the reverse of what many people expect from a merge.
  • During a merge, "ours" is the branch that was checked out when the merge started, and "theirs" is the branch being merged in.

Getting this backward is a common source of resolving a rebase conflict exactly wrong while believing it was done correctly — when in doubt, read the actual diff rather than trusting which side "ours" and "theirs" intuitively feel like.

sections.title: Using git mergetool for a Genuinely Messy Conflict
sections.content:
Some conflicts are small enough to resolve directly in an editor — a single line, an obvious choice. Others involve overlapping changes across many lines where reading raw markers becomes genuinely hard to reason about correctly. For those, a visual merge tool is worth reaching for instead of hand-editing:

git mergetool

This launches whichever merge tool is configured — common choices include vimdiff, kdiff3, meld, or an IDE's built-in three-way merge view. It presents the base version, both sides, and the merged result as separate panes, allowing individual changes to be picked visually rather than parsing marker syntax under pressure.

git config --global merge.tool vscode
git config --global mergetool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait $MERGED'

Once the tool reports the file resolved, it stages the result automatically in most configurations; confirm with git status, then continue the operation the same way as any other conflict — rebase --continue or cherry-pick --continue, matching whichever operation triggered it.

sections.title: Merge Conflict vs Rebase/Cherry-Pick Conflict: The Contrast
sections.content:
The markers are identical in every case. What differs is the command that comes after resolving them, and getting this wrong is the single most common point of confusion when a conflict happens mid-operation rather than during a plain merge:

  • Merge conflict: resolve, git add, git commit (creates one new merge commit).
  • Rebase conflict: resolve, git add, git rebase --continue (never a manual commit — the rebase creates it).
  • Cherry-pick conflict: resolve, git add, git cherry-pick --continue (same pattern as rebase).

Running git commit in the middle of a rebase, instead of --continue, is a mistake worth specifically watching for — it can create a stray commit that confuses the remaining steps of the rebase, since the rebase machinery is not expecting a manual commit to appear mid-sequence.

The reliable habit: before touching a single conflict marker, run git status. It states plainly which operation is in progress — "rebase in progress", "You are currently cherry-picking", or a plain merge conflict — and that answer determines which continuation command comes next.

sections.title: A Rebase Conflict Under Real Time Pressure
sections.content:
A release branch needs one urgent fix cherry-picked over from main before a deploy in twenty minutes. The branch has diverged enough that a conflict is likely:

git checkout release/2.4
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/payments/gateway.ts

First, confirm exactly what state things are in rather than guessing:

git status
# You are currently cherry-picking commit a1b2c3d.
git diff

The diff shows the conflict is a single overlapping condition check — small enough to resolve directly rather than pulling up a merge tool. Edit the file, remove the markers, keep both the release branch's existing null check and the incoming retry logic:

git add src/payments/gateway.ts
git cherry-pick --continue

The cherry-pick finishes, creating a single new commit on release/2.4 with the fix applied. Push it and the deploy proceeds on schedule:

git push origin release/2.4

Had the diff revealed something more tangled — say, the retry logic depended on a function signature that had changed entirely — git cherry-pick --abort would have been the right call: back out cleanly, get the fix properly reviewed, and retry once there is time to do it right.

sections.title: Why Branching Strategy Is a Real Decision
sections.content:
Every team using Git ends up answering the same set of questions, whether deliberately or by accident: how long does a branch live before merging back? Does main always reflect what's in production, or does a separate branch track releases? How many branches typically exist at once, and how much process surrounds getting a change from a developer's laptop into production?

Different answers to these questions are not equally good or bad in the abstract — they are better or worse fits for a team's actual release cadence, team size, and QA process. A strategy built for shipping a mobile app twice a year looks nothing like one built for a SaaS product deploying fifty times a day, and applying one team's process to the other's situation creates friction rather than discipline.

This lesson compares three real, widely used branching strategies concretely — their actual branch structure, a rough timeline from commit to production, and the kind of team each one fits — as a foundation for choosing deliberately rather than by default.

sections.title: Git Flow: Structure and Timeline
sections.content:
Git Flow is the most structured of the three, built around two long-lived branches and several categories of short-lived supporting branches:

  • main — always reflects exactly what is currently in production.
  • develop — the integration branch where finished features accumulate between releases.
  • feature/* — branched from develop, merged back into develop when done.
  • release/* — branched from develop when preparing a release, used for final QA and stabilization, then merged into both main and develop.
  • hotfix/* — branched directly from main for urgent production fixes, merged into both main and develop.
git checkout develop
git checkout -b feature/checkout-redesign
# ...work, then merge back into develop...
git checkout develop
git checkout -b release/2.5.0
# ...stabilize, QA signs off...
git checkout main
git merge release/2.5.0
git tag -a v2.5.0 -m "Release 2.5.0"

Commit-to-production timeline is measured in days to weeks: a feature merges into develop, sits alongside other in-progress work until a release branch is cut, goes through a dedicated stabilization and QA cycle, and only then reaches main and production.

sections.title: Git Flow: Where It Fits
sections.content:
Consider a team shipping enterprise desktop software on a quarterly release train, with a dedicated QA team that runs a two-week regression pass before every release. Features land continuously in develop throughout the quarter; nothing touches main until QA has signed off on a release branch as a whole. If a critical bug surfaces in the field between releases, hotfix/* gives a clean path to patch production without pulling in unfinished work sitting in develop.

This is exactly the situation Git Flow is built for: a real gap between "code is written" and "code is in production," filled by a deliberate, scheduled stabilization phase.

The same structure is a poor fit for a team deploying continuously — the extra branches and merge steps (develop, then a release branch, then main) add real ceremony with no purpose when every change goes to production within hours anyway. A team in that position typically finds Git Flow slows delivery down without buying anything, since there is no scheduled release window for the release-branch stabilization step to actually serve.

sections.title: GitHub Flow: Structure and Timeline
sections.content:
GitHub Flow strips branching down to almost nothing: one long-lived branch, main, plus short-lived feature branches that merge directly back into it.

git checkout main
git pull
git checkout -b add-export-csv
# ...commit work...
git push -u origin add-export-csv
# open a pull request against main
# after review and CI pass, merge directly into main

There is no develop branch and no dedicated release branch. main is deployable at all times by convention — every merge into it is expected to be safe to ship, often triggering an automatic deploy. A feature branch typically lives for hours to a few days, not weeks, since the whole model depends on branches staying small enough to review and merge quickly.

Commit-to-production timeline is measured in hours: a pull request merges into main, and deployment follows immediately or on the next scheduled deploy, without a separate stabilization phase standing between merge and production.

sections.title: GitHub Flow: Where It Fits
sections.content:
Consider a small SaaS product team of six engineers, deploying to production several times a day, with test coverage and CI trusted enough that a green build is treated as ready to ship. A developer branches off main for a new feature, opens a pull request within a day, gets it reviewed, and merges — the change is live within the hour.

This is the situation GitHub Flow fits well: a small enough team that a long-lived integration branch would add coordination overhead without a corresponding benefit, and a deploy pipeline trusted enough that "merged" and "safe to ship" are treated as effectively the same thing.

It fits poorly for a team that needs a real stabilization window before release — say, a product requiring a manual QA pass across many device configurations before anything reaches users. Without a release branch to hold candidate changes still while that QA pass runs, GitHub Flow offers nowhere to put that process; every merge to main is expected to go out essentially immediately.

sections.title: Trunk-Based Development: Structure and Timeline
sections.content:
Trunk-Based Development goes further than GitHub Flow: branches, when used at all, live for under a day, and many changes are committed directly to trunk (main) behind a feature flag rather than through a branch and pull request at all.

git checkout main
git pull
# small change, feature-flagged
git add src/checkout/new-flow.ts
git commit -m "Add new checkout flow behind feature flag CHECKOUT_V2"
git push origin main

The defining mechanic is the feature flag: incomplete or unreleased functionality is merged into main continuously, wrapped in a runtime flag that keeps it inactive in production until it is ready. This decouples "merged to trunk" from "visible to users" entirely, which is what makes committing directly to trunk safe even for work spanning multiple days.

Commit-to-production timeline is measured in minutes to hours — often the shortest of the three — since there is no branch-based review gate standing between a commit and the next deploy; safety instead comes from strong automated testing, small incremental commits, and flags controlling exposure.

sections.title: Trunk-Based Development: Where It Fits
sections.content:
Consider a large engineering organization with hundreds of developers committing to a shared codebase, deploying continuously throughout the day, with a mature automated test suite and feature-flagging infrastructure already in place.
