Long-lived feature branches in this environment become a liability: with that many people working in parallel, a branch that lives for a week accumulates enough drift from trunk that merging it back becomes its own multi-day project of conflict resolution.

This is exactly what Trunk-Based Development is optimized for — keeping every branch's lifespan short enough that divergence never has room to build up, at the scale where CI/CD throughput matters more than any individual change having a dedicated review branch.

It fits poorly for a small team without mature test automation or flagging infrastructure already in place — committing straight to trunk without a strong safety net (thorough CI, feature flags to control exposure) risks shipping broken or half-finished functionality directly to production with no review gate catching it first.

sections.title: The Three Side by Side
sections.content:
• Branch lifespan: Git Flow — weeks (release branches); GitHub Flow — hours to days; Trunk-Based — hours or less, often no branch at all.
  • Long-lived branches: Git Flow has two (main, develop); GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based each have one (main).
  • Stabilization phase: Git Flow has a dedicated release branch for it; GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based have none — safety comes from CI and, for Trunk-Based, feature flags instead.
  • Commit-to-production time: Git Flow — days to weeks; GitHub Flow — hours; Trunk-Based — minutes to hours.
  • Review mechanism: Git Flow and GitHub Flow both rely on pull requests before merge; Trunk-Based often skips this for trunk commits, relying on automated tests and flags instead.

None of these differences make one strategy universally better — each trades process and ceremony against speed differently, and the right trade depends entirely on what a specific team actually needs.

sections.title: Choosing a Strategy
sections.content:
Three factors decide which strategy actually fits a given team, more reliably than any general preference for "simpler" or "more structured":

  • Team size. Small teams coordinate informally and tolerate a lighter process; large teams need branch lifespans short enough that parallel work does not constantly collide, which pushes toward Trunk-Based as headcount grows.
  • Release cadence. A scheduled, infrequent release (monthly, quarterly) benefits from Git Flow's dedicated release branch to hold things still during stabilization. Continuous deployment, releasing many times a day, gets no benefit from that same structure and is better served by GitHub Flow or Trunk-Based.
  • QA process. A manual or lengthy QA pass needs somewhere to hold a release candidate still while it runs — a release branch. A team relying primarily on automated tests and feature flags for safety does not need that holding branch at all.

A useful gut check: a team currently on Git Flow that has quietly stopped doing real release-branch stabilization is probably better served by GitHub Flow. A GitHub Flow team growing past a few dozen engineers and hitting constant merge conflicts on main is probably outgrowing it toward Trunk-Based. The strategy should match the team's actual release process, not the other way around.

title: Feature Branch Workflow, End to End

sections.title: Starting the Ticket
sections.content:
Maya picks up ticket CM-482: add CSV export to the reports page. Before writing any code, the first step is making sure the new branch starts from the latest version of main, not from whatever was checked out last:

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout -b feature/CM-482-csv-export

Branching from a stale local main is a common, avoidable source of pain later — every commit made on the new branch inherits whatever the local main was missing, which surfaces as extra, unrelated-looking changes the first time the branch is rebased or compared against the real, current main. Pulling first costs a few seconds and avoids that entirely.

The branch name follows the team's convention — a short type prefix, the ticket number, and a brief description — which makes the branch identifiable in git branch, in CI logs, and in the eventual pull request without needing to open the ticket to remember what it was for.

sections.title: Committing Incrementally
sections.content:
Rather than writing the entire feature and committing it as one large change at the end, Maya commits in small, logical steps as the work actually progresses through the day:

git add src/reports/export-csv.ts
git commit -m "Add CSV export utility function"

git add src/reports/reports.component.ts
git commit -m "Wire export button to CSV utility"

git add src/reports/reports.component.spec.ts
git commit -m "Add tests for CSV export"

Each commit message describes what changed and stays specific enough to be useful later — "Add CSV export utility function" tells a reviewer or a future git blame reader something real, unlike a generic "update" or "wip" that would need the diff opened just to understand what happened.

Small commits also make the branch easier to review later: a reviewer can follow the feature being built up logically, and if something later needs to be reverted, a small targeted commit is far easier to back out than one enormous one bundling unrelated changes together.

sections.title: Keeping the Branch Current With Rebase
sections.content:
Two days into the ticket, main has moved — a teammate merged an unrelated change to the same reports module. Rather than letting the branch drift further out of sync, Maya rebases onto the latest main partway through the work:

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout feature/CM-482-csv-export
git rebase main

This replays each of the branch's commits, one at a time, on top of the current tip of main, rather than creating a merge commit tangling the two histories together. If a conflict comes up during the replay, it is resolved the same way as any rebase conflict: fix the file, git add it, then git rebase --continue rather than a manual commit.

git push --force-with-lease

Rebasing rewrites the branch's commit hashes, so pushing the updated branch requires a force push. --force-with-lease is the safer form — it refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else has pushed to it since it was last fetched, which a plain --force would silently clobber.

sections.title: Pushing and Opening the Pull Request
sections.content:
With the feature functionally complete, Maya pushes the branch and opens a pull request against main:

git push -u origin feature/CM-482-csv-export

The -u flag sets up tracking between the local branch and its remote counterpart, so future pushes and pulls on this branch need no further arguments. The pull request description references the ticket, briefly explains the approach, and calls out anything a reviewer should pay particular attention to — in this case, that the export intentionally excludes archived reports, a decision worth flagging rather than leaving for a reviewer to question independently.

CI runs automatically against the pushed branch — tests, linting, a build check — and the pull request is not considered ready for review until that passes cleanly. Opening the PR early, even before every commit is polished, gives teammates visibility into work in progress and lets CI catch problems well before the branch is considered done.

sections.title: Responding to Review Feedback
sections.content:
A reviewer leaves two comments: one asking for a null check on an edge case, the other pointing out that a variable name is misleading. Maya addresses both, and the choice of how to commit the fix depends on what the comment actually calls for:

git add src/reports/export-csv.ts
git commit -m "Add null check for empty report set"
git push

For the null check — a real, separate piece of logic — a new commit keeps the change visible in the PR's commit history and easy for the reviewer to re-review in isolation, without re-reading the entire diff again.

The variable rename is cosmetic and belongs to the same commit it should have been part of originally, so it is folded in with an amend instead of adding a fourth trivial commit:

git add src/reports/export-csv.ts
git commit --amend --no-edit
git push --force-with-lease

Both are legitimate choices depending on the nature of the feedback — new commits for substantive changes worth reviewing on their own, --amend or an interactive rebase for cleanup that would just be noise as a standalone commit.

sections.title: Cleaning Up History Before Merge
sections.content:
By the time review wraps up, the branch has seven commits, several of them small fixups like "typo" and "fix test" that added no real value once the feature was working. Before merge, Maya squashes the noisy ones together with an interactive rebase:

git rebase -i main
# pick a1b2c3d Add CSV export utility function
# squash c9d8e7f typo
# pick f4e5d6c Wire export button to CSV utility
# squash 7f8e9d0 fix test
# pick 3c4d5e6 Add null check for empty report set

Changing pick to squash (or its shorthand s) folds that commit into the one directly above it, and Git then prompts for a combined commit message for each squashed group. The result is a smaller set of commits, each one representing a real, reviewable unit of the change, rather than the raw, messy sequence the work actually happened in.

This step is a judgment call, not a mandatory one — some teams prefer preserving the exact commit-by-commit history of how a change was developed. Whether to clean up before merge should follow the team's actual convention rather than personal preference alone.

sections.title: Merge Commit vs Squash vs Rebase Merge
sections.content:
At merge time, the team's convention for the PR itself determines which of three options is used, and each leaves a different shape in main's history:

  • Merge commit — keeps every commit from the branch, plus one new merge commit tying them together. Preserves the full, exact history of how the branch developed, at the cost of a busier main-line history with merge commits scattered through it.
  • Squash merge — combines every commit on the branch into a single new commit on main, discarding the branch's individual commit boundaries entirely. Keeps main's history linear and gives every feature exactly one commit, at the cost of losing the granular development history (still viewable on the closed PR itself, just not in main's log).
  • Rebase merge — replays the branch's individual commits directly onto main with no merge commit at all, keeping history linear while still preserving each individual commit.

For Maya's ticket, the team uses squash merge as its default — a small, well-scoped feature like this is more useful in main's history as one clean commit referencing CM-482 than as five. Larger, multi-day features where the individual commits carry real meaning are more often merge-committed or rebase-merged instead, at the team's discretion.

sections.title: Deleting the Branch After Merge
sections.content:
Once the pull request merges, the feature branch has served its purpose and should not linger. Most Git hosting tools offer a one-click delete on the remote branch right after merge; the equivalent from the command line:

git push origin --delete feature/CM-482-csv-export

The local copy still exists after the remote is deleted and needs its own cleanup:

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feature/CM-482-csv-export

git branch -d (lowercase) only deletes a branch that Git can confirm is already fully merged, refusing otherwise — a useful safety check against accidentally deleting unmerged work. -D (uppercase) forces deletion regardless, which is occasionally necessary after a squash merge specifically, since squashing produces a new commit on main that Git does not recognize as identical to the branch's original commits, causing -d to incorrectly report the branch as unmerged.

Leaving merged branches around indefinitely clutters git branch and git branch -r output for the whole team, making it harder to spot which branches represent real, active work.

sections.title: The Whole Day, End to End
sections.content:
Put together, Maya's ticket moved through one continuous sequence: branch from an up-to-date main, commit incrementally through the day's work, rebase onto main when it moved underneath the branch, push and open a pull request, respond to review with a mix of new commits and an amend, squash the noisy commits before merge, and let the team's squash-merge convention fold the branch into one clean commit on main.

git checkout main && git pull
git checkout -b feature/CM-482-csv-export
# ...commits through the day...
git rebase main
git push -u origin feature/CM-482-csv-export
# ...review, fixup commits, amend, interactive rebase...
git push --force-with-lease
# ...PR squash-merged via the hosting tool...
git checkout main && git pull
git branch -d feature/CM-482-csv-export
git push origin --delete feature/CM-482-csv-export

Nothing in this sequence is unusual or advanced on its own — each command is one covered individually elsewhere. What makes a feature branch workflow work in practice is exactly this: running the right one at the right point in a single ticket's lifecycle, from the first commit to the branch's final deletion.

sections.title: Feature Freeze and Why Release Branches Exist
sections.content:
Picture a team preparing version 1.4.0 of a product. Feature work for this release is done, but main does not stand still — other developers keep merging commits for the next release the moment their pull requests are approved. If QA tests directly against main, the code under test changes underneath them every time someone merges something new.

The fix is to declare a feature freeze: agree on a cutoff commit, then cut a dedicated release/1.4.0 branch from it. From that point forward, main is free to accept new feature work for 1.5.0 while release/1.4.0 stays frozen except for the bug fixes QA actually finds.

git checkout main
git pull origin main
# confirm the freeze commit is the tip of main right now
git log -1 --oneline

This separation is the backbone of every release strategy in this lesson: one branch keeps evolving, one branch gets stable enough to ship.

sections.title: Cutting release/1.4.0 From main
sections.content:
With the freeze point confirmed, create the release branch and push it so the whole team can see it and branch fixes from it.

git checkout -b release/1.4.0 main
git push -u origin release/1.4.0
# release/1.4.0 now exists on the remote, identical to main at this moment

From here, release/1.4.0 and main diverge on purpose. Anyone opening a pull request for a new feature targets main. Anyone fixing a bug that QA reports against the release targets release/1.4.0 instead.

Naming the branch after the version (release/1.4.0) rather than something generic like release lets multiple releases be stabilized in parallel if a team ever needs to patch an older version while preparing a newer one.

The release branch is not a snapshot that gets thrown away after shipping — it stays alive for as long as that version might need a patch, which becomes important later in this lesson.

sections.title: Stabilization: Bug Fixes Only, No New Features
sections.content:
Once release/1.4.0 exists, the team enters stabilization mode. The rule is strict: only commits that fix a defect QA has actually found are allowed onto the release branch. No new features, no impromptu refactors while you are in there, no dependency upgrades that are not fixing a reported bug.

The reason is risk. Every change carries a chance of introducing a new problem, and a release branch close to shipping has no time left to catch a fresh regression. A team that keeps adding scope to a release branch never actually stabilizes — the finish line keeps moving.

git checkout release/1.4.0
git checkout -b fix/login-timeout
# ...fix the bug...
git commit -am 'fix: correct session timeout calculation'
git checkout release/1.4.0
git merge --no-ff fix/login-timeout
git push origin release/1.4.0
If a fix was already made on main for unrelated reasons, do not merge all of main into the release branch to pick it up — that would drag in every other feature merged since the freeze too. Use git cherry-pick <commit> to bring across only that one commit.

sections.title: Tagging the Release Candidate v1.4.0-rc.1
sections.content:
Once the team believes the release branch is stable, they do not tag it v1.4.0 immediately. They tag a release candidate first, giving QA a specific, immutable commit to test against.

git checkout release/1.4.0
git tag -a v1.4.0-rc.1 -m 'Release candidate 1 for 1.4.0'
git push origin v1.4.0-rc.1

An annotated tag (-a) is used rather than a lightweight one because it records who created it, when, and why — useful history for a version that might ship or might get rejected by QA.

The candidate build gets deployed to a staging environment from this exact tag, and QA signs off against that exact commit, not against whatever release/1.4.0 happens to contain by the time they finish testing.

sections.title: QA Sign-off and Promoting to v1.4.0
sections.content:
Suppose QA finds a real bug during testing of v1.4.0-rc.1. The fix lands on release/1.4.0 the same way as before, and a new candidate is cut for re-testing:

git tag -a v1.4.0-rc.2 -m 'Release candidate 2 for 1.4.0'
git push origin v1.4.0-rc.2

This can repeat several times — rc.3, rc.4 — until QA signs off with no open defects. Once that happens, the exact commit that passed is tagged as the final release, with no code changes in between:

git tag -a v1.4.0 -m 'Release 1.4.0'
git push origin v1.4.0

v1.4.0 and the last release candidate point at the identical commit. That is the whole point: whatever QA actually approved is exactly what ships, with zero last-minute changes sneaking in between sign-off and release.

sections.title: Life After Release: main Keeps Moving
sections.content:
After v1.4.0 ships, release/1.4.0 does not get deleted. It stays as the permanent home for anything that might need to patch version 1.4.x in the future. Meanwhile main has been accumulating 1.5.0 feature work the entire time and continues to do so without interruption.

git branch -a
# main
# release/1.4.0
# release/1.5.0   (does not exist yet -- cut later, at the next freeze)

This is the payoff of the whole strategy: shipping 1.4.0 never blocked 1.5.0 development, and 1.5.0 development never destabilized what QA had already approved. The two branches simply diverge and each does its own job.

That calm does not last forever, though — production bugs have a way of showing up right after a release goes out.

sections.title: A Production Bug Forces a Hotfix
sections.content:
A week after v1.4.0 ships, a customer reports that exports silently fail for accounts with more than 10,000 rows. This is not something QA can wait for in the next scheduled release — it needs a hotfix, a small, urgent patch built directly from the exact code that is in production.

The hotfix branches off the release tag, not off main and not off whatever release/1.4.0 currently contains, because 1.5.0 feature work may already be flowing into main and the release branch may already have unrelated fixes queued for a future 1.4.x. The tag is the one guaranteed-stable starting point that matches what is actually running in production.

git checkout -b hotfix/1.4.1 v1.4.0
# fix the export pagination bug
git commit -am 'fix: paginate export queries above 10k rows'

The branch name signals both urgency and target version, making it obvious in a branch listing what it is for and how critical it is.

sections.title: Tagging v1.4.1 and Backporting to Both Branches
sections.content:
Once the hotfix is verified, it gets merged into release/1.4.0 and tagged as a patch release:

git checkout release/1.4.0
git merge --no-ff hotfix/1.4.1
git tag -a v1.4.1 -m 'Hotfix: export pagination for large accounts'
git push origin release/1.4.0 v1.4.1

This is the step teams most often get wrong: the fix must also be merged (or cherry-picked) into main. If it is not, the bug is only fixed in the 1.4.x line. When 1.5.0 is cut from main later, it will not contain this fix, and the same export bug reappears in production the moment 1.5.0 ships — a customer files what looks like a brand-new bug report for something that was already fixed once.

git checkout main
git cherry-pick <hotfix-commit-sha>
git push origin main
A hotfix that never gets backported to main is one of the most common causes of a bug coming back in the very next release. Treat the backport as part of finishing the hotfix, not an optional follow-up.

sections.title: Common Mistakes That Sink a Release
sections.content:
The mechanics above are simple; most release problems come from skipping a step under time pressure. Watch for these:

  • Releasing straight from main. Without a dedicated release branch, QA is testing a moving target and a late feature merge can slip into a release that already looked finished.
  • Letting new features onto the release branch. Once stabilization starts, every extra change is extra risk with no extra time to catch it.
  • Skipping the release candidate tag. Tagging only the final version means there is no immutable reference for what QA actually tested versus what shipped.
  • Branching a hotfix from main or from the release branch's tip instead of from the release tag, pulling in unrelated, untested changes into an urgent fix.
  • Forgetting the backport. The single most common mistake: fixing production but never merging that fix into main, guaranteeing the bug returns in the next release.
  • Deleting the release branch after shipping. It needs to stay around for as long as that version might need a future patch release.

A release strategy is only as strong as its least-followed step. Every branch, tag, and backport in this lesson exists to answer one question with certainty: what exact code is running in production right now, and where did it come from?

sections.title: What a Git Hook Actually Is
sections.content:
A Git hook is a script that Git runs automatically at a specific point in its workflow — before a commit is finalized, after a commit is made, before a push leaves the machine, and so on. Hooks are not a Git feature bolted on from outside; Git itself calls them by name at the right moment, checking whether a matching script exists and, if so, running it.

Critically, hooks are local by default. They run on the developer's own machine, using whatever script is sitting in that developer's own repository. Nothing forces every teammate to have the same hooks installed, which is both the appeal (fast, no network round trip) and the weakness (easy to skip or simply not have) of this mechanism.

ls .git/hooks
# pre-commit.sample  commit-msg.sample  pre-push.sample  ...

Every fresh Git repository ships with a folder full of .sample hook scripts as examples. None of them run until the .sample suffix is removed and the file is made executable.

sections.title: Where Hooks Live: .git/hooks/
sections.content:
Hooks live inside the repository's own .git directory, at .git/hooks/. Each hook is simply a file named after the event it responds to — pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push, and dozens of others — with no file extension required, as long as the file is executable and Git can run it (a shell script, a Node script with a shebang line, a Python script, anything the operating system can execute).

cp .git/hooks/pre-commit.sample .git/hooks/pre-commit
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

To confirm a hook actually fires, a simple one-line script that just echoes a message is a good first test before writing real logic:

#!/bin/sh
echo 'pre-commit hook is running'

If a hook script exits with a non-zero status, Git treats that as a failure and aborts the action it was guarding — a commit does not get created, a push does not go out.

sections.title: Why Hooks Aren't Committed or Shared by Default
sections.content:
The .git directory is deliberately excluded from what a repository tracks and shares — it is Git's own internal bookkeeping, not part of the project's file history. That means hooks placed in .git/hooks/ live only on the machine where they were created. Cloning the repository fresh gives a brand-new, empty .git/hooks/ folder with none of the team's hooks installed.

For a solo project this rarely matters. For a team, it means a hook that everyone should have needs to be distributed and installed by some other mechanism, since Git itself provides no way to version and share hook scripts through a normal commit.

This is exactly the gap tools like Husky fill: they store hook scripts inside the versioned project (commonly under a .husky/ folder) and wire them up automatically when a teammate runs the project's install step, so the whole team ends up running the same checks without manually copying files into .git/hooks/.

Whether a team uses a tool like that or manages hooks manually, the underlying mechanism this lesson covers — a script, an event name, an exit code Git respects — stays exactly the same.

sections.title: pre-commit: Catching Problems Before They're Committed
sections.content:
The pre-commit hook runs after git commit is invoked but before the commit is actually created, and before the commit message editor even opens. It is the natural place to run a linter or a fast subset of tests against the files about to be committed — catching an obvious mistake before it ever enters history.

#!/bin/sh
npm run lint
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo 'Lint failed -- commit aborted'
  exit 1
fi

Because this hook runs on every single commit, it needs to stay fast. A full end-to-end test suite that takes ten minutes does not belong here — it will train developers to reach for git commit --no-verify just to get on with their day, which defeats the purpose entirely.

Keep pre-commit checks scoped to only the files being committed (most linters support a staged-files-only mode) rather than re-checking the entire codebase on every commit.

sections.title: commit-msg: Enforcing a Commit Message Convention
sections.content:
The commit-msg hook runs after the developer writes a commit message but before the commit is finalized. It receives the path to a temporary file containing the message, and can inspect or reject it based on whatever rule the team wants enforced.

A widely used rule is Conventional Commits: every message starts with a type such as feat:, fix:, or chore:, optionally followed by a scope, describing what kind of change the commit makes.

feat(auth): add password reset flow
fix(export): paginate queries above 10k rows
chore(deps): bump typescript to 5.6

A minimal hook can reject anything that does not match the pattern:

#!/bin/sh
MSG=$(cat "$1")
if ! echo "$MSG" | grep -qE '^(feat|fix|chore|docs|refactor|test)(\(.+\))?: '; then
  echo 'Commit message must start with a type, e.g. fix: correct timeout bug'
  exit 1
fi

sections.title: Why Conventional Commits Enables Automated Changelogs
sections.content:
The feat: / fix: / chore: convention is not enforced for its own sake — it is enforced because it makes commit history machine-readable. A tool can walk every commit between two tags and mechanically sort them into features, fixes, and everything else, without a human reading and categorizing each one by hand.

git log v1.3.0..v1.4.0 --oneline --grep='^feat'
git log v1.3.0..v1.4.0 --oneline --grep='^fix'

This connects directly back to how a release actually gets documented: a changelog generator can produce a what's-new summary for every release, grouping every feat: commit under Features and every fix: commit under Bug Fixes, purely from the discipline enforced at commit time by the commit-msg hook.

Without this convention, generating a changelog means someone manually reading through dozens of commit messages after the fact and guessing what mattered — slow, inconsistent, and easy to skip under deadline pressure.

sections.title: pre-push: Running the Full Suite Before Code Leaves the Machine
sections.content:
The pre-push hook runs after git push is invoked but before any data actually reaches the remote. Because it only fires once per push rather than once per commit, it is the right place for a heavier check that would be too slow for pre-commit — typically the full automated test suite.

#!/bin/sh
npm test
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo 'Tests failed -- push aborted'
  exit 1
fi

This gives a developer one more chance to catch a broken test locally, before teammates ever see the broken commit on the shared remote. It does not replace continuous integration, though — a developer can always bypass a local hook, and CI is where a check becomes non-optional.

git push --no-verify skips every push hook entirely. A local hook is a helpful reminder, not a guarantee — treat anything that must never be skipped as a job for the CI pipeline instead.

sections.title: From Local Hooks to CI Gates
sections.content:
Every check described so far — lint, commit message format, test suite — can be bypassed locally with a flag or simply by a developer not having the hook installed. That is why the same checks get run again, this time somewhere a developer cannot opt out of: a continuous integration pipeline.

When a pull request is opened, CI runs the linter, the test suite, and often a commit message check again on the server. The pull request is configured so it cannot be merged until those checks pass, regardless of what happened on anyone's laptop. The same pattern extends to releases: a pipeline can require every check to pass before a tag is allowed to trigger a deployment.

# typical CI pipeline steps, conceptually
npm ci
npm run lint
npm test
# only if all of the above succeed does the pipeline continue to build and deploy

Local hooks and CI checks are not redundant with each other — they are two layers of the same discipline. The hook gives fast, private feedback before a commit or push even happens; CI gives the slower but unavoidable final answer before code is allowed to merge or ship.

sections.title: A Commit's Journey Through Every Gate
sections.content:
Walk one small change through the whole system to see how the pieces connect. A developer fixes a bug where an export silently fails for large accounts.

  • They stage the fix and run git commit -m 'fix: paginate export queries above 10k rows'. The pre-commit hook runs the linter against the changed files and passes.
  • The commit-msg hook checks the message against the Conventional Commits pattern. fix: matches, so the commit is created.
  • They run git push. The pre-push hook runs the full test suite locally; it passes, and the branch reaches the remote.
  • They open a pull request. CI runs lint and tests again on the server, independent of what happened locally, and reports success on the pull request.
  • A teammate approves the review, and because every required check is green, the pull request is allowed to merge into main.
  • When the next release is tagged, a changelog generator scans every feat: and fix: commit since the last tag — including this one — and lists it automatically under a Bug Fixes heading in the release notes.

No single check in that chain was exotic. What made it reliable was that the same discipline — lint, message format, tests — was enforced twice: once locally for fast feedback, and once on the server where it could not be skipped.

sections.title: The Problem With Many Releases Behind You
sections.content:
A team that has shipped a handful of tagged releases has a manageable history. A team that has shipped fifty releases over two years has a different problem: knowing exactly which commit a given build came from, summarizing what changed between any two releases, and — the hardest one — figuring out which of hundreds of intervening commits introduced a bug that only just got reported.

Tags remain the anchor for all of this, but at scale a team needs tools that operate across tags rather than looking at one tag at a time.

git tag --list 'v1.*' | sort -V
# v1.0.0
# v1.1.0
# v1.2.0
# v1.3.0
# v1.4.0
# v1.4.1

The three tools in this lesson — git describe, tag-range logs, and git bisect — are exactly the ones that scale from a handful of releases to years of release history without the process getting slower.

sections.title: git describe: Turning a Commit Into a Version String
sections.content:
Every build a team ships eventually needs a human-readable version identifier baked into it — something visible in an error report, a support ticket, or an about screen. Typing out the exact commit SHA is precise but meaningless to a person. git describe bridges the gap.

git describe
# v1.4.0-12-g8f3d2a1

Run with no arguments, git describe finds the most recent tag reachable from the current commit and reports how far the current commit is from it. It is built specifically for turning a position in history into a compact, sortable string suitable for a version label.

Add --tags if lightweight tags should also be considered, and --dirty to append a marker when the working tree has uncommitted local changes — useful in a build script that stamps a version into the compiled output.

sections.title: Reading a git describe Output
sections.content:
The output v1.4.0-12-g8f3d2a1 is three pieces of information joined by dashes, each answering a specific question:

  • v1.4.0 — the nearest ancestor tag reachable from this commit.
  • 12 — the number of commits made since that tag.
  • g8f3d2a1 — the current commit's short hash, prefixed with g for git to disambiguate it from a plain number.

If the current commit is the tag exactly — for instance, running git describe right after checking out v1.4.0 itself — the output is simply v1.4.0 with no suffix, because zero commits separate them.

git checkout v1.4.0
git describe
# v1.4.0

This single string answers what a build was built from more precisely than a version number alone ever could, since two different commits both twelve commits past v1.4.0 would be impossible — the hash makes every build's identity unique.

sections.title: Using describe Output as a Build Version
sections.content:
Because the format is compact and unambiguous, build scripts commonly capture git describe at build time and embed it directly into the shipped artifact — a footer string, a log line printed at startup, or an HTTP header on an API response.

BUILD_VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty)
echo "Building version: $BUILD_VERSION"
# stamp $BUILD_VERSION into the application, e.g. an env var or generated file

When a bug report comes in referencing build v1.4.0-12-g8f3d2a1, the exact source commit is recoverable in one step, with no guessing about which of the twelve commits after v1.4.0 the report might correspond to.

git show 8f3d2a1 --stat

This is a small habit that pays for itself the first time a customer reports a bug against a build nobody can otherwise identify.

sections.title: Building a Changelog From Tag to Tag
sections.content:
Summarizing what changed between two releases is a matter of asking Git for the commit range between their tags. v1.3.0..v1.4.0 means every commit reachable from v1.4.0 that is not also reachable from v1.3.0 — exactly the commits introduced by that release.

git log v1.3.0..v1.4.0 --oneline
# 8f3d2a1 feat(auth): add password reset flow
# 6c1e9b0 fix(export): paginate queries above 10k rows
# a45f102 chore(deps): bump typescript to 5.6

Combined with a Conventional Commits discipline (covered in the hooks lesson), this range can be filtered into sections automatically:

git log v1.3.0..v1.4.0 --oneline --grep='^feat'
git log v1.3.0..v1.4.0 --oneline --grep='^fix'

Many teams script exactly this pair of commands into their release process, pasting the grouped output straight into release notes rather than reconstructing the list from memory.

sections.title: A Regression Appears: Since When?
sections.content:
Now the harder scenario. A customer reports that CSV exports have started producing garbled data. Nobody can say exactly when this started — it worked in v1.2.0, and it is broken now in v1.4.1, but somewhere across dozens of commits and two-plus releases, something changed.

Checking out each release one at a time and manually testing would work, but with dozens of commits between the last known-good tag and the first known-bad one, that could mean many slow, manual checkouts before finding the culprit.

git log v1.2.0..v1.4.1 --oneline | wc -l
# 47

Forty-seven candidate commits is exactly the kind of search Git has a purpose-built tool for: a binary search across history that finds the exact commit in a handful of steps instead of up to forty-seven.

sections.title: git bisect: Starting the Search
sections.content:
git bisect performs a binary search over commit history. It needs two boundaries: one commit known to be good (the bug was not present) and one known to be bad (the bug is present). Between those two points, Git checks out the midpoint commit and asks the developer to test it.

git bisect start
git bisect bad                # HEAD (or a specific bad commit) has the bug
git bisect good v1.2.0         # v1.2.0 is known to be fine
# Bisecting: 23 revisions left to test after this (roughly 5 steps)
# Git automatically checks out the midpoint commit

At each step, the developer tests the currently checked-out commit — running the app, reproducing the export, checking whether the garbled output happens — and reports back with a single word.

git bisect good   # the bug is NOT present here
# -- or --
git bisect bad    # the bug IS present here

Git uses that answer to narrow the range by half and automatically checks out the next midpoint, repeating until only one candidate commit remains.

sections.title: Stepping Through to the Culprit
sections.content:
Continuing the export bug search, a full session might look like this, testing and reporting at each automatic checkout:

git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good v1.2.0
# Bisecting: 23 revisions left to test after this (roughly 5 steps)

# ...test the checked-out commit, export still garbled...
git bisect bad
# Bisecting: 11 revisions left to test after this (roughly 4 steps)

# ...test again, export looks fine here...
git bisect good
# Bisecting: 5 revisions left to test after this (roughly 3 steps)

# ...repeat a few more times...
# a1b2c3d is the first bad commit
git show a1b2c3d --stat

Git reports the exact first commit where the bug appears, together with what that commit changed — usually enough on its own to see what went wrong. Once the culprit is found, end the session and return to the original branch:

git bisect reset

git bisect reset is not optional cleanup — skipping it leaves the working tree checked out at whatever commit the search landed on, detached from any branch.

sections.title: Why Bisect Beats Manual Checkouts
sections.content:
Bisect's advantage is mathematical, not just convenient. Checking commits one at a time in order means testing up to every single commit in the range in the worst case. Bisect halves the range at every step, so even a genuinely large range collapses fast:

  • 47 candidate commits: roughly 6 tests to find the culprit, not 47.
  • 500 candidate commits: roughly 9 tests, not 500.

A few habits keep a bisect session productive rather than frustrating:

  • Skip untestable commits with git bisect skip rather than guessing good or bad — a commit that does not even build cannot be honestly tested.
  • Automate the test when possible: git bisect run <script> lets a script report good or bad automatically via its exit code, turning a multi-step manual session into one command.
  • Always run git bisect reset when done — forgetting it leaves the repository in a detached, checked-out-at-a-random-commit state that confuses whatever is tried next.
  • Pick real boundaries. A good commit that is not actually confirmed bug-free just relocates the confusion instead of resolving it.

For any regression with more than a handful of suspect commits, bisect turns a search that could burn an afternoon of manual checkouts into a search that takes minutes.

sections.title: Git Rarely Actually Loses Data
sections.content:
Most panics about breaking Git share a common shape: something disappeared from view, and it feels like it is gone forever. In the overwhelming majority of cases, it is not. Git almost never deletes a commit the moment it stops being reachable from a branch — it just stops showing it in the usual places, like git log, until something eventually cleans it up much later.

That gap — between not visible and actually deleted — is where every recovery technique in this lesson lives. Understanding it turns a moment of panic into a short, methodical process: find the commit, point something at it again, move on.

git log --oneline
# shows only commits reachable from the current branch --
# it is not a complete list of every commit Git still has

The tool that reveals what is still actually there, even after it has scrolled out of normal view, is the reflog.

sections.title: git reflog: The Safety Net Explained
sections.content:
The reflog is a chronological record of every place HEAD has pointed in this repository — every commit, every branch switch, every reset, every rebase step, every checkout. It is not the same thing as commit history; it is a log of where you have been, kept separately.

git reflog
# 8f3d2a1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# 6c1e9b0 HEAD@{1}: commit: fix export pagination bug
# a45f102 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to fix/export-bug
# ...

Two things about the reflog matter for recovery. First, it is local only — it lives in this one repository's .git directory and is never pushed, pulled, or shared, so it cannot rescue a mistake made only on someone else's machine. Second, entries expire after a default retention period (commonly 90 days for reachable entries, 30 for unreachable ones), so it is a safety net, not permanent history.

Within its retention window, the reflog can recover from almost any local mistake: a bad reset, an abandoned rebase, an accidentally deleted branch. It is the single most useful command to remember when something appears to have vanished.

sections.title: Recovering a Lost Commit After git reset --hard
sections.content:
Suppose three commits of real work get wiped out by an overly aggressive git reset --hard HEAD~3, run by mistake while meaning to undo just one commit. The branch pointer now sits three commits earlier, and git log shows no trace of the work that was just there.

git reset --hard HEAD~3
git log --oneline
# the last three commits are gone from view

The commits themselves still exist — only the branch pointer moved. The reflog remembers exactly where HEAD was one step before the reset:

git reflog
# 4d9a1c2 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# 8f3d2a1 HEAD@{1}: commit: add export retry logic
# ...

git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
# branch now points back at the commit that was thought lost

Alternatively, a specific commit can be recovered without moving the whole branch back, by creating a new branch at that point instead:

git branch recovered-work 8f3d2a1

sections.title: When a Rebase Goes Wrong Mid-Flight
sections.content:
An interactive rebase that hits a bad merge conflict, or one where the wrong commits get squashed together by mistake, does not have to be fought through to completion. As long as the rebase is still in progress — Git has not yet reported it finished — it can simply be cancelled:

git rebase --abort

git rebase --abort puts the branch back exactly where it was before the rebase started, as if it had never been attempted. This is the calmest possible outcome: no recovery technique needed at all, because nothing was ever actually changed.

A rebase paused on a conflict is not broken — it is waiting. git status during a paused rebase lists the conflicted files and reminds you of both --continue and --abort, so it is always visible which commit the rebase is currently replaying.

The harder case is a rebase that ran to completion with an unwanted result, which is covered next.

sections.title: Recovering a Rebase That Already Completed
sections.content:
If a rebase finishes — commits rewritten, history rearranged — and only afterward does it become clear something went wrong, --abort is no longer available. The reflog is the recovery path here too, because every intermediate state the rebase passed through was recorded as HEAD moved.

git reflog
# a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature
# 9f8e7d6 HEAD@{1}: rebase (pick): fix export retry logic
# ...
# 4d9a1c2 HEAD@{5}: rebase (start): checkout main

git reset --hard HEAD@{5}
# branch restored to its state immediately before the rebase began

This reliably works as long as the rebased branch has not left the local machine. If the branch was already force-pushed after the rebase, the remote now reflects the rewritten history too, and any teammate who pulled it has the rewritten commits in their own history. Fixing that requires coordinating a second force-push after recovery, and warning teammates to reset their own local copies — the local reflog alone cannot undo what a force-push already did to a shared remote.

Rewriting and force-pushing a branch other people have already pulled is the one situation where reflog recovery on your own machine is not the whole fix — the remote and every teammate's clone need to be brought back in line too.

sections.title: Understanding Detached HEAD
sections.content:
Normally, HEAD points at a branch name, and the branch name points at a commit. In detached HEAD state, HEAD points directly at a commit with no branch name in between. Git is not broken when this happens — it is a deliberate, ordinary state, but one that behaves differently from working on a branch.

The most common way to land here is checking out a tag or a specific commit by its hash instead of a branch name:

git checkout v1.4.0
# Note: switching to 'v1.4.0'.
# You are in 'detached HEAD' state...

Git's own message at this point is informative, not an error: it explains exactly what happened and what to do about it. Looking around, running tests, or checking out old code in this state is completely safe. The risk appears only if new commits get made here — commits made in detached HEAD are not attached to any branch, so nothing automatically keeps them findable once something else is checked out.

sections.title: Escaping Detached HEAD Safely
sections.content:
If nothing was committed while detached, escaping is trivial — just switch back to wherever you were before:

git switch -
# switches back to the previously checked-out branch

The situation that actually needs care is when real commits were made while detached — for example, testing a fix directly against an old tag and it worked, so the fix was committed right there. Those commits are not lost, but they are not on any branch either, so simply switching away would make them hard to find later (though still recoverable via the reflog, per the earlier section). The right move is to give them a home before leaving:

# still in detached HEAD, with new commits made here
git branch rescue-fix
git switch rescue-fix
# the commits now belong to a real branch and are safe to keep working on

From there, rescue-fix behaves like any other branch and can be merged, rebased onto main, or pushed like normal.

sections.title: Cleaning Up a Messy Local Branch
sections.content:
A feature branch with fifteen small wip and fix typo commits works fine locally but makes for a confusing pull request. Two different tools fix two different versions of this problem.

To reshape a whole string of commits — squashing several into one, reordering them, rewriting messages — use interactive rebase against the point the branch diverged from:

git rebase -i main
# opens an editor listing every commit since main;
# change pick to squash (or s) to combine a commit into the one before it

To undo the most recent commit or two but keep all the actual code changes, staged and ready to be re-committed more sensibly, git reset --soft is faster than a full interactive rebase:

git reset --soft HEAD~2
git status
# changes from the last 2 commits are staged, ready to re-commit as one clean commit
git commit -m 'feat: add export retry logic'
Reach for reset --soft when undoing just the last commit or two on your own unpublished branch; reach for interactive rebase when reordering or combining commits scattered further back in the branch's history.

sections.title: A Full Recovery, Start to Finish
sections.content:
Put the pieces together with one realistic afternoon. A developer is cleaning up a messy branch, runs git rebase -i main to squash a dozen small commits into three clean ones, and midway through resolving a conflict, panics and runs git reset --hard origin/feature thinking it will cancel the rebase — instead it just detaches things further and the three intended commits seem to vanish.

# first, check whether the rebase itself is still in progress
git status
# status shows no rebase in progress -- too late for --abort, need the reflog instead

# find where things stood right before the trouble started
git reflog
# f7a2b91 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to origin/feature
# 3c8d4e5 HEAD@{1}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature
# ...

git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
git log --oneline
# the three squashed commits are back, exactly as the rebase left them

Along the way, checking an old tag to compare behavior left the developer briefly in detached HEAD:

git switch -
# back on feature, no commits were made while detached, nothing to rescue

Nothing here required panic. Every step was the same pattern repeated: notice something looks wrong, check git status and git reflog to see what actually happened, and point a branch or HEAD back at the right commit. Git kept every piece around the entire time — the only thing that was ever actually missing was a moment of calm.

title: Relational Databases & the Relational Model
summary: How a relational database organises data into tables, rows and columns, and how primary and foreign keys identify every record and connect related records across tables.

sections.title: Why Databases Exist
sections.content:
Picture a growing online shop that keeps customers in one spreadsheet and orders in another. Two staff edit the same file at once and one overwrites the other. Someone types a customer's email three different ways. An order points to a customer who was deleted last week.

A relational database solves exactly these problems. It stores data in a structured, shared place that many users and applications can read and change at the same time, while the database itself enforces rules that keep the data valid.

Almost every business system you use, from banking to ticket booking, sits on one.

sections.title: Tables, Rows and Columns
sections.content:
Data lives in tables. Each table describes one kind of thing, such as customers or orders. A column is one attribute that every row has, and a row (also called a record) is one instance of the thing.

customers
 id | name         | email             | city
----+--------------+-------------------+-----------
  1 | Ana Silva    | ana@example.com   | Lisbon
  2 | Ravi Kumar   | ravi@example.com  | Pune
  3 | Mei Chen     | mei@example.com   | Singapore

Here every row has the same four columns. That predictable shape is what lets the database validate, index and query the data efficiently.

sections.title: Every Column Has a Type
sections.content:
When a table is created, each column gets a data type: whole numbers, decimals, text, dates, true/false. The database then refuses values that don't fit, so a date column can never hold the word "tomorrow".

The full set of tables, columns, types and rules is called the schema. It is defined up front, before data arrives, and changed deliberately later. That is the opposite of a spreadsheet, where any cell can hold anything.

A fixed schema can feel restrictive at first, but it is what makes the data trustworthy. Every query can rely on every row having the same shape.

sections.title: Primary Keys: One Row, One Identity
sections.content:
A primary key is a column, or set of columns, that uniquely identifies each row. Its values must be unique and can never be NULL.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

Most tables use a simple, meaningless number such as id. Names and emails make poor keys because they can repeat or change. With a primary key, an UPDATE or DELETE can always target exactly one row, and other tables have something stable to point at.

sections.title: Foreign Keys: Connecting Tables
sections.content:
A foreign key is a column that points to the primary key of another table. Each order stores the id of the customer who placed it:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  total       DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

Instead of copying the customer's name and email onto every order, the order just holds customer_id = 2. The database can enforce that customer 2 actually exists, so orphaned orders pointing at nothing become impossible.

sections.title: One Fact in One Place
sections.content:
Because orders reference customers by id, each customer's details exist in exactly one row. When Ravi changes his email, one update fixes it everywhere, and every order still points to the right person.

This is the central idea of the relational model: store each fact once, and relate rows to each other through keys. When you need the combined picture, such as orders with customer names, SQL brings the tables back together with a join, which you will meet in the Joining Tables lesson.

The word "relational" comes from mathematics: a table is formally called a relation. In everyday use it is easiest to remember it as "tables related through keys".

sections.title: What the Database Engine Does for You
sections.content:
The software that manages a relational database is an RDBMS (relational database management system). Popular ones include PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite. Behind every query, it:

  • Enforces types and constraints, such as unique emails and valid foreign keys.
  • Lets many users read and write at once without corrupting each other's work.
  • Groups related changes into transactions that succeed or fail together.
  • Works out the fastest way to answer each query.
  • Recovers committed data after a crash.

You describe what you want in SQL; the engine figures out how.

sections.title: Relational or NoSQL?
sections.content:
Relational databases are the default choice when data is structured and related, and correctness matters: orders, payments, inventory, accounts.

NoSQL stores fit narrower jobs. Document databases such as MongoDB suit self-contained records whose shape varies a lot. Key-value stores such as Redis suit caching and very fast lookups by key.

Many real systems use both: a relational database as the source of truth, with a NoSQL store alongside for caching or a specialised workload. Learning SQL first pays off either way, because the ideas of keys, constraints and queries carry over.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Tables hold one kind of thing; rows are records and columns are typed attributes.
  • The schema defines tables, columns, types and rules before data arrives.
  • A primary key uniquely identifies every row: unique and never NULL.
  • A foreign key points to another table's primary key and represents a relationship.
  • Store each fact once and connect rows through keys; joins combine them when needed.
  • The RDBMS enforces rules, handles concurrency and transactions, and plans queries.

title: Querying Data: SELECT, WHERE & ORDER BY
summary: Write single-table queries that pick columns, filter rows with WHERE, match lists, ranges and patterns, remove duplicates, sort and page results, and understand the order SQL really runs in.

sections.title: Your First Query
sections.content:
Every read in SQL starts with SELECT: which columns you want, and FROM which table.

SELECT name, price
FROM products;

The result is itself a small table: one row per product, with just the two columns you asked for. The products table is not changed in any way. A SELECT only reads.

SQL keywords are not case-sensitive, but writing them in capitals is a common convention that makes queries easier to scan. A semicolon marks the end of a statement.

sections.title: Choosing and Naming Columns
sections.content:
Besides plain columns, SELECT can compute values and give them names with AS:

SELECT name,
       price,
       price * 1.18 AS price_with_tax
FROM products;

The alias price_with_tax only exists in the result; nothing is stored. SELECT * returns every column, which is handy while exploring but best avoided in application code. It fetches data you don't need, and its shape changes whenever someone adds a column.

sections.title: Filtering Rows with WHERE
sections.content:
WHERE keeps only the rows for which a condition is true:

SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price < 20;

The usual comparison operators work: =, <> (or !=), <, <=, >, >=. Text values go in single quotes, as in WHERE category = 'books'. Note that SQL uses a single = for comparison, not ==.

sections.title: Combining Conditions
sections.content:
AND requires both conditions, OR requires either, and NOT negates one. Watch the precedence: AND is evaluated before OR.

-- Returns ALL books, plus games under 20
WHERE category = 'books' OR category = 'games' AND price < 20

-- Returns books and games that are both under 20
WHERE (category = 'books' OR category = 'games') AND price < 20

Whenever a condition mixes AND and OR, add parentheses. It costs nothing and prevents one of the most common filtering bugs.

sections.title: Lists, Ranges and Patterns
sections.content:
Three operators make common filters shorter and clearer:

  • IN matches any value in a list: WHERE country IN ('US', 'CA', 'MX').
  • BETWEEN matches an inclusive range: WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 50 includes both 10 and 50.
  • LIKE matches text patterns, where % means any number of characters and _ means exactly one: WHERE name LIKE 'An%' finds Anna and Andrew.

A pattern that starts with %, such as '%son', works but cannot use a normal index, so it gets slow on large tables.

sections.title: Removing Duplicates with DISTINCT
sections.content:
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result:

SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM customers;

Each city appears once, however many customers live there. With several columns, DISTINCT applies to the whole combination: SELECT DISTINCT city, country keeps each distinct pair.

If you find yourself adding DISTINCT to "fix" unexpected duplicates, pause: the duplicates usually point to a query problem worth understanding, often a join that matched more rows than expected.

sections.title: Sorting with ORDER BY
sections.content:
Without ORDER BY, SQL guarantees no particular row order, even if results seem sorted today.

SELECT name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC, name;

ASC (the default) sorts low to high and DESC high to low. Extra columns break ties: here, products with the same price are sorted by name. Any time the order matters to a user or to your code, say so explicitly with ORDER BY.

sections.title: Limiting and Paging Results
sections.content:
LIMIT caps how many rows come back, and OFFSET skips rows first, which is the basis of simple pagination:

-- Page 3, with 20 products per page
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

Standard SQL writes the same thing as OFFSET 40 ROWS FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY, and SQL Server also has TOP. Always pair a limit with ORDER BY; otherwise "the first 20" can be different rows every time.

sections.title: The Order SQL Really Runs In
sections.content:
A query is written starting with SELECT, but it is logically evaluated in a different order: FROM, then WHERE, then SELECT, then DISTINCT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT.

This explains a classic error:

SELECT price * 1.18 AS gross
FROM products
WHERE gross > 100;   -- error: gross does not exist yet

WHERE runs before SELECT creates the alias, so repeat the expression instead: WHERE price * 1.18 > 100. Aliases do work in ORDER BY, because it runs after SELECT.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• SELECT picks columns, FROM names the table, and nothing is changed by reading.
  • AS names computed columns; avoid SELECT * in application code.
  • AND binds tighter than OR: add parentheses when mixing them.
  • IN, BETWEEN (inclusive) and LIKE (%, _) shorten common filters.
  • Row order is only guaranteed with ORDER BY; pair every LIMIT with one.
  • Logical order: FROM → WHERE → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

title: NULLs, Data Types & Expressions
summary: Choose sensible column types, handle missing values correctly with three-valued logic, COALESCE and NULLIF, branch with CASE, and use everyday text, number and date functions.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Data Type
sections.content:
A column's type decides what it can hold, how values compare and how much space they take. The common families:

  • Integers: INTEGER, or BIGINT for ids and counters that may grow very large.
  • Exact decimals: DECIMAL(p, s), also called NUMERIC.
  • Text: VARCHAR(n) for bounded text, TEXT for long text.
  • Dates and times: DATE, TIMESTAMP.
  • Flags: BOOLEAN.

Never store numbers or dates as text. As strings, '10' < '9' is true and dates sort incorrectly.

sections.title: Money Needs Exact Numbers
sections.content:
FLOAT and DOUBLE store binary approximations, and many decimal fractions, such as 0.1, have no exact binary form. Across thousands of rows the tiny errors add up, and a check like amount = 19.99 can unexpectedly fail.

CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  amount DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL   -- exact: up to 10 digits before the point, 2 after
);

Use DECIMAL for money and anything else that must not drift. Some teams instead store the smallest unit, such as cents, in an integer column; both approaches keep the arithmetic exact.

sections.title: What NULL Really Means
sections.content:
NULL means a value is missing or unknown. It is not zero and not an empty string, both of which are real, known values.

Because NULL is unknown, almost any calculation involving it is unknown too:

SELECT 5 + NULL;          -- NULL
SELECT 'abc' || NULL;     -- NULL in standard SQL

A customer with no phone number has phone = NULL, which really means "we don't know a phone number". That subtle meaning is the source of most NULL surprises, as the next slide shows.

sections.title: Three-Valued Logic
sections.content:
SQL conditions can be true, false or unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. Comparing anything with NULL gives unknown, even NULL = NULL.

WHERE email = NULL       -- never matches anything
WHERE email IS NULL      -- correct
WHERE status <> 'active' -- also silently skips rows where status IS NULL

The same logic makes NOT IN dangerous: id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) returns no rows at all, because one comparison is always unknown. Use IS NULL, IS NOT NULL and, for subqueries, NOT EXISTS.

sections.title: Replacing NULLs: COALESCE and NULLIF
sections.content:
COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument, which makes it the standard way to supply a fallback:

SELECT name,
       COALESCE(phone, email, 'no contact') AS contact
FROM customers;

NULLIF(a, b) does the reverse: it returns NULL when a equals b. Its classic use is avoiding division by zero:

SELECT revenue / NULLIF(order_count, 0) AS avg_order
FROM monthly_stats;   -- NULL instead of an error when order_count is 0

sections.title: Branching with CASE
sections.content:
CASE is SQL's if/else. It checks conditions in order and returns the value of the first one that matches:

SELECT id,
       amount,
       CASE
         WHEN amount < 50  THEN 'small'
         WHEN amount < 200 THEN 'medium'
         ELSE 'large'
       END AS order_size
FROM orders;

Because branches are checked top to bottom, the second one only needs amount < 200. Without an ELSE, rows that match nothing get NULL, so it is good practice to include one. CASE works anywhere an expression does, including ORDER BY and inside aggregates.

sections.title: Everyday Text Functions
sections.content:
A few functions cover most text work:

  • LOWER() and UPPER() change case: WHERE LOWER(email) = LOWER('Ana@Example.com') matches regardless of capitalisation.
  • TRIM() removes surrounding spaces, a common cleanup for imported data.
  • LENGTH() returns the number of characters.
  • Concatenation joins strings: first_name || ' ' || last_name in standard SQL and PostgreSQL, CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) in MySQL.

Function names vary a little between databases. When a query has to run on more than one engine, check each function in that engine's documentation.

sections.title: Dates, Casting and Arithmetic
sections.content:
CAST converts between types: CAST('2024-05-01' AS DATE) turns text into a real date that can be compared and sorted. Date functions differ by engine, for example CURRENT_DATE, DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) in PostgreSQL, and DATE_FORMAT() in MySQL.

One arithmetic trap: in PostgreSQL, dividing two integers discards the remainder.

SELECT 7 / 2;      -- 3 in PostgreSQL, 3.5000 in MySQL
SELECT 7.0 / 2;    -- 3.5 everywhere

When a ratio matters, make at least one side a decimal or cast it explicitly.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Pick types deliberately; never store numbers or dates as text.
  • Use DECIMAL for money, not FLOAT.
  • NULL means unknown: comparisons with it are unknown, so use IS NULL.
  • <> and NOT IN quietly skip or break on NULLs.
  • COALESCE supplies fallbacks; NULLIF avoids division by zero.
  • CASE is if/else inside a query; include an ELSE.
  • Watch integer division and engine-specific function names.

title: Aggregation & Grouping
summary: Summarise data with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, group rows with GROUP BY, filter groups with HAVING, and understand exactly how NULLs and DISTINCT change the numbers.

sections.title: From Rows to Answers
sections.content:
Most business questions are summaries: how many orders came in today, what was last month's revenue, what is the average basket size per country. Answering them by reading individual rows would be hopeless at scale.

Aggregate functions collapse many rows into a single value, and GROUP BY lets you compute that value separately for each group, such as each country or each month. Together they turn raw records into the numbers people actually make decisions with.

sections.title: The Core Aggregate Functions
sections.content:
Five functions do most of the work:

SELECT COUNT(*)    AS orders,
       SUM(total)  AS revenue,
       AVG(total)  AS avg_order,
       MIN(total)  AS smallest,
       MAX(total)  AS largest
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid';

Without a GROUP BY, all rows that pass the WHERE filter form one group, so the query returns exactly one row. MIN and MAX also work on text and dates: MAX(created_at) is the most recent order.

sections.title: Three Ways to Count
sections.content:
COUNT has three forms, and they answer different questions:

  • COUNT(*) counts rows.
  • COUNT(coupon_code) counts rows where that column is not NULL.
  • COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) counts different non-NULL values.

For 10 orders where 3 used no coupon and 7 came from 4 different customers, these return 10, 7 and 4. Comparing COUNT(*) with COUNT(column) is also a quick way to see how many values are missing.

sections.title: Grouping Rows with GROUP BY
sections.content:
GROUP BY splits rows into groups that share a value, and each aggregate is computed per group:

SELECT country,
       COUNT(*)   AS customers,
       SUM(spend) AS total_spend
FROM customers
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;

The result has one row per country. Grouping by several columns, as in GROUP BY country, city, creates one group for every distinct combination, so two cities with the same name in different countries stay apart.

sections.title: The GROUP BY Rule
sections.content:
After grouping, each output row stands for many input rows. So every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate:

-- Rejected by most databases: which employee's name per department?
SELECT department, name, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

The database can't pick one name for a whole department. Either group by it, aggregate it (MAX(name)), or, if you really want the detail row behind each group, use a window function, covered in Advanced SQL. Older MySQL settings allowed this and returned an arbitrary name, a silent bug that modern defaults now block.

sections.title: Filtering Groups with HAVING
sections.content:
WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it can't use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation:

SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spend
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'   -- rows: only this year
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total) > 1000;          -- groups: only big spenders

Put every condition on individual rows in WHERE, even in grouped queries. Filtering early means fewer rows to group, which is both correct and faster.

sections.title: How NULLs Affect Aggregates
sections.content:
Every aggregate except COUNT(*) ignores NULL values:

  • AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15, not 10, because it divides by the two known values.
  • SUM of a group where every value is NULL is NULL, not 0.

Decide what a missing value should mean and say so explicitly:

SELECT AVG(COALESCE(score, 0))   AS avg_counting_missing_as_zero,
       COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)  AS total_or_zero
FROM results;

sections.title: Putting It Together: A Monthly Report
sections.content:
A typical report combines everything in this lesson:

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) AS month,
       COUNT(*)                         AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)      AS customers,
       SUM(total)                       AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND created_at >= '2024-01-01'
  AND created_at <  '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;

Rows are filtered first, grouped by month, aggregated, then sorted. DATE_TRUNC is PostgreSQL; MySQL groups by DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m'). Months with no orders won't appear at all, a gap you will learn to fill with joins.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) collapse rows into values.
  • COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) non-NULL values, COUNT(DISTINCT col) different values.
  • GROUP BY computes aggregates per group; every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.
  • WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
  • Aggregates skip NULLs; wrap with COALESCE when missing should count as zero.

title: Joining Tables
summary: Combine related tables with INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, self and cross joins, find rows with no match, and avoid the duplicate-row and ON-versus-WHERE traps that break real reports.

sections.title: Why Joins Exist
sections.content:
A well-designed database stores each fact once: customers in one table, orders in another, linked by orders.customer_id. That keeps data consistent, but most questions need both at once, such as "show each order with the customer's name".

A join combines rows from two tables wherever a condition matches, usually a foreign key equal to a primary key. The result has columns from both tables side by side. Joins are how the relational model gives you the full picture without ever duplicating data.

sections.title: INNER JOIN
sections.content:
An INNER JOIN returns only pairs of rows that match on both sides:

SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;

JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN. The short aliases o and c keep the query readable, and qualifying every column with its alias avoids "ambiguous column" errors when both tables share a name such as id.

Customers who never ordered, and orders whose customer is missing, simply don't appear.

sections.title: LEFT JOIN: Keeping Unmatched Rows
sections.content:
A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table. Where nothing matches on the right, the right-hand columns are NULL:

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;

Every customer appears: once per order if they have orders, and once with order_id = NULL if they have none. Choose the join type by the question: "customers and their orders" is an inner join; "all customers, with orders if any" is a left join.

sections.title: Finding What Is Missing
sections.content:
Those NULLs are useful. Filtering on them finds rows with no match, a pattern called an anti-join:

-- Customers who have never ordered
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

The same question can be written with NOT EXISTS, which reads very naturally and handles NULLs safely. You will meet it in the Subqueries lesson. Typical uses include inactive customers, products never sold, and users who never verified their email.

sections.title: RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN
sections.content:
A RIGHT JOIN is a left join with the tables swapped: it keeps every row from the right-hand table. Most teams simply write left joins to keep queries consistent.

A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides, which is useful for reconciling two lists:

SELECT b.id AS bank_id, l.id AS ledger_id, b.amount, l.amount
FROM bank_transactions b
FULL OUTER JOIN ledger_entries l ON l.reference = b.reference;

Rows with NULL on one side are the mismatches. MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN; there it is emulated with a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN combined using UNION.

sections.title: Self Joins
sections.content:
Sometimes rows in a table refer to other rows in the same table, such as each employee's manager. A self join uses two aliases so the table can play both roles:

SELECT e.name AS employee,
       m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id;

The LEFT JOIN keeps employees without a manager, such as the CEO. Self joins also help compare rows with each other, for example products in the same category with similar prices.

sections.title: CROSS JOIN and the Cartesian Product
sections.content:
A CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of another. Three sizes and four colours give 12 combinations, which is useful when you really do want every pairing:

SELECT s.label AS size, c.label AS colour
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colours c;

The same explosion happens by accident when a join condition is forgotten. 100 customers and 1,000 orders listed without one produce 100,000 rows. If a query suddenly returns far too many rows, check every join condition first.

sections.title: The Duplicate-Row Trap
sections.content:
Joining a table to two independent one-to-many tables multiplies rows. A customer with 3 orders and 2 support tickets produces 3 × 2 = 6 rows, so summing order amounts counts each order twice:

-- Wrong: totals are inflated
SELECT c.id, SUM(o.total)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o          ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN support_tickets t ON t.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;

The fix is to aggregate each child table on its own first, in a subquery or CTE, and then join the per-customer totals. DISTINCT hides the duplicate rows but does not fix the sums.

sections.title: ON Versus WHERE in Outer Joins
sections.content:
With a LEFT JOIN, where you put a condition on the right-hand table matters:

-- Drops customers without shipped orders (behaves like INNER JOIN)
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'shipped'

-- Keeps every customer, attaching only their shipped orders
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'shipped'

Unmatched rows have NULL in o.status, and WHERE throws them away. Conditions that decide which right-hand rows may match belong in ON; conditions on the left table belong in WHERE.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Joins combine related tables through keys, usually foreign key = primary key.
  • INNER JOIN keeps matches only; LEFT JOIN keeps every left row with NULLs for no match.
  • LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows with no match.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both sides; self joins use two aliases; CROSS JOIN pairs everything.
  • Joining two one-to-many tables multiplies rows; aggregate first, then join.
  • In outer joins, put right-table filters in ON, not WHERE.

title: Changing Data: INSERT, UPDATE & DELETE
summary: Add, change and remove rows with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, merge data with upserts, fetch generated values with RETURNING, and follow the habits that keep data changes safe in production.

sections.title: Adding Rows with INSERT
sections.content:
INSERT adds new rows. Always name the columns you are filling:

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city)
VALUES ('Ana Silva', 'ana@example.com', 'Lisbon');

Columns you leave out take their default, such as an auto-generated id or a created_at timestamp, or NULL if they have none. Without a column list, values are matched to columns by position, so adding or reordering a column later silently breaks the statement or puts values in the wrong place.

sections.title: Inserting Many Rows at Once
sections.content:
Several rows can go in one statement, with one parenthesised list per row:

INSERT INTO tags (name)
VALUES ('sql'), ('databases'), ('performance');

Rows can also come from a query, which is how data is copied between tables:

INSERT INTO archived_orders (id, customer_id, total, created_at)
SELECT id, customer_id, total, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE created_at < '2023-01-01';

This copies old orders. The originals stay put until a separate DELETE removes them.

sections.title: Changing Rows with UPDATE
sections.content:
UPDATE changes existing rows. SET lists the new values, and WHERE chooses the rows:

UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 50,
    updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE id = 7;

The right-hand side can use the row's current values, so balance - 50 reduces whatever the balance is now. Letting the database do the arithmetic like this, rather than reading a value into your code and writing it back, also prevents lost updates when two requests change the same row at once.

sections.title: Removing Rows with DELETE
sections.content:
DELETE removes whole rows that match its WHERE condition:

DELETE FROM sessions
WHERE expires_at < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;

It removes rows, never columns. Dropping a column is ALTER TABLE, and dropping the table is DROP TABLE. If other tables reference the rows through foreign keys, the delete may be rejected or may cascade to child rows, depending on how the constraint was defined. You will learn those options in the DDL lesson.

sections.title: The Missing WHERE Clause
sections.content:
An UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE affects every row in the table:

UPDATE products SET price = 0;   -- every product is now free
DELETE FROM customers;           -- every customer is gone

The database runs these without complaint. Some client tools, such as MySQL Workbench in safe-update mode, try to block them, but that is a convenience, not a guarantee.
