Before running any UPDATE or DELETE, read the WHERE clause twice. It is the single most important habit when changing data.

sections.title: DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP
sections.content:
• DELETE FROM logs WHERE … removes matching rows one by one and fires row triggers. It can be rolled back inside a transaction.
  • TRUNCATE TABLE logs empties the entire table in one fast operation and usually resets identity counters. PostgreSQL can roll it back inside a transaction; MySQL commits it immediately.
  • DROP TABLE logs removes the table itself: structure, data, indexes and permissions.

Use DELETE for selected rows, TRUNCATE to clear a staging table quickly, and DROP only when the table should no longer exist.

sections.title: Upserts: Insert or Update
sections.content:
Often you want "insert this row, or update it if it already exists", such as counting page views per product. An upsert does it atomically:

-- PostgreSQL
INSERT INTO product_views (product_id, views)
VALUES (42, 1)
ON CONFLICT (product_id)
DO UPDATE SET views = product_views.views + 1;

-- MySQL
INSERT INTO product_views (product_id, views)
VALUES (42, 1)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE views = views + 1;

It relies on a unique key on product_id. Doing a SELECT and then deciding between INSERT and UPDATE in code has a race: two requests can both see no row and both try to insert. SQL Server and Oracle use MERGE.

sections.title: Getting Values Back with RETURNING
sections.content:
After an insert, the application usually needs the generated id. PostgreSQL returns it in the same statement:

INSERT INTO users (email)
VALUES ('ravi@example.com')
RETURNING id, created_at;

RETURNING also works with UPDATE and DELETE, for example to see which rows were changed. SQL Server offers OUTPUT, and MySQL applications typically call LAST_INSERT_ID(). Getting the value back in one round trip is faster and avoids guessing which row was "the latest".

sections.title: Changing Data Safely
sections.content:
A simple routine prevents most accidents with real data:

  1. Preview: run a SELECT with exactly the same WHERE and check the count and a sample of rows.
  2. Use a transaction: BEGIN, run the change, check the affected row count, then COMMIT, or ROLLBACK if it looks wrong.
  3. Batch large changes into chunks so locks stay short.

Most clients run in autocommit mode, where each statement is committed the moment it succeeds. Without an explicit BEGIN, there is nothing left to roll back; only a backup can undo the change.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• INSERT adds rows; always list the columns. INSERT … SELECT copies rows from a query.
  • UPDATE … SET … WHERE changes rows and can use current values (balance - 50).
  • DELETE … WHERE removes rows; without WHERE, it removes all of them.
  • TRUNCATE empties a table fast; DROP removes the table itself.
  • Upserts (ON CONFLICT, ON DUPLICATE KEY, MERGE) insert or update atomically.
  • Preview with SELECT, wrap risky changes in a transaction, and remember autocommit.

title: Creating Tables: DDL & Constraints
summary: Define and evolve tables with CREATE, ALTER and DROP, pick column types, and protect data with NOT NULL, DEFAULT, UNIQUE, CHECK, primary keys, foreign keys and the right ON DELETE behaviour.

sections.title: Defining Structure with DDL
sections.content:
SQL has two halves. DML (Data Manipulation Language) reads and changes data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DDL (Data Definition Language) defines the structure that data lives in: CREATE, ALTER and DROP.

DDL is where you decide what a valid row looks like. Every rule you encode here, such as "every order has a customer" or "prices are never negative", is enforced on every write from every application, script and import. That makes the schema the most reliable place to protect your data.

sections.title: Creating a Table
sections.content:
A CREATE TABLE statement names each column, its type and its rules:

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku         VARCHAR(40)    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        VARCHAR(200)   NOT NULL,
  price       DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  status      VARCHAR(20)    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft',
  created_at  TIMESTAMP      NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

Read it line by line and you can see the business rules: every product has a unique SKU, a name and a non-negative price, and new products start as drafts. The next slides look at each kind of rule.

sections.title: NOT NULL and DEFAULT
sections.content:
NOT NULL rejects any row that leaves the column empty. Use it for every column that must always have a value, which in a well-designed schema is most of them. A nullable column should mean "this genuinely may be unknown", not "we didn't think about it".

DEFAULT supplies a value when an INSERT doesn't mention the column:

INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price)
VALUES ('BK-101', 'SQL Pocket Guide', 14.99);
-- status becomes 'draft', created_at becomes the current time

Defaults keep inserts short and make sure audit columns such as created_at are never forgotten.

sections.title: UNIQUE and CHECK
sections.content:
UNIQUE guarantees a value, or combination of values, never repeats:

email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
UNIQUE (user_id, product_id)   -- one rating per user per product

CHECK rejects rows where a condition is false: CHECK (price >= 0) or CHECK (status IN ('draft', 'published', 'archived')).

MySQL only enforces CHECK from version 8.0.16; older versions parsed it and silently ignored it. Most databases also allow several NULLs in a UNIQUE column, because two unknown values are not considered equal.

sections.title: Primary Keys and Identity Columns
sections.content:
Every table should have a primary key: unique, never NULL, and stable. The usual choice is a generated number:

id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY   -- standard SQL, PostgreSQL 10+
id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY                 -- MySQL
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY                             -- older PostgreSQL style

The database hands out the next value for each new row. Expect gaps: values used by failed or rolled-back inserts are never reused, so ids jumping from 105 to 108 is normal. Ids identify rows; they are not a count of them. A composite primary key, such as PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id), is also common on junction tables.

sections.title: Foreign Keys and Referential Integrity
sections.content:
A foreign key declares that a column must point to an existing row elsewhere:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  total       DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL
);

Inserting an order for customer 999 now fails if that customer doesn't exist. The referenced column must be a primary key or have a UNIQUE constraint, so every reference identifies exactly one row. This is referential integrity: no orphans, ever, no matter which code path wrote the data.

sections.title: What Happens on Delete
sections.content:
When a referenced parent row is deleted, the foreign key's ON DELETE action decides what happens to the children:

  • RESTRICT / NO ACTION (the default): the delete is rejected while children exist. Right for important history, such as customers with invoices.
  • CASCADE: children are deleted too. Right when children mean nothing alone, such as order lines.
  • SET NULL: children survive with the reference cleared. Right for optional links, such as a deleted coupon; the column must be nullable.

Cascades can chain through several tables and remove far more than expected. Use them only for clear ownership relationships.

sections.title: Changing Tables Safely
sections.content:
ALTER TABLE evolves a live schema: adding columns, constraints and indexes. Changes to big production tables need care. In PostgreSQL, adding a NOT NULL column to a table with rows fails unless it has a DEFAULT, so the safe pattern is: add it nullable, backfill in batches, then add the constraint.

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN country VARCHAR(2);
UPDATE users SET country = 'IN' WHERE country IS NULL;   -- in batches
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN country SET NOT NULL;

Teams apply schema changes through versioned migration scripts (Flyway, Liquibase, or an ORM's tool), so every environment gets the same changes in the same order.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) defines structure; DML reads and changes data.
  • NOT NULL by default; DEFAULT fills omitted columns.
  • UNIQUE stops repeats; CHECK enforces conditions.
  • Every table needs a stable primary key; identity gaps are normal.
  • Foreign keys must reference a primary key or unique column; they prevent orphans.
  • ON DELETE: RESTRICT protects history, CASCADE removes owned children, SET NULL clears optional links.
  • Change production schemas in stages, through versioned migrations.

title: Data Modeling & Relationships
summary: Turn business requirements into entities, attributes and keys, model one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships, and handle hierarchies, history and statuses the way real systems do.

sections.title: From Requirements to Entities
sections.content:
Data modeling starts with listening, not SQL. Read the requirements and underline the nouns the business cares about: "Customers place orders for products, pay for them, and have them shipped to an address." Those nouns are your candidate entities: customer, order, product, payment, address.

Each entity usually becomes a table. Then ask how they relate: can a customer have many orders? Can an order contain many products? The answers decide where keys go. Getting this right early is far cheaper than reshaping a live schema later.

sections.title: Attributes and Keys
sections.content:
Each entity has attributes that become columns: a product has a name, a SKU and a price. Ask of every attribute: does it describe this entity, or something else?

An order's shipping city describes an address, not the order, which hints that addresses deserve their own table. Every entity also needs an identifier, its primary key.

Modelers sketch all of this as an ER diagram (entity-relationship diagram): boxes for entities, lines for relationships. In the common crow's foot notation, a three-pronged end on a line means "many" and a single bar means "one".

sections.title: One-to-Many Relationships
sections.content:
The most common relationship: one customer has many orders, and each order belongs to exactly one customer. The foreign key always goes on the "many" side:

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  placed_at   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);

If you tried the reverse, an order_id column on customers, each customer could only ever have one order. When the relationship is optional, such as an order that may or may not use a coupon, the foreign key simply allows NULL.

sections.title: Many-to-Many and Junction Tables
sections.content:
An order contains many products, and a product appears in many orders. Neither table can hold the other's key, so a junction table sits in the middle with a foreign key to each side:

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   BIGINT REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id BIGINT REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity   INT NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

The composite primary key stops the same product appearing twice on one order. Attributes of the pairing itself, such as quantity and the price paid, live here. That is why junction tables often deserve real names, like order_items or enrollments.

sections.title: One-to-One Relationships
sections.content:
Sometimes each row in one table matches at most one row in another, such as a user and their seller profile. It is modeled as a foreign key that is also UNIQUE, or that is itself the primary key:

CREATE TABLE seller_profiles (
  user_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id),
  store_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  payout_iban VARCHAR(34)
);

Split a table like this only for a reason: the columns are optional and sparse, they are sensitive and need separate permissions, or they are large and rarely read. Otherwise, keep the columns in one table.

sections.title: Surrogate or Natural Keys?
sections.content:
A natural key is a real-world value that's already unique, such as an email or an ISBN. A surrogate key is a meaningless generated value, such as an auto-incrementing id or a UUID.

Most teams use surrogate primary keys, for one main reason: keys are copied into every referencing table, so they must never change, and natural values change all the time. When a user updates their email, a surrogate key means nothing else has to change.

Keep the natural value protected too: a surrogate id as the primary key, plus a UNIQUE constraint on email.

sections.title: Modeling Hierarchies
sections.content:
Categories inside categories, employees reporting to managers, comments replying to comments: all are hierarchies. The simplest model is a self-referencing foreign key, called an adjacency list:

CREATE TABLE categories (
  id        INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  parent_id INT REFERENCES categories(id)   -- NULL for top-level categories
);

It supports any depth with a single table, and recursive CTEs (in the Advanced SQL track) can walk the whole tree. Fixed level1, level2, level3 columns look simpler but break the moment the hierarchy grows one level deeper.

sections.title: Modeling History and Status
sections.content:
Three patterns come up in almost every real system:

  • Facts at a point in time: store the price paid on order_items at checkout. Today's product price may change; what the customer paid must not. This is not harmful duplication, because the two values mean different things.
  • Lookup tables: when statuses need labels or sort orders, give them their own table and reference it by key, instead of repeating text everywhere.
  • Soft deletes: a deleted_at column keeps rows for audit, but every normal query must then filter WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Start from the business nouns: entities become tables, attributes become columns.
  • One-to-many: the foreign key goes on the "many" side.
  • Many-to-many: a junction table with a composite key and the pairing's own attributes.
  • One-to-one: a foreign key that is also unique; split only for a reason.
  • Prefer stable surrogate keys, plus UNIQUE on natural values.
  • Model hierarchies with a parent_id; capture historical facts where they happened.

title: Normalization & Denormalization
summary: See why redundant data causes insert, update and delete anomalies, normalize tables to first, second and third normal form, and learn when deliberate denormalization is worth its cost.

sections.title: Why Redundancy Hurts
sections.content:
Imagine a single orders spreadsheet-style table that stores the customer's name, email and address on every order. It looks convenient: everything in one place, no joins.

Then a customer with 40 orders changes their email. Forty rows must change, and if one is missed the database now holds two different emails for the same person. Nothing tells you which is right.

Normalization is the discipline that prevents this. It organises tables so that each fact is stored in exactly one place, which makes contradictions impossible by design rather than by careful coding.

sections.title: The Three Anomalies
sections.content:
Redundant designs suffer three kinds of anomaly. Take a table course_enrollments(student, course, instructor, instructor_email):

  • Update anomaly: an instructor's email is repeated on hundreds of rows, and changing only some leaves conflicting values.
  • Insert anomaly: a new instructor can't be recorded until a student enrolls in one of their courses.
  • Delete anomaly: when the last student drops a course, the only record of who teaches it disappears.

All three come from the same root cause: facts about different things crammed into one table.

sections.title: First Normal Form (1NF)
sections.content:
A table is in 1NF when every column holds a single value: no lists, no repeating groups.

-- Not 1NF: several values packed into one column
products(id, name, tags)            -- tags = 'red,sale,cotton'

-- 1NF: one row per product and tag
products(id, name)
product_tags(product_id, tag)

Packed lists can't be indexed, constrained or queried reliably: searching for 'sale' with LIKE also matches 'wholesale'. Repeating columns such as phone1, phone2, phone3 break 1NF in spirit too, and cap how many values you can store.

sections.title: Second Normal Form (2NF)
sections.content:
A table is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and every non-key column depends on the whole primary key. This only matters for composite keys.

-- Primary key: (order_id, product_id)
order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name)

quantity depends on both the order and the product, so it belongs. product_name depends only on product_id, so it repeats for every order of that product. Move it to the products table, and order_items keeps just the keys and the pairing's own facts.

sections.title: Third Normal Form (3NF)
sections.content:
A table is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and no non-key column depends on another non-key column, meaning there are no transitive dependencies.

-- Primary key: id
employees(id, name, department_id, department_name)

department_name is determined by department_id, not by the employee, so it repeats for everyone in the department. It belongs in a departments table.

The classic summary of 1NF to 3NF: every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

sections.title: Normalizing a Real Table
sections.content:
Start with one flat table: orders(order_id, customer_name, customer_email, products, total).

  1. 1NF: the products list becomes rows in order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price).
  2. 2NF: product names and list prices move to products(id, name, price), leaving order_items with only facts about the pairing.
  3. 3NF: customer name and email describe the customer, not the order, so they move to customers(id, name, email) and orders keep customer_id.

The result is four focused tables, each with one job. Every fact now lives in one place, and joins put the full picture back together on demand.

sections.title: When to Denormalize
sections.content:
Denormalization deliberately stores redundant data to make important reads cheaper, accepting extra write work and a consistency risk. Common, justified cases:

  • A counter or summary read constantly, such as order_count on customers.
  • A measured, frequent query that stays too slow after indexing and tuning.
  • Historical facts that must not change, such as the price on an invoice line.

Denormalize on evidence, not instinct. Give every duplicated value one clear owner and one update path (a transaction, trigger or scheduled job), and consider a materialized view first.

sections.title: Transactional and Analytical Schemas
sections.content:
Application databases (OLTP, online transaction processing) handle many small reads and writes, so they are normalized, usually to 3NF, to keep writes cheap and data consistent.

Analytics warehouses (OLAP, online analytical processing) answer big read-only questions over history, so they are often deliberately denormalized into a star schema: a central fact table, such as one row per order line, surrounded by dimension tables for date, customer and product.

Data flows from one to the other through ETL or ELT pipelines (extract, transform, load), so each schema can be shaped for its own job.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Normalization stores each fact once, preventing update, insert and delete anomalies.
  • 1NF: one value per column, no lists or repeating groups.
  • 2NF: non-key columns depend on the whole composite key.
  • 3NF: no non-key column depends on another non-key column.
  • "The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."
  • Denormalize deliberately, on measured need, with a clear update path.
  • OLTP schemas are normalized; analytics star schemas are denormalized by design.

title: Subqueries & Set Operations
summary: Answer multi-step questions with scalar, IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries and derived tables, combine result sets with UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT, and choose between subqueries and joins.

sections.title: Queries Inside Queries
sections.content:
Some questions take two steps: "which products cost more than average?" first needs the average, then the comparison. A subquery is a complete SELECT nested inside another statement, and its result feeds the outer query.

Subqueries can appear in WHERE, in FROM, in the SELECT list, and even inside INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. What a subquery returns, whether one value, a list or a whole table, decides where it can be used, as the next slides show.

sections.title: Scalar Subqueries
sections.content:
A scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column, so it can stand anywhere a single value can:

SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);

If a subquery used with = or > returns more than one row, the query fails with an error such as "more than one row returned by a subquery". That usually means you wanted a list, which is what IN is for.

sections.title: IN and EXISTS
sections.content:
IN compares a value against every value a subquery returns:

SELECT * FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 500);

EXISTS only asks whether the subquery returns any row, and the database can stop at the first match:

SELECT * FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN for "has none" questions: if the subquery ever returns a NULL, NOT IN silently returns nothing at all.

sections.title: Correlated Subqueries
sections.content:
A correlated subquery refers to columns of the outer query, so it is conceptually re-evaluated for each outer row:

-- Employees paid above their OWN department's average
SELECT e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (
  SELECT AVG(x.salary)
  FROM employees x
  WHERE x.department_id = e.department_id
);

They express "compared with its own group" questions very naturally. Planners often rewrite them as joins, but when they can't, a correlated subquery over a large table can be slow. Aggregating once and joining, or using a window function, are the usual alternatives.

sections.title: Derived Tables
sections.content:
A subquery in FROM produces a temporary result that the outer query reads like a table. It is called a derived table:

SELECT t.customer_id, t.order_count
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
) AS t
WHERE t.order_count >= 5;

This "aggregate first, then filter or join" pattern is extremely common. MySQL and SQL Server require the alias (AS t); PostgreSQL made it optional in version 16, but naming it is a good habit everywhere. CTEs, in the next lesson, express the same idea more readably.

sections.title: Combining Results with UNION
sections.content:
Set operations stack the rows of two queries. The queries must return the same number of columns, with compatible types, in the same order:

SELECT email FROM customers
UNION
SELECT email FROM newsletter_subscribers;

UNION removes duplicate rows, which costs a sort or hash over the whole result. UNION ALL keeps every row and is cheaper, so prefer it whenever duplicates are impossible or acceptable. A single ORDER BY at the very end sorts the combined result.

sections.title: INTERSECT and EXCEPT
sections.content:
Two more set operations compare results instead of stacking them:

-- Customers who bought in both years
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2023
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2024;

-- Customers who bought in 2023 but not in 2024
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2023
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM orders_2024;

Order matters for EXCEPT: swapping the queries answers a different question. MySQL supports both from version 8.0.31, and Oracle calls EXCEPT MINUS. Where they aren't available, EXISTS and NOT EXISTS do the same job.

sections.title: Subquery, EXISTS or JOIN?
sections.content:
The same question can often be written several ways. A practical guide:

  • Need columns from the other table? Use a JOIN.
  • Only checking whether related rows exist? Use EXISTS or NOT EXISTS. They never duplicate outer rows and handle NULLs safely.
  • Comparing with a single computed value? Use a scalar subquery.
  • Aggregate, then use the result? Use a derived table or a CTE.

Modern planners often execute IN, EXISTS and equivalent joins with the same plan, so choose for correctness and readability, and check EXPLAIN when performance matters.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Subqueries nest a SELECT inside another statement.
  • Scalar subqueries return one value; use IN when a subquery returns a list.
  • EXISTS tests for any row; prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN.
  • Correlated subqueries reference the outer row and can be slow on big tables.
  • Derived tables (subqueries in FROM) need an alias in most engines.
  • UNION deduplicates, UNION ALL doesn't; INTERSECT and EXCEPT compare results.

title: CTEs & Recursive Queries
summary: Write complex queries as readable named steps with WITH, chain several CTEs together, and use recursive CTEs to generate sequences and walk hierarchies such as org charts, safely.

sections.title: Naming the Steps with WITH
sections.content:
A common table expression (CTE) gives a subquery a name at the top of the statement, so the main query can use it like a table:

WITH recent_orders AS (
  SELECT customer_id, total
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
)
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spend
FROM recent_orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

The CTE exists only for this one statement. Reading top to bottom, you see each step with a name that explains its purpose, instead of decoding nested parentheses from the inside out.

sections.title: Building a Query in Stages
sections.content:
One WITH can define several CTEs, separated by commas, and each can use the ones before it:

WITH paid AS (
  SELECT customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid'
),
spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS total_spend
  FROM paid
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, s.total_spend
FROM spend s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id
ORDER BY s.total_spend DESC
LIMIT 10;

Each stage has one job: filter, aggregate, present. While debugging, you can run any stage on its own by selecting from it directly.

sections.title: CTEs, Subqueries and Views
sections.content:
All three package a query, but they differ in reach:

  • A subquery is anonymous and lives inside one part of one statement.
  • A CTE is named, can be referenced several times within one statement, and can be recursive.
  • A view is saved in the database and reusable by any query, in any session.

A good rule: reach for a CTE when one statement has several logical steps or needs the same intermediate result twice. Promote the logic to a view when many different queries need it.

sections.title: Recursion: The Idea
sections.content:
A recursive CTE refers to itself. It has two parts joined by UNION ALL:

  1. An anchor query that produces the starting rows.
  2. A recursive query that produces the next rows from the ones found in the previous step.

The database runs the anchor, then repeats the recursive step on the newest rows, appending each new batch, until a step produces nothing. PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and SQLite require the keyword WITH RECURSIVE; SQL Server and Oracle accept a plain WITH.

sections.title: A First Recursive Query
sections.content:
The smallest useful example generates a sequence of numbers:

WITH RECURSIVE n AS (
  SELECT 1 AS x              -- anchor: start at 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT x + 1 FROM n        -- step: add one
  WHERE x < 5                -- stop condition
)
SELECT x FROM n;             -- 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

Trace it: the anchor yields 1; each step adds one while the previous value is below 5; when x reaches 5 the condition fails, no row is added, and recursion ends. Sequences like this are handy for filling date gaps in reports.

sections.title: Walking a Hierarchy
sections.content:
Recursion's real strength is hierarchies stored with a parent_id or manager_id:

WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
  FROM employees
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL                 -- anchor: the top of the tree

  UNION ALL

  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id        -- step: the next level down
)
SELECT name, depth FROM org ORDER BY depth, name;

Each iteration finds the direct reports of everyone found in the previous one, so the whole org chart unfolds level by level. An index on manager_id keeps each step fast.

sections.title: Guarding Against Endless Recursion
sections.content:
If the data contains a cycle, such as A reporting to B and B reporting to A, or "friend of a friend" links, the recursion can revisit the same rows forever.

  • Track the path visited so far and stop when a row is already on it.
  • Cap the depth: WHERE depth < 20.
  • Use UNION instead of UNION ALL when whole rows repeat, so duplicates end the recursion.
  • In PostgreSQL 14+, the built-in CYCLE clause does the tracking for you.

MySQL stops runaway recursion with its cte_max_recursion_depth setting, 1000 by default.

sections.title: A Note on Performance
sections.content:
CTEs are mainly a readability tool. In PostgreSQL 12+, MySQL 8 and SQL Server, a simple CTE referenced once is usually inlined: optimised exactly like the equivalent subquery, so it costs nothing extra.

A CTE can instead be materialized, computed once and stored, which helps when an expensive result is used several times but blocks the planner from pushing filters inside. PostgreSQL lets you choose with AS MATERIALIZED or AS NOT MATERIALIZED. Before version 12, PostgreSQL always materialized CTEs, which is why older articles call them optimisation fences.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A CTE names a subquery with WITH and lasts for one statement.
  • Chain several CTEs with commas; each can use the earlier ones.
  • Use CTEs for multi-step logic, views for logic shared across queries.
  • Recursive CTEs: an anchor plus a self-referencing step, joined by UNION ALL.
  • Recursion stops when a step adds no rows; always include a stop condition.
  • Guard against cycles with path tracking, depth limits or CYCLE.
  • Simple CTEs are inlined; materialization is a deliberate choice.

title: Window Functions
summary: Rank, compare and total rows within groups without collapsing them, using OVER, PARTITION BY, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, running totals and window frames for moving averages.

sections.title: Calculations That Keep Every Row
sections.content:
GROUP BY answers "what is each department's average salary?" but loses the individual employees. Often you want both at once: each employee next to their department's average, their rank within it, or the running total up to their row.

Window functions do exactly that. They compute across a set of related rows, the window, while keeping every row in the result. They unlock rankings, running totals, period-over-period comparisons and "latest row per group" queries in a single, readable statement.

sections.title: OVER and PARTITION BY
sections.content:
Adding OVER (…) after an aggregate turns it into a window function. PARTITION BY decides which rows form each window:

SELECT name,
       department,
       salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg,
       salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS vs_avg
FROM employees;

Every employee is still listed, with their department's average beside them. An empty OVER () makes the whole result one window, so sales / SUM(sales) OVER () gives each row's share of the grand total.

sections.title: Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
sections.content:
Ranking functions number rows in the order given inside OVER. They differ only on ties. For scores 90, 85, 85, 80:

  • ROW_NUMBER() gives 1, 2, 3, 4. Every row is unique, and ties are broken arbitrarily unless you add a tie-breaker.
  • RANK() gives 1, 2, 2, 4. Ties share a rank and a gap follows, like a race result.
  • DENSE_RANK() gives 1, 2, 2, 3. Ties share a rank, with no gap.
SELECT name, score,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS position
FROM exam_results;

sections.title: Top N per Group
sections.content:
"The three best-selling products in each category" is a classic window function job. Number the rows within each partition, then keep the first three:

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, name, units_sold,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY category
           ORDER BY units_sold DESC, name
         ) AS rn
  FROM product_sales
)
SELECT category, name, units_sold
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;

The filter must be in an outer query or CTE, because window functions are computed after WHERE. Some engines, such as Snowflake, BigQuery and DuckDB, add a QUALIFY clause for exactly this.

sections.title: Running Totals
sections.content:
Adding ORDER BY inside OVER makes the window grow row by row, so aggregates become cumulative:

SELECT sale_date,
       amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS running_total
FROM daily_sales;

Each row shows the total of all sales up to and including its date. Add PARTITION BY region and the running total restarts for each region. Without ORDER BY, every row would simply show the grand total.

sections.title: Comparing Rows with LAG and LEAD
sections.content:
LAG reads a value from an earlier row in the window's order, and LEAD from a later one, with no self join needed:

SELECT month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly_revenue;

The first month has no previous row, so LAG returns NULL. A third argument supplies a default instead: LAG(revenue, 1, 0). Typical uses include month-over-month growth, time between a user's sessions, and detecting status changes.

sections.title: Window Frames and Moving Averages
sections.content:
A frame narrows the window to rows near the current one. A 7-day trailing average, with one row per day:

SELECT day,
       visits,
       AVG(visits) OVER (
         ORDER BY day
         ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS avg_7d
FROM daily_visits;

With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default runs from the first row to the current row and includes tied rows together. That is why LAST_VALUE() often seems to return the current row: extend its frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

sections.title: Latest Row per Group
sections.content:
One of the most useful patterns in practice: each customer's most recent order.

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM orders o
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

The same shape removes duplicates: number the copies of each email from newest to oldest, then delete everything numbered above 1. In PostgreSQL, DISTINCT ON (customer_id) is a shorter alternative for the latest-row case.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Window functions compute across related rows but keep every row.
  • OVER (PARTITION BY …) defines the groups; OVER () covers the whole result.
  • ROW_NUMBER never ties; RANK leaves gaps; DENSE_RANK doesn't.
  • Top N or latest per group: number rows per partition, then filter in an outer query.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER makes totals cumulative.
  • LAG and LEAD compare with earlier and later rows.
  • Frames (ROWS BETWEEN …) give moving averages; mind the default frame.

title: Views, Stored Procedures & Triggers
summary: Package queries as views and materialized views, encapsulate logic in functions and stored procedures, react to changes with triggers, and judge when logic belongs in the database or the application.

sections.title: Views: Saved Queries
sections.content:
A view is a named SELECT stored in the database. Queries read from it as if it were a table, and the database runs the underlying query each time:

CREATE VIEW active_customers AS
SELECT c.id, c.name, c.email, MAX(o.created_at) AS last_order_at
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name, c.email
HAVING MAX(o.created_at) >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days';

SELECT * FROM active_customers WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com';

A regular view stores no data, so it is always up to date, and it is exactly as fast as the query inside it.

sections.title: Views for Simplicity and Security
sections.content:
Views earn their place in two main ways.

Simplicity: a reporting team queries active_customers instead of repeating a multi-table join, and the underlying tables can be reorganised without breaking their queries, as long as the view keeps its shape.

Security: a view can expose only certain columns or rows. Analysts can be granted SELECT on a view that leaves out email addresses and payment details, without any access to the base table.

GRANT SELECT ON orders_without_pii TO analyst;

sections.title: Updatable Views and Their Limits
sections.content:
Simple views over a single table, without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or set operations, can usually accept INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, which the database applies to the base table. More complex views need INSTEAD OF triggers to accept writes.

One surprise to watch for: PostgreSQL and MySQL expand SELECT * into a fixed column list when the view is created, so columns added to the table later don't appear in the view until it is recreated.

List columns explicitly in view definitions. It documents the view's contract and avoids the SELECT * surprise.

sections.title: Materialized Views
sections.content:
A materialized view runs its query once and stores the result, so reads are as fast as reading a table:

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at) AS day, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1;

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_revenue;   -- needs a unique index

The trade-off is staleness: the data is a snapshot until the next refresh, usually run on a schedule. That suits expensive dashboards that can be a few minutes or hours behind. MySQL has no native materialized views; a summary table refreshed by a scheduled job achieves the same thing.

sections.title: Stored Functions and Procedures
sections.content:
Databases can store named, reusable logic. A function returns a value and can be used inside queries; a procedure is run with CALL and, in PostgreSQL 11+, can commit transactions partway through.

CREATE FUNCTION price_with_tax(p DECIMAL) RETURNS DECIMAL AS $$
  SELECT ROUND(p * 1.18, 2);
$$ LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE;

SELECT name, price_with_tax(price) FROM products;

Procedures shine for heavy, set-based data work, such as nightly aggregation or bulk corrections, where running next to the data avoids moving millions of rows to an application.

sections.title: Triggers
sections.content:
A trigger runs automatically when a table event happens: INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE, either BEFORE or AFTER the change, inside the same transaction.

  • BEFORE triggers can inspect and modify the incoming row, or reject it.
  • AFTER triggers see the stored row and suit follow-up work, such as writing an audit record.
  • Row-level triggers fire once per affected row; statement-level triggers fire once per statement.

Good uses are small and self-contained: audit trails, timestamps and enforcing an invariant the database must always hold.

sections.title: A Practical Trigger: updated_at
sections.content:
Keeping an updated_at column current is the classic trigger example. In PostgreSQL, a trigger calls a trigger function:

CREATE FUNCTION set_updated_at() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at := CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER products_set_updated_at
BEFORE UPDATE ON products
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at();

It is a BEFORE trigger because it changes the row (NEW) before it is written. MySQL doesn't need a trigger for this: ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on the column does it.

sections.title: Database Logic or Application Logic?
sections.content:
Logic inside the database is powerful but less visible. Triggers in particular run implicitly, so a simple UPDATE can set off changes nobody sees in the application code, which makes behaviour hard to test, debug and tune.

  • In the database: integrity rules, audit logs, set-based data processing, and reusable read logic as views.
  • In the application: business rules that change often, workflows that call other services, and anything that benefits from normal testing and deployment.

Never call external systems, such as email or payment APIs, from a trigger. They can't be rolled back and they slow every write.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A view is a saved query: always current, no faster than its query.
  • Views simplify complex SQL and restrict which columns and rows users see.
  • Simple single-table views can be updatable; list columns explicitly.
  • Materialized views store results for fast reads and must be refreshed.
  • Functions return values usable in queries; procedures are run with CALL.
  • Triggers fire on table events; keep them small, few and free of external calls.

title: Indexes in Depth
summary: How B-tree indexes find rows, how to design composite, covering, unique, partial and expression indexes, and how to weigh every index against its write and storage cost.

sections.title: Why Queries Get Slow
sections.content:
Without help, the only way for a database to find the orders of customer 42 is to read every row in the table and check each one: a full table scan. On a thousand rows nobody notices. On fifty million rows, the same query takes seconds and competes with every other query for disk and memory.

An index is a separate structure that lets the database jump straight to the matching rows, the way a book's index takes you to the right page without reading the whole book. Most real-world performance work starts with indexes.

sections.title: How a B-tree Index Works
sections.content:
The default index type in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle is a B-tree: a balanced tree that keeps keys in sorted order, with each key pointing to its rows.

Finding a key means walking from the root down a handful of levels, even for millions of rows. Because keys are sorted, a B-tree also handles ranges (BETWEEN, >, <) and ordering: the database finds the first matching key and reads forward.

Other index types exist for special cases: hash indexes for pure equality, GIN for arrays, JSON and full-text search, GiST for geometry. B-trees cover the vast majority of everyday needs.

sections.title: Creating and Using an Index
sections.content:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);

SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42;   -- can now use the index

You never tell a query to use an index; the planner decides for each query, based on how many rows it expects to match. Primary keys and UNIQUE constraints get an index automatically.

Foreign keys are a common gap: MySQL's InnoDB indexes them automatically, but PostgreSQL does not. Index them yourself, because joins and parent deletes look up child rows by those columns.

sections.title: Composite Indexes and the Leftmost Prefix
sections.content:
A composite index covers several columns, sorted by the first, then by the second within each first value, and so on. It helps queries that filter on a leftmost prefix of its columns:

CREATE INDEX idx_tasks_status_created ON tasks (status, created_at);

-- Uses the index well: equality on status, then range or sort on created_at
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE status = 'open' ORDER BY created_at;

-- Cannot use it efficiently: skips the leading column
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE created_at > '2024-06-01';

Order composite index columns as: equality filters first, then the range or sort column.

sections.title: Covering Indexes
sections.content:
Normally an index lookup finds matching keys, then visits the table to fetch the other columns. If the index already contains every column the query needs, the table visit is skipped. This is an index-only scan, using a covering index:

-- Query: SELECT created_at, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_cover
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (total);   -- PostgreSQL 11+, SQL Server

In MySQL, extra columns are simply added to the index key. Covering indexes are a targeted tool for very frequent queries; wider indexes cost more space and slower writes. This is also one more reason to avoid SELECT *.

sections.title: Unique, Partial and Expression Indexes
sections.content:
• Unique: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON users (email) both speeds lookups and enforces uniqueness on every write.
  • Partial (PostgreSQL): indexes only rows matching a condition, staying small when queries focus on a subset, such as … ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'.
  • Expression (functional): indexes a computed value, so a query filtering on it can use the index.
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users (LOWER(email));

SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = LOWER('Ana@Example.com');

The query's expression must match the indexed expression exactly.

sections.title: What Indexes Cost
sections.content:
Indexes are not free:

  • Writes slow down: every INSERT and DELETE, and every UPDATE of an indexed column, must also update each index.
  • Storage and memory: indexes compete with table data for cache.
  • Low selectivity wastes them: if a filter matches most of the table, scanning is cheaper and the planner ignores the index.

Indexing every column "just in case" is a common mistake on write-heavy tables. Fourteen indexes on a busy table can make each insert many times slower.

sections.title: Choosing Indexes Wisely
sections.content:
Work from real queries, not guesses:

  1. Find the most expensive queries by total time, using the slow query log or pg_stat_statements.
  2. Index columns those queries filter, join and sort on, and design composite indexes around their exact shape.
  3. Check the plan with EXPLAIN to confirm the index is used.
  4. Periodically find unused or redundant indexes and drop them: an index on (a) is usually redundant next to (a, b).

In PostgreSQL, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds an index without blocking writes on a live table.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• An index lets the database jump to rows instead of scanning the whole table.
  • B-trees keep keys sorted, supporting equality, ranges and ordering.
  • Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: equality columns first, then range or sort.
  • Covering indexes enable index-only scans.
  • Unique, partial and expression indexes solve specific problems.
  • Every index costs write speed and storage; index real queries and drop unused ones.
  • Index foreign keys yourself in PostgreSQL.

title: Query Plans & Optimization
summary: Read execution plans with EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, understand join algorithms and statistics, write sargable predicates, and fix N+1 queries and slow pagination with a repeatable tuning workflow.

sections.title: How the Planner Decides
sections.content:
SQL says what you want, never how to get it. For each query, the database's planner (optimizer) considers many possible strategies: which index to use or whether to scan, which table to read first, which join algorithm to apply. It estimates the cost of each and picks the cheapest.

Those estimates come from statistics about your data, such as row counts and how values are distributed. When the statistics are accurate, the planner is remarkably good. When they are stale or misleading, it can choose a plan that is thousands of times slower than the best one.

sections.title: Reading EXPLAIN
sections.content:
EXPLAIN shows the plan the database intends to use, as a tree of steps:

EXPLAIN
SELECT o.id, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2024-06-01';

Read it from the most indented node outwards: those run first and feed their parents. For each node, check the type (a sequential scan, an index scan, or an index-only scan), the join method, and the estimated rows. A sequential scan over a huge table in a query that should return a few rows is the most common red flag.

sections.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Plans Meet Reality
sections.content:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and adds the real time and real row count for every node, so you can compare the planner's guesses with what happened:

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
-- ... (cost=... rows=12 ...) (actual time=... rows=480000 loops=1)

A huge gap between estimated and actual rows, here 12 against 480,000, means the planner misjudged the data, and every decision built on that guess may be wrong. Because it really executes, wrap EXPLAIN ANALYZE of an UPDATE or DELETE in BEGIN … ROLLBACK.

sections.title: Join Algorithms
sections.content:
The planner chooses between three main ways to join:

  • Nested loop: for each outer row, look up matches in the inner input. Excellent when the outer side is small and the inner join column is indexed; disastrous for two large inputs.
  • Hash join: build a hash table from the smaller input, then probe it with each row of the larger one. Good for large, unsorted inputs joined on equality.
  • Merge join: walk two inputs already sorted on the join key, side by side.

A nested loop chosen because the planner expected 10 rows, when the real number is 2 million, is a classic cause of sudden slowdowns.

sections.title: Sargable Predicates
sections.content:
A condition is sargable when an index can evaluate it, which generally means the column stands alone on one side of the comparison:

-- Not sargable: the function hides the column from the index
WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024
-- Sargable
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01'

-- Not sargable: leading wildcard, or a type conversion on the column
WHERE name LIKE '%son'
WHERE phone = 5551234      -- phone is VARCHAR: MySQL converts every row

Rewrite the condition when you can. When you can't, an expression index on exactly that expression is the alternative.

sections.title: Statistics and Bad Estimates
sections.content:
Statistics go stale after big data changes, such as bulk imports, mass deletes or rapid growth. Refreshing them is cheap and often fixes a mysteriously bad plan:

ANALYZE orders;          -- PostgreSQL
ANALYZE TABLE orders;    -- MySQL

PostgreSQL's autovacuum and MySQL refresh statistics automatically, but not always soon enough after a large change. Some problems come from correlated columns, such as city and postcode, which the planner assumes are independent; PostgreSQL's extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS) can teach it about those relationships.

sections.title: The N+1 Query Problem
sections.content:
Many slow pages are slow because of how many queries they run, not because any single query is slow:

const orders = await Order.findAll({ limit: 50 });   // 1 query
for (const o of orders) {
  o.customer = await Customer.findByPk(o.customerId); // 50 more queries
}

Each query takes a millisecond, but 51 round trips add up. The fix is to load related rows in one query, with a join or a single WHERE id IN (…), usually through the ORM's eager loading (include, joinedload, JOIN FETCH). Query logs showing the same statement repeated per item are the giveaway.

sections.title: Pagination at Scale
sections.content:
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000 looks cheap, but the database still produces and throws away 200,000 rows before returning 20, so deep pages get steadily slower. Keyset pagination continues from where the previous page ended instead:

SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM articles
WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

With an index on (created_at, id), every page costs the same. The trade-off is that users move next and previous, rather than jumping to page 5,000, which suits infinite scroll and APIs.

sections.title: A Tuning Workflow
sections.content:
1. Measure first: rank queries by total time (time per call × number of calls) using pg_stat_statements, the slow query log or APM traces.
  2. Reproduce the slowest with realistic parameter values.
  3. Read the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE: scans on big tables, bad estimates, spilled sorts, huge loop counts.
  4. Fix the cause: an index, a sargable rewrite, fresh statistics, a query restructure, or an N+1 fix in the application.
  5. Verify with the plan and production metrics.

Change one thing at a time. Otherwise you can't tell which change helped, and which quietly made something else worse.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• The planner picks the cheapest plan it can estimate, based on statistics.
  • EXPLAIN shows the plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows actual rows and times.
  • Large estimate-versus-actual gaps point to stale statistics; run ANALYZE.
  • Keep predicates sargable: no functions, conversions or leading wildcards on indexed columns.
  • Fix N+1 queries with joins or batched IN lookups.
  • Use keyset pagination for deep pages.
  • Measure, reproduce, read, fix, verify: one change at a time.

title: Transactions & ACID
summary: Group changes so they succeed or fail together with BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK and savepoints, understand what each ACID property guarantees, and place transaction boundaries correctly in real applications.

sections.title: Why Transactions Exist
sections.content:
Transferring money takes two updates: subtract from one account, add to another. If the server crashes between them, money vanishes. If two transfers interleave badly, balances end up wrong.

A transaction groups several statements into one unit of work that either happens completely or not at all. Other users never see it half done, and once it is committed it survives crashes.

Transactions are what let developers reason about multi-step changes as if each were a single, safe action, which is one of the main reasons relational databases are trusted with money, orders and inventory.

sections.title: BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK
sections.content:
BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (1, 2, 100);

COMMIT;

BEGIN (or START TRANSACTION) opens the transaction. COMMIT makes every change permanent and visible to others at once. ROLLBACK discards everything since BEGIN.

The application checks that the first update affected exactly one row, meaning there were enough funds, and rolls back otherwise.

sections.title: Atomicity and Consistency
sections.content:
ACID names the four guarantees transactions give. The first two:

  • Atomicity: all of a transaction's changes happen, or none do. A crash midway leaves no trace of the partial work, so a debit never happens without its matching credit.
  • Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. Constraints such as foreign keys, CHECK (balance >= 0) and uniqueness hold at every commit; if a change would break one, the transaction fails instead.

Consistency is shared work: the database enforces declared constraints, while the application is responsible for business rules it hasn't declared.

sections.title: Isolation and Durability
sections.content:
• Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere in ways that break correctness. How strictly depends on the isolation level, covered in the Concurrency lesson.
  • Durability: once COMMIT returns, the changes survive crashes and power loss.

Durability comes from write-ahead logging (WAL in PostgreSQL, the redo log in InnoDB). Before a commit is acknowledged, a record of its changes is written sequentially to a log and flushed to disk. After a crash, the database replays the log to recover any committed work that hadn't reached the data files yet. The same log feeds replication and point-in-time recovery.

sections.title: Autocommit and Transaction Boundaries
sections.content:
Most clients and drivers run in autocommit mode: each statement is its own transaction, committed as soon as it succeeds. Grouping statements requires an explicit transaction, which frameworks usually manage for you, for example with Spring's @Transactional or an ORM's transaction() helper.

await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  await tx.query('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2', [100, 1]);
  await tx.query('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2', [100, 2]);
}); // commits if the function succeeds, rolls back if it throws

A transaction should wrap exactly the work that must succeed or fail together.

sections.title: Savepoints
sections.content:
A savepoint marks a point inside a transaction that you can roll back to, without abandoning the whole transaction:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (7, 120.00);
SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
UPDATE coupons SET used_count = used_count + 1 WHERE code = 'SAVE10';
-- coupon turned out to be invalid:
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
COMMIT;   -- the order is kept, the coupon change is not

Savepoints suit optional steps that may fail. ORMs also use them to implement "nested" transactions.

sections.title: Errors and DDL Inside Transactions
sections.content:
Databases differ in how they treat a failed statement mid-transaction:

  • PostgreSQL marks the transaction as aborted and rejects every further statement until ROLLBACK, or ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT.
  • MySQL lets the transaction continue after most errors, so application code must decide to roll back explicitly.

Schema changes differ too. PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so a failed migration can roll back cleanly. MySQL and Oracle commit implicitly around most CREATE and ALTER statements, so a failed multi-step migration can leave the schema half-changed.

sections.title: Keep Transactions Short
sections.content:
Locks taken inside a transaction are held until it ends, so long transactions block other users and, under MVCC, delay cleanup of old row versions.

  • Never wait for user input inside a transaction.
  • Never call slow external services, such as payment gateways or email APIs, inside one. They can't be rolled back, and they hold locks while you wait.

For workflows that span services, use separate local transactions with clear states and compensating actions, known as the saga pattern. Create the order as pending, charge the card outside the transaction with an idempotency key, then mark the order paid or release the stock.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A transaction groups statements into one all-or-nothing unit.
  • BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK; savepoints allow partial rollback.
  • Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability; durability comes from write-ahead logging.
  • Autocommit runs each statement as its own transaction.
  • PostgreSQL aborts a transaction after an error and supports transactional DDL; MySQL doesn't.
  • Keep transactions short; keep external calls outside them.

title: Concurrency: Isolation, Locking & MVCC
summary: Predict what concurrent transactions see under each isolation level, prevent lost updates and phantoms with locks or optimistic versioning, understand MVCC, and avoid and handle deadlocks.

sections.title: When Users Collide
sections.content:
Two people book the last seat at the same moment. Both requests read seats_left = 1, both decide a booking is fine, and both write seats_left = 0. Two tickets are sold for one seat. This is a lost update: one change silently overwrote the other.

Every multi-user system faces problems like this. The database gives you tools to prevent them: isolation levels control what concurrent transactions can see, and locks and versioning control who can change what, and when. Choosing among them is a trade-off between correctness and throughput.

sections.title: Read Anomalies
sections.content:
Weaker isolation allows three classic read anomalies:

  • Dirty read: seeing another transaction's uncommitted change, which might later be rolled back.
  • Non-repeatable read: reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values, because someone committed a change in between.
  • Phantom read: re-running the same query and getting new rows, because someone inserted rows that match the condition.

Add the lost update from the previous slide and you have the main ways concurrent transactions can produce wrong answers.

sections.title: Isolation Levels
sections.content:
The SQL standard defines four levels, from weakest to strongest:

  • READ UNCOMMITTED: allows dirty reads. PostgreSQL treats it as READ COMMITTED.
  • READ COMMITTED: each statement sees only data committed before it began. This is the default in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle.
  • REPEATABLE READ: rows you have read don't change for the rest of the transaction. This is the default in MySQL's InnoDB.
  • SERIALIZABLE: results equal some one-at-a-time ordering of the transactions; conflicting ones are aborted and must be retried.
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;   -- PostgreSQL syntax

sections.title: MVCC: Many Versions of a Row
sections.content:
PostgreSQL, MySQL's InnoDB and Oracle use MVCC (multi-version concurrency control). An update writes a new version of the row instead of overwriting it, and the old version stays available to any transaction whose snapshot still needs it.

Each transaction, or each statement under READ COMMITTED, reads a consistent snapshot. The result: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. Only writers changing the same row wait for each other.

Old versions must be cleaned up: by VACUUM in PostgreSQL, usually through autovacuum, and by the purge thread in InnoDB. Long-running transactions hold back that cleanup, so tables bloat. That is another reason to keep transactions short.

sections.title: Row Locks and SELECT … FOR UPDATE
sections.content:
For read-then-write logic, pessimistic locking locks the rows while reading them, so nobody else can change them until you commit:

BEGIN;
SELECT seats_left FROM flights WHERE id = 17 FOR UPDATE;   -- others now wait
-- application checks seats_left > 0
UPDATE flights SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = 17;
INSERT INTO bookings (flight_id, user_id) VALUES (17, 42);
COMMIT;

Simpler still, when the check can be expressed in SQL: one atomic conditional update, UPDATE flights SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = 17 AND seats_left > 0. Zero affected rows means sold out.

sections.title: Optimistic Locking
sections.content:
Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare and detects them at write time, holding no locks in between. Each row carries a version number:

-- Read: version = 7
UPDATE documents
SET body = :new_body, version = version + 1
WHERE id = :id AND version = 7;
-- 0 rows updated means someone else saved first: reload and retry

It suits long user edits and low-contention data, where holding a lock while someone types would be wasteful. For hot rows updated constantly, retries pile up, and pessimistic locking is the better fit.

sections.title: Deadlocks
sections.content:
A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs: A locks account 1 and wants account 2, while B locks account 2 and wants account 1. Neither can proceed, so the database detects the cycle and aborts one of them with an error.

  • Lock in a consistent order, such as always the lower account id first. This prevents the cycle entirely.
  • Keep transactions short, and index the columns in UPDATE … WHERE so fewer rows get locked.
  • Retry transactions aborted by deadlocks. Under heavy concurrency they can be reduced, never fully eliminated.

sections.title: Pattern: Job Queues with SKIP LOCKED
sections.content:
Several workers pulling jobs from one table would normally queue up behind each other's locks. SKIP LOCKED makes each worker pass over rows that are already locked and grab the next free ones:

BEGIN;
SELECT id, payload
FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 10
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
-- mark them 'running', then COMMIT
COMMIT;

Supported in PostgreSQL 9.5+ and MySQL 8, it turns an ordinary table into a reliable work queue. Add a sweep that resets jobs stuck in running in case a worker crashes.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Concurrency bugs: lost updates, dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads.
  • Isolation levels trade correctness for throughput; READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL) and REPEATABLE READ (MySQL) are the defaults.
  • SERIALIZABLE prevents every anomaly but requires retries.
  • MVCC keeps row versions so readers and writers don't block each other.
  • Pessimistic: SELECT … FOR UPDATE; optimistic: version checks with retry.
  • Prefer atomic conditional updates when the check fits in SQL.
  • Prevent deadlocks with a consistent lock order, and retry when they happen.

title: Security & Access Control
summary: Stop SQL injection with parameterized queries and allowlists, apply least privilege through roles and grants, isolate data with row-level security, and protect sensitive data with encryption and safe handling.

sections.title: What We Are Protecting Against
sections.content:
A database usually holds an organisation's most valuable and most sensitive data: customer details, payments, credentials. Attacks and accidents tend to fall into a few groups:

  • Injection: attackers smuggling SQL through application input.
  • Over-privileged access: accounts and people able to do far more than they need.
  • Data exposure: sniffed connections, stolen disks or backups, leaked test copies.
  • Insider mistakes: a well-meaning person running the wrong statement.

Good database security is layered: each layer limits the damage when another one fails.

sections.title: SQL Injection
sections.content:
SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, so the input can change the query itself:

// Vulnerable
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email +
            "' AND password_hash = '" + hash + "'";
// email entered as:  ' OR '1'='1' --

The input closes the string, adds a condition that is always true, and comments out the password check, so the query returns every user. Similar input can read other tables, change data or drop tables entirely. Injection has been one of the most damaging web vulnerabilities for over two decades, and it is entirely preventable.

sections.title: Parameterized Queries
sections.content:
The defence is parameterized queries, also called prepared statements. The SQL text and the values travel separately, so input is never parsed as SQL:

// Safe: the email is bound as a value
const { rows } = await db.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = $1',
  [email]
);

Every driver and ORM supports this, using placeholders such as $1, ? or :email. ORMs are safe by default, but their "raw SQL" escape hatches are not, so use their parameter binding there too. Hand-written escaping, input length limits and hidden error messages help a little, but they don't replace parameters.

sections.title: Identifiers Need an Allowlist
sections.content:
Parameters replace values only, not table names, column names or keywords such as ASC. When users choose a sort column, map their choice to a fixed set in code:

const SORTS = {
  newest: 'created_at DESC',
  cheapest: 'price ASC',
};
const orderBy = SORTS[req.query.sort] ?? SORTS.newest;
const sql = `SELECT id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY ${orderBy} LIMIT $1`;

User input only ever selects a key; the SQL text always comes from your code. Anything not on the list falls back to a safe default.

sections.title: Least Privilege and Roles
sections.content:
Every account should have only the permissions it needs:

CREATE ROLE app_rw;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA shop TO app_rw;

CREATE ROLE analyst;
GRANT SELECT ON orders, products TO analyst;

GRANT app_rw TO shop_api;      -- the application's login
REVOKE analyst FROM former_contractor;

Use separate accounts for the application (data changes only), migrations (schema changes), reporting (read-only, ideally on a replica) and each person, with no shared logins. Granting to roles keeps permissions consistent and makes offboarding a single REVOKE.

sections.title: Row-Level Security
sections.content:
In a multi-tenant application, every query must filter by tenant, and one forgotten WHERE leaks another customer's data. PostgreSQL's row-level security (RLS) enforces the filter inside the database:

ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int);

Once the application sets app.tenant_id for its session, every query on invoices automatically sees only that tenant's rows. RLS is a strong safety net for shared-table multi-tenancy and for restricting rows per user.

sections.title: Encryption in Transit and at Rest
sections.content:
• In transit: enable TLS (Transport Layer Security) on database connections, so queries, results and credentials can't be read or altered on the network. This is essential whenever traffic crosses shared or cloud networks.
  • At rest: encrypt data files, backups and snapshots, through disk encryption, transparent data encryption or managed cloud options. This protects against stolen disks and leaked backup files.

Neither stops someone who can log in and query normally. That is the job of permissions, row-level security and, for the most sensitive fields, application-level encryption with keys stored outside the database.

sections.title: Handling Sensitive Data
sections.content:
• Passwords: never store them, even encrypted. Store salted hashes from a slow password-hashing algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2, so a leaked table is very hard to crack.
  • Error messages: show users a generic message and log details server-side. Raw database errors reveal table names and query structure to attackers.
  • Test data: use masked or synthetic data instead of raw production copies, which spread personal data to laptops and test servers with weaker controls.
  • Secrets: keep database credentials in a secrets manager, not in source code.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Security is layered: each layer limits damage when another fails.
  • SQL injection comes from concatenating input into SQL; parameterized queries prevent it.
  • Use allowlists for identifiers such as sort columns.
  • Least privilege: separate accounts, permissions granted through roles.
  • Row-level security enforces tenant and user filters in the database.
  • TLS protects data in transit; encryption at rest protects disks and backups.
  • Hash passwords with bcrypt or Argon2, hide raw errors, mask test data.

title: Backup, Replication & Scaling
summary: Plan backups and point-in-time recovery around RPO and RTO, use replication, read replicas and failover, handle replication lag, and scale step by step with pooling, partitioning and sharding.

sections.title: Planning for Failure
sections.content:
Disks fail, servers crash, regions go offline, and people run the wrong DELETE. The question is not whether something will go wrong, but how much you lose and how long you are down when it does. Two numbers frame every plan:

  • RPO (recovery point objective): the most data the business can afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of 5 minutes means losing at most the last 5 minutes of changes.
  • RTO (recovery time objective): the longest acceptable downtime before service is restored.

Backup frequency, log archiving, replication and failover are all chosen to meet these two targets.

sections.title: Logical and Physical Backups
sections.content:
• Logical backups (pg_dump, mysqldump) export the schema and data as SQL or a portable format. They are flexible, work across versions and can restore single tables, but they are slow to restore for large databases.
  • Physical backups (pg_basebackup, Percona XtraBackup, storage snapshots) copy the database's data files directly. They are much faster to restore at scale, and they are the foundation for point-in-time recovery.

Larger systems typically rely on physical backups plus continuous log archiving, keeping logical dumps for migrations and selective restores. Managed cloud databases handle much of this automatically, but you still choose retention and test the restores.

sections.title: Point-in-Time Recovery
sections.content:
Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores a base backup and then replays the archived transaction log (PostgreSQL WAL or MySQL binlog) up to any chosen moment, such as one minute before an accidental DROP TABLE.

For a mistake made an hour ago on a busy system, don't roll the whole database back, which would erase an hour of legitimate work. Restore to a separate instance as of just before the mistake, then copy back only the lost rows.

Replication is not a backup. Replicas copy every change, including the bad DELETE, within seconds. Only backups with log history can bring the old data back.

sections.title: Test Your Restores
sections.content:
A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan. Backups fail silently: missing files, corrupt archives, expired credentials, or a restore procedure nobody has tried.

  • Restore regularly, ideally automatically, into a scratch environment.
  • Verify the restored data: row counts, recent records, application smoke tests.
  • Time the restore. That is your real RTO, and it is often much longer than people assume.
  • Keep copies off-site, in another region or account, and protected from deletion, so ransomware or a compromised account can't destroy them along with production.

sections.title: Replication and Read Replicas
sections.content:
In primary/replica replication, the primary streams its transaction log to one or more replicas, which replay it to stay in sync. Replicas serve two purposes:

  • High availability: if the primary fails, a replica can take over.
  • Read scaling: reports, dashboards, search and other read-heavy work move to read replicas, leaving the primary free for writes.

In standard setups, replicas are read-only, and all writes go to the primary.

sections.title: Replication Lag and Failover
sections.content:
With asynchronous replication, replicas apply changes slightly after the primary commits them, usually within milliseconds but sometimes seconds under load. A user who saves a profile and is then served by a replica can see stale data. A common fix is to route each user's reads to the primary briefly after they write.

Synchronous replication waits for a replica to confirm before acknowledging a commit: no committed data is lost on failover, but every write pays the extra round trip.

Failover promotes a replica to primary when the primary fails. Tools such as Patroni, and managed cloud services, automate it to stay within the RTO.

sections.title: Partitioning
sections.content:
Partitioning splits one large table into smaller pieces inside the same database, for example one partition per month:

CREATE TABLE events (
  id         BIGINT,
  created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  payload    JSONB
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE events_2024_06 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-06-01') TO ('2024-07-01');

Queries filtering on created_at read only the relevant partitions (partition pruning), and retention becomes cheap: dropping an old month is a quick metadata operation instead of a huge DELETE. Partitioning does not add capacity beyond the single server.

sections.title: Sharding
sections.content:
Sharding spreads rows across several independent database servers by a shard key, such as customer_id. Each shard holds part of the data and handles part of the write load, which is how the largest systems grow beyond a single primary.

The cost is high: joins, aggregates and transactions across shards need application logic or distributed tooling, every query must be routed to the right shard, and rebalancing data between shards is operationally heavy.

Distributed SQL databases and extensions such as Citus or Vitess automate parts of sharding, but the design trade-offs remain. Treat sharding as a last step, not a starting point.

sections.title: Scaling Step by Step
sections.content:
When a database approaches its limits, work through the options roughly in order of cost:

  1. Optimise the top queries: indexes, sargable rewrites, N+1 fixes.
  2. Pool connections with an application pool or PgBouncer, because thousands of connections can exhaust a server long before its CPU.
  3. Cache hot, rarely changing reads.
  4. Scale up to a bigger machine: simple, with no code changes.
  5. Add read replicas for read-heavy work.
  6. Partition very large tables.
  7. Shard only when write volume truly exceeds one primary.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• RPO is how much data you can lose; RTO is how long you can be down.
  • Logical backups are flexible; physical backups plus log archiving enable point-in-time recovery.
  • Replication is not a backup: it copies mistakes too.
  • Test restores regularly, time them, and keep off-site, protected copies.
  • Replicas give high availability and read scaling; plan for replication lag.
  • Partitioning splits tables within one server; sharding splits data across servers.
  • Scale in order: optimise, pool, cache, scale up, replicate, partition, then shard.

title: Monorepos and Nx
summary: Why teams keep many projects in one repository, how a monorepo differs from a monolith, and what Nx core, plugins and Nx Cloud each add.

sections.title: Why One Repository?
sections.content:
Imagine a company with a web app and an admin app in two separate repositories. Both need the same date-formatting utility. There are two common options, and both hurt:

  • Copy it into each repository. The copies drift apart as each team fixes bugs in its own version.
  • Publish it as a package. Every change now needs a new release, and each app must update to that version before it can use the fix.

A monorepo removes this friction: both apps import the utility directly from the same repository, so a fix is available to everyone the moment it is merged.

sections.title: Monorepo vs Monolith
sections.content:
The two words sound alike but describe different things.

  • A monorepo is about where code lives: many separate projects, such as apps and libraries, in one repository. Each project can still be built, tested and deployed on its own.
  • A monolith is about architecture: one large application that is deployed as a single unit.
