You can have either without the other. A monorepo can hold a dozen small services that are deployed independently, and a monolith can live alone in its own repository. Choosing a monorepo does not mean merging your apps into one.

sections.title: Atomic Changes
sections.content:
Because a library and every project that uses it live together, one commit can change both. Say you rename formatDate to formatDisplayDate in a shared library:

  • in a monorepo, the same commit renames the function and updates every caller in every app
  • reviewers see the whole change in one pull request
  • the repository is never in a half-updated state where some apps are broken

With separate repositories, the same rename means publishing a new library version, opening a pull request in each app, and keeping the old name around until all of them have upgraded.

sections.title: The Scaling Problem
sections.content:
A monorepo has a cost if nothing understands its structure. With plain scripts, CI has no idea which projects a change touches, so the safe choice is to build and test everything on every pull request.

With 5 projects that is fine. With 60 projects, a one-line fix to a single library still rebuilds and retests all 60, and CI time keeps growing as the repository grows. Developers wait longer, and the benefits of sharing code start to feel like a burden.

This is the problem Nx exists to solve: make a large monorepo feel as fast as a small one.

sections.title: What Nx Adds
sections.content:
Nx is a build system for monorepos. It adds four capabilities that the rest of this subject builds on:

  • A project graph: a map of every project and which projects depend on which.
  • Task orchestration: running builds, tests and lints in the right order, in parallel where possible.
  • Caching: never running the same task twice when nothing it depends on has changed.
  • Affected runs: running tasks only for the projects a change can impact.

On top of these sit tools that keep a growing codebase organised, such as module boundary rules and code generators.

sections.title: Nx Core, Plugins and Nx Cloud
sections.content:
Nx comes in three layers, and only the first is required.

  • Nx core is the task runner. It builds the project graph, runs tasks and caches results on your machine. It works on its own, even with plain package.json scripts.
  • Nx plugins, such as @nx/react or @nx/vite, teach Nx about specific tools. They create tasks from config files and provide generators for new projects.
  • Nx Cloud is an optional hosted service. It shares the cache across the team and CI, spreads tasks across machines and adds CI features such as flaky task retries.

sections.title: Package-Based and Integrated Setups
sections.content:
Nx workspaces usually follow one of two styles.

  • Package-based: every project has its own package.json and dependencies, linked together by npm, pnpm or Yarn workspaces.
  • Integrated: dependencies are declared once at the root, and projects are wired together through Nx and TypeScript configuration.

Many integrated workspaces follow a single version policy: one version of each dependency, such as React, for the whole repository. Shared libraries then always work with every app. The trade-off is that an upgrade has to be made and tested across all projects at once.

sections.title: When a Monorepo Does Not Fit
sections.content:
A monorepo pays off when projects share code or change together. It is a weaker fit when:

  • products are unrelated and share no code
  • teams must not see each other's code, since one repository makes access control harder
  • nobody can own the shared tooling and CI

Language is rarely the reason to say no. Besides JavaScript and TypeScript, official plugins support Gradle, Maven and .NET projects, so a Java backend and a TypeScript frontend can share one workspace and get the same caching and affected runs.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A monorepo is many separate projects in one repository; a monolith is one app deployed as a unit
  • Monorepos make code sharing and atomic changes easy
  • Without tooling, a growing monorepo builds and tests everything on every change
  • Nx adds a project graph, task orchestration, caching and affected runs
  • Nx core works alone; plugins add tool knowledge; Nx Cloud is optional
  • Package-based setups give each project a package.json; integrated setups share root dependencies
  • A single version policy keeps projects compatible but makes every upgrade workspace-wide
  • Unrelated products or strict access rules are reasons to keep repositories separate

title: Workspace Structure
summary: Create a workspace or add Nx to an existing repo, organise apps and libraries, and know what nx.json, project.json and package.json each control.

sections.title: Creating a Workspace
sections.content:
To start a new monorepo from scratch, run:

npx create-nx-workspace@latest acme

The command asks a few questions, such as which stack or template to start from, and then creates a repository with Nx already set up: an nx.json, a package.json and, depending on your choices, a first app.

Starting this way means every convention, from folder layout to task configuration, is consistent from day one. For a repository that already exists, there is a gentler option, covered next.

sections.title: Adding Nx to an Existing Repo
sections.content:
Most teams do not start fresh. To add Nx to a repository that already exists, run:

npx nx init

nx init installs Nx, creates nx.json and asks which scripts are safe to cache, such as build, test and lint. It does not move any folders.

Existing commands keep working, and the same scripts can now be run through Nx, for example npx nx build web, to get caching and correct ordering. Teams can then adopt more features step by step instead of restructuring everything at once.

sections.title: Apps and Libraries
sections.content:
An Nx workspace holds two kinds of projects.

  • Apps are entry points that get deployed or run: a web app, an admin panel, an API.
  • Libraries hold code that apps and other libraries import: UI components, data access, utilities, feature logic.

A common guideline is to keep apps thin. An app wires libraries together and adds configuration, while most real code lives in libraries. Smaller projects make Nx's caching and affected runs more precise, because a change touches fewer projects. The libraries lesson covers how to split and organise them.

sections.title: How Nx Finds Projects
sections.content:
Nx does not rely on folder names. A folder is a project when it contains:

  • a project.json file, or
  • a package.json that Nx picks up, for example through the package manager's workspaces

Folders such as apps/, libs/ or packages/ are conventions that help people find things. They are not requirements. Many large workspaces group projects by business area instead:

shop/app
shop/feature-cart
admin/app
shared/ui-buttons

Whatever the layout, npx nx show projects lists every project Nx found.

sections.title: nx.json: Workspace Settings
sections.content:
nx.json at the root holds settings for the whole workspace:

{
  "plugins": ["@nx/vite/plugin"],
  "targetDefaults": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "cache": true }
  },
  "namedInputs": {
    "default": ["{projectRoot}/**/*"],
    "production": ["default", "!{projectRoot}/**/*.spec.ts"]
  },
  "defaultBase": "main"
}
  • plugins registers plugins that create tasks
  • targetDefaults applies settings to every target with that name
  • namedInputs defines reusable file sets for caching
  • defaultBase is the branch affected runs compare with

sections.title: A Project's Own Configuration
sections.content:
Each project can have its own settings in project.json, or in an nx section of its package.json:

{
  "name": "shop",
  "tags": ["scope:shop", "type:app"],
  "implicitDependencies": ["shared-assets"],
  "targets": {
    "build": { "outputs": ["{projectRoot}/dist"] }
  }
}

Project configuration holds what is specific to that project: its tags, links Nx cannot detect on its own, and any target settings that differ from the workspace defaults. A good rule: set things once in nx.json, and only override in a project when it genuinely needs something different.

sections.title: Package Manager Workspaces
sections.content:
How does an app import a library by name, as in import { Button } from '@acme/ui'? In package-based workspaces, the package manager does it.

npm, pnpm and Yarn all support workspaces: you list the folders that hold packages, in pnpm-workspace.yaml or the workspaces field of the root package.json, and the package manager links each local package into node_modules by its name.

packages:
  - "apps/*"
  - "libs/*"

The app then imports @acme/ui as if it came from a registry, while actually using the code in the repository.

sections.title: Everyday Tools
sections.content:
A few details make daily work smoother.

  • Nx Console is an extension for VS Code, Cursor and JetBrains IDEs. It lists projects and their tasks, runs generators through a form and opens the project graph.
  • npx nx always runs the Nx version installed in the workspace, so everyone, including CI, gets the same results. Upgrades happen deliberately with nx migrate.
  • The .nx folder holds the local cache and data Nx computes about the workspace. It is specific to each machine, belongs in .gitignore and can always be rebuilt.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• create-nx-workspace starts a new workspace; nx init adds Nx to an existing repo without moving folders
  • Apps are deployed or run; libraries hold shared code. Keep apps thin
  • A folder with a project.json, or a package.json Nx picks up, is a project
  • apps/ and libs/ are conventions, not rules
  • nx.json holds workspace settings: plugins, targetDefaults, namedInputs and defaultBase
  • Project configuration holds tags, implicit dependencies and overrides
  • Package manager workspaces link local packages by name
  • npx nx uses the workspace's own Nx version; .nx stays out of Git

title: Running Tasks
summary: Run targets on one project or many, chain tasks with dependsOn pipelines, handle long-running servers with continuous tasks, and explore the workspace with nx graph.

sections.title: Targets and Tasks
sections.content:
Everything Nx runs is described with two words.

  • A target is a named operation a project can perform, such as build, test, lint or serve.
  • A task is one target run on one project, such as shop:build.

Targets come from three places: package.json scripts, project configuration, and plugins that create them from tool config files. However a target is defined, you run it the same way, and Nx treats every task the same when it orders, runs and caches work.

sections.title: Running One Task
sections.content:
The everyday pattern is nx, then the target, then the project:

npx nx build web
npx nx test web
npx nx run web:build

The first two lines run the build and test targets of the web project. The last line is the longer form of the first, useful when a target name could be mistaken for an Nx command.

Nx does more than run one script. It checks whether the task needs other tasks first, such as building libraries, and whether a cached result already exists.

sections.title: Running Many Tasks
sections.content:
run-many runs targets across several projects at once:

npx nx run-many -t test
npx nx run-many -t build lint -p shop admin
  • -t (or --targets) lists one or more targets
  • -p (or --projects) picks projects; without it, every project that has the target is included

The first command tests every project. The second runs build and lint for only shop and admin, four tasks in total. To run tasks only for projects a change can affect, Nx has a separate command, nx affected, covered in the caching lesson.

sections.title: Task Pipelines
sections.content:
Some tasks must wait for others. An app's build needs its libraries built first. You describe this with dependsOn, usually once in nx.json:

"targetDefaults": {
  "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"] },
  "test": { "dependsOn": ["build"] }
}
  • ^build means "run build on the projects I depend on first"
  • build without the caret means "run my own build first"

With these rules, nx build shop builds every library shop uses, then shop itself. Nobody has to remember the order, and it is the same on every machine.

sections.title: Parallel Runs
sections.content:
When you run many tasks, Nx builds a task graph and runs independent tasks at the same time. Two rules decide the schedule:

  • a task never starts before the tasks it depends on have finished
  • no more than a set number of tasks run at once
npx nx run-many -t build --parallel=5

The --parallel option, or the parallel setting in nx.json, sets that limit. Match it to the machine: too low wastes cores, while too high makes tasks compete for memory and can make a small CI machine slower or unstable.

sections.title: Continuous Tasks
sections.content:
Some tasks never finish. A dev server keeps running until you stop it. If an e2e target depends on serve, a normal dependency would make the tests wait forever.

Marking the target as continuous fixes this:

"targets": {
  "serve": { "continuous": true },
  "e2e": { "dependsOn": ["serve"] }
}

Nx now starts serve and runs e2e alongside it instead of waiting for the server to exit. When the tests are done and nothing else needs the server, Nx stops it. Watch processes are another common continuous task.

sections.title: The Terminal UI
sections.content:
When ten tasks run in parallel, ten streams of logs would normally be mixed together in one terminal. The Nx Terminal UI keeps them apart.

  • a list shows every task and its status: running, finished, failed or restored from the cache
  • select a task to see only its output
  • search the task list and view several tasks side by side

It turns a long multi-project run from a wall of text into something you can follow and debug. In CI and other non-interactive terminals, Nx falls back to plain logs.

sections.title: Exploring and Wrapping Scripts
sections.content:
Two more commands come up often.

nx graph opens an interactive map of the workspace in the browser. You can see which projects depend on which, focus on one project, trace the path between two projects and view the tasks a command would run. It is the fastest way to understand an unfamiliar codebase.

nx exec runs any command as an Nx task, so a root script can be cached too:

"scripts": {
  "docs": "nx exec -- node scripts/docs.js"
}

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A target is a named operation; a task is one target on one project
  • Run one task with nx build web or nx run web:build
  • run-many -t picks targets and -p picks projects
  • dependsOn: ["^build"] builds dependencies first; without the caret it means the same project
  • Independent tasks run in parallel up to the --parallel limit, never before their dependencies
  • Mark dev servers continuous: true so dependent tasks do not wait forever
  • The Terminal UI separates each task's output
  • nx graph maps the workspace; nx exec makes any script a cacheable task

title: Project Graph and Inferred Tasks
summary: How Nx builds its project and task graphs, how plugins infer tasks from tool config files, and how to see and override the final configuration.

sections.title: The Project Graph
sections.content:
The project graph is Nx's map of every project and how they depend on each other. Nx builds it automatically by:

  • scanning source files for imports, such as import { Button } from '@acme/ui', and working out which project each import belongs to
  • reading package.json dependencies between local packages

Plugins can add more, for example links between Gradle projects. Almost everything smart Nx does starts here: task order, which projects a change affects, what goes into a cache hash and whether an import breaks a boundary rule. The graph updates as the code changes, with no list to maintain by hand.

sections.title: From Project Graph to Task Graph
sections.content:
The project graph shows how projects relate. When you run a command, Nx turns it into a task graph, which shows how the tasks for that command relate.

Say shop uses ui, ui uses util, and builds have dependsOn: ["^build"]. For nx build shop, Nx:

  1. looks up what shop depends on in the project graph
  2. applies the pipeline rule, adding ui:build and util:build
  3. orders them: util:build, then ui:build, then shop:build

That task graph is what Nx runs and caches, and nx graph can display it.

sections.title: Inferred Tasks
sections.content:
Most tools already have a config file that says how a project is built or tested. With inferred tasks, a plugin reads that file and creates the targets for you.

If a project contains vite.config.ts and the @nx/vite plugin is registered, the project automatically gets targets such as build, serve and test, each with sensible cache inputs and outputs. Nothing has to be written in project.json.

Before inferred tasks, every target was written out by hand in each project's configuration, often with long, repeated options. Now project files only hold real exceptions. Delete a tool's config file and its inferred tasks disappear with it.

sections.title: Registering Plugins
sections.content:
Plugins that infer tasks are listed in the plugins array of nx.json, either by name or as an object with options:

"plugins": [
  "@nx/eslint/plugin",
  {
    "plugin": "@nx/jest/plugin",
    "options": { "targetName": "unit-test" }
  }
]

Here the ESLint plugin uses its defaults, while the Jest plugin names its inferred target unit-test instead of test, for every project at once. Plugin options are the clean way to adjust inferred tasks across the workspace, without touching individual projects or editing plugin code.

sections.title: Seeing the Final Configuration
sections.content:
With settings coming from plugins, defaults and project files, it helps to see the end result. Run:

npx nx show project shop
npx nx show project shop --web

The output lists every target the project has, with its command, options, inputs, outputs and dependencies. The --web version opens the same details in the browser and shows where each setting came from: a plugin, targetDefaults or the project's own file.

When a task runs with settings you did not expect, this is the first place to look.

sections.title: Who Wins: Configuration Layers
sections.content:
A target's settings can come from three layers, merged in order:

  1. Plugins: what a plugin infers from the tool's config file
  2. targetDefaults in nx.json: settings for every target with that name
  3. Project configuration in project.json or package.json

Later layers win. A workspace default can override what a plugin inferred, and a single project can always override the default.

The practical rule is to fix a setting in the layer it belongs to. A change for every project goes in targetDefaults or plugin options; a true exception goes in the project.

sections.title: Implicit Dependencies
sections.content:
Nx finds dependencies through imports, so a link that only exists at runtime is invisible to it. A common case: a shop-e2e project tests the shop app through a browser and never imports its code.

Declare the link by hand with implicitDependencies:

{
  "name": "shop-e2e",
  "implicitDependencies": ["shop"]
}

Now a change to shop makes shop-e2e affected, and pipelines order their tasks correctly. Use this only for links Nx genuinely cannot see. Adding a fake import just to create a link hides the real reason and confuses readers.

sections.title: Plugin Order and Config Inputs
sections.content:
Two details explain some surprising results.

  • Plugin order matters. Plugins are processed in the order they are listed. If two plugins create a target with the same name for a project, the plugin listed last wins. Give one of them a different target name to avoid the clash.
  • Config files are inputs. When a plugin infers a task, it includes the tool's config file in the task's inputs, since it changes the result. Editing vite.config.ts therefore reruns that project's build instead of replaying it from the cache, while other projects keep their cache hits.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• The project graph comes from imports and package.json dependencies, and updates itself
  • For each command, Nx combines the project graph with dependsOn rules into a task graph
  • Plugins infer targets, inputs and outputs from tool config files such as vite.config.ts
  • Register plugins in the plugins array of nx.json; options rename or tune their targets
  • nx show project shows the final configuration and where each setting came from
  • Layers merge in order: plugin, then targetDefaults, then project configuration
  • implicitDependencies declare links Nx cannot see in code
  • The last plugin listed wins a target-name clash; config files are task inputs

title: Caching and Affected
summary: How Nx decides a task can be replayed from the cache, how to declare inputs and outputs correctly, and how nx affected runs only what a change can impact.

sections.title: Doing Less Work
sections.content:
As a monorepo grows, the biggest cost is repeated work: rebuilding and retesting code that has not changed. Nx tackles this with two ideas.

  • Caching: never run the same task twice. If nothing a task depends on has changed, Nx replays the saved result.
  • Affected: never run tasks a change cannot touch. If a pull request only changes the cart library, there is no reason to test the admin app.

Both rely on the project graph, and both are only as good as the information Nx has about your tasks. This lesson shows how to give it the right information.

sections.title: How a Task Hash Is Built
sections.content:
Before running a task, Nx computes a hash: a fingerprint of everything that could change the result. It includes:

  • the project's input files
  • the command and its options
  • environment variables and runtime values declared as inputs
  • the relevant inputs or outputs of the projects it depends on

If a task with the same hash ran before, locally or in a shared remote cache, Nx restores its outputs and replays its terminal output in a fraction of the time. Who runs the task, and when, plays no part in the hash.

sections.title: Inputs and Outputs
sections.content:
Every cacheable task has two lists, and each has a different job.

  • inputs decide when to rerun. Change any input and the hash changes.
  • outputs decide what to save. On a cache hit, these files are put back on disk.
"build": {
  "inputs": ["production", "^production"],
  "outputs": ["{projectRoot}/dist"]
}

Missing outputs give a cache hit that restores nothing, so the folder you expected is not there. Missing inputs are worse: they give a stale result that looks correct.

sections.title: Named Inputs: default and production
sections.content:
Writing file patterns into every target would be repetitive, so nx.json defines reusable sets called namedInputs.

"namedInputs": {
  "default": ["{projectRoot}/**/*"],
  "production": ["default", "!{projectRoot}/**/*.spec.ts"]
}

default is every file in the project. production is the same set minus spec files, so builds can use it while tests use default.

The result: editing only a test reruns that project's tests, while its build, and the builds of apps that use it, stay cache hits. The caret in ^production applies the same set to the projects this one depends on.

sections.title: Declaring Environment Inputs
sections.content:
Nx can only react to what it knows about. Suppose a build bakes API_URL into the bundle but never declares it:

  • someone changes API_URL
  • no input changed, so the hash stays the same
  • Nx replays the old build, with the old URL inside

The fix is to declare the variable as an input:

"build": {
  "inputs": ["production", "^production", { "env": "API_URL" }]
}

Treat a wrong cache hit as a bug in the inputs. Running nx reset hides it once; declaring the missing input fixes it for good.

sections.title: What Not to Cache
sections.content:
Caching assumes the same inputs always give the same result. Tasks that change the outside world break that assumption.

  • Deploys and publishes: replaying one from the cache would skip the real deployment.
  • Dev servers and watchers: they never finish with a result to store.

Switch caching off for such targets:

"deploy": { "cache": false }

When something seems stuck locally, nx reset clears the local cache and workspace data and stops the Nx daemon, so the next command starts fresh. It never touches your source files.

sections.title: Affected: Only What Changed
sections.content:
nx affected -t test runs a target only for the projects a change can impact. Nx maps the changed files to projects, then follows the graph to every project that depends on them.

Take this workspace: shop and admin both use ui, and ui uses util. A change to ui affects:

  • ui, because it changed
  • shop and admin, because they use it

util is not affected, because a change in ui cannot change util. Dependencies flow one way, which is why a library every project imports makes every change affect everything.

sections.title: Base and Head
sections.content:
To know what changed, affected compares two points:

  • base: by default the defaultBase branch in nx.json, usually main
  • head: your current state, including uncommitted changes
npx nx affected -t lint test build
npx nx affected -t test --base=origin/main --head=HEAD

On a feature branch the defaults are usually right. In CI, pipelines pass explicit commits, typically the last successful run on main, so nothing that failed earlier slips through. The CI lesson covers how to find that commit.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Nx skips work two ways: caching (same inputs, replay the result) and affected (only projects a change can impact)
  • A task's hash covers its input files, command, declared env values and dependencies
  • inputs decide when to rerun; outputs decide what is restored
  • Define file sets once with namedInputs; production keeps test edits from rebuilding apps
  • Declare every environment variable a task reads, or expect stale results
  • Set cache: false on deploys and other tasks with side effects
  • Affected includes dependents, never dependencies
  • affected compares the working copy with defaultBase; CI passes explicit base and head

title: Libraries and Module Boundaries
summary: Split code into libraries, tag them, enforce which projects may depend on which, and keep TypeScript references and dependencies clean.

sections.title: Why Split Code into Libraries
sections.content:
Nx caches results and works out what is affected per project. If an app holds all its code, any change reruns everything for that app. Split the same code into libraries and a change only reruns tasks for the library touched and the projects that use it.

Libraries bring other benefits too:

  • clear ownership, since a team can own shop/feature-cart
  • reuse between apps without copying
  • boundaries that tooling can enforce

Splitting too finely has a cost: dozens of one-file libraries add configuration and make the graph hard to read. Start with libraries per feature and type, and split further when one grows large.

sections.title: Library Types
sections.content:
A widely used convention sorts libraries into four types, each with clear rules about what it may use:

  • feature: smart components and pages for one use case; may use every other type
  • ui: presentational components; may use only ui and util
  • data-access: API calls and state; may use data-access and util
  • util: pure helpers such as formatting; may use only util

The rules keep layers clean. A button in a ui library never pulls in API code, so it stays easy to reuse and test. Apps sit on top and are never imported by libraries.

sections.title: Tagging Projects
sections.content:
To enforce rules, Nx needs to know each project's role. That is what tags are for: labels in a project's configuration.

{
  "name": "shop-feature-cart",
  "tags": ["scope:shop", "type:feature"]
}

Most workspaces tag along two dimensions:

  • scope: which part of the business, such as scope:shop, scope:admin or scope:shared
  • type: the library type, such as type:ui or type:util

Tags also work in commands: nx run-many -t test -p tag:scope:shop tests every shop project.

sections.title: Enforcing Boundaries
sections.content:
Tags become rules through the @nx/enforce-module-boundaries ESLint rule and its depConstraints:

"depConstraints": [
  { "sourceTag": "scope:shop", "onlyDependOnLibsWithTags": ["scope:shop", "scope:shared"] },
  { "sourceTag": "type:ui", "onlyDependOnLibsWithTags": ["type:ui", "type:util"] }
]

If a shop project imports a library tagged scope:admin, lint fails in the editor and in CI. TypeScript and the package manager would allow the import; only this rule knows the intended architecture.

The same rule also reports circular dependencies and imports that reach into another project's internals.

sections.title: Public APIs and Deep Imports
sections.content:
Every library has an entry point, usually an index.ts, that exports what other projects may use. That file is the library's public API.

// Good: through the public API
import { Button } from '@acme/ui';

// Bad: reaching into internals
import { theme } from '@acme/ui/src/lib/internal/theme';
import { theme } from '../../libs/ui/src/lib/internal/theme';

Deep imports couple your code to files the library's owners may rename or delete at any time, and relative paths into another project tie code to the folder layout. Import by name, and if something is genuinely needed, export it from the entry point.

sections.title: Buildable, Publishable and Non-Buildable
sections.content:
Libraries differ in whether they have a build step of their own.

  • Non-buildable: no build target. The app that imports it compiles its source as part of the app's build.
  • Buildable: has its own build target, so it can be built and cached separately.
  • Publishable: buildable, plus set up to be released to a registry such as npm, with a package name and version.

For most libraries inside an app workspace, non-buildable is the simplest default. They still get their own lint and test targets and caching. Make a library publishable when it is used outside the repository, or buildable when separate builds clearly save time.

sections.title: TypeScript References and nx sync
sections.content:
Modern TypeScript workspaces often use project references: each tsconfig.json lists the projects it depends on, so TypeScript can build and type-check them incrementally. Keeping those lists right by hand is tedious and easy to get wrong.

Nx keeps them in step with the project graph using sync generators:

npx nx sync
npx nx sync:check

nx sync updates the references to match the graph, and tasks can also prompt you to sync when they are out of date. nx sync:check changes nothing and fails if anything is stale, which makes it a good CI step.

sections.title: Breaking Circular Dependencies
sections.content:
A circular dependency means two libraries import each other, directly or through others: data-access uses util-format, and util-format uses data-access. Neither can be understood, built or tested on its own, and tools get confused about order.

The usual fix:

  1. find the code both sides need
  2. move it into a new, lower-level library, such as util-dates
  3. make both libraries import the new one

Dependencies now point in one direction. The module boundaries rule reports cycles as soon as they appear, so they are caught in review instead of months later.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Nx caches and computes affected per project, so smaller libraries mean more precise runs
  • Feature, ui, data-access and util libraries each have rules about what they may use
  • Tag projects by scope and type in their configuration
  • @nx/enforce-module-boundaries turns tags into lint rules through depConstraints
  • Import through a library's entry point, never its internals or a relative path
  • Non-buildable is the default; buildable and publishable libraries are for real needs
  • nx sync keeps TypeScript references in step; nx sync:check guards CI
  • Break a cycle by moving shared code into a new lower-level library

title: Generators and Plugins
summary: Create projects and code consistently with generators, add and explore plugins, and extend Nx with local generators and plugins for your team's tools.

sections.title: What Generators Do
sections.content:
A generator creates or updates files in the workspace. For example:

npx nx g @nx/react:library libs/shop/feature-cart

This creates a React library with its source folder, test setup, lint configuration and TypeScript settings already wired together. Writing all of that by hand takes time and comes out slightly different each time.

Generators exist for apps, libraries, components and more. The g in nx g is short for generate. Generators also power upgrades: nx migrate uses them to update code when Nx changes.

sections.title: Preview with --dry-run
sections.content:
Before a generator touches anything, you can see exactly what it would do:

npx nx g @nx/react:library libs/shop/feature-cart --dry-run

The output lists every file the generator would create, update or delete, and no file is written. Adjust the options until the result looks right, then run the same command without --dry-run.

Dry runs are especially useful for unfamiliar generators and for generators that change existing files, such as ones that add a library to an app's configuration. Nx Console shows the same preview as you fill in its form.

sections.title: Adding Plugins with nx add
sections.content:
Plugins must match the workspace's Nx version. The safest way to install one is:

npx nx add @nx/vite

nx add does three things that a plain npm install does not:

  • picks the plugin version that matches your Nx version
  • installs it
  • runs its setup step, which typically registers it in the plugins array of nx.json so it starts inferring tasks

A mismatched plugin version is a common cause of confusing errors, so nx add is worth making a habit.

sections.title: Exploring a Plugin
sections.content:
To see what is installed, and what a plugin offers:

npx nx list
npx nx list @nx/react

The first command lists installed plugins and others available to add. The second lists everything one plugin provides: its generators, such as application, library and component, and any executors.

Official framework plugins usually provide two things: generators that create correctly configured projects, and inferred tasks for the tools those projects use. The tools themselves, such as Vite or Vitest, remain their own packages.

sections.title: Generator Defaults
sections.content:
Typing the same options every time is tedious and easy to forget. Set defaults once in the generators section of nx.json:

"generators": {
  "@nx/react:library": {
    "unitTestRunner": "vitest",
    "bundler": "none"
  }
}

Anyone running nx g @nx/react:library now gets Vitest and no bundler unless they pass a different value on the command line. Defaults like these keep new projects consistent across a team without anyone having to remember the house rules.

sections.title: Local Generators for Team Conventions
sections.content:
Teams often have conventions no official generator knows about: tags on every library, a README, a standard folder layout. Instead of checking these by hand in review, write a local generator.

A local generator lives in a plugin inside the workspace. A typical one:

  1. calls the official library generator
  2. adds the team's tags to the new project
  3. writes a README and any extra files from templates

Now one command creates a library that is correct from the start. When a convention changes, you update one generator instead of fixing dozens of libraries, which is why a generator beats copying a template folder.

sections.title: Local Plugins and createNodesV2
sections.content:
A local plugin is a project in the workspace, often under tools/, that holds generators and can also infer tasks. It is versioned with the code it serves and needs no publishing.

Suppose an in-house tool reads check.config.json. A local plugin can use the createNodesV2 API to:

  • match every **/check.config.json file
  • add a check target to the project that contains it
  • declare the target's inputs and outputs so it can be cached

Official plugins infer tasks with the same API, so your tool gets the same treatment as Vite or Jest.

sections.title: Executors vs Inferred Tasks
sections.content:
You will meet two ways of defining how a task runs.

  • Executors are functions provided by a plugin. A target names the executor and passes options, usually in project.json, and Nx calls the plugin's code.
  • Inferred tasks usually run the tool's own command, such as vite build, reading the tool's normal config file.
"build": {
  "executor": "@nx/vite:build",
  "options": { "outputPath": "dist/shop" }
}

Both are cached and ordered the same way. Newer workspaces lean on inferred tasks, so the tool's own documentation applies directly.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Generators create or update files so new projects start correctly configured
  • Add --dry-run to preview every file a generator would change
  • nx add installs a plugin at the matching Nx version and registers it
  • nx list shows plugins; nx list @nx/react shows what one provides
  • Set generator defaults in the generators section of nx.json
  • Local generators encode team conventions and are updated in one place
  • Local plugins can infer tasks for in-house tools with createNodesV2
  • Executors run plugin code; inferred tasks run the tool's own CLI

title: Nx in CI
summary: Build CI pipelines that only do the work a change needs, with the right base commit, remote caching, task distribution and help for flaky or failing tasks.

sections.title: What CI Should Do in a Monorepo
sections.content:
In a large monorepo, most pull requests touch only a few projects. A good pipeline follows two rules:

  • Only do the work a change needs. Run tasks for affected projects, not the whole repository.
  • Never repeat work. If a task with the same inputs already ran, on any machine, reuse its result.

With both in place, CI time grows with the size of the change, not the size of the repository. This lesson covers the pieces that make that work: the right base commit, remote caching, distribution across machines, and help with flaky or failing tasks.

sections.title: A Typical Pipeline
sections.content:
Most Nx pipelines follow the same shape, whatever the CI provider:

  1. check out the code with enough Git history to reach the base commit
  2. install dependencies, using the package manager's own cache
  3. set the base and head commits
  4. run affected tasks, reusing the remote cache
  5. run checks such as nx sync:check
npm ci
npx nx affected -t lint test build
npx nx sync:check

The commands stay short because the hard parts live elsewhere: choosing the base commit and sharing the cache, covered next.

sections.title: Choosing the Base Commit
sections.content:
affected compares a base commit with a head commit, and in CI the base matters:

  • on a pull request, the base is usually where the branch split from main
  • on main, the base should be the last commit where CI succeeded, so anything that failed since then is checked again

The nx-set-shas GitHub Action finds that commit and sets NX_BASE and NX_HEAD, which Nx reads automatically. Other CI systems have equivalents.

A shallow clone with a fetch depth of 1 contains only the latest commit, so the base is missing and affected fails or treats everything as affected. Fetch enough history.

sections.title: Remote Caching
sections.content:
The local cache only helps the machine that ran a task. A remote cache shares results with everyone.

  • a build that ran in CI can be a cache hit on a developer's laptop
  • a test a teammate already ran on the same code is replayed in your pull request
  • rerunning a failed pipeline only redoes the tasks that actually failed

Nx Cloud provides a remote cache, and self-hosted options exist for teams that must keep artifacts on their own infrastructure. The cache key is the same task hash used locally, so remote hits are exactly as trustworthy as local ones, as long as inputs are declared correctly.

sections.title: Keeping the Remote Cache Safe
sections.content:
A shared cache needs trusted writers. If anyone could write to it, a malicious pull request could store a tampered build output that other machines later restore as a cache hit.

  • give untrusted runs, such as pull requests from forks, read-only access
  • keep access tokens in CI secrets, with separate read and read-write tokens
  • never let task outputs contain secrets, since outputs are shared
  • choose hosting, Nx Cloud or self-hosted, that meets company rules

Read-only access still lets untrusted runs benefit from the cache; it only stops them from changing it.

sections.title: Parallelism vs Distribution
sections.content:
There are two ways to run more tasks at once.

  • Parallelism runs several tasks on one machine, up to the --parallel limit. It is capped by that machine's cores and memory; past a point, more parallel tasks just compete with each other.
  • Distribution spreads tasks across several machines. Nx uses the task graph to decide what runs where and in what order, and shares outputs between machines so dependent tasks have what they need.

When hundreds of tasks are affected and one machine is the bottleneck, distribution adds real capacity. Nx Cloud provides it, and each machine still runs tasks in parallel.

sections.title: Flaky Tasks and Self-Healing CI
sections.content:
Because Nx knows every task's inputs, it can spot problems other CI setups miss. Both features below are part of Nx Cloud.

  • Flaky task detection: a task that fails and then passes with exactly the same inputs must be flaky. Nx Cloud can detect this, retry such tasks automatically and report them, so one unreliable test does not fail a pull request.
  • Self-healing CI: when a task fails, Nx Cloud can look at the failure and the change, and propose a fix. Developers review it and apply it locally or let it be pushed to the pull request. Nothing changes without someone approving it.

sections.title: When Affected Runs Everything
sections.content:
Sometimes affected is working correctly, yet almost every pull request still runs everything. The usual cause is the project graph, not CI.

If a catch-all shared-utils library is imported by all 50 projects, any change to it affects all 50. The fix is structural: split it into focused libraries, such as util-dates and util-currency, so a change only affects the projects that use that part.

Two smaller checks help too: compare cache hit rates, since low rates often mean inputs are too broad, and match --parallel to the CI machine so tasks are not starved of memory.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Good CI does only the work a change needs and never repeats work
  • A typical pipeline: checkout with history, install, set base and head, nx affected, checks
  • On main, the base is the last successful commit; nx-set-shas finds it
  • A depth-1 clone breaks affected because the base commit is missing
  • Remote caching shares results between CI and every developer
  • Untrusted runs get read-only cache access; tokens stay in CI secrets
  • Parallelism uses one machine; distribution spreads the task graph across many
  • If affected runs everything, split catch-all libraries

title: Versioning and Releases
summary: Version, document and publish packages from a monorepo with nx release: fixed or independent versions, conventional commits, dependents, dry runs and CI.

sections.title: What nx release Does
sections.content:
Libraries that others install, from npm or a private registry, need versions, changelogs and publishing. nx release handles all three for the packages in a workspace:

  1. Version: decide each package's new version and update its package.json
  2. Changelog: write changelog entries from the commits since the last release
  3. Publish: upload the packages to the registry
npx nx release

It is aimed at packages, not deployments. Deploying an app to a server is a separate concern, usually a CI job of its own. Settings live in the release section of nx.json.

sections.title: Running Steps Separately
sections.content:
Each step also has its own command:

npx nx release version
npx nx release changelog
npx nx release publish

Running steps separately helps when they belong in different places. A common setup:

  • one job versions the packages, writes changelogs and creates the release commit and tags
  • a later job, after tests pass on the tagged commit, publishes

It also lets teams plug individual steps into scripts they already have, for example keeping their own changelog tooling while using Nx for versioning and publishing.

sections.title: Fixed vs Independent Versioning
sections.content:
nx release supports two relationships between packages.

  • Fixed (the default): every released package shares one version, and they are released together. Users know that version 5.2 of every package works together.
  • Independent: each package has its own version and is only bumped when it changes.
"release": {
  "projectsRelationship": "independent"
}

Choose fixed for packages designed to be used together, like a framework's core and add-ons. Choose independent for separate products with their own users and pace, so a fix in one does not force new versions of the rest.

sections.title: Release Groups
sections.content:
One workspace does not have to follow one rule. Release groups apply different settings to different sets of packages:

"release": {
  "groups": {
    "core": { "projects": ["core", "cli"], "projectsRelationship": "fixed" },
    "plugins": { "projects": ["plugin-*"], "projectsRelationship": "independent" }
  }
}

Here core and cli always share a version, while each plugin is versioned on its own. Each group can also have its own changelog and tag settings, so one workspace can mix tightly coupled packages with loosely related ones.

sections.title: Conventional Commits Decide the Bump
sections.content:
Choosing versions by hand is slow and inconsistent. With conventional commits, the commit messages decide.

feat: add CSV export          -> minor (1.4.0 to 1.5.0)
fix: handle empty input        -> patch (1.4.0 to 1.4.1)
feat!: remove the legacy API   -> major (1.4.0 to 2.0.0)

A feat commit signals a new feature, fix a bug fix, and ! or a BREAKING CHANGE note a breaking change. With conventional commits enabled, nx release reads the commits that touched each package since its last release and picks the bump. The same messages also give tidy changelog entries.

sections.title: Updating Dependents
sections.content:
When a library gets a new version, the packages that depend on it may need one too. Suppose cli depends on core, and core gets a fix:

  • core is released as a patch
  • cli should be bumped as well, so its dependency range points at the new core

The updateDependents setting controls whether nx release does this automatically. In independent mode it is what keeps dependents in step, while packages with no changes and no link to core keep their versions.

Run a dry run after changing this setting to see exactly which packages would be bumped.

sections.title: Tags, Commits and the First Release
sections.content:
By default, nx release commits the version and changelog changes and creates Git tags, named by a configurable pattern such as v1.4.0 or core@1.4.0. Those tags matter: the next release uses them to find the commits since the previous version.

A package that has never been released has no previous tag to look for. The --first-release option tells nx release this is the first one, so it does not fail searching:

npx nx release --first-release

After that, the tags it creates are used automatically.

sections.title: Dry Runs and Releasing from CI
sections.content:
Releases should be predictable and reviewed. Two habits help.

Dry runs show the versions, changelog entries and file changes without touching files, Git or the registry:

npx nx release --dry-run

Running this on pull requests catches configuration mistakes before anything ships.

Publish from CI, only from main. Releases then come from reviewed code, the registry token stays in protected CI secrets instead of on laptops, and every release is reproducible. If publishing fails halfway, the tags show what was released and the publish step can be rerun on its own.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• nx release versions, writes changelogs and publishes packages
  • Each step can run alone: nx release version, changelog or publish
  • Fixed versioning (the default) shares one version; independent versions each package
  • Release groups apply different rules to different sets of packages
  • Conventional commits decide bumps: feat is minor, fix is patch, a breaking change is major
  • updateDependents bumps packages that depend on a changed library
  • Release commits and tags mark where the next release starts; use --first-release the first time
  • Dry run on pull requests and publish only from main in CI

title: Maintaining a Healthy Workspace
summary: Upgrade Nx safely with nx migrate, bring in other repositories with nx import, keep cache results trustworthy, and keep a large shared repo easy to own and debug.

sections.title: Workspaces Age
sections.content:
A monorepo that lasts for years keeps changing: new projects, new tools, new Nx versions, more teams. Without care, three things drift:

  • Versions: Nx and its plugins fall behind, and upgrades get harder
  • Trust in the cache: new scripts read files nobody declared as inputs
  • Ownership: it gets unclear who should review what

This lesson covers the tools that keep each of these under control, plus how to debug problems and how to help AI coding agents work safely in a large workspace.

sections.title: Upgrading with nx migrate
sections.content:
Nx upgrades in two deliberate steps:

npx nx migrate latest
npm install
npx nx migrate --run-migrations
  1. nx migrate latest updates the versions of Nx and related packages in package.json and writes the code changes needed into migrations.json. No code changes yet.
  2. After reviewing the plan and installing packages, --run-migrations applies each migration, updating configuration and code for the new version.

Nx Console offers a Migrate UI to review and run migrations one by one. Finish by running your tasks and committing.

sections.title: Upgrading Across Major Versions
sections.content:
Migrations are written to move from one version to the next. If a workspace has fallen several major versions behind, jumping straight to the latest is risky.

The safer path is one major version at a time:

npx nx migrate 21
npx nx migrate 22

After each step, install packages, run the migrations, run the affected tasks and commit. Each step stays small, the right migrations run in order, and if something breaks it is obvious which step caused it. Doing upgrades in their own branch, apart from feature work, keeps reviews simple.

sections.title: Bringing Repositories In
sections.content:
Monorepos often grow by absorbing existing repositories. nx import moves another repository, or a folder of it, into the workspace:

npx nx import https://github.com/acme/billing.git apps/billing
  • the imported code keeps its Git history, so git log and git blame still work
  • Nx detects the tools the code uses and helps add the matching plugins

Afterwards, align dependency versions with the workspace, add tags so boundary rules apply, update CI and check the result with nx graph. Archive the old repository once the team has switched.

sections.title: Keeping Cache Results Trustworthy
sections.content:
The cache is only as good as the declared inputs and outputs. As a workspace grows, new scripts start reading files nobody listed, and stale cache hits creep in.

Habits that help: prefer inferred tasks, reuse namedInputs, declare environment variables, and treat every wrong cache hit as a bug in the inputs.

Task sandboxing, an Nx Cloud add-on, goes further: it traces the files each task really reads and writes and compares them with what it declared. An undeclared read is reported as a violation. Fix it by adding the file to the inputs; exclusions are only for harmless reads, such as caches, because excluded files stop being tracked.

sections.title: Ownership in a Shared Repository
sections.content:
When many teams share one repository, every change still needs the right reviewer. Most hosting platforms solve this with a CODEOWNERS file:

/apps/shop/          @acme/shop-team
/libs/shop/          @acme/shop-team
/libs/shared/ui/     @acme/design-system
/nx.json             @acme/platform

GitHub and similar platforms read this file and request a review from the matching team automatically. Combined with scope tags and boundary rules, it keeps ownership clear: teams control their own projects, and changes to shared configuration such as nx.json go through the platform team.

sections.title: Diagnostics: nx report and the Daemon
sections.content:
When something goes wrong, two tools help.

nx report prints the versions of Node.js, the package manager, Nx and every installed Nx plugin. Mismatched plugin versions are a common cause of strange errors, and this output is what to paste into a bug report.

The Nx daemon is a background process that watches the workspace and keeps the project graph ready, so commands do not recompute it each time. If the graph seems out of date or commands hang, nx reset stops the daemon and clears local data. Setting NX_DAEMON=false turns the daemon off, which some CI setups do.

sections.title: Working with AI Agents
sections.content:
AI coding agents work best when they understand the workspace the way Nx does, instead of guessing from file names.

npx nx configure-ai-agents

This command sets up instructions and Nx skills for agents such as Claude, Codex or Cursor, so they use Nx commands and can read workspace information like the project graph. A well-configured agent:

  • checks which projects a change affects before editing
  • verifies its work with nx affected -t lint test
  • uses generators and respects boundary rules

The same structure that helps new team members helps agents.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Over time, versions, cache trust and ownership drift unless maintained
  • nx migrate latest plans the upgrade; --run-migrations applies it
  • Upgrade one major version at a time, testing and committing after each
  • nx import brings in a repository with its Git history
  • Keep inputs complete; Nx Cloud task sandboxing flags undeclared file reads
  • A CODEOWNERS file routes reviews to the team that owns each project
  • nx report prints versions for bug reports; nx reset restarts the daemon
  • nx configure-ai-agents teaches coding agents to work the Nx way

title: Getting Started with Express
summary: What Express adds on top of Node.js, how to install Express 5, and how to create, start and run your first server.

sections.title: What Express Is
sections.content:
Express is a small web framework for Node.js. It runs on top of Node's built-in http module and makes the common jobs of a web server simple: matching requests to the right code, reading what the client sent and sending back a response.

Express is deliberately minimal and unopinionated. It gives you routing and middleware, and leaves the rest, such as folder structure, database and template engine, to you. That flexibility is why it powers so many APIs and websites, and why most Node.js developers meet it early.

sections.title: Express vs Plain Node.js
sections.content:
With Node's http module alone, you inspect every request yourself:

http.createServer((req, res) => {
  if (req.method === 'GET' && req.url === '/users') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
    res.end(JSON.stringify(users));
  }
});

Express replaces that plumbing with three things:

  • Routing: app.get('/users', handler)
  • Middleware: shared steps such as parsing JSON or logging
  • Response helpers: res.json(), res.status()

sections.title: Installing Express 5
sections.content:
Express 5 is the current major version and the one npm installs by default. It needs Node.js 18 or higher.

npm init -y
npm install express

You can import it in either module system:

// CommonJS
const express = require('express');

// ES modules ("type": "module" in package.json)
import express from 'express';

This subject teaches Express 5 throughout. Older tutorials written for Express 4 still work for most ideas, but some syntax has changed.

sections.title: Your First Server
sections.content:
A complete Express server takes a few lines:

const express = require('express');
const app = express();

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Hello from Express');
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
  console.log('Listening on http://localhost:3000');
});
  • express() creates the application
  • app.get registers a handler for GET requests to /
  • app.listen starts an HTTP server on port 3000 and keeps running

sections.title: How a Request Flows
sections.content:
An Express app is a pipeline. When a request arrives, Express walks through the middleware and routes in the order you registered them.

  1. Each middleware whose path matches runs and either responds or calls next() to continue.
  2. The first route that matches the method and path handles the request and sends a response.
  3. If nothing responds, Express sends its default 404, such as Cannot GET /about.

Almost everything you build in Express fits this picture, which is why the order of your code matters so much.

sections.title: Startup Errors in Express 5
sections.content:
app.listen returns Node's http.Server, and in Express 5 startup errors, such as a port already in use, are passed to its callback:

const server = app.listen(3000, (err) => {
  if (err) {
    console.error('Could not start:', err.code); // e.g. EADDRINUSE
    process.exit(1);
  }
  console.log('ready');
});

Keeping the server reference is useful later: you call server.close() for a graceful shutdown or attach a WebSocket server to the same port.

sections.title: Choosing the Port
sections.content:
Hard-coding port 3000 works on your laptop, but hosting platforms and containers usually tell the app which port to use through the PORT environment variable.

const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
app.listen(port);

Reading the variable, with a sensible fallback for local development, lets the same code run everywhere without changes. The same pattern applies to other settings, such as database URLs, covered in the lesson on structuring an app.

sections.title: A Smooth Development Loop
sections.content:
A Node.js process loads your code once, so edits do not take effect until the server restarts. Node's built-in watch mode does that for you:

node --watch app.js

Every time a watched file changes, Node restarts the app. It replaces what tools such as nodemon were commonly used for, with nothing extra to install.

Add it as a script so the whole team uses the same command:

"scripts": {
  "dev": "node --watch app.js",
  "start": "node app.js"
}

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Express is a minimal, unopinionated web framework built on Node's http module
  • It adds routing, middleware and response helpers
  • Express 5 is the npm default and needs Node.js 18 or higher
  • express() creates the app; app.listen starts the server and returns an http.Server
  • Requests flow through middleware and routes in registration order
  • Unmatched requests get the default 404, such as Cannot GET /about
  • In Express 5, startup errors such as EADDRINUSE arrive in the listen callback
  • Read the port from process.env.PORT; use node --watch during development

title: Routing
summary: Match requests to handlers with route methods, parameters and query strings, use the Express 5 path syntax, and organise routes with express.Router.

sections.title: Method, Path and Handler
sections.content:
A route has three parts: an HTTP method, a path and a handler function.

app.get('/users', listUsers);
app.post('/users', createUser);
app.delete('/users/:id', deleteUser);

Each method has its own function: app.get, app.post, app.put, app.patch and app.delete. A route only handles its own method, so app.get('/users') does not answer POST /users.

The handler receives req and res, reads what it needs from the request and sends exactly one response.

sections.title: Route Parameters
sections.content:
A segment that starts with a colon is a route parameter. Its value lands in req.params:

app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => {
  res.json({ id: req.params.id }); // GET /users/42 gives { id: '42' }
});

Two details catch people out:

  • Parameter values are always strings, because they come from the URL. Convert them with Number() and validate them before use.
  • A parameter matches one whole segment, so /users/:id does not match /users/42/orders.

sections.title: Query Strings
sections.content:
Everything after the ? is the query string. It is not part of route matching, and Express parses it into req.query:

// GET /search?q=express&page=2
app.get('/search', (req, res) => {
  const { q, page } = req.query; // 'express', '2'
  res.json({ q, page: Number(page) });
});

Use parameters for which resource, and query values for optional modifiers such as filters, sorting and pagination. In Express 5, the default parser keeps keys flat, so ?filter[name]=ana gives the key filter[name], not a nested object.

sections.title: Route Order Matters
sections.content:
Express checks routes in the order they are defined and uses the first match. That can surprise you:

app.get('/users/:id', getUser);
app.get('/users/new', newUserForm); // never reached

/users/new matches /users/:id first, so getUser runs with req.params.id set to 'new'.

Register specific routes before general ones: /users/new first, then /users/:id.

sections.title: Wildcards in Express 5
sections.content:
Express 5 changed how wildcards work. A wildcard must have a name, and its value is an array of path segments:

app.get('/files/*splat', (req, res) => {
  // GET /files/docs/a.txt gives ['docs', 'a.txt']
  res.send(req.params.splat.join('/'));
});

A wildcard needs at least one segment, so /*splat does not match the root path. Wrap it in braces to make it optional: /{*splat} matches / and every deeper path, which is handy for catch-all routes. A bare /* is no longer valid.

sections.title: Optional Segments, No Regex
sections.content:
Express 5 marks optional parts of a path with braces:

app.get('/:file{.:ext}', (req, res) => {
  // /report     gives { file: 'report' }
  // /report.pdf gives { file: 'report', ext: 'pdf' }
  res.json(req.params);
});

Regular expressions inside path strings, such as /:id(\d+), were removed, partly because some patterns allowed regular expression denial of service. Such a route now throws an error. Match /users/:id and validate the format in middleware or the handler instead.

sections.title: Grouping Routes with express.Router
sections.content:
A router is a mini app with its own routes and middleware. Mount it with app.use to give all its routes a common prefix:

const router = express.Router();
router.get('/', listUsers);      // GET /api/users
router.get('/:id', getUser);     // GET /api/users/42

app.use('/api/users', router);

Inside a mounted router, paths are relative to the mount point. req.baseUrl holds the mount path, /api/users, and req.path holds the rest, /42. Routers are how large apps stay organised, one per feature.

sections.title: app.route and app.all
sections.content:
Two helpers reduce repetition.

app.route(path) chains several methods on one path:

app.route('/books')
  .get(listBooks)
  .post(createBook);

app.all(path, handler) matches a path for every HTTP method. It is useful for things like a health check or a method-not-allowed response:

app.all('/health', (req, res) => res.sendStatus(200));

Neither matches deeper paths: /health/db needs its own route.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• A route is a method, a path and a handler: app.get('/users', handler)
  • Route parameters go to req.params and are always strings
  • Query strings are not part of matching; they go to req.query
  • Routes match in definition order, so put specific routes before parameter routes
  • Express 5 wildcards are named, /*splat, and give an array; /{*splat} also matches /
  • Optional parts use braces, /:file{.:ext}; regex in paths was removed
  • express.Router groups routes; mounted paths are relative, with req.baseUrl
  • app.route chains methods; app.all matches every method

title: Request and Response
summary: Read params, query, body, headers and cookies from req, and send JSON, status codes, redirects and files with res, exactly once per request.

sections.title: Two Objects, Two Jobs
sections.content:
Every handler and middleware receives two objects:

  • req, the request: everything the client sent, including the path, query string, headers and body
  • res, the response: everything you send back, including the status code, headers and body

Both are Node's own request and response objects with extra Express helpers attached. The same two objects travel through every middleware for that request, which is how earlier steps can share information with later ones.

sections.title: Params, Query and Body
sections.content:
A request carries data in three places, each with its own property:

// POST /orders/7?notify=true   body: { "item": "pen" }
app.post('/orders/:id', (req, res) => {
  req.params.id;    // '7'
  req.query.notify; // 'true'
  req.body.item;    // 'pen' (only after express.json() has run)
});

In Express 5, req.body is undefined until a body parser such as express.json() runs. Values from the path and query string are always strings, so convert and validate them before use.

sections.title: Headers and Cookies
sections.content:
Read headers with req.get, which ignores case:

req.get('Content-Type');  // same as req.get('content-type')
req.get('Authorization');

Express can set cookies, but not read them. Add the cookie-parser middleware to fill req.cookies:

app.use(cookieParser());

res.cookie('theme', 'dark', {
  httpOnly: true,   // hidden from page JavaScript
  secure: true,     // HTTPS only
  sameSite: 'lax',  // limits cross-site sending
});

sections.title: Sending JSON and Status Codes
sections.content:
For APIs, res.json is the workhorse: it serialises the value and sets the application/json content type.

res.json(user);                       // 200 by default
res.status(201).json(newUser);        // created
res.status(400).json({ error: 'Invalid email' });
res.sendStatus(204);                  // no body

res.status sets the code and returns res, so it chains. res.sendStatus sets the code and sends immediately; for 204 No Content the body is empty. In Express 5, res.status only accepts valid codes from 100 to 999 and throws otherwise.

sections.title: One Response per Request
sections.content:
Sending a response does not stop your function. Forget a return and the code keeps going:

app.get('/user/:id', (req, res) => {
  const user = users[req.params.id];
  if (!user) {
    return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' });
  }
  res.json(user);
});

Without that return, an unknown id would send the 404 and then try to send a second response, which fails with Cannot set headers after they are sent. Make every response the last thing its code path does.

sections.title: Redirects
sections.content:
res.redirect sends the client to another URL. The status comes first in Express 5, and defaults to 302:

res.redirect('/login');          // 302 Found
res.redirect(301, '/new-home');  // permanent

Express 5 removed the old res.redirect(url, status) order and the special 'back' value. To send users back where they came from, use the Referrer header with a fallback:

res.redirect(req.get('Referrer') || '/');

Never redirect to a URL taken straight from user input; that creates an open redirect.

sections.title: Sending Files
sections.content:
Two helpers stream a file to the client:

const path = require('node:path');

// Displayed in the browser where possible
res.sendFile(path.join(__dirname, 'files', 'report.pdf'));

// Saved as a download, with a file name
res.download(path.join(__dirname, 'files', 'report.pdf'), 'report.pdf');

res.sendFile needs an absolute path, or a root option; a relative path throws an error. res.download adds Content-Disposition: attachment, so the browser offers to save the file instead of showing it.

sections.title: res.locals: Data for One Request
sections.content:
res.locals is an object that lives for a single request. Middleware can put values there for later handlers and templates:

const { randomUUID } = require('node:crypto');

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  res.locals.requestId = randomUUID();
  next();
});

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.render('home'); // the template can read requestId
});

Values in res.locals are available to every template rendered with res.render for that request. App-wide values, such as the site name, belong in app.locals instead.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• req holds what the client sent; res builds what you send back
  • Path values go to req.params, the query string to req.query, the parsed body to req.body
  • req.body is undefined until a parser runs; params and query values are strings
  • req.get reads headers case-insensitively; reading cookies needs cookie-parser
  • Use res.status(code).json(data), or res.sendStatus(204) for no body
  • Send exactly one response: return after early responses
  • res.redirect(301, url) puts the status first in Express 5
  • res.sendFile needs an absolute path; res.download saves the file

title: Middleware
summary: How middleware functions run in order and call next, where to register them, which built-in and third-party middleware to use, and how to write your own.

sections.title: What Middleware Is
sections.content:
Middleware is a function that runs as part of the request pipeline:

function logger(req, res, next) {
  console.log(req.method, req.originalUrl);
  next();
}

app.use(logger);

A middleware can read or change req and res, end the request by sending a response, or call next() to pass control on. Almost everything in Express is built this way: parsing bodies, logging, authentication, CORS, and even routers themselves.

sections.title: next() and Ending the Request
sections.content:
Every middleware must do one of two things:

  • call next() to let the next middleware or route run, or
  • send a response to end the request.

If it does neither, Express waits forever and the client eventually times out. The reverse mistake is just as common: calling next() after sending a response lets a later handler try to respond again, which fails with Cannot set headers after they are sent.

Calling next(err) with an error is different again: Express skips straight to the error-handling middleware.

sections.title: Order Is Everything
sections.content:
Express runs middleware and routes in registration order, and stops at the first response. This bug is a classic:

app.use('/api', apiRouter);
app.use(express.json()); // too late for /api

The router answers /api requests before the JSON parser runs, so req.body is undefined in every API route. A reliable order for most apps:

  1. security and logging
  2. body parsers
  3. routes
  4. the 404 handler
  5. the error handler

sections.title: Where Middleware Applies
sections.content:
The same function can run for different scopes depending on how you register it:

app.use(logger);                     // every request
app.use('/api', apiKeyCheck);        // paths under /api

const admin = express.Router();
admin.use(requireAuth);              // only this router's routes

app.get('/reports', requireAuth, getReports); // one route only

Route-level middleware runs left to right: requireAuth runs first, and getReports only runs if it calls next(). Router-level middleware is a clean way to protect a whole feature at once.

sections.title: Built-in Body Parsers
sections.content:
Express ships with parsers for common body types:

app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));  // application/json
app.use(express.urlencoded());              // HTML form posts
  • Each parser only handles its own Content-Type. A JSON body sent as text/plain is skipped, and req.body stays undefined.
  • In Express 5, express.urlencoded() defaults to extended: false, so user[name]=ana stays a flat key. Pass { extended: true } for nested objects.
  • limit caps the body size; larger bodies are rejected with 413.

sections.title: Third-Party Middleware
sections.content:
Much of Express's power comes from its middleware ecosystem. A few you will see in almost every API:

  • morgan or pino-http: a log line for each request
  • cors: lets browser apps on other origins call the API
  • helmet: sets security headers
  • cookie-parser: fills req.cookies
  • express-rate-limit: limits requests per client
app.use(helmet());
app.use(cors({ origin: 'https://app.example.com' }));
app.use(morgan('tiny'));

Each is just a function with the (req, res, next) signature, configured once and registered like any other middleware.

sections.title: Writing Your Own
sections.content:
Custom middleware often attaches data for later steps. This one measures how long each request takes:

function requestTimer(req, res, next) {
  const start = Date.now();
  res.on('finish', () => {
    console.log(`${req.method} ${req.originalUrl} took ${Date.now() - start}ms`);
  });
  next();
}

app.use(requestTimer);

The response finishes after next() returns, so the timer listens for the finish event. Register it early so it times everything.

sections.title: Configurable Middleware
sections.content:
When middleware needs settings, write a function that returns a middleware. This is the pattern behind express.json(options) and cors(options):

const requireRole = (role) => (req, res, next) => {
  if (req.user?.role === role) return next();
  res.status(403).json({ error: 'Forbidden' });
};

app.delete('/users/:id', requireAuth, requireRole('admin'), deleteUser);

Calling requireRole('admin') creates a middleware configured for one role. The same factory serves every role without duplicating code.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Middleware has the signature (req, res, next)
  • Each middleware must call next() or send a response, never both
  • next(err) jumps to error-handling middleware
  • Order decides what runs: security and parsers first, then routes, then 404 and error handlers
  • Register globally, by path, per router or per route
  • Parsers only handle their own Content-Type; Express 5 urlencoded defaults to extended: false
  • Ecosystem middleware covers logging, CORS, security headers, cookies and rate limits
  • A function that returns middleware makes it configurable

title: Static Files and Views
summary: Serve static assets with express.static, handle Express 5 dotfile rules and caching, render server-side pages with a template engine, and serve a single-page app.

sections.title: Serving Static Files
sections.content:
Images, stylesheets and browser scripts do not need any code to serve. Express's built-in express.static middleware maps URLs to files in a folder:

app.use(express.static('public'));

With public/logo.png on disk, a request for /logo.png returns that file. Requests that do not match a file simply continue to the next middleware or route, so static files and API routes can live in the same app.

sections.title: Absolute Paths and Prefixes
sections.content:
A relative folder name is resolved from the directory the process starts in. Start the app from somewhere else, as process managers and containers often do, and it points to the wrong place. Build an absolute path instead:

const path = require('node:path');

app.use('/static', express.static(path.join(__dirname, 'public')));

The first argument is a virtual prefix: public/logo.png is now served at /static/logo.png. The folder name itself never appears in the URL.

sections.title: Several Folders and Caching
sections.content:
Static folders are middleware, so they are tried in order. The first folder that has the file wins:

app.use(express.static('public'));
app.use(express.static('assets')); // only used for files public lacks

The maxAge option sets a Cache-Control header, so browsers and CDNs can reuse files without asking again:

app.use(express.static('public', { maxAge: '1d' }));

Long cache times work best with fingerprinted names such as app.3f9c.js, which change whenever the content changes.

sections.title: Dotfiles in Express 5
sections.content:
Express 5 ignores dotfiles by default, and now also checks folders: anything under a hidden folder such as .well-known returns 404. That protects files like .env from being served by accident.

When you do need a hidden folder, for example for domain verification or security.txt, opt in for that path only:

app.use('/.well-known',
  express.static(path.join(__dirname, 'public/.well-known'), { dotfiles: 'allow' }));

Never set dotfiles: 'allow' on a folder that might contain secrets.

sections.title: Template Engines
sections.content:
For server-rendered pages, Express works with template engines such as EJS or Pug. Install one and tell Express to use it:

app.set('view engine', 'ejs');
app.set('views', path.join(__dirname, 'views'));

By default Express looks for templates in a views folder under the working directory; setting views explicitly avoids surprises, just like static paths. In production, with NODE_ENV=production, Express caches compiled templates for speed.

sections.title: Rendering with Data
sections.content:
res.render fills a template with data and sends the HTML:

app.get('/profile', (req, res) => {
  res.render('profile', { name: 'Ana', orders: 3 });
});

Here Express renders views/profile.ejs, where the template can use name and orders. Values in res.locals and app.locals are available too.

In Express 5, res.render is asynchronous for every engine, so rendering errors reach the error handler consistently. Pass a callback if you need the HTML as a string instead of sending it.

sections.title: Serving a Single-Page App
sections.content:
A React, Angular or Vue build is static files plus client-side routing. Refreshing /settings would return 404, because no such file exists. Add a fallback that sends index.html:

app.use('/api', apiRouter);
app.use(express.static(path.join(__dirname, 'dist')));
app.get('/{*splat}', (req, res) => {
  res.sendFile(path.join(__dirname, 'dist', 'index.html'));
});

Order matters: API routes first, then static files, then the catch-all, so /api paths are never answered with the app's HTML.

sections.title: Static Files in Production
sections.content:
