express.static is fine for small apps, but at scale, static files are usually served by something closer to the user:

  • a CDN caches files at locations around the world
  • a reverse proxy such as nginx serves files efficiently and frees Node for application logic

Even then, keep the same habits: absolute paths, long cache times for fingerprinted assets, a short or no cache for index.html, and dotfiles kept out of anything that is served.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• express.static serves files from a folder; unmatched requests continue
  • Build static and view paths with path.join(__dirname, ...)
  • A mount path is a virtual prefix: /static/logo.png
  • Several static folders are tried in order; maxAge sets Cache-Control
  • Express 5 ignores dotfiles and hidden folders unless you allow them per path
  • Set view engine and views, then res.render(view, data)
  • A single-page app needs a final /{*splat} fallback to index.html
  • At scale, a CDN or reverse proxy usually serves static files

title: Error Handling
summary: Catch errors from sync and async handlers in one place with error-handling middleware, add a 404 handler, map custom errors to status codes and never leak internals.

sections.title: One Place for Errors
sections.content:
Databases go down, input is invalid and bugs slip through. A good API fails predictably: the same JSON shape, the right status code and no internal details, whatever went wrong.

Express makes this possible by sending errors to special error-handling middleware. Instead of a try/catch with its own response in every route, routes and services throw errors, and one handler at the end of the pipeline decides what the client sees. This lesson builds that setup step by step.

sections.title: Error-Handling Middleware
sections.content:
An error handler is middleware with four parameters. Express recognises it by that signature:

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  console.error(err);
  res.status(500).json({ error: 'Internal error' });
});
  • Declare all four parameters, even if next is unused; with three, Express treats it as normal middleware.
  • Register it after all routes. Errors travel forward through the stack, so a handler registered before a route never sees that route's errors.
  • It must send a response or call next(err), or the request hangs.

sections.title: How Errors Reach the Handler
sections.content:
An error gets to the error handler in three ways:

// 1. Thrown synchronously
app.get('/a', () => { throw new Error('boom'); });

// 2. Passed to next
app.get('/b', (req, res, next) => next(new Error('fail')));

// 3. A rejected promise from an async handler (Express 5)
app.get('/c', async () => { await db.query('...'); });

Calling next(err) makes Express skip every remaining normal middleware and route and jump to the next error handler.

sections.title: Async Handlers in Express 5
sections.content:
In Express 4, a rejected promise from an async handler was ignored: the request hung and Node reported an unhandled rejection. Teams wrapped every route in a helper like asyncHandler to fix it.

Express 5 does this itself. When a handler returns a promise that rejects, Express calls next with the error:

app.get('/users/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const user = await db.users.find(req.params.id); // may reject
  res.json(user);
});

No try/catch, no wrapper. Existing wrappers still work, but they are no longer needed.

sections.title: Errors Outside the Request
sections.content:
Express only sees errors thrown during the handler call or from the promise it returns. Code that runs later, in a callback, escapes it:

app.get('/later', (req, res, next) => {
  setTimeout(() => {
    try {
      doWork();
      res.send('done');
    } catch (err) {
      next(err); // hand it to Express yourself
    }
  }, 10);
});

Without the try/catch, an error thrown inside the timer becomes an uncaught exception and can crash the process. Prefer promises you await, which Express 5 handles automatically.

sections.title: A Catch-All 404 Handler
sections.content:
When no route matches, Express sends a small HTML page. APIs usually want their own JSON instead. A 404 handler is just normal middleware registered after every route:

app.use('/api', apiRouter);

app.use((req, res) => {
  res.status(404).json({ error: `No route for ${req.method} ${req.path}` });
});

app.use(errorHandler); // last of all

It only runs when nothing earlier responded. It goes before the error handler, which is reserved for real errors.

sections.title: Custom Error Classes
sections.content:
Give errors a status code where they are created, and let one handler use it:

class NotFoundError extends Error {
  constructor(message) {
    super(message);
    this.statusCode = 404;
    this.expose = true; // safe to show the message
  }
}

// in a service
if (!user) throw new NotFoundError('User not found');

The error handler then picks the status from the error, falling back to 500 for anything unexpected. Services stay free of HTTP details, and every route reports errors the same way.

sections.title: Safe, Consistent Responses
sections.content:
A production error handler protects both clients and the system:

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err);
  const status = err.statusCode ?? 500;
  if (status >= 500) logger.error({ err, reqId: req.id });
  res.status(status).json({
    error: err.expose ? err.message : 'Internal error',
  });
});
  • If a response already started, pass the error to Express's default handler, which closes the connection.
  • Log full details on the server; send clients only safe messages.
  • Never send stack traces in production. Express's own default handler hides them when NODE_ENV is production.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Error handlers have four parameters, (err, req, res, next), and go after all routes
  • Errors arrive from throws, next(err) and, in Express 5, rejected async handlers
  • next(err) skips normal middleware and jumps to error handlers
  • Async wrappers are no longer needed in Express 5
  • Errors thrown in later callbacks escape Express; catch them and call next(err)
  • A 404 handler is normal middleware placed after the routes
  • Custom error classes carry a status code for one central handler
  • Check res.headersSent, log details, send safe messages, never stack traces

title: Validation and File Uploads
summary: Validate body, params and query with a schema before your logic runs, return clear 400 errors, limit body sizes and accept file uploads safely with multer.

sections.title: Never Trust Input
sections.content:
Anything in a request can be wrong or hostile: a missing field, a string where a number belongs, an extra role: "admin", or a 50 MB body. Checks in the frontend help users, but anyone can call the API directly with curl or a script.

So an Express API validates at the edge: as soon as a request arrives, before any business logic or database call. Invalid requests are rejected early with a clear 400, and the rest of the code can trust the data it receives.

sections.title: Validating with a Schema
sections.content:
A schema library such as Zod describes the shape you expect. A small middleware factory makes it reusable:

const { z } = require('zod');

const createUser = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  name: z.string().min(1).max(100),
});

const validate = (schema) => (req, res, next) => {
  const result = schema.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!result.success) {
    return res.status(400).json({ errors: result.error.issues });
  }
  req.body = result.data; // only the validated fields
  next();
};

app.post('/users', validate(createUser), createUserHandler);

safeParse never throws; it returns success and either data or error.

sections.title: Using express-validator
sections.content:
express-validator takes a different approach: each rule is a middleware in the route.

const { body, validationResult } = require('express-validator');

app.post('/signup',
  body('email').isEmail(),
  body('password').isLength({ min: 12 }),
  (req, res) => {
    const errors = validationResult(req);
    if (!errors.isEmpty()) {
      return res.status(400).json({ errors: errors.array() });
    }
    // ... create the account
  });

The rules only record problems. If the handler forgets to call validationResult, invalid data goes straight through.

sections.title: Params and Query Are Strings
sections.content:
Validation is not only for the body. Route parameters and query values come from the URL, so they are always strings:

// items have numeric ids
items.find((i) => i.id === req.params.id); // never matches: 7 !== '7'

Validate and convert them like any other input, for example with a schema that coerces types:

const idParam = z.object({ id: z.coerce.number().int().positive() });

const parsed = idParam.safeParse(req.params);
if (!parsed.success) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Invalid id' });

sections.title: Clear Errors, Clean Data
sections.content:
When validation fails, respond with 400 Bad Request and say which fields failed and why, so the client can fix the request:

{ "errors": [ { "field": "email", "message": "Invalid email" } ] }

When it passes, use the validated result, not the raw body. Passing req.body straight to the database lets a client set fields they should never touch, such as role or isVerified. This is called mass assignment. A schema that lists only the allowed fields prevents it.

sections.title: Limiting Body Size
sections.content:
Body parsers read the whole body into memory, so size limits protect the server from huge payloads:

app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));

A larger body is rejected with 413 Payload Too Large, which reaches your error handler. 100 kB is also the default, so raising the limit should be a deliberate choice, ideally only on the routes that need it:

app.post('/imports', express.json({ limit: '5mb' }), importHandler);

sections.title: File Uploads with multer
sections.content:
File uploads arrive as multipart/form-data, which express.json() ignores. multer parses them:

const multer = require('multer');
const upload = multer({ dest: 'uploads/' });

app.post('/avatar', upload.single('avatar'), (req, res) => {
  // req.file: path, size, mimetype, originalname
  // req.body: the text fields from the same form
  res.status(201).json({ size: req.file.size });
});

upload.single accepts one file from one field and fills req.file. upload.array and upload.fields accept several files into req.files.

sections.title: Uploading Safely
sections.content:
The file name and type are chosen by the client, so treat them as untrusted:

const upload = multer({
  dest: 'uploads/',
  limits: { fileSize: 2 * 1024 * 1024, files: 1 },
  fileFilter: (req, file, cb) => cb(null, ['image/png', 'image/jpeg'].includes(file.mimetype)),
});
  • Limit size and count; oversized files are rejected with an error.
  • Filter types, and check the real content where it matters.
  • Use generated names and store files outside the web root or in object storage.
  • Serve uploads with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and as attachments.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Validate every input on the server, at the edge, before business logic
  • Schemas such as Zod describe the expected shape; safeParse returns success or errors
  • express-validator rules need a validationResult check in the handler
  • Params and query values are strings: validate and convert them
  • Respond 400 with field-level errors; use only the validated data
  • Set body size limits; oversized bodies get 413
  • multer parses multipart uploads into req.file or req.files
  • Limit upload size and type, generate names and store uploads safely

title: Authentication and Authorization
summary: Implement session-based and token-based login in Express, protect routes with authentication and role middleware, store passwords safely and handle logout.

sections.title: Two Questions
sections.content:
Protecting an API means answering two separate questions on every request:

  • Authentication: who is making this request?
  • Authorization: is this person allowed to do this?

In Express, each answer is usually its own middleware. An authentication middleware identifies the user and attaches them to req; authorization middleware then checks roles or ownership. Keeping them separate makes routes easy to read: requireAuth, requireRole('admin'), handler.

sections.title: Session Login with express-session
sections.content:
With sessions, login state lives on the server, and the browser holds only a cookie with a session ID:

const session = require('express-session');

app.use(session({
  secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
  resave: false,
  saveUninitialized: false,
  cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' },
}));

app.post('/login', async (req, res, next) => {
  const user = await checkCredentials(req.body);
  if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid login' });
  req.session.regenerate((err) => {
    if (err) return next(err);
    req.session.userId = user.id;
    res.sendStatus(204);
  });
});

sections.title: Secure Sessions
sections.content:
A few settings make the difference between sessions that are safe and sessions that leak:

  • Cookie flags: httpOnly hides the cookie from page scripts, secure sends it only over HTTPS and sameSite limits cross-site sending.
  • A real store: the default MemoryStore leaks memory, loses sessions on restart and is not shared between processes. Use Redis or a database in production.
  • Regenerate on login: req.session.regenerate() issues a fresh ID, which prevents session fixation.
  • saveUninitialized: false avoids storing empty sessions for anonymous visitors.

sections.title: Token Login with JWTs
sections.content:
With tokens, the server signs a JSON Web Token at login and the client sends it with each request:

const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');

app.post('/login', async (req, res) => {
  const user = await checkCredentials(req.body);
  if (!user) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid login' });
  const token = jwt.sign({ sub: user.id, role: user.role }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, {
    expiresIn: '15m',
  });
  res.json({ token });
});

The client sends it in the Authorization header as Bearer followed by the token. The server keeps no record of it: the signature proves it is genuine, and the expiry limits how long it works.

sections.title: An Authentication Middleware
sections.content:
One middleware verifies the token and attaches the user to the request:

function requireAuth(req, res, next) {
  const token = req.get('Authorization')?.replace('Bearer ', '');
  try {
    req.user = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
    next();
  } catch {
    res.status(401).json({ error: 'Unauthorized' });
  }
}

router.use(requireAuth); // protects every route in this router

jwt.verify checks the signature and expiry, and throws for a missing, tampered or expired token. Later handlers simply read req.user.

sections.title: Role-Based Authorization
sections.content:
Once req.user is set, authorization middleware decides what the user may do:

const requireRole = (role) => (req, res, next) =>
  req.user.role === role ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: 'Forbidden' });

app.delete('/users/:id', requireAuth, requireRole('admin'), deleteUser);
  • 401 Unauthorized: no valid credentials; the client is not authenticated.
  • 403 Forbidden: the user is known but not allowed.

Roles cover broad permissions. Rules about specific records, such as users editing only their own orders, belong in the service, which checks ownership against req.user.

sections.title: Storing Passwords
sections.content:
Passwords must never be stored in a form that can be turned back into the password. Hash them with an algorithm designed to be slow and salted, such as bcrypt or argon2:

const bcrypt = require('bcrypt');

const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12);   // at sign-up
const ok = await bcrypt.compare(password, hash); // at login

Fast hashes such as plain SHA-256 are the wrong tool: attackers can test billions of guesses per second against a stolen database. Pair safe hashing with rate limiting on the login route.

sections.title: Logout and Passport
sections.content:
Logout is simple with sessions: req.session.destroy() deletes the session on the server, and the cookie becomes useless.

JWTs are harder, because the server does not store them: a copied token keeps working until it expires. Common answers are short-lived access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens, or a denylist of revoked token IDs.

For logins through providers such as Google or GitHub, Passport offers ready-made strategies that plug into Express. Storing users and building login pages remains your job.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Authentication asks who you are; authorization asks what you may do
  • Sessions keep state on the server; the browser holds only a session ID cookie
  • Use httpOnly, secure and sameSite cookies, a real session store and regenerate on login
  • JWTs are signed tokens sent as Authorization: Bearer, verified on every request
  • An auth middleware sets req.user or responds 401
  • Role middleware responds 403 when a known user lacks permission
  • Hash passwords with bcrypt or argon2, never plain or fast hashes
  • JWTs need short expiry plus refresh tokens or a denylist for logout

title: Structuring an Express App
summary: Organise routes, controllers and services by feature, separate the app from the server, load configuration safely, share resources and refactor large route files.

sections.title: Why Structure Matters
sections.content:
Express does not prescribe a project layout. That is freedom on day one and a problem on day three hundred, when a single file holds hundreds of routes, business rules are copied between handlers and nobody can test anything without starting the server.

A good structure makes three things easy: finding the code for a feature, testing logic without HTTP, and changing one part without breaking another. The patterns in this lesson are widely used conventions, not rules Express enforces.

sections.title: Routes, Controllers and Services
sections.content:
Split each feature into three layers:

  • Routes map paths and methods to controllers and attach middleware.
  • Controllers translate HTTP: read req, call a service, send the response.
  • Services hold business logic and data access, with no knowledge of req or res.
// users.controller.js
exports.getUser = async (req, res) => {
  const user = await userService.get(Number(req.params.id));
  res.json(user);
};

Because services are plain functions, they can be reused by background jobs and tested directly.

sections.title: Feature-Based Folders
sections.content:
Group files by feature rather than by type:

src/
  app.js
  server.js
  config.js
  users/
    users.routes.js
    users.controller.js
    users.service.js
    users.test.js
  orders/
    ...
  middleware/
    auth.js
    error-handler.js

Everything about users lives in one folder, so a change to that feature stays in one place. Type-based folders, with all controllers in one directory and all services in another, scatter a single feature across the whole project as it grows.

sections.title: Separating App from Server
sections.content:
Keep the code that builds the app apart from the code that starts it:

// app.js
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use('/api/users', usersRouter);
app.use(errorHandler);
module.exports = app;

// server.js
const app = require('./app');
app.listen(process.env.PORT || 3000);

Tests import app and send requests in memory with Supertest, without opening a port. server.js is the place for listening, connecting to the database and graceful shutdown.

sections.title: Configuration
sections.content:
Settings such as the database URL and secrets come from environment variables, never from code committed to Git. Read them in one module and validate them at startup:

// config.js
const { z } = require('zod');

const env = z.object({
  PORT: z.coerce.number().default(3000),
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
}).parse(process.env);

module.exports = env;

A missing setting now fails immediately with a clear message. Recent Node.js versions load a local .env file with node --env-file=.env server.js; keep .env out of Git.

sections.title: Sharing Resources
sections.content:
Expensive resources, such as a database connection pool, are created once at startup and shared. Connecting per request is slow and can exhaust the database's connection limit.

Passing dependencies in, rather than importing them everywhere, keeps code testable:

function createUserRouter(userService) {
  const router = express.Router();
  router.get('/:id', async (req, res) => {
    res.json(await userService.get(Number(req.params.id)));
  });
  return router;
}

app.use('/api/users', createUserRouter(userService));

Tests can build the same router with a fake service.

sections.title: Nested Routers and Versioning
sections.content:
Routers can nest. For resources like a user's orders, the child router needs mergeParams to read the parent's parameters:

const orders = express.Router({ mergeParams: true });
orders.get('/', (req, res) => listOrders(req.params.userId));

users.use('/:userId/orders', orders);

Without mergeParams, req.params would be empty inside the child.

Mounting everything under a version prefix such as /api/v1 lets you introduce /api/v2 later for breaking changes, while existing clients keep working.

sections.title: Refactoring a Large Route File
sections.content:
When one file has grown to thousands of lines, refactor in small, safe steps:

  1. Add tests around the current routes, so behavior is locked in.
  2. Split by feature into routers mounted with app.use.
  3. Extract services from handlers, one feature at a time.
  4. Move repeated steps into middleware, such as auth checks, validation and loading a record by id.
  5. Centralise errors: replace scattered try/catch blocks with thrown errors and one handler.

Keep the tests green after each step instead of attempting one big rewrite.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Routes map URLs, controllers translate HTTP, services hold business logic
  • Group code by feature so each change stays in one place
  • app.js builds and exports the app; server.js starts it
  • Read settings from environment variables and validate them at startup
  • Create pools and clients once; pass dependencies into router factories
  • Child routers need mergeParams: true to read parent params
  • Version APIs with prefixes such as /api/v1
  • Refactor large files in small steps, with tests first

title: Security in Express
summary: Harden an Express app with security headers, strict CORS, rate limiting, trust proxy, injection-safe queries, CSRF protection, safe redirects and patched dependencies.

sections.title: Security Is Opt-In
sections.content:
Express is minimal, and that includes security: a fresh app sends no security headers, accepts requests from any origin and has no rate limits. None of that is a flaw; it simply means protection is something you add deliberately.

This lesson covers the baseline every production Express API should have. Validation, authentication and safe error responses, covered in earlier lessons, are part of the same picture: security comes from several layers working together, not from one package.

sections.title: Security Headers with helmet
sections.content:
helmet sets a group of response headers that tell browsers to block common attacks:

const helmet = require('helmet');

app.use(helmet());
  • Content-Security-Policy limits where scripts and other resources may load from
  • Strict-Transport-Security tells browsers to use HTTPS only
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops browsers guessing content types

helmet also removes X-Powered-By: Express, which advertises your framework. Without helmet, app.disable('x-powered-by') does that one job.

sections.title: CORS Done Right
sections.content:
CORS is a browser rule: a page from one origin can only read responses from another origin if that server allows it. Tools such as curl and Postman ignore it, which is why an API can work there and still fail in the browser.

const cors = require('cors');

app.use(cors({
  origin: ['https://app.example.com'],
  credentials: true, // only if the browser must send cookies
}));

List the exact origins that need access. Never combine credentials with a wildcard origin. And remember CORS is not authentication: it protects users' browsers, so every route still needs proper auth.

sections.title: Rate Limiting and trust proxy
sections.content:
express-rate-limit caps requests per client, which slows down password guessing and abuse:

const { rateLimit } = require('express-rate-limit');

app.use('/login', rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, limit: 5 }));

The sixth attempt within 15 minutes gets 429 Too Many Requests. Limits are counted per IP, so behind a load balancer every client appears as the proxy's address. Tell Express how many proxies to trust:

app.set('trust proxy', 1); // req.ip now comes from X-Forwarded-For

Use the real number of proxies, not true, or clients could fake their IP.

sections.title: Preventing Injection
sections.content:
Never build a query by pasting request input into it:

// Vulnerable: name could be  ' OR '1'='1
db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '${req.query.name}'`);

// Safe: the driver sends the value separately
db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1', [req.query.name]);

Parameterised queries, or a query builder or ORM that uses them, keep data from ever being read as SQL. The same idea applies elsewhere: do not pass request input into shell commands, file paths or NoSQL query objects without validating it first.

sections.title: CSRF and Cookies
sections.content:
Browsers attach cookies to requests automatically, including requests triggered by other websites. With cookie-based sessions, a malicious page can make a logged-in user's browser send a request your app trusts. This is cross-site request forgery.

  • Set session cookies to sameSite: 'lax' or 'strict'.
  • Add CSRF tokens to state-changing forms and requests in cookie-based apps.
  • Never change data on GET requests.

APIs that only accept tokens in an Authorization header are not exposed in the same way, because browsers never add that header by themselves.

sections.title: Redirects and Uploaded Files
sections.content:
Two smaller holes are easy to leave open.

Open redirects. res.redirect(req.query.next) lets an attacker craft a link to your real login page that sends users to their site afterwards. Only redirect to relative paths or an allowlist:

const next = req.query.next;
res.redirect(typeof next === 'string' && next.startsWith('/') && !next.startsWith('//') ? next : '/');

Uploaded files. A file claiming to be an image could be HTML that runs scripts on your domain. Serve uploads with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Content-Disposition: attachment, ideally from a separate domain.

sections.title: Keeping Dependencies Patched
sections.content:
A typical Express app depends on hundreds of packages, and vulnerabilities are found in them regularly. Keeping them patched is part of security, not just maintenance:

npm audit
npm audit fix
  • Run npm audit in CI so new vulnerabilities fail the build.
  • Use automated update pull requests, such as Dependabot or Renovate, and merge them often.
  • Stay on a supported Express and Node.js version; old majors stop receiving fixes.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Express ships without security defaults; add protections deliberately
  • helmet() sets security headers and removes X-Powered-By
  • CORS is a browser rule: allow exact origins, and still authenticate every route
  • express-rate-limit returns 429; set trust proxy to the real number of proxies
  • Use parameterised queries, never string-built SQL
  • Cookie sessions need sameSite cookies and CSRF tokens
  • Redirect only to safe paths; serve uploads as nosniff attachments
  • Audit and update dependencies continuously

title: Testing Express Apps
summary: Test Express APIs over HTTP with Supertest, assert status, headers and bodies, cover error paths, auth and sessions, unit test middleware and keep tests reliable.

sections.title: What to Test
sections.content:
For an Express API, the best value usually comes from HTTP-level integration tests: send a real request through the app and check the response. One test exercises routing, middleware, validation, the service and the error handler together, and still runs in milliseconds.

Around those, add:

  • unit tests for complex services and individual middleware
  • tests for error paths: bad input, missing auth, failing dependencies

Testing Express's own router is unnecessary; test your contract with clients.

sections.title: Supertest Basics
sections.content:
Supertest sends requests to an Express app and lets you assert on the response. It works with any runner, such as Jest, Vitest or Node's built-in node:test:

const request = require('supertest');
const app = require('../src/app');

test('lists users', async () => {
  await request(app)
    .get('/api/users')
    .expect(200)
    .expect('Content-Type', /json/);
});

You never call app.listen: given an app that is not listening, Supertest binds it to a temporary port for the request, so test files do not clash over ports.

sections.title: A Testable App
sections.content:
Supertest needs the app, not a running server, so the module that builds the app must not start it:

// src/app.js: builds and exports, never listens
module.exports = createApp({ userService });

// src/server.js: the only place that listens
require('./app').listen(process.env.PORT || 3000);

Going one step further, a factory such as createApp({ userService, db }) lets each test pass in its own dependencies, including fakes that throw on demand.

sections.title: Asserting Responses
sections.content:
A useful test checks what clients rely on: the status, key headers and the important fields of the body.

const res = await request(app)
  .post('/api/users')
  .send({ name: 'Ana', email: 'ana@example.com' })
  .expect(201)
  .expect('Content-Type', /json/);

expect(res.body).toMatchObject({ name: 'Ana', email: 'ana@example.com' });
expect(res.body.id).toBeDefined();

A test that only checks that nothing threw would still pass if the API returned the wrong status or data, so always assert on the response itself.

sections.title: Error Paths and Auth
sections.content:
Errors are where APIs break most often, so test them on purpose:

test('invalid email gives 400', async () => {
  await request(app).post('/api/users').send({ email: 'nope' }).expect(400);
});

test('database failure gives a safe 500', async () => {
  const app = createApp({ userService: { create: async () => { throw new Error('db down'); } } });
  const res = await request(app).post('/api/users').send(validUser).expect(500);
  expect(res.body.error).toBe('Internal error');
});

For protected routes, sign a token with the test secret and send it with .set('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + token), so the real auth middleware is tested too.

sections.title: Sessions with request.agent
sections.content:
A plain request(app) forgets cookies after each request, so session logins do not carry over. An agent keeps them, like a browser:

const agent = request.agent(app);

await agent.post('/login').send({ email, password }).expect(204);
await agent.get('/profile').expect(200); // session cookie sent automatically

await request(app).get('/profile').expect(401); // a fresh client is not logged in

Use one agent per simulated user to test flows such as login, actions and logout end to end.

sections.title: Testing Middleware Alone
sections.content:
Middleware is just a function, so you can call it directly with simple fakes:

test('requireAuth rejects a missing token', () => {
  const req = { get: () => undefined };
  const res = { status: jest.fn().mockReturnThis(), json: jest.fn() };
  const next = jest.fn();

  requireAuth(req, res, next);

  expect(res.status).toHaveBeenCalledWith(401);
  expect(next).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
});

mockReturnThis lets res.status(401).json(...) chain as it does in Express. These tests are fast and pin down edge cases precisely.

sections.title: Reliable Test Data
sections.content:
Tests that pass alone but fail randomly in CI usually share something they should not:

  • Use a separate test database, selected by an environment variable, never the development one.
  • Reset data before each test, or wrap each test in a transaction that is rolled back.
  • Close resources such as database pools in teardown hooks, so the runner can exit.
  • Await every request and avoid fixed sleeps.

Test doubles are faster and great for forcing failures; a real test database catches query bugs. Most teams use both.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• HTTP-level tests with Supertest give the most confidence per test
  • Supertest needs the app, not app.listen; it uses a temporary port
  • Export the app separately from the server, ideally from a factory
  • Assert status, Content-Type and body fields, not just that nothing threw
  • Test error paths and auth with real tokens and failing fakes
  • request.agent keeps session cookies between requests
  • Unit test middleware with fake req, res and next
  • Isolate test data: separate database, reset between tests, close resources

title: Performance and Deployment
summary: Run Express reliably in production: NODE_ENV, compression and caching, non-blocking handlers, using every core, logging, health checks, graceful shutdown and timeouts.

sections.title: Production Is Different
sections.content:
An app that works on your laptop is not yet ready for production. Real traffic brings many simultaneous users, slow clients, deployments that stop and start processes, and failures you only discover through logs.

Running Express well in production comes down to a handful of habits: the right environment settings, efficient responses, code that never blocks, several processes, good observability, and clean starts and stops. None is complicated on its own; together they make an app reliable.

sections.title: NODE_ENV=production
sections.content:
Express and many libraries change behavior based on NODE_ENV:

NODE_ENV=production node server.js
  • Express caches compiled view templates instead of reading them on every render.
  • Its default error handler stops sending stack traces to clients.
  • Many libraries skip development-only checks and logging.

Forgetting it means slower pages and leaked internals. Platforms usually let you set it as an environment variable for the service.

sections.title: Compression and Caching
sections.content:
Smaller and fewer responses are the cheapest speedup.

const compression = require('compression');
app.use(compression()); // gzip responses when the client supports it
  • Compression shrinks JSON and HTML considerably. Many deployments let the reverse proxy or CDN do it instead, saving Node's CPU.
  • ETags: Express adds an ETag to responses by default. A client that sends it back in If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified with no body when nothing changed.
  • Cache-Control on static files lets browsers and CDNs skip requests entirely.

sections.title: Never Block the Event Loop
sections.content:
Node runs your JavaScript on one thread. While a handler does slow synchronous work, every other request waits:

// Blocks the whole server while the file is read
app.get('/report', (req, res) => {
  res.send(fs.readFileSync('big-report.csv'));
});

// Streams it without blocking
app.get('/report', (req, res) => {
  res.sendFile(path.join(__dirname, 'big-report.csv'));
});

Avoid synchronous file, crypto and compression calls in handlers, and move CPU-heavy work, such as image processing or big reports, to worker threads or a background job queue.

sections.title: Using Every Core
sections.content:
One Node.js process uses roughly one CPU core. To use more, run several processes behind a load balancer:

  • the built-in cluster module
  • a process manager such as PM2 in cluster mode
  • several containers, the usual approach on Kubernetes and similar platforms

This only works if the app is stateless: sessions in a shared store such as Redis, uploads in object storage, and shared counters, such as rate limits, in a shared store. Anything kept in one process's memory is invisible to the others.

sections.title: Logging and Health Checks
sections.content:
In production you learn what happened from logs. Use a structured logger that writes JSON with levels and context:

const pinoHttp = require('pino-http');
app.use(pinoHttp()); // one structured log line per request, with a request id

app.get('/health', async (req, res) => {
  await db.query('SELECT 1');
  res.json({ status: 'ok' });
});

A health endpoint lets load balancers and orchestrators check whether an instance can serve traffic, and route around or restart it when it cannot.

sections.title: Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
Deployments stop processes all the time, usually with SIGTERM. A graceful shutdown finishes in-flight requests instead of cutting them off:

const server = app.listen(port);

process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  server.close(async () => {   // stop new connections, wait for current ones
    await db.end();            // then release resources
    process.exit(0);
  });
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref(); // never hang forever
});

Failing the health check first gives the load balancer time to stop sending new traffic before the server closes.

sections.title: Proxies, Managers and Timeouts
sections.content:
A few more pieces complete a production setup:

  • A reverse proxy such as nginx, or the platform's load balancer, terminates HTTPS, buffers slow clients and can serve static files. Set trust proxy to match.
  • A process manager or orchestrator restarts crashed processes and handles rolling deployments.
  • Server timeouts stop slow clients from holding connections open:
server.headersTimeout = 10_000;  // time to send request headers
server.requestTimeout = 30_000;  // time to send the whole request

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Set NODE_ENV=production for view caching and hidden stack traces
  • Compress responses and use ETags and Cache-Control to avoid repeat work
  • Never block the event loop; stream files and offload CPU-heavy work
  • Run several processes or containers, and keep the app stateless
  • Use structured logs with request IDs and a health check endpoint
  • On SIGTERM, server.close(), finish requests, release resources, exit
  • Put a reverse proxy and process manager or orchestrator in front
  • Set server timeouts so slow clients cannot tie up connections

title: Upgrading to Express 5
summary: Upgrade an Express 4 app safely: prepare with tests and Node.js 18, run the official codemods, fix route paths and removed APIs, review behavior changes and roll out gradually.

sections.title: Why Upgrade
sections.content:
Many production apps still run Express 4. Express 5 keeps the same programming model, routes and middleware, but fixes long-standing rough edges:

  • Promise support: rejected async handlers reach the error handler automatically.
  • Safer routing: a newer path matcher that removed patterns open to regular expression denial of service.
  • A cleaner API: long-deprecated methods are gone.
  • Modern Node.js: Express 5 targets Node.js 18 and later.

Most apps need a modest amount of work. This lesson walks through it in a safe order.

sections.title: Prepare First
sections.content:
Two things make an upgrade safe before any code changes:

  1. Tests that cover the important routes, including error paths and auth. They are what tells you the upgrade worked.
  2. A supported Node.js version, 18 or higher, upgraded and deployed on its own first, so any problems are not mixed with the Express change.

Then do the upgrade in a dedicated branch, separate from feature work, so the change is easy to review and to roll back.

npm install express@5

sections.title: Run the Codemods
sections.content:
The Express team publishes codemods that rewrite many breaking changes automatically:

npx codemod@latest @expressjs/v5-migration-recipe

They handle mechanical changes such as renamed methods and old res.send and res.redirect signatures. They cannot understand every pattern, especially route paths and behavior that depends on how your app uses requests, so review the diff and work through the following slides by hand.

sections.title: Route Path Changes
sections.content:
Route paths are where most upgrades need manual work:

// Express 4                     // Express 5
app.get('*', handler);           app.get('/{*splat}', handler);
app.get('/files/*', handler);    app.get('/files/*splat', handler);
app.get('/:file.:ext?', h);      app.get('/:file{.:ext}', h);
app.get('/user/:id(\\d+)', h);   app.get('/user/:id', h); // validate id in code
  • Wildcards must be named, and their value is now an array of segments.
  • Optional parts use braces instead of ?.
  • Regex groups throw at startup, which at least makes them easy to find.

sections.title: Removed and Renamed APIs
sections.content:
Calls that were deprecated in Express 4 are gone:

app.del(path, h)           // use app.delete(path, h)
req.param('id')            // use req.params.id, req.body.id or req.query.id
res.sendfile(p)            // use res.sendFile(p)
res.send(404)              // use res.sendStatus(404)
res.json(obj, 400)         // use res.status(400).json(obj)
res.redirect(url, 301)     // use res.redirect(301, url)
res.redirect('back')       // use res.redirect(req.get('Referrer') || '/')
req.acceptsCharset()       // use req.acceptsCharsets()

One is quietly dangerous: res.send(404) no longer sends a 404. It sends status 200 with the body 404, so search for it explicitly.

sections.title: Behavior Changes
sections.content:
Some code compiles fine but behaves differently. Review anything that relies on:

  • req.body being {}: it is now undefined until a parser runs.
  • Nested query objects: the default query parser no longer expands filter[name]; set app.set('query parser', 'extended') if you need it.
  • Writing to req.query: it is now a read-only getter, and assignments are silently ignored.
  • req.host: it now includes the port; use req.hostname for the name alone.
  • res.clearCookie: it ignores maxAge and expires.

sections.title: Defaults That Changed
sections.content:
A few defaults changed too:

  • express.urlencoded() uses extended: false; pass { extended: true } to keep nested form fields.
  • express.static ignores dotfiles and now hidden folders as well; allow folders like .well-known explicitly.
  • app.listen passes startup errors such as EADDRINUSE to its callback.
  • res.render is asynchronous for every template engine.

Also check your middleware packages: most popular ones support Express 5, but older or unmaintained ones may rely on removed APIs.

sections.title: Roll Out Safely
sections.content:
Once the tests pass, release the upgrade like any risky change:

  1. Remove async wrappers and try/catch blocks that only forwarded errors; Express 5 does it for you.
  2. Deploy to a staging environment and exercise the main user flows.
  3. Roll out gradually, for example to a few instances first, while watching error rates, 404s and latency.
  4. Keep the previous version ready to roll back.

A sudden rise in 404s usually points to a route path that changed meaning; a rise in 500s often points to code relying on old request behavior.

sections.title: Things to Remember
sections.content:
• Express 5 keeps the model but adds promise support, safer routing and a cleaner API
  • Prepare with good tests and Node.js 18 or higher, in a dedicated branch
  • Run npx codemod@latest @expressjs/v5-migration-recipe, then review by hand
  • Rewrite wildcards as named, optional parts with braces, and drop regex groups
  • Replace removed APIs; res.send(404) now sends a 200
  • Check code relying on req.body, nested queries, req.query writes and req.host
  • Note changed defaults for urlencoded, static dotfiles, listen errors and render
  • Roll out gradually and watch 404 and 500 rates
